Surviving blank-line blocks in the OCR are retained; because the plain OCR suppresses most printed paragraph indentation, long blocks are subdivided into citation paragraphs of at most 25 mechanically segmented sentences. These numbered paragraphs and sentences are navigation units for the Multitext Viewer, not a claim to reproduce the printed paragraphing.

div.head: I. Rectoratsrede zur Feier des Jahrestages Seiner Majestät des hochseligen Königs Friedrich Wilhelms III. gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 3. August 1847.
Ueber die Lage und Verhältnisse der Preufsischen Universitäten, vorzüglich der Berliner, während der Regierung des Königs Friedrich Wilhelm III.

p.s: This day, esteemed listeners, on which we commemorate the memory of the founder of our university in grateful recollection, has been, since the beginning of this creation of his, a festive and joyful day for the older among us through a long series of years, and its memory has made a deep impression on us all.

But to whom could it have left a deeper impression than to me, who on that day appeared twenty-five times as ceremonial orator, in order to give expression, in the name of our academic body, to the veneration, the gratitude, and the love for Frederick William III — I, that is, who had the occasion and the duty to consider year after year the actions of that same king, at least insofar as they touched our university directly or indirectly, and, following the impression of events, to grasp the sentiments of men's minds — always the same in devotion to the king, yet nonetheless varying with circumstances and conditions — and to express them insofar as my ability, my position, and the limits allowed, which were set for the public orator by the times, now happy and serene, now grave and clouded, and by the very purpose of the celebration!

This day, which was then a festive and joyful one for us, is so still today; but not so much, as formerly, through the feeling of the present, as rather by our going back into the past: and only where we harvest the fruits of what Frederick William III planted does the past, in his memory, link itself with the present, indeed even with the future.

But in proportion
as each person faithfully preserves the memory of him, the melancholy mingles with the feeling of joy that is aroused by it; and if we did not feel this melancholy, would he then really still be worthy of a day of festal commemoration?

No one can acknowledge more fully and more deeply than I what we owe to the exalted heir of his throne, what we have gained through him, what we have become through him; but the mourning for him who has been torn from us still retains its full right, even after seven years in which the outlook of the nations and the spiritual temper of the fatherland have been almost entirely transformed — its full right for the older generation, who were witnesses of the government of Frederick William III, and by the younger these witnesses will not be heard unwillingly.

These [times] Prussia knew in the times which immediately preceded its deepest humiliation, in the times when, under a wavering policy abroad that in its final consequences was disastrous, it had, at home, like almost all German lands, no political stirring or standing whatever, but rested on the enjoyment of the blessings of peace and on the full contentment of a willing population, on the strength of its administration and on a seemingly formidable military power which had nevertheless outlived itself; on the strength of an administration which, despite some defects peculiar to the age, was yet distinguished by that which most directly concerns our own profession, namely that it honored and promoted the sciences and protected the freedom of thought.

You have known Prussia during the six years of the humiliation of a just pride that awakened no love, years in which, the stronger the pressure, the greater the elasticity it gained, in which those who governed strove by every means to awaken and to heighten the strength of the people, and the people was intimately entwined with the king by the closest bond, the bond of suffering.

You have lived through the swiftly flown years of enthusiasm, of the highest upsurge of national feeling, of the greatest military glory, which Frederick William won with a loyal people capable of every sacrifice, and you have witnessed how this sacred flame, out of anxiety that it might consume the whole edifice of the state, was damped down until only a spark still glimmered beneath the ashes: here the opinion that aroused hopes and promises would not be fulfilled, impatient expectations, youthful aberrations, and in isolated cases even
crimes; there fear of innovations, suspicion even of the nobler sort; gradually again almost general calm and the return of the old indifference; toward the end of the cherished life, religious excitements, to take the place of the appeased political ones, and amid all the change of views and feelings, the same goodness, friendliness toward the citizens, moderation, and dignity of the aged king, the same veneration and love for him among all the estates of the people!

It is not the orator's business to narrate like a historian; and how could I, within the measure of time allotted to me, present Frederick William III's life, his experiences and hard trials, his actions in peace and in war, in their entanglement with the greatest European affairs and with the most memorable events of the century?

Nor do I wish, as some philosophers are accustomed to do, to search after a so-called principle of the noble King's spiritual personality—a principle that cannot be discovered from his manifold utterances, which are in many ways conditioned by circumstances and events, without the danger of deception, because the particular personality cannot be determined conceptually, but, like a work of art, is grasped only in immediate intuition.

Rather, esteemed listeners, may it suffice for you, as it does for me, if I confine myself to a subject lying within the circle of my own experience, one that seems to me the most fitting for our celebration: if I consider the situation and circumstances of the Prussian universities, and especially of our own, during the reign of Frederick William III, yet direct my gaze more toward the sense and spirit in which they were guided, toward their position in relation to the moving forces of the age, toward the temper of minds, than toward achievements in specialized scholarship, or toward numbers and names and the whole external scaffolding and skeleton of our small commonwealth—finally, without these observations, grounded in fact, being able even to encompass the most important of this within the narrow frame of a speech.

I shall speak openly, as one is entitled to speak of the past; I shall speak with sympathy, but without passion, without undue partiality or aversion. Frederick William III, at
the beginning of his reign, found—to leave lesser institutions out of account—the universities of Halle, Königsberg, Frankfurt an der Oder, and Erlangen already in existence.
Among these, Halle and Königsberg had exercised the most significant influence on German education.
In Halle a freer development of philosophy, and soon of criticism as well, early became predominant, and this did not fail to exert its influence on theology.

Christian Thomasius, who eradicated the crudest remnant of ancient barbarism and of the old superstition, the witch trials, and who secured for the mother tongue admission to the lectures of the universities, found there a refuge from the persecutions at Leipzig; Christian Wolf, from there, dominated Germany for a time as a philosopher; driven out by sanctimonious opponents, he was restored to his chair by Frederick the Great.
Theology there received a freer direction, chiefly through Semler, whose representative in the early years of Frederick William III's reign was still above all Nösselt.

In Königsberg, distinguished by a fine union of intellectual powers that at all times stepped boldly and undauntedly into the lists, Kant became the teacher first of all Germany, and brought about a rejuvenation not merely of philosophy but of almost all the sciences, especially of jurisprudence and of theology.

Before Frederick William III ascended the throne, the freedom of teaching of the Halle theologians and of the great Kant had been assailed by Wöllner and his assistants; Frederick William III removed these attacks together with their authors, and restored the freedom of teaching, while at the same time encouraging the freedom of communication through the press.

From this alone one can see that he did not regard the universities as institutions for the drilling of servants in prescribed doctrines, but as nurseries of free knowledge, which is also to have its effect on the servants to be trained for the state; but he demonstrated this even more clearly in the last years before the fateful day of Jena.

Shortly before this, Jena had been the principal seat of German philosophy; the boldest and freest thinker of modern times, Fichte, accused by Electoral Saxony of blasphemy, as so many noble seekers after truth had been since Anaxagoras, left Jena and found
refuge and protection in Prussia; he taught in alternation, half-yearly, at Erlangen and Berlin, here at first in freely formed circles of those eager for knowledge, since in this capital at that time respect and love for philosophy were widespread among the nobler minds, and later as one of the first and fairest ornaments of the young university: at the same time he intervened powerfully in life, and worked toward the awakening of the German national feeling and of liberal views with his thought-rich, primevally vigorous, sharp word.

Here it became evident once again, as it has always proved true, that the freedom of thought, when it is checked in one place and for a short time, breaks forth all the more brilliantly elsewhere—sometimes, to be sure, only later; almost without exception, all those whom the nobility and the learned, or the lowly and ignorant mob of their time, accused as godless—whether because they combated the prevailing superstition, or because, like Aristarchus of Samos and Copernicus and Galileo, they advanced only certain doctrines wholly independent of religion, which seemed contrary to religion to their prejudiced contemporaries—have been acquitted by posterity and highly praised as proclaimers of the truth: suppression itself gives the truth the stronger power of reaction.

For Halle, too, the decline in the splendor of the University of Jena was used to give the national university new ornaments; several professors were called there from Jena, and in order to found there a new center of scholarly activity, the Allgemeine Literaturzeitung, at that time very influential, was drawn over from Jena to Halle—whatever the success at the very beginning, not without sacrifices; without fear of the new ideas, which once again undermined the ground of the old conceptions already undermined by Kant, the new views were transplanted there, though not directly from Jena: I name only Schleiermacher, who, a declared admirer of the pagan Plato and of the disreputable Spinoza, was installed as teacher of philosophy and theology, and Steffens, who was to represent in Halle the equally much-slandered philosophy of nature, which only later proved harmless.

Although not all traces of the old coarseness had vanished, there nevertheless prevailed in Halle—which at that time, like Göttingen, attracted a considerable number of foreigners—a
more animated, genuinely scholarly spirit, full of youthful enthusiasm, owing to the old forces, among whom Fr. Aug. Wolf was the most effective, and equally or even more so to the younger ones.

The struggle against Napoleon had already, in those years, awakened the students—as befits the flower of patriotic youth—to patriotic feelings, though they were otherwise not yet politically stirred: the free spirit of the German universities had long been hateful to the world ruler; this spirit already seemed so formidable at that time that the Emperor, immediately upon his arrival, dissolved the University of Halle and drove all the students from the city, the poorer ones with a thaler for travel money.

Just as the crushing reduction in the extent and power of the state called forth only a rejuvenation and rebirth of what remained to it in all branches, so too in the universities: here as well we find for them the turning point toward better things in the most essential respects.

What had been lost in physical strength was to be replaced by intellectual strength, which had already elevated the state in earlier times and is the surest foundation for the renewal of states; for physical strength is the limited strength of the mass, the mass that is once and for all the same and can be increased only by the addition of other mass; intellectual strength is in itself infinite and, without any external addition, is capable, through its own tension, of immeasurable increase and multiplication.

At the same time, it could not be overlooked that young forces had to be formed; the education and upbringing of the young, alongside the liberation of the people from old fetters and a more popular order of the army, was that on which the new state had to be founded.

No wonder, then, that precisely in the most oppressive distress and hardship a sum as large as never before was allocated for the improvement and founding of the scientific institutions of the capital; the greatest part of this sum fell to the new university, which indeed initially took the place of the lost Halle institution and made fine acquisitions from it, but was not to become a provincial institution, but rather a general German, indeed a European one.

Not yet in more recent times had a Protestant university been established at the seat of a princely house; indeed, the freer life of the students seemed incompatible with the
proximity of a court: it proved an exceptional love of the sciences that this prejudice was overcome, that a university was regarded as an ornament of the capital and that from it, precisely at this location, a fruitful activity was expected; and Berlin had to seem especially suited for this, on account of the manifold scholarly resources that were already united here and could easily be increased, no less on account of the scholars already present and on account of the inhabitants' inclination toward scholarly cultivation.

At the same time, the principle was adopted of locating the universities preferentially in the capitals; and by this means the horizon of the teachers has indisputably been broadened, petty frictions among them have been forestalled, and many a foolish and harmful custom among the students has been eradicated or mitigated.

The University of Frankfurt was indeed initially strengthened by excellent new teachers, but it would scarcely have attained any significant flourishing, and it suffered especially from the bad habit of the old tone; its transfer to Breslau and union with the Catholic university there proceeded from the same principle as the founding of the one here.

The Halle university was strengthened, after the restoration of the Empire, through the remnants of the Wittenberg university in a purposeful union; the Königsberg and the newly acquired Greifswald universities were raised according to circumstances; eight years after the founding of the university here, the Bonn university was founded and flourished quickly.

Here the government appears to have abandoned the principle that should itself have found application for Dresden too, had it come to Prussia—namely, of conferring universities on the most important cities of the land; if external reasons also contributed to this—the old claim of the place where Maximilian Frederick, the Archbishop of Cologne, had established a university, the friendliness of the city, large palace buildings well suited to housing a scholarly institution—then it is no less known to me from the mouths of those who at that time directed these affairs that it was feared the new foundation would be exposed to clerical and hierarchical influences in the venerable old seat of the archbishopric.
Thus, gradually, every German province of the realm received a university, counting the Academy at Münster as well.

But I go back to the first years of our
own.

This institution had been called into being amid the liveliest sympathy and expectation of all Germany; from the outset it was well organized and prudently directed, without too great an interference of the government in its internal affairs; hence the finest community spirit among the teachers, the highest joy in the office itself even under uncertain and threatening prospects; that spirit was not a little strengthened by two men who are now ministers of His Majesty: I mean the man to whom the supreme direction of the scholarly and ecclesiastical affairs of the whole state is now entrusted, then syndic of the university, and the man who gave legal studies a principal direction, established their flourishing condition at our university, and especially here trained numerous students, as third rector of the university.

Thus this single quiet yet vigorous activity, in youthful freshness, exerted its influence and already drew numerous listeners to it, until in the third year of its existence the sorely tried King called to arms.

His call to the uprising of the people, to the liberation of the country from foreign rule, had made a great impression at the universities; at the local one only a few students unfit for service or foreign students remained behind, while the teachers as well, some of whom themselves went into the field, occupied themselves with armament and war preparations: from the spring of the year 1813 onward, for some half a year, the lectures ceased, except for a few attended by the very smallest number of listeners.

Formerly, those who were permitted to devote themselves to their studies were almost entirely distinguished from the men liable for military service; only one who was free from the obligation to serve could with certainty devote himself to the sciences, and many a good mind, if in particular it had the misfortune to sit on a long and strong body, was suddenly and forever torn from its career, in order to be brought into that servitude from which heroism was supposed to spring, and earlier, to be sure, under a great hero-king had also sprung.

But now we see the educated youth on the field of battle in separate armed hosts, and we have admired their bravery at once in the very first battles; with the change in the whole military constitution, the sharp contrast between citizens and soldiers disappeared, and with
it at the same time the constant quarrels between the two, and especially at the universities between the students and the younger officers: the two qualities had now frequently been united in one and the same person.

From that time on, no one was any longer irrevocably excluded by military service from his studies and from a career in the pursuits of peace; everyone fulfills the duty of training himself to be a defender of the fatherland.

Art and science, though the noblest goods of humanity, can nevertheless, when cultivated one-sidedly, make people soft and inactive; through hardening of the body and practice in arms, which again, cultivated one-sidedly and as in a caste, leads to the opposite faults, the proper balance, together with those, and the full health of body and soul are established.

Now that the state has realized this equilibrium within itself, we may pride ourselves on the finest eulogy that the great Pericles gave the Athenians: "We love the beautiful without extravagant display, and we love wisdom without softness." With the new military order, which is an immortal merit of the king now resting in God and is all the more to his credit the more his opinions, absorbed from youth on, and long habit resisted it, the position of the academic youth in the state has been essentially changed.

It would be incomprehensible if the enthusiasm of that time of struggle had not also aroused in the academic bodies of the university the wish to prove their veneration to the foremost heroes of the great struggle; and I may the less regard the mention of this as petty, since my predecessor in office did not disdain it either: when on August 3, 1814, after the ceremonial address on the great deeds of the king and the people, which I delivered as appointed speaker of the whole university, Solger, as dean of the philosophical faculty, besides the prince state chancellor, named the supreme army commanders doctors, this peculiar celebration seemed neither improper nor pedantic.

The expectations that were attached to the glorious successes of the struggles seized none less than those whose hearts were above all set on intellectual development; for this is not independent of political development.

What almost everyone at that time hoped for as the improvement of political conditions was a constitution: that this
wish also did not remain foreign to the university is shown by another oratorical monument from that period and by the same man whom I have just named.

Solger delivered the ceremonial oration of August 3 in the year 1815; he highlighted the promised introduction of the estates, of which no further mention was later made at this place, because—to say nothing of the period of expectation—the provisional settlement of this great matter by the late king, which seemed satisfactory to only a few, receded behind more influential acts of state.

The orator observed that antiquity, celebrated for the sake of its freedom, had lacked the most excellent of all forms of government, which remained foreign to it: the form in which, under the auspices of the royal majesty, assemblies of select men, the representatives of the whole people, deliberate on the laws and public burdens. In the history of the more recent nations, especially the Germanic peoples, he recalled, there lay many beginnings and developments of this best form, but the Germanic estates constitution had conceded too much to individuals and their particular advantages; in the form of government he praised, it would not be the voices of individuals that were heard, disputing over their rights and powers, but the voice of the people, which can will nothing other than the king: for the king wills the advantage of the people, and therefore it must be of concern to him that he act with the people, not with individuals.

Assemblies should therefore be established that represent the place not of individuals or of a single estate, but of the whole people, and that work together with the king toward this end: that the state present the most nearly perfect image of justice.

Admittedly, such assemblies could also be constituted in such a way that they had only the semblance of right and gave a cosmetic veneer to despotism, as under Napoleon and one of his brothers; but we, it was said, had come so far that that most beautiful state order, which otherwise only emerges from many conflicts and hardships, should be established among us in mutual trust and love between king and subjects, and everyone would here too remember the royal word: "The cause that I lead is common to me with my people." So spoke at that time a man whom no one could count among the agitators, a man who had won his fame through speculative profundity
and a noble and refined aesthetic cultivation.

The fair custom that on this day—which is, as it were, a festival of the dead for us—the busts of our departed teachers that have newly been added to adorn our hall are to be set up, bids me renew his memory today; and instead of speaking of him separately, as it were in an appendix, I prefer to show him in connection with the events of the age, as he appeared now two-and-thirty years ago on this same day and in this place, so as to give expression not, perhaps, to the self-interested hopes of our academic body, but to the common hopes of the fatherland, in which we have the root of our life.

If, then, in the years that followed the struggle for Germany's external independence, there formed at the universities, alongside eager scholarly endeavor and a very considerable improvement in morals, a political tendency among the youth nourished by secret societies, that youth was not so much led into this by individual spokesmen as thrust into it by the earlier, favored spirit: how could one expect that the movement would halt at an arbitrarily fixed goal or bend itself aside?

For it was a necessary consequence of the events, of the participation of the student youth in the wars, from which they had returned home grave and with early life experiences, and soon also of the conflict between the internal policy already intimated in the foundations of the Holy Alliance and a widely prevalent spirit of the age.

Since the time of Napoleon's power hostile to the universities in Germany, the year 1819 has been the most threatening for them; yet under prudent and mild rulers, and for us under Frederick William III, it passed without far-reaching disadvantages.

Already in January, a threat directed against the professors aroused anxious apprehensions and moved our Senate to request a more specific declaration of the Royal will, one that would afford the assurance that in all cases where the censor's approval did not already secure the writer against every claim, no public teacher would be removed on account of alleged press offenses without trial and justice.

Then, to begin with, that fanatical outrage committed against a world-renowned man then living as a guest in Germany brought about the loss of a dear colleague; and
although time has also drawn its veil over the matter, the sympathy may nonetheless be revealed that we paid to his fate out of natural communal feeling.

If the King found himself compelled by his conscience to dismiss this man, the Senate felt itself no less compelled, addressing itself directly to the throne on his behalf, to declare that we have found cause to esteem this man highly as much for the seriousness, honesty, and openness of his character as for his knowledge and his zeal in teaching, and to request that the strictest investigation be ordered by the superior authority into the manner in which he has worked in his teaching office and into the principles he has disseminated therein, and that until its completion the dismissal already decreed be stayed.

After this request, as well as a subsequent motion of the Senate, had proved fruitless, and the man who had been dismissed without any prior investigation or judgment was left his salary, they secured for the dismissed man, until better times, the amount of his salary—something that at that time could only be done in secret—and to this not only friends but also opponents contributed.
Meanwhile the Bund had passed the resolutions against the universities, which not so much [were directed] at these to the...
...served to harm them, than to the debasement of men who were accustomed to an honorable position.
It will be permissible, after twenty-eight years, as a contribution to the appreciation of our academic body in that period, to publish what at the time remained hidden.

On the same day on which the last use [service] for the dismissed colleague had been decided upon, the Rector and Senate, in the feeling of duty fulfilled and of injury suffered, wrote: "In the introduction to the draft laws which by the Imperial

On September 20, 1819, the Austrian federal legation laid before the high Federal Assembly the harshest accusations against the German universities in general and against the teachers active at them, accusations that wounded their honor most painfully: not only was a large portion of academic teachers charged with having misjudged the true and original purpose of the universities, with having substituted for it an arbitrary and often pernicious one, and, instead of forming young men for the service of
the state and for the good of the fatherland, with having filled them with empty dreams and with aversion to the existing legal order; but a dangerous degeneration of the German universities was even asserted, and that in a generality little limited by a few vaguely left exceptions, and in the same generality there was even talk of definite hostilities which were said to have proceeded from this quarter against the principles and the order on which the existing constitution and the internal peace of Germany rest.
On the other hand, we believed that we owed it to the dignity of our institution and to our obligations toward it not to pass over in silence accusations put forward without any citation of facts.

If individual academic teachers had misconducted themselves—a matter on which judgment does not lie with us—then these individuals might be affected by the measures available to the governments; but that not even the slightest suspicion of such guilt falls upon the great majority of the teachers, on that point we may confidently appeal to the judgment of the world.

If a large part of the youth of Germany has been seized by a dangerous presumption, then any impartial investigation will show that this evil is to be ascribed not so much to the universities as rather to other causes acting harmfully upon them from outside as well.

If, finally, this evil could be checked in no other way than by rigorous scholarship in the lecture courses and a serious academic discipline, then these two means, which alone lead to the goal, would have to lose their effectiveness if the academic authorities and the teachers themselves were publicly disparaged in the eyes of those entrusted to their care and of their students.

We would have the reassuring consciousness that our university has remained faithful to its well-recognized scholarly vocation, and that even in these admittedly precarious times it has striven always to keep itself worthy of its true calling; and on account of the conduct of our teaching office, the administration of the discipline entrusted to us, and the spirit and behavior of the great majority of our students, we might confidently appeal to the testimony of our superior authority.

In this consciousness, and in the conviction that the same
holds true of the German universities in general and of the far greater number of their teachers, we felt ourselves, the more we abhorred the conduct laid to our charge and acknowledged its unconditional punishability, all the more obliged to protest most solemnly, on behalf of the German universities and of ours in particular, against the accusations mentioned above, taken in their generality as they were pronounced. The ever most benevolent Minister von Altenstein, requested "to be so good as to forward this our protestation to the high Federal Assembly," willingly transmitted it to the Prince State Chancellor.

When, shortly thereafter, the assembly of ministers at Vienna had been opened, the Rector and Senate also sent a copy of their protest to the State Chancellor, so that it might be laid before that conference.
The prince retained the original and the copy, and informed us of this with the graciousness that adorned, as it did the king, so his foremost servant.

The subordination of the university to a royal extraordinary plenipotentiary, introduced by virtue of those resolutions, brought discord on every side from the very outset; soon the supervising ministry, in sympathy and principles in agreement with the university, again entered into direct connection with it, until the first plenipotentiary was dismissed.
From his successor she experienced only goodwill, and she sincerely regretted his sudden dismissal.

Since that time there existed only a deputyship of this supervisory authority from the midst of our own academic body, soon exclusively through the elected Rector with the associate appointment of the judge.

Without constricting forms, everything was yet well ordered; even under dubious circumstances that renewed themselves from time to time, no offense or embarrassment arose on any side: the university soon reached the highest number of listeners; no proof of perfection, to be sure, but still of a widely spread reputation and of public confidence.

In the winter of 1833–1834 it counted 2,001 enrolled students, and together with the others entitled to hear the lectures, 2,561 listeners; a number such as no German university had been able to show in recent times.

And what was most gratifying, we again enjoyed the full confidence of a government that loved learning
and of a king receptive to the expression of love and reverence that the academic youth also showed him.

He recognized the inner worth of these universities, and they survived the times of a suspicion that reached far beyond their own domain—a suspicion which, I am unfortunately not at liberty to conceal, had almost first originated with a member of our university, an otherwise well-disposed and amiable colleague who had been the first rector of this university.

It is — I say this in the full feeling of truth, after forty years of service in office — it is an inextinguishable vital force, an indestructible kernel of health in these Protestant universities of Germany, so long as they remain true to themselves; and those who, in their urge to reshape everything, would fain destroy even this remnant of old times do not know that they are laying hands on a noble and sacred inheritance, a palladium of German spiritual freedom and unity, which is handed down from generation to generation, from parents to children, like the light of life.

I have spoken of the collision between the universities and politics, from which, according to earlier principles, they were to remain aloof: their relationship to the church has at all times been no less a cause for concern.
But under Frederick William III, apart from that hierarchical movement toward the end of his reign, which scarcely touched the Protestant universities, these affairs took a quiet course.

He had set himself the purpose—a fine one, in my judgment—of bringing about a churchly union of the Protestants, who, to use his own words, were still divided by inherited forms, by traditional hallowed words, by the dead letter of the confession.
In this he indisputably had the spirit and sentiment of the majority on his side; with few exceptions, all the Protestants of Germany strove toward that end.

He encountered less opposition in this union than in the establishment of new forms, even if milder ones; in doing so he exercised little constraint upon the people, whose appropriateness one may rightly debate; he complained more about the theologians.

Yet, apart from transient complications involving individual professors, the universities have been little affected by this, much less hard-pressed or
unsettled. The princes' love of the sciences springs from very different sources and is of very different kinds.
I pass over ignoble sources in silence; the nobler ones are chiefly of two kinds.

The one springs from the understanding of the ruler: he recognizes that the noblest good of the people is knowledge, that the state can be well governed only by those who know, that the state is ennobled and elevated when understanding gradually permeates all its parts.

A prince who holds this conviction can, even without any genuine personal love of the sciences, promote them as a statesman, because he regards them as a necessary element of life; just as a prince without any warlike inclination can devote all requisite care to the armed forces: it is not self-interest, not selfishness, but a correct estimation of their worth that leads him to favor the sciences.

Thus, it seems to me, did Frederick William III promote and love the sciences; educated and instructed, he possessed, like the true statesman, a full overview of all the branches of the state and let every one of them receive its due; as a model not merely of royal but of human prudence and modesty, he at the same time gladly listened to the most judicious.
Thus he did extraordinary things for the sciences in his lands, systematically and uniformly, without favoring one and neglecting another, just and generous toward all.

The other kind of love of princes for the sciences rests on an innate, invincible impulse toward knowledge itself, which might perhaps have destined the king's son to be a scholar, had he not been destined to be a king. Yet such men are not necessarily the most effective promoters of the sciences in their state; still, they will be more fond of the company of scholars.
Frederick the Great had this disposition and direction.

If I have ventured to go so far into personal matters in my judgment of the revered and admired kings of our ruling house, then let it likewise be ventured—although personal comparisons easily become unjust or unseemly—to indicate in a few strokes Frederick William IV's relation to the sciences as well, without fearing that those who know him will accuse me of flattery.

Frederick William IV combines the sublime father's all-around promotion of science and art as a matter of
national concern with Frederick the Great's personal love for the same and for their representatives: and herein lies a step forward, just as the times have also advanced in other respects.

May this, especially for you too, dear younger citizens of our scholarly commonwealth, be a spur to love of the gracious ruler, and to attachment not only to the fatherland but also to the hallowed person of him in whom the fatherland has its visible unity; no less may it be for you a powerful incentive to genuine scholarship and morality.
Yet this day belongs to the father—the noble, virtuous, glory-crowned King!
However the world may transform itself, his memory remains in honor!

div.head: II. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1848.
Ueber das Verhältnifs des Staates zum Unterrichtswesen

p.s: If today, highly esteemed assembly, I speak on the same festival day on which, ever since the accession of Frederick William IV, I have appeared here every year, I cannot—however inappropriate this may seem—following the mood and feeling of my heart, suppress, right at the outset, the deep sorrow that this day is no longer, as formerly, a day of unclouded joy.

This fateful year has, almost throughout all Europe, shaped into deeds mighty thoughts, feelings, and designs that had long been prepared and that were nourished and ripened by the resistance of a governing art that was too late undeceived—deeds by which especially France, Italy, and Germany have been shaken. However magnificent these may be, and, in their further consequences, hopefully beneficial, yet through them have arisen struggles, divisions, and discords that have blasted a deep and wide and scarcely any longer fillable chasm between princes and peoples who were formerly bound, or seemed to be bound, by a mutual bond of piety.

But the celebration for which we are assembled is a celebration of precisely this piety—a piety tender and gentle, free of calculation and, as it were, unconscious, which has its seat neither in the understanding nor, like enthusiasm, in the imagination, but is a secret stirring of the heart, closely akin first of all to gratitude and to religious feeling: amid the great movements of the age, the mighty strivings of the unfettered spirits, the passionate indignation of the parties, the sharp and disintegrating criticism, the tirelessly active sophistry, the wit and mockery that is seldom harmless and mostly cutting and insolent—amid all this, this feeling of piety is gradually dying away in almost all its directions and applications.

Indeed, how could it remain alive in a political upheaval, when even in the religious
sphere, where it ought truly to be at home, the almost inevitable excess that accompanies every new formation so utterly destroys all those feelings that even the founder of Christianity cried out the harsh word to the disciple who, before following him, wished to fulfill the duty most sacred to the natural man—to bury his father: "Let the dead bury their dead"; that the same messenger of love, of divine peace and of the divine kingdom could say that he had not come to send peace on earth, but the sword, to set the son against the father, the daughter against the [father].

Mother against daughter-in-law, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law; a man's enemies would be his own household; whoever loves father and mother, whoever loves son or daughter more than him, is not worthy of him!

I am to say that every fanatical or demonic agitation, whether religious or political or of whatever kind, and however noble and exalted in its origin, however fully justified in its occasions, however beneficent in its effects, devours, like a grave, during the period of fermentation all other spiritual stirrings and all other activities of the soul, and brings the more human feelings, by which the heart is gently moved in the still and quiet flow of life, as a bloody sacrifice to itself.

Indeed, since piety by its nature loves retirement and is seldom paired with strong vigor of action, it scarcely ventures, even where it is still present, to step forward decisively before those of a different mind and to speak out openly, and thus it then seems even less alive than it really is: seldom do we find the just man who holds fast to his principles, the man whom, in the poet's words, "neither the fury of the citizens commanding what is base, nor the countenance of the threatening tyrant shakes in his firm resolve."

The purest and richest source of human well-being, dispassionate prudence, which weighs things with the correct weight and prefers what is possible and useful to the utmost, unattainable, or dangerous consistency, meets in such times with the reproach of half-heartedness: and yet the oldest and simplest wisdom of the Ascraean singer has already known that the half is more than the whole.

Today and in this place I can speak only under the
gratifying presupposition that in your hearts, esteemed listeners, who have come together for this celebration, piety has not yet been extinguished, and that the friends, teachers, and disciples of science—whatever color each individual may belong to—do not lack prudence.

Yet I do not count on applause; for even in times when calmer reflection was to be expected, and although for many years I had devoted myself to spreading liberal views—with moderation, to be sure, but not without danger—I had nonetheless learned from experience that even the best opinion and intention was abandoned to misinterpretation and unintelligent misjudgment, and indeed from both sides, on account of some ill-regarded word that had not been carefully weighed.

Accustomed, however, to speaking not in my own name but as the representative of an academic body, and to immersing myself in the spirit of the majority of those whom I am to represent, I shall endeavor, if not to give expression to this spirit so far as I know it, at least as far as possible to merge my own particular conception with it.
We are gathered here in solemn celebration, honored gentlemen, to commemorate the birthday of the King.

We satisfy only our own piety, in full accord with the truth, when we commemorate his warm-hearted kindness, his enthusiasm for all that is noble and beautiful, his open and lively sense for science and art, and his self-sacrificing self-renunciation.

We satisfy truthfulness only when we acknowledge that he was the first to open the path for the freer political development of this realm; if that development proceeded and was realized further by another route and in another form, then not only piety but even political wisdom—which is greater in the lifting and reconciling of opposites than in their perpetuation—commands us not to quarrel with the past; still less does it become nobler minds to revile or scold the men who were once powerful after they have become powerless.

What has happened cannot be undone: we can only learn from it, in order to make better what was done badly, although, as is well known, people are wont to learn nothing from it because of willfulness and conceit; and if better
conditions make the people happy, the earlier errors may be forgotten, on whomever the blame for them may fall.
Rather, let us remember the good!

And truly, we have had many and great reasons to acknowledge and praise even many of the absolute princes of this land: for they founded its flourishing, its greatness, its glory; but Frederick William the Fourth is the first constitutional, and therefore in truth wholly lawful, king of this land, and in the measure that, as such, he has greater need of the power of the people's love in compensation, in that same measure he has a higher claim to it.

That such purely human gratitude and love, even toward an absolute ruler—how much more, then, for the constitutional one, who is far removed from any slavish spirit—is possible, I have learned from that people to which I owe the greater part of my education; but not I alone, rather the entire educated world, have learned it from the Hellenic people, which first in life and then also in scholarship gave the most complete and noblest expression to political freedom, first among all peoples—and that is, if we except the great form of constitutional monarchy, which it did not attain, and the institution of slavery, which it did not overcome, and with which even today's model state of freedom is still afflicted.

Theron, the mighty tyrant—to cite only this one example—had by cunning and force obtained a wholly illegitimate sole rule; yet gratitude for his mildness and greatness, for his services to the fatherland, since in concert with the princes of Syracuse he had rescued Sicily from the hand of the Carthaginians, seemed so little incompatible with the regained freedom of the Acragantines that after his death they honored him as a hero, just as during his life he had been loved throughout all Sicily.

But Frederick William IV is not only the first constitutional king of this land; he was also the first, precisely with that enthusiasm peculiar to him, to take up the cause of the Germans—not merely in words but in deed, not at others' expense but with heavy sacrifices borne by this land, and moreover without thanks.

All else, honored listeners, I leave to your own hearts, to your own reflection; least of all do I intend a political speech,
since such speeches are delivered everywhere and in the closest proximity, whether from private or public calling and in the more suitable free form of extemporaneous production—not, as the otherwise quite legitimate custom of these celebrations bids us, read from the page.

Rather, I turn to a particular subject that is political in nature only insofar as it has often been called into doubt, both formerly and also nowadays, whether and how far it falls to the state—to a subject that concerns first and foremost ourselves and, to be sure, also our relation to the commonwealth: I mean public education.

If we proceed from the so-called Rechtsstaat, which, without reference to the morality of actions, can restrict natural freedom or arbitrary will only to the extent that the freedom or arbitrary will of others is not thereby violated, then there follows directly from this the most unrestricted freedom to give and to receive instruction: for no person's freedom is thereby directly violated or restricted by my having unconditional freedom to teach and to have myself taught, or also not to have myself taught; it will therefore be open to everyone to come to an agreement with another concerning instruction, and the law will have to decide only whether the contract is a valid one and whether it has been kept or not.

Meanwhile, the question whether the contract is a valid one already includes the thought that the content of the doctrine, or the principles on which it rests, may be of such a kind that through the freedom to teach and to learn the freedom of others is indirectly impaired—as, for instance, if someone wished to give instruction in the art of thieving or robbing, or in immorality generally, or in doctrines that by prevailing conviction are held to be harmful to the common good, for example in atheism; yet the consistent thinker will reply to this that, so long as such things are taught theoretically and have not passed over into criminal deeds, preventive measures against them belong not to the state of law but to the reprehensible police state, and that, to keep to the points cited, it must first still be determined by science what is moral or not, what atheism is or merely seems to some, indeed who has right on his side, the worshiper of God or the denier of God, and whose doctrine
is more beneficial for humanity, and whether property is a real right and not rather, as one has already heard, the harshest injustice and violation of natural freedom.

The constitutional state, therefore, if it is fully consistent, will have to grant not only the personal freedom of instruction but also the complete freedom of teaching with respect to its content, even at the risk of its own dissolution: it has no occasion to found educational institutions or even merely to supervise teaching.

The matter presents itself quite differently if we regard the state as something more positive and more substantial than an institution founded by human beings, an institution in which the reason and morality of the human race are to be realized—and thus, to be sure, freedom as well, since freedom consists in the dominion of reason and morality.

Reason and morality—the latter taken at its highest level, as conscious virtue—rest, however, on knowledge; and the means of attaining knowledge, apart from the rare cases in which outstanding minds, by the path of wholly independent self-instruction, arrive at no slight degree of cultivation, is instruction, joined with one's own activity.

From this standpoint, to which I profess allegiance, without being able here, within the compass of this lecture, to justify it over against the former one, the state is not merely entitled but obligated to take the educational system, or the entire school system, into its own hands; whoever, however, concedes this standpoint with its consequences for the school must, incidentally, equally concede that the church too falls within the domain of the state, or else he would have to exclude the church—which is, after all, nothing other than the institution founded for the realization of the religious life of humanity—and, along with the church, religion itself from the domain of reason and morality and knowledge, and confine it to the dead confession of an uncomprehended dogma and the symbolic usages connected therewith, whereas the church nevertheless lays claim to this: that the faith which it confesses contains the highest wisdom, exalted above all human science, a wisdom which has not seldom been asserted by it as authoritative for all science, and whereas one equally lays claim to the church:
that it, whether through instruction or through influence upon feeling and heart and conscience, spread and strengthen general morality.

If, then, the state wishes to exercise its right and its duty to direct instruction in the greatest possible extent, all the means and institutions of instruction will be supplied and supervised by the state authority; we then obtain—since the state itself transforms itself almost into an educational institution—an exclusive, though indeed a very popular, state education, which, like the Spartan, for all its beauty and all the advantages connected with it, easily leads to Chinese or Egyptian drilling, uniformity, and strict seclusion, and whose constricting compulsion does not suit the free course of development of European culture and of this age.

For the good of the human race, such consistency is rare: few states have been built entirely according to theories, and least of all nowadays can any lasting duration be promised to a theoretical structure of this kind; rather, here too the truth proves to be that the half is more than the whole: expediency and necessity advise relaxing the rigor of the system, and, as it were, erecting only the foundation pillars and walls of the edifice of knowledge by state authority, while expecting various additions and embellishments from individuals, insofar as the state can count on them.

But he can count on this least of all among those who feel the need for instruction least and lack the means for it most: his most sacred duty, therefore, is to give the poorer and humbler the possibility of instruction, and they obtain this only through free teaching in public schools.

The state must establish the various institutions of higher learning all the more, the more considerable the expense they require in an age in which the sciences have branched out in manifold ways and have gained an infinite extension, and the less a comprehensive and systematic establishment of those institutions can be hoped for from the private association of individuals.

The summit of these higher schools is the universities; their calling is accordingly the teaching of science itself for all who devote themselves to it as their particular purpose in life, but not—as has often been asserted from a subordinate
standpoint—the preparation for state service; yet the servants of the state are to be educated and prepared through science, and therefore pre-eminently here, because, if the state is to be the realization of the life of reason, those who serve the state—that is, who are to participate in some sphere in its government—must first of all be educated through science.

If, however, the state assumes responsibility for the institutions of higher education, it does not follow from this that it must also bear all the costs of this education: it is enough and more than enough if it provides the means of instruction to the point that the wealthy disciple of science, so long as there are still wealthy people, makes a not burdensome personal contribution for his personal education, and regards this, as the name of this contribution indicates, as a matter of honor.
It would be no less deeply to be lamented if the state's concern for science and education wished to exclude all private cooperation therein.

After all, in classical antiquity, which had reached a high level of culture, almost the whole of instruction, with few exceptions, was left to private care apart from gymnastics and music; in later times the benevolence of private individuals has directed great support to the sciences, and private schools can only be accepted with gratitude as a welcome aid toward achieving the general and particular purposes of the whole, and in a free state they can no more be contested than ecclesiastical or religious private associations.
But how, then, do matters stand in the state of reason and morality with regard to the freedom of teaching and of doctrine?
Certainly no worse than in the state of law: for freedom is the first condition of reason and morality; reason that is not free, morality that is not free, is no longer reason and morality.

To go further into detail with only a few sentences: since everyone is master in his own house and family, any restriction of domestic instruction to specially authorized persons—something that has been attempted elsewhere and also among us—lacks sufficient justification. But when instruction emerges into the public sphere, as it does even in the private school, then reason and morality are necessary preconditions for
the teacher's authorization; and since both qualities do not reside in all persons, an exclusion from the right to teach is indeed not unfounded, however difficult this may be in practice if freedom is not to be endangered.

That the teaching itself must be free follows from what has been said without further ado; if at other times I have often spoken in favor of freedom of teaching, it now stands in no need of advocacy, and as a representative of the university I need not first proclaim that the university is devoted to it with its whole soul, since it is precisely the university that has defended and protected the freedom of teaching as far as its powers allowed, though without the recognition it deserved.

Oral teaching, however, cannot claim any greater freedom—or rather, impunity—than the press; if, then, the offenses of the latter are subject to punishment even in those states in which political freedom is realized in the fullest measure, so too the man who resists this cannot deny that the same may befall the public teacher and that no special privilege is due to him.

The freedom of teaching is violated only when the latter is proceeded against in another way and according to other provisions than those by which all citizens are governed—by arbitrary suppression, not by judgment and law, according to arbitrary ordinances and exceptional laws, as they have been made against the teachers, not according to the universally valid laws which the free state must enact as are appropriate to a free people; it is violated only when the state power seeks to clip the wings of the spirit's flight and to ban and fetter thought by prescribed magic formulas of power.

Although these views on the relation of the state to the educational system do not presuppose an ideal and unattainable condition of society, such as, for instance, a Platonic state, the existing state can nevertheless fall far short even of those presuppositions under which what has been said holds good.

For although we make the demand of the state that it be the realization of reason and morality, the state as it appears only approaches this idea, and indeed more or less according to the diversity of constitutions
and the deviations from them which, commonly, are nonetheless also called constitutions.
All these are usually determined by the prevailing power.

But unfortunately it still remains true, however philosophically false and however factually true, what Thrasymachus the Sophist said more than two thousand years ago, with a sure grasp of the given conditions: that the just is the advantageous of the stronger, or more precisely that which the stronger, even though doubtless caught up in great error, regards as advantageous to himself. The expression of right is law, and the sum of public right and law is the constitution, so that, according to that doctrine, the constitution is the sum of what the stronger in the relation of the state regards as advantageous to himself.
Accordingly, the position of education and of science in relation to the actual state becomes very different.
Let it be permitted to give a few examples.

In theocracy, or rather hierarchy, the priest rules by virtue of the recognition that has fallen to his ordinances, and firm faith in their divinity, together with the submission of consciences arising therefrom, is the guarantee of this rule: a free development of the.

Science, and instruction free of prejudice, is therefore not conducive to such a state power and stands in contradiction to its consistent spirit; almost every advance in knowledge would thus be impossible under it, were it not that, on the one hand, the prudence of the priesthood tolerated many things that do not agree with its ordinances, in that it wrests from them the appearance of compatibility with them or of indifference toward them, and, on the other hand, the human spirit itself broke through the established limits in defiance of dungeon, fire, and sword: evidence of which is too well known to be cited here.

So long, however, as the people stand at a low level of education, the priesthood is a capable preserver of inherited means of education, and church and monasteries have earned merit through this preservation.

The strict aristocracy of a caste-like hereditary nobility—that is, one moderated by no cooperating power of another estate—rests essentially on its separation from the lesser, so that the noble metal may not be falsified by admixture of the common ore; it must therefore be averse to the cultivation of the governed, so that these
may not through their education gain the appearance or the claim of equality of birth, and since education is itself a power, become dangerous to the aristocracy: how often does one hear from this side that the common people are more easily governed if they remain in ignorance, and that they lose in happiness what they gain in enlightenment!

The highly educated Thirty Men at Athens forbade the teaching of the art of rhetoric, and in particular forbade Socrates to associate with shoemakers, builders, and metalworkers, whom he had already properly worked over.
In such an aristocracy, then, education cannot descend very far, and moreover, even in the higher circles, it all too easily passes over into sham education.

Absolute sole rule—whether one calls it despotism or tyranny or absolute monarchy—exerts, according to the spirit of the ruler or of influential advisers, on which in it the manner of its operation alone depends, a very different influence on scholarship and instruction, and from very different motives.

In its essential nature, science is not conducive to unmoderated autocracy, because freedom is the goal and the vital air of science; and conversely, a tyrannical pressure continued through many ages, especially in alliance with a corrupt hierarchy, as in the Byzantine Empire, infallibly kills the spirit. But there are, so to speak, quiet and withdrawn sciences that affect life slightly or slowly, that do not stir it up and do not disturb it; there is a learned craft that has no influence at all on the spiritual temper of the people. This kind of learning the statesman of the most absolute principles may indifferently leave to whatever pursuit he pleases, or, as he sees fit, even promote it, because it paralyzes those active in it more than it awakens them.

Furthermore, deeper science and art also withdraw from the agitated life of the state, and can therefore be employed by absolute rule as a means of calming and diversion, as a plaything and for delight, like the theater and other amusements: of which I have treated earlier on another occasion: both furthermore spread a splendor around the throne, and elevate the state in public opinion.

For these and similar reasons, and for the most part also out of their own love of art
and desire for learning, either art or science or both were already cultivated—not without brilliant and beneficent success—by the Pisistratids and by Polycrates of Samos, by the Ptolemies and the princes of Pergamon, by Augustus and the Medici, by the French kings Charles the Wise, Francis the First, and Louis the Fourteenth; and if we already acknowledge in these men respect and love for art and science, then our kings assuredly deserve in equal measure the glory of these and other noble grounds for their promotion of the same.

From these noble grounds I single out two more, which have also determined absolute rulers: the one that Frederick the Great advances, that it is easier to convince a people of just things, a people that has sufficient education to accept reason, than one stubborn and recalcitrant in its ignorance; the other, that the well-disposed and moderate autocrat indeed wishes to make his people partakers of all good and well knows that the people's dearest good is knowledge: but in putting this principle into practice, he himself slackens the reins of mere power and prepares the way for the dissolution of this form of state.

Democracy, finally, seems especially favorable to the cultivation of the sciences and arts and of education, because in its idea it grants the full freedom of thought, although it has not confirmed this in Anaxagoras and Socrates, in Protagoras and Diagoras; because it further arouses and gives wings to the spirit of the people; and because it is beneficial to it that knowledge spread through all classes of the population; people also commonly draw the historical proof of this proposition from the flowering of the arts and of all liberal culture in democratic Greece.

In fact, only antiquity, from which the experience of many centuries in the history of many and distinguished states lies before us, can give us greater instruction concerning democracy and its consequences; and it would be foolish presumption to close our eyes before this bright mirror of self-knowledge, to fancy ourselves grown out of such old-fashioned wisdom, or even merely to suppose that our conditions are too different from those to be measured by one and the same standard.

Let us set Plato aside, who denies any distinction between democracy and
democracy and rejects them all alike, and hold to the view that moderate democracy is truly a constitution, while immoderate democracy, or ochlocracy, is a transgression; and we shall find that the former, under favorable attendant circumstances, is fruitful for art and science, while the latter is unconditionally fatal to them.

To speak first of the moderate [form of government]: the highest proof of moderation on the part of that democratic-minded people, so well practiced in political affairs, was its distrust of its own insight and its trust in a higher one. Thus Athens, in a time of great turmoil, placed its entire constitutional affair in the hand of the one man Solon, and Cyrene likewise had its whole state ordered by a foreign arranger specially entreated for the purpose, Demonax of Mantinea: no one thought of raising the slightest objection to any ordinance of theirs.
I pass over many other examples.

The foundation of the moderate democracy at Athens was precisely that constitution of the noble Solon; after he had lifted the pressure from the people, he gave to the democracy its surest moderation through a timocratic addition and through the aristocracy of proven ability and insight bound up with it in the high council of the Areopagus, the anchor of the state and, as Aeschylus calls it, the saving bulwark for country and city.

Thus he united the opposing parties, as he himself says in his simply beautiful words: "For to the people I granted as much power as sufficed for them; I did not curtail their honor, nor did I raise it too high; and to those whom power distinguished, and whom possessions distinguished as well, I, mindful of these too, gave according to their due."
Embracing both with a mighty shield I stood, and I allowed no victories of either party contrary to justice." Thus he won for all time the double glory of the sage and of a true friend of the people.

When, under the pressure of circumstances, the delimitation of the rights of government according to the assessment of property had become untenable, and the Areopagus too had suffered a weakening, yet by no means did every influence of the propertied class disappear, and still less that of insight; the latter was transferred especially to the surpassing mind of Pericles, who, with the omnipotence of a prudent and artistically cultivated speech, in popular assemblies which,
consecrated by religious celebration, were held only under the presidency of the state authorities, guided a people capable of every sacrifice for the power and glory of the state in war and peace; and there existed, as Thucydides says, in word a democracy, but in fact the sole rule of the first man, over a period of approximately forty years.

What Polybius remarks about true democracy—that it is not the democracy in which the people can do whatever happens to please them at any given moment, but the one in which it is an old custom and habit to fear the gods, to honor one's parents, to show respect to age, to obey the laws—that was the spirit of that democracy; even in far more corrupt times, before every deliberation the herald's call went forth first of all: "Who wishes to speak from among those who are over fifty years old?" The noble youth, accustomed by the strictness of the Gymnasien and by tactical exercise to discipline and measure, was, like many of our own, so far as it was led into battle, the brave executor of what had been resolved and was held back from the orator's platform; military service was regulated according to the property assessment; the authorities were held in high esteem and in their competence were hampered by no popular will; the laws were subject to change only under very stringent provisions.
And above all, that age was distinguished by unconditional obedience to the existing law; this kept all passions in check, and no resolution of the people was more valid than the law.

The same Sophocles who proclaimed the watchword of democracy, "The state that belongs to one man is no longer a state," said to his fellow citizens in the same tragedy: "The greatest of evils is disobedience."

It undermines the states, it brings about the fall of the noble houses; in the battle of spears it breaks flight into the ranks: if they stand in order, obedience preserves many from destruction." And as a reward for giving expression to such principles and to a deep reverence for the divine, that people placed him, together with Pericles, at the head of an army.

What wonder that this democracy, under the firm leadership of the greatest man of his age, among a highly gifted and industrious people, borne up by an extensive power, supported by the generous contributions of wealthy citizens, and commanding the tribute
of perhaps a thousand cities, unfolded the highest blossoms of the spirit and all the beauty of human nature?

But the same antiquity also experienced and frankly admitted the worst of its evils in the state, ochlocracy, in which a stormy mob assumes the role of the tyrant, no longer ruling according to law but according to the arbitrary will of popular decrees, with the dissolution of the power of the authorities, in whose place there step forward not, to be sure, great demagogues such as Themistocles, Cimon, and Pericles were, but men such as Cleon and Hyperbolus.

Such men are, as Aristotle says, to the people what flatterers are to the tyrant; and just as the latter teach the tyrant, so the former teach the people that it is free to do whatever it pleases, and likewise whatever it considers expedient.
But in his delusion he held it to be beneficial to distribute the property of the rich; and this, says the same Aristotle, he regards even as right: the surest way to make everyone poor.

With this there was joined, as the harshest expression of democratic envy, an ostracism of intelligence and of every kind of distinction: "Let no one among us be the best," said the Ephesians in the decree of the people, when they drove out their best man.
Thus unreason and violence are raised to the throne.

How can one still believe that in such a state of affairs the arts and sciences—except perhaps the most utterly material of them—could be regarded as beneficial, honored, cultivated, indeed even merely tolerated?

Even granted that the people should remain industrious and not, as in antiquity, grow idle in an idle ochlocracy, the spiritual will nonetheless be pressed down by the sensual, the ideal by the earthly; the noble cultivation that lives in the harmony of those two elements, imagination and poetry, inquiry and philosophy, will die out.

If the despotism of the absolute ruler can still tolerate art and science up to a certain degree, and may even promote them, then under ochlocratic despotism both necessarily perish, unless the latter, as commonly happens, soon reverts to the former.

If today, a year later, at this very place, in agreement with the judgment of the most learned, most experienced, and most judicious teachers of statecraft in ancient and modern times—even those of Hellas and Rome, who had
actually put the republic to the test—I declared the mixed form of government, which is perfected in a properly composed constitutional monarchy, to be the best and one that lastingly satisfies all the needs of society, then, faithful to my conviction, I now add that it is also the most beneficial to the sciences and arts, because, without oppressive surveillance or tutelage, without favoring those tendencies toward retrogression, in the state as in scholarship, and generally without arbitrary favor or disfavor, it places no fetter on the free soaring of genius and at the same time is able to supply all the aids that the teaching and practice of the sciences and arts require.
If, amid the general confusion of thought, wisdom, moderation, and concord are to be capable of preserving for us the new good, then we go forward with the hereditary prince toward a brighter future.
God preserve the King and his House!

div.head: III. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1849.
Ueber die Einheit der Preufsischen Monarchie und über die Einheit Deutschlands

p.s: We are assembled today, highly esteemed listeners, first in order to celebrate a festival within the narrower circle of this university, a festival in which the whole fatherland takes part; and then in order to be present at an act which indeed concerns this academic body alone, but which is rightly linked to that general celebration, not merely because the one and the other are accidentally bound to the same day, but because the existence of our academic body is essentially rooted in the whole of the fatherland, and is an outflow of the royal house's esteem and love for learning and for the education of the people.

If those who perform the latter act have a given subject in the office that the one lays down and the other takes up, then for the man who likewise speaks by virtue of his office—and thus not, as in the Hellenic age the orators at some panegyris were appointed speaker for the former by the special confidence of the community—in this joyful occasion only the genre of the speech is prescribed, and indeed the panegyric genre, while for the subject, provided only that it has some relation to the one honored, a wide scope is left open.

For among the three kinds of speech that were set forth by the ancients, the sole models and teachers of eloquence, the deliberative and the judicial, because they work toward an intended decision or action, have a direction determined by the circumstances of each occasion, which with some practice is not easily missed, and are therefore also alone suited to free improvisation, to the application of all means of persuasion, and also to passion and the manifold play of so-called bodily eloquence: the third, called by the ancients the demonstrative, to which the panegyric belongs, far removed from such working and struggling and advancing only in pomp and splendor, has its essence in general
contemplation, and consequently, as regards its subject, its starting point, and its goal, a great indeterminacy; it requires Isocratean considered choice, is, as Aristotle teaches, of all kinds most directed toward written composition, and its work, says the same author, is reading.

If one were to say that the panegyrical speech, too, has its own securely prescribed purpose—to celebrate and praise the subject of the festival—then I reply that, through an abuse of linguistic usage, as it has been reshaped and entrenched in flattering times, the meaning of a eulogy has been foisted upon the panegyrical speech; that the acknowledged and expressly stated intention of bestowing praise, especially upon an individual, deprives the speaker of dignity and the praise of value; that finally the panegyrical speech, in this respect somewhat akin to the church sermon, in its original and proper sense had only the purpose of bringing a solemnly assembled multitude, through noble words and thoughts suited to the circumstances—which are not given with unalterable necessity—into a mood appropriate to the celebration; and that the praise of the person to whom the celebration is directed is indeed a very suitable means to this end, but that any censure of that person would be a discord in the harmony of the festival.

In the storm and whirl of a much-agitated age, when sentiment ebbs and flows, in the periodic recurrence of one and the same festivity, even after the lapse of a single year, the same sentiment can no longer be presupposed in either speaker or hearer, nor can it seem adequate to the celebration—not merely because we ourselves change along with the times, but because even he who, amid the change of things around him, remains firm in his own being and on his principles, comes to occupy a different position toward this changing element and is differently affected by it.
Happy the one being honored, happy his admirers, if the mood has changed from a sorrowful and oppressed one into a serene and joyful one!
Today the King and his loyal followers, among whom I count myself, must feel this happiness especially keenly, above all when they transport themselves back to the same-named day of last year.

At that time, in this same place where I speak today, at the very opening of my address I could not suppress
the deep distress that this day was no longer, as formerly, a day of unclouded joy; I had to look into the yawning gulf that had been torn open between prince and people; I had to mourn the decline of the most profound of feelings in noble minds, the feeling of piety, and to lament the constraint under which most, even of those in whom this feeling had not yet been extinguished, shut this very feeling within themselves for lack of strength and courage and let it fall silent.

This gloomy mood could have been moderated by joyful hopes, if even then it had been recognizable that the reversal into the opposite lay quite near; but however movable and volatile the crowd may be in its inclinations, in favor and disfavor, however clearly history also teaches that the immoderate has no duration, however swiftly also in this age, just as spaces, so too changes and events that formerly required generations of men, are traversed in close compression, this rapidity of reversal could scarcely be expected.
Nevertheless, and perhaps precisely because of this rapidity, much is still lacking for us to attain full reassurance, since much is still lacking for our concord.

For just as the individual spirit is at rest only when all its soul-powers harmoniously accord, while their discord wears it down, so unity and concord are the purest source also of the public good, and discord its ruin; and although in all natural and human things diversity and opposition are necessary for life to arise, yet, if life is not to be destroyed in eternal strife and all forms to disintegrate, dissolved into their various constituent parts, the opposite must join together into unity.

Driven by its original destiny, the human race has created for itself this unity in the state, the greatest edifice of the human spirit—a unity in which all the various strivings are absorbed without being destroyed; within it the church too must be absorbed, if it is not to form a state within the state. The endeavor to dissolve the state in order to attain an even higher stage of culture is a gigantic presumption against human nature and at the same time a piece of sheer folly.

In order to achieve the greatest possible unity, in the
