earliest times the highest power was entrusted to the hands of a single man, because rule by many did not foster piety; and since unity is not possible without continuity, absolute monarchy was tied to the right of hereditary succession.
When this no longer seemed tolerable to the rising people, the hereditary monarchy was abolished in many places, and free states of every kind and form were established.

These proved their worth as long as they rested on the virtue of the citizens, though for the most part they were again directed by an outstanding spirit as their actual ruler, and as long as circumstances were small, simple, and easy to survey.

The more manifold and intricate these became, and the larger the states grew, the more necessary it was, in the face of greater manifoldness and multiplicity, to shape a firmer unity; and so almost all the more extensive states, and at the same time those further advanced in development, found their satisfaction—with brief and for the most part very turbulent interruptions—in monarchy, whose truest form is rightly held to be the constitutional, provided it is not mere semblance, which kills everything, but truth, which alone has vital power.
It is into this form that our state has presently turned from absolute monarchy.

Undoubtedly the latter has in full measure given it the unity and continuity through which the monarchy is beneficial to the peoples: it would be more loss than gain if the new transformation made the monarchy unfit to effect that for which it seems pre-eminently called.
But that is not the case!
Far from being less capable of preserving the unity and stability of the state, a monarchy moderated and limited by wise laws preserves them rather in a nobler manner than an absolute one.

For the absolute ruler attains it only by having taken all power into his own hands and holding the people down with the full weight of that power; the constitutional ruler allows the people, in its representatives—and indeed, in a sensible constitution, according to the measure of worthiness, or, as one of the ancients expresses it, according to geometric and not arithmetic equality, and yet without excluding any class—the due influence over the legislation which it is to obey and over the regulation of the taxes which it is to pay; but he retains the fairest
prerogative of moderating those powers through his requisite consent, and thereby of uniting all elements, whether they be democratic or aristocratic or whatever else they may be or be called, and of hovering, in untroubled impartiality, above the change of persons and opinions, the oppositions and parties, like the eternally One and Existent above the many and the becoming.

Thus Plato, comparing the royal art to the art of weaving half in jest and yet with deep seriousness, already placed its business in the interlinking and interweaving of the various natures, soft and hard, gentle and vehement.

Then, in a limited monarchy, once it has first been fully ordered, stability is increased by the fact that changing the laws is made more difficult, because it no longer depends on individual whim—unless, that is, the popular representation, in the manner of an ochlocracy, presumes to be able to pass resolutions binding even against the existing law.

Moreover, even the absolute prince cannot give the state a unified and firm form unless between the ruling house and the ruled there exists, or is assumed to exist, so living a reciprocal interaction that the prince counts as the bearer of the fundamental ideas of his people, and the people presuppose in him the expression of national character embodied in one person: how much more intimate, however, is this reciprocal interaction between the king who rules constitutionally and the people, since it lies realized before our eyes in all acts of state!

Finally, in the hereditary monarchy the unity and duration of the state receive yet a special guarantee through the fact that its lesser members, who are not all capable of the degree of political virtue that is necessary to the citizen of a free state if the latter is to enjoy a happy continuance, conceive a heartfelt affection for the hereditary supreme head of the realm, and that even those who stand in the widest and outermost circles of political life are drawn by spiritual attraction, and as it were according to the natural law of gravity, which is mirrored in the moral sphere, toward the one center.

If in free states—at least those of antiquity—love of country has spurred men on to the most admirable deeds and sacrifices, this sacred flame is still more abundantly nourished and more
vividly kindled by the inherited love of a gracious and citizen-friendly king, and by the soulful devotion and loyalty dedicated to him: at his call all follow, as warriors follow the battle cry of their commander; and when the idea, that mighty lever of deeds, no longer suffices for the work, feeling for the person still harbors powerful driving forces of enthusiasm.

It has been observed that even under unlimited autocracy, provided only that it observes some measure of restraint, the people hold the good and throne-reverent belief that of whatever in the acts of government appears to them unreasonable or oppressive the prince knows nothing; otherwise it would long since have been remedied: and since even the most prudent and active prince cannot enter into all details, still less penetrate them—something that even Frederick the Great, in his striving after it, did not always succeed in doing—that belief is not without all justification.

But the principle of constitutional kingship, which lays all responsibility upon the servants of the Crown, will, in place of that belief, establish the conviction that whatever seems oppressive is approved by the King not with arbitrary force but after mature deliberation and with the assent of the people's representatives, and that if an error has occurred in this, its origin lies not in the will or judgment of the ruler; besides, even in the limited monarchy, countless opportunities remain to him to win the love of the people and to assure himself of their attachment.

This attachment, now that the passionate agitations of the past year have been overcome, has again awakened so powerfully in this country as well that today we can give ourselves wholly to the mood that alone is fitting for this day: joy over the rule of this royal house, joy over the restored happiness of a prince whose goodness of heart and fullness of love for his people, and deep enthusiasm for all that is good and noble, no slander has been able to obscure.

Even if we do not yet walk on fully leveled ground, even if here and there a spark still glimmers beneath our soles, we may yet hope that this disposition in our fatherland will more and more lead all minds back to the old concord, but will banish
discord—that daughter of night and mother of poverty—and give room only to that moderate opposition which is recognized as necessary for a healthy public life.

In antiquity, beneath the veil of figurative expression, we find the principle stated—that it is well, in a stormy night, to have let down two anchors from the ship into the seabed—namely, that the individual comes to share in a greater security when he has a double fatherland and is a citizen of several states.

The German has, even without this, a twofold fatherland: the German fatherland and the particular fatherland of his particular land; but it is doubtful whether this confers such an advantage on the individual, and still more doubtful whether it does so on the whole.

Certainly not for the whole, and consequently not for the majority of individuals either, so long as discord arises from the multiplicity of states, so long as the unity of the many has not yet been found; here too, I repeat what I have said, much is still lacking for our full reassurance.

Although I know very well how to distinguish the place from which I speak here from the political orator's platform, and have already distinguished it in the opening of my address, and although I further know that Solon's demand that in civil strife everyone should take a side can easily be outweighed by the teaching of his descendant that under certain circumstances and conditions the philosopher does best to refrain from participation in the existing state, and that, given the impossibility of helping, many may be led to the principle of Asinius Pollio, adopted as obstinacy against the ruling power, of being willing to be the victor's spoil; yet the position which the universities have occupied in Germany for a long time seems to me not only to entitle but to require them not to fall silent when the German fatherland is spoken of.

Even if one or another among us should not join in, yet in this rare misfortune of the times he will still permit what Tacitus called a rare good fortune of the times—freedom to think what one will and to say what one thinks; indeed, impossible as it is, in matters of importance, to please everyone, I may even hope that, with the disposition which is firmly suited to the present King, I may speak of the German Fatherland
in harmony with it, because it is in harmony with the innermost feeling, the declared direction, and the earnest striving of the King, which had already been indicated by unambiguous signs before the fateful convulsion of Germany.

The German universities have long been regarded as a common good and jewel of the whole fatherland: Emperor and Empire have granted them privileges and, in cases where it was necessary, prescribed laws for them, and the Federal Diet, established in the place of Emperor and Empire, has continued this legislation, no matter in which direction; even the Germans' enemy in war has recognized them all together as his enemies.

For a common bond has embraced all German universities, with the sole exception of the Austrian and, earlier, also the Bavarian; all have exercised the most intimate mutual interaction upon one another in teachers and students.

No wonder that on them the idea of German unity especially took root, and that from them—after the cosmopolitanism and indifference toward all things patriotic, so often urged upon scholars and teachers, to which they were to some extent entitled by the equally frequent admonitions to occupy themselves only with science and learning, had also in these yielded to the stirrings of the national spirit—that from them, I say, endeavors proceeded which, taken up by youthful minds, strayed from the right path in their untimeliness, immaturity, and excess, and fell under the law!

And yet it is a fact that cannot be argued away, whether it be pleasing or displeasing: whatever genuine element lay in that direction—indeed, even much that was spurious along with it—has prevailed within the course of scarcely a single generation, and, down to the outward signs, the presentiment has been fulfilled which, as I recall, a great teacher of this university, long since deceased, expressed in a ceremonial address precisely in this connection: that the future would probably bring to realization much of what at that time was scarcely permitted to be uttered.

However many may have become doubtful of German unity and oneness, it least of all befits the universities to become disloyal to the German fatherland; and this university, whose spokesman I have the honor to be, is, I think, just as far from this as it was the previous year
from even allowing the mere appearance to arise against it that it were casting its gaze toward a power standing outside the Prussian fatherland: for it knew that it had, from its government—though sorely pressed at that time—in the experience of the past, a sure pledge of faithful care and nurture for the future.

Thus we Prussians are with our whole soul: but we will not cease to be Germans and to lament all that which gives nourishment to the discord of our common fatherland—a discord which, alas, is as old a disgrace of the Germanic name as its memory reaches back, and which draws on through almost all the centuries down into our own days.

There by the Teutoburg Forest they raise a colossus to the Cheruscan prince, the victory-crowned, unfortunate hero in whose fate the future of his people is already foreshadowed—to him who in the bloom of manhood became a victim of dynastic discord, of personal arrogance, of the envy that strikes everything outstanding, and finally of the freedom misunderstood by his own people: against him stands his own brother in the ranks of the Romans, against him his father-in-law Segestes out of an old private feud, his uncle Inguiomer because, an old man, he deems it unworthy to obey his youthful nephew, the Suevian king Marbod because Hermann's fame threatens to eclipse his own; and after the Romans refused the poison with which a prince of his own stock had undertaken to kill him, he falls through the machinations of his own blood-kin, because he strove for the power and dominion through which alone he could become the liberator of the Germans.
They raise a monument to this hero of the Germanic peoples, and they kill him anew when they perpetuate the discord that brought about his downfall.

We see that a neighboring people, through prolonged internal strife, has become the prey of the adjoining kingdoms, and, driven from its land—the Messenians of our time—carries the firebrand, shall I say of Eris or of Nemesis, through Europe: and yet many of the Germans resist our unity!
Are the divisions within the German people really so deeply rooted and insurmountable as they are presented to us by some — partly in good faith?

Admittedly, the evils that are unsettling Germany are not few, and among them
the struggle between the poor and the propertied, between aristocracy or oligarchy or timocracy and democracy with all its adventurous and rampant varieties and excrescences, together with the distress of individual classes of the population, is the most dangerous; but that struggle, with few passing exceptions, does not divide state from state, but undermines the interior of the particular states.

What is supposed to make the unity of the Germans a mere figment of the imagination is, as this person and that have argued, the diversity of language, of national character, of customs, of religion, of material advantages.
Let us draw closer to these assertions!

When Germany was torn entirely apart under Napoleon's yoke, it seemed a consolation that its language, and whatever is closely connected with it, its scholarship, was still a firm bond of its national unity: now that this has been brought near to us, this last anchor of distress too is cut away from us, and we hear with shame that language divides the German tribes!

As if in Germany the question were whether to force Germans and Slavs of every kind, and Magyars and Italians, together into one unity; as if other states, such as France and Great Britain, where it succeeded early to overcome the rule of many, did not, with the firmest union of their constituent lands, exhibit many very different dialects; as if it created or justified discord when one person uses this word-form and another that, pronounces a letter, a syllable, an ending this way or that, or stresses and modulates his speech this way or that!

Anyone who wished to establish a political separation by this means would also have to divide the townspeople and the rural population into different states, and have a different state begin every five or six miles, as was also formerly the case in part in the districts of Germany: for, to use a delightful expression of the so-called German Philosopher of Görlitz, "the principal languages twist themselves in the mouths of the common people every five or six miles according to the character of the air in their ruling constellation"!
What holds of language also holds of national character and customs; their diversity is not so great that the Germans thereby ceased to be one people.

The difference between the East and the West is in this respect no less than that between the
North and the South; and yet we see the farthest East and the farthest West united not merely, say, into a federal unity, but under Frederick William's mild scepter into a full unity of state, whose possibility is thus proved by actuality, at least wherever no dynastic impediment arises: indeed, we have even seen these farthest Prussian lands allied in the same political direction.

If one speaks of the liveliness, imagination, and warmth of feeling of the German South, and of the calm and cold rationality of the North, here too the account is exaggerated: the Berlin tongue is quicker than the Swabian, and in the North action has shown itself no less quick and even rash than in the South; on the sandy plains of the Mark, too, imaginative poetry has grown, and the inhabitants of the Baltic and North Sea coasts are just as warm-hearted as the neighbors of the Alps.

In the age of Frederick the Great, the more educated among the South Germans looked with love and admiration toward the North; only later did Romantic spirits undertake to disparage the culture of the German North, and under Napoleonic rule, from a certain point onward, the opposition between North and South was asserted with particular zeal and self-seeking passion.

More alarming could be the difference of religion, which is exploited with the greatest success by instigators of disunity: for at all times religion has been misused for political purposes, to which, according to the teaching of the divine founder of ours, it is entirely foreign; indeed, people even speak openly of a Catholic politics, just as a few years ago they fabulated about a Catholic philosophy.

Unfortunately, to be sure, the religion of love and peace, denying its origin less than its calling, has transplanted that intolerance—which in antiquity only the less cultivated peoples, especially the Oriental ones, the Persians, Egyptians, and Jews, practiced to a greater degree and against others—onto European soil and into the heart of peoples and states, certainly with less justification, since the religions of antiquity were more closely interwoven with national character and the fanatical struggle of one against the other rested at the same time on the mutual repulsion of national characters.
I deny, however, that in Germany—to dwell on this country alone—the difference of confessions is connected with a national diversity, especially of the North and the South.
Permit me, highly esteemed listeners, to consider by means of a few examples how the confessions are delimited locally, and how these delimitations came about.

The greater part of the North is, to be sure, Protestant; but I need only name Westphalia, Hildesheim, the Eichsfeld, and Ermeland, in the far East entirely enclosed by Protestant territory, to recall that Catholicism—and indeed a very decided Catholicism—is not foreign to the North either.

The south is mostly Catholic, and this confession reaches right up to Saxony; but in the southwest, in the former Swabian Circle and the neighboring districts, Protestant and Catholic regions are jumbled together: Württemberg and the territories of the former Margraviate of Baden-Durlach are Protestant, those of the former Margraviate of Baden-Baden Catholic, quite strictly according to the earlier boundary lines of these small states; alongside them, between them, and partly right in the midst of the Protestant regions, the Breisgau—that old possession of Austria—Hohenzollern, many former possessions of ecclesiastical lords, and a portion of the former imperial cities are likewise Catholic.
A similar demarcation is evident in the various old territories of the Franconian Circle.

This juxtaposition, intermingling, and interpenetration of landscapes of different confessions clearly shows what history also teaches: that neither in the South nor in the North was the spirit of the people effective in the separation of confessions; that rather, lands and small lands whose population is of the same stock are divided into different confessions merely according to former political boundaries; and that only dynastic power imposed the various religious forms in the times of the struggle over the latter—above all, Catholicism upon the South. For had the House of Habsburg not counteracted Protestantism under the direction of the Jesuits and with the help of the Wittelsbachs, and violently eradicated it in Bohemia and in Austria proper, where it had already gained considerable ground, Protestantism would be as widespread in the South as in the North.

The diversity of confessions in Germany
is therefore a consequence of dynastic separation, not a result of different national characters.
But, it will be said, the religious division is now indeed present and stands in the way of unification as an obstacle.

To be sure, if the discords are deliberately created and cunningly nourished, if they are busily stirred up and fanned into flame, as has already been attempted in this kingdom even under the late lamented King.

It is certainly true that uniformity of religion is more conducive to the tranquility of a state; but that different religious parties, if only they are not artificially stirred up, can coexist within one and the same state, and how much more so within a federal state, is taught by the example of our own country and of Bavaria and other German states, which, amid the shifting of territorial distributions, have grown together out of several territories that had formerly been dynastically and religiously separate.

Finally, as regards the diversity of material advantages, this speaks rather for than against unity; for the greater and more intimate union of kindred peoples, especially in relation to foreign lands, is precisely what makes possible mutual complementation, the easier satisfaction of one people's needs by the products of another, and the sale of what one has in abundance and the other needs. The merchant comes to the aid of the farmer, and the coastal dweller and seafarer come to the aid of the inland people.

Individual imbalances and hardships in the various branches of economic activity are temporary and even out in time, and indeed more easily within a larger and closer association; most of the German states have themselves felt the benefit of such a union, in that they have joined the customs union founded by Prussia.

Away, then, with those glossings-over of self-interest and private cravings which have more than once plunged the whole fatherland into ruin, made Germany's soil the battlefield of the European peoples, and even made Germans allies of foreigners against Germans.
What can be placed in the balance against the advantages of unity?
Is it, perhaps, that in the case of that separation, a person unjustly persecuted in one state finds protection and refuge in another?

We hope rather that such persecutions, which formerly occurred especially against
scholars, will have reached their end with constitutional freedom.

But how often has one heard it said that Germany, like Hellas, owes the manifold flowering of the sciences and arts to its fragmentation; that through closer unity, as in France, everything significant would be drawn together and absorbed into a single center, and that the fairest glory of the fatherland would thereby be diminished!

That this fear is unfounded, the Prussian state shows: it too is already a great unity of many, and yet not everything significant has been swallowed up by the capital; rather, there are not a few points of light within it, and under a mild and sensible government there always will be.
And the particularities are surely not to be obliterated but rather to be unified; even noble attachment to hereditary ruling families is not incompatible with this unification.

Moreover, a great capital city, in which many resources are concentrated together, is a center of gravity of power whose importance was recognized, even in antiquity—despite all its predilection for isolation—with a correct political eye.

If people have so often and emphatically stressed that beneficial quality of manifold separation, then I leave it to reflection whether, in amiable self-deception and for consolation, people have not still sought to discover something good in the evil.
And truly, it would be worse than bad if a great evil did not after all enclose within itself some atoms of good!
Highly esteemed assembly: without unity, no power!

When our city and our country were abandoned to the Hydra of discord, we trembled for the throne: the return of concord has restored to the realm its old, and—so far as human works can defy time, to which even great Rome succumbed—its indestructible vitality, and has led its armies to victory as far as the outermost marches of Germania.
If the King, if the country has made heavy sacrifices, then we share the glory that in antiquity glorious Athens strove for and won.

Even against him, native particularism raised the charge that he was squandering his strength in order to bring help to the Hellenes, who themselves did little or nothing; but the great-hearted Demosthenes, the true friend of his country, recognizes Athens' greatness precisely
in this: that for honor and glory, for the first prize of virtue, for the common advantage of the Hellenes, it had expended more money and manpower than the others had for themselves; that it did not let this grieve it, did not believe itself to be at a disadvantage if it furnished twice as many ships as all the others together, but rather gave thanks to the gods for this, that in the common danger of the Hellenes it was able to accomplish more than the others.

This disposition had made the state the foremost of the Hellenic states: it was the high point of Hellenic life when, under the de facto sole rule of a Pericles, Athens commanded the greater part of the Hellenic financial power and military power.

But the arrogance in prosperity, the lack of moderation even of the most civilized national community toward its kindred allies, especially after the defeat of brothers who had fallen away, aroused hatred and prepared the fall of the strongest pillar of Hellenism.

The duality in Hellas, embodied in Sparta and Athens as in aristocracy and democracy, consumed the noblest powers: when, finally, through the claims of a Boeotianism that had fallen behind in the cultivation of mind and feeling, a three-headed rule had arisen, Hellas succumbed to the Macedonians, and later, amid similar dissensions, to the Romans.
May the lessons of history finally, for once, not go unheard!
The "natural law of mass attraction" also assigns leadership, in the life of human beings among kindred peoples, to the ruler of the state who predominates in armed might and intellectual power.

May Frederick William IV, the nobly minded, benevolent, richly endowed in spirit and heart, our dearest King, now that he has pacified his own land and the lands of his allies, also succeed in the sublime mission of permanently establishing Germany's unity along the path now marked out for him; may the House of Hohenzollern reconcile, winning their hearts, the German South, from which it springs, and the North, where through bravery, wisdom, justice, and mildness it has acquired its power, and with equal glory and a happier fortune than the gifted House of its old castle neighbors, the Hohenstaufen, spread the splendor of the Prussian and likewise of the Germanic name!

But if this is
not possible, if self-interest and presumption or any influence whatsoever thwarts the successes of our efforts and postpones the fulfillment of German hopes to an indefinite future; then may at least this land continue to flourish under this royal house, and even in a less favorable position remain forever Germany's protection and shield against all internal and external enemies!
God bless the King and his House!
Böckh, Speeches 11.

div.head: IV. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1850.
Ueber die Umbildung der Deutschen Universitäten

p.s: Among the manifold reflections that present themselves to anyone who gives some attention to the life of mortals, highly esteemed listeners, one of the oldest and most significant is this: that no great happiness tends to endure for long; that the higher an individual is placed, the harder the blows of fate to which he is subject and the more keenly felt the attacks to which he is exposed; that the destinies of men, like the currents of the air, turn about in unforeseen and rapid change, and in manifold oscillations move by leaps from the pleasant to calamity, from evil to good.

It is precisely to these fluctuations—indeed, in certain periods of development, to an almost rhythmically regulated ebb and flow—that the great communities of human beings, the states, are also subject; and the faster the pace of our times, the more surely does the truth of this age-old view of life prove itself in them.

Thus on the day that is devoted to the joyful birthday celebration of the most gracious King, two years ago we had sorrowfully to lament that, amid the fateful upheavals of most of the kingdoms of the European continent, almost all reverence for the princes of the peoples and their houses had died out, and also the reverence of no insignificant portion of our people for the royal house by which Prussia's glory and splendor and power had been founded and continually increased; the vigorous and fortunate overcoming of the most perilous internal conditions soon afterward cast rays of hope down upon this land, and today a year ago I could joyfully acknowledge and proclaim that that attachment to the King and his house, on which internal concord rests and which in the earlier governing years of Frederick William IV and his nearest forebears had been the fairest bond between throne
and people, had again powerfully awakened and the happiness of the noble ruler had been restored.

I do not wish to say that in the course of the present year this recovered good has suffered diminishment; but the sacrilegious and abominable attack upon the sacred person of the hereditary father of his country—although it was calculated to win the hearts of all good men, indeed even of those who had not been attached to him and held fast to him with their whole and fullest soul, all the more surely to the sorely threatened and aggrieved King, and to bind them to him all the more intimately—this infamous assault, I say, points once again to the inconstancy and mutability of human fortune, and to the highest dangers that are bound up with the highest station; dangers which, from a less pure conception of antiquity, are derived from the envy of the gods, whose lightning strikes the lofty trees and the palaces, whereas we, according to the worthier estimation of Christian doctrine, recognize in them trials of Providence, from which the man hard struck emerges, like the noble metal from the fire, more purified and brighter, when God's gracious hand has shielded the sufferer from the utmost extremity, as it repeatedly shielded the most beloved King.

Thanks and praise to the Giver of all good things, to the Ruler of all destinies, for the protection which he allowed to be bestowed upon him; fervent prayer and supplication to the Most High, that he may avert further perils from the beloved head, and also stifle the seeds of every evil and disaster-laden impulse in criminally demoralized or confused minds!
May Providence also not withdraw its help from the German and Prussian fatherland, and may it lead the same, along the inscrutable paths that it has marked out for the nations, to a fruitful goal!
For his deeds and sufferings too, especially in the last years, give us a sad example of vicissitudes and fluctuations which followed one upon another, each destroying the other.

Frederick William IV was the first prince to grasp the great idea of putting in place of the Federal Diet—as despised as it was detested—a more effective union of the German tribes and states, such as the dignity of the German people, the consciousness of its inner unity, and the need and the urgency of
the times demanded.

When he first declared to Prussia his resolve to place himself at the head of this undertaking, without wishing to impair the position of any of the other co-princes, he and Prussia were spurned and thrust back; before long, the very assembly that had turned away from him toward another side offered him the imperial crown.
Magnanimously, one offered to him by the people.

Scorning the power and dignity with which the greater among the German princes were not in agreement, he drew up the plan of a new confederation, and soon found himself rewarded, in return for his magnanimity, with fresh resistance, indeed even with defection on the part of those very men whose rescuer he had been: yet there remained to the German people one last ray of hope, a hope that also inspired me when last year, at this same celebration and on this very spot, I spoke of German unity and gave expression to the ardent wish that the much-beloved king, so rich in spirit and in heart, might yet succeed in the sublime mission of establishing Germany's unity on a lasting foundation.

But again and again such great difficulties and obstacles have been placed in the way of this noble work that, at the time of Germany's deepest humiliation, to many it seemed that all our hopes had been carried to the grave with shame and sorrow.

But let us not yet despair that a new turn of events—and this one from bad to good—will raise the fatherland again. Only let me be forgiven—I who otherwise gladly seize upon this day the most important phenomena of the present in order, in connection with them, to set the spirit and mind of the celebrated king in the light—only let me be forgiven if I now withdraw from these distasteful confusions and instead choose a subject of contemplation which, while it directly touches our academic body, is at the same time not without all relation to the circumstances of the times and to the common German fatherland, and is certainly fully suited to be discussed on the birthday celebration of Frederick William IV.

Frederick William is the most magnanimous and most generous protector of the sciences, whose foremost representatives in Germany are rightly held to be the universities; these are a common good of the common fatherland, and precisely for that reason they have
been drawn into its movement, and in the attempted transformation of all the conditions of the German states, a remolding or improvement of the universities has also been intended and held out in prospect.

Permit me, therefore, highly esteemed listeners, to dwell upon this subject, without claiming to offer more than a few fleeting remarks, since the time allotted to me does not allow a full and detailed discussion even of the most important points.

Just as every organic growth is already prefigured in the germ and contained there together with its full destiny, so too is the origin of human institutions and establishments of great importance for their history; and if one wished to say that what matters in this regard is not so much their first beginning as their highest perfection, not the unemancipated age of childhood but the maturity of manhood, I reply that in a development that follows nature and is independent, undisturbed by external circumstances, the later cannot stand in contradiction to the earlier, although changed conditions, situations, and surroundings may over the course of time divert an institution somewhat from its original form, just as a plant develops differently, or even perhaps stunted, in another climate and another soil.

Already in the Hellenic age, in certain cities distinguished for learning and science—such as Athens, Rhodes, Apollonia in Epirus, Alexandria, and Tarsus in Cilicia, where the natives themselves were especially devoted to study—many teachers of various schools, particularly philosophers and rhetoricians, had come together; although these were not bound into an academic body by any common bond, and even before states or princes had assigned them salaries, there nevertheless appears in this assembly of teachers a resemblance to the universities of a later time, even though the latter had not consciously taken those as their model: and as the fundamental character of these universities there emerges outward and inward freedom, that is, the freedom of the teachers with respect to the arrangements to be made for their instruction, and the freedom of teaching itself, which in Hellas underwent restrictions only
rarely and briefly, and in Rome too was only unsuccessfully contested in the time of the free state, when in old-fashioned simplicity people still believed they could put a dam against the spread of Hellenic culture, and later suffered a hard blow only from tyrannical emperors, as from Domitian through the complete expulsion of the philosophers from Italy, for some years.
The same is true of the emergence of the universities in the Middle Ages.

The eminent scholars who in the twelfth century taught the sciences, and even theology itself, in various cities were independent men, bound by no spiritual vow; unless they had voluntarily bound themselves to the city by an oath, they left the place where they had appeared as teachers whenever they pleased, and were followed by their students.

Teachers and students themselves drew up the constitution and laws by which the university community was ordered, and they elected their superiors entirely freely, both without any action on the part of the municipal authorities and without being hindered in this by them.

The universities were therefore in fact recognized academic bodies, and indeed long before charters of foundation or privileges were conferred upon them; such conferral was at first mostly only a confirmation of the rights previously acquired and possessed by custom and tacitly, and therefore usually took place only when these rights—as notably that of independent jurisdiction—had been violated or contested.
For the validity of a university, a document issued by a state authority did not at all seem to be required.

"Because the origin of the university of Padua," says Meiners, founding on good sources, "and its constitution and privileges went back beyond all history, several of the oldest jurists already raised the question whether a university which, like the University of Padua, had been founded or confirmed by no pope or emperor, and which therefore could also produce no letters of foundation or confirmation, was to be regarded as a true privileged university; and the jurists answered this question in the affirmative, because custom is just as much a source of valid privileges as the grace and letters of grace of princes, and because some universities arose solely
through the privileges of princes, others merely through themselves or through long-standing custom, and still others through custom as well as through the privileges of princes." All of this concerns only external freedom: for the content of the teaching itself there was, to be sure, no proper supervision by superiors; accusations of heresy on the part of ecclesiastical authorities were, by contrast, admittedly very frequent, and the form of teaching was indeed not a very free one, since one mostly dictated: only toward the time of the Church Reformation and after the invention of the art of printing did free lectures become more common, and the studies of ancient literature spread in Germany chiefly through Reuchlin and his followers worked powerfully to awaken a freer spirit, a more unprejudiced inquiry, and a more cultivated taste; yet this young and more vigorous life was exposed to the persecutions of an opposing party and especially of the Cologne theologians, who sought to uphold the old truths, as they called them, and to exterminate the new errors.

However manifold the restrictions and supervision to which the universities may have been subjected in later times and down to our own day, that spirit of freedom has nevertheless remained the inextinguishable vital principle of them, and especially of the Protestant universities.

That this was bound up with certain excesses, of which the Middle Ages were still less free of a lack, cannot be denied; and since what individuals incurred as guilt was laid to the charge of the whole, or even guiltless conduct was stamped as guilt, the universities were affected by the harsh measures of the German Confederation which I have already deplored earlier at this place, and which, in particular, Frederick William IV's mildness and high esteem for the sciences had already, many years before the dissolution of the Federal Diet, brought back to a more correct and lesser measure.

The spirit of freedom native to the universities, combined with the earlier pressure, necessarily produced a reaction, and it is therefore not to be wondered at if they too were seized by the movements of the year 1848; but we may say it to their credit that precisely those universities which until then had enjoyed a greater freedom—that especially the Prussian universities, apart from
the offenses of individuals and as academic bodies, preserved full loyalty to the lawful power and the lawful gracious King, paid homage to the principles of preservation in the face of a wild violence that was overthrowing everything, and precisely thereby also themselves experienced that change in human affairs, in that they, but a short time before praised as champions of free sentiment, were now attacked and reviled as rotten remnants of medieval learned guilds.

Nevertheless, that general movement also gave them the incentive and the impulse toward real or supposed improvements: just as deliberative associations formed in all estates and classes of the people, so assemblies were held partly by the students and partly by the teachers of all the German universities, because all German universities are imbued with the consciousness of belonging to the whole fatherland; but at the same time special deliberative assemblies formed at individual universities, partly on one and the same university opposing ones of the younger and the older teachers.

With good forethought the highest state authority took this matter in hand early, and at its request legally constituted assemblies at every Prussian university deliberated on timely changes to their constitution, until the Royal Minister—whom we now see, with joy and grateful recognition of his friendly, benevolent, and wise leadership, at the head of this branch of administration—summoned elected delegates from all Prussian universities here for joint deliberation on these matters.

One could reproach the university here and the other Prussian universities for not having taken part in the general assembly of delegates of the German universities: but far from these refusals having had their ground in the pernicious craving for separation from the unity of the Germanic people, or from our not having recognized that the bearers of German learning must above all also be the bearers of German unity and that all German universities must feel themselves to be one great whole; so it would have been an inner contradiction and sheer superfluity if the Prussian universities had reported almost simultaneously
to their own government and had wished to cooperate in common resolutions of delegates of all German universities, and indeed at a time when the general confusion of Germany and the dissensions between the individual states gave reason to expect not the slightest success of such advisory resolutions and motions to be adopted for the whole fatherland.
Science had been declared free.
Almost all attempts and proposals for improving the university system attach themselves to this idea.
That freedom is, as already said, partly an inner freedom and partly an outer one.

By the inner freedom we understand the freedom of teaching, which consists in this: that what is presented in writing or orally receives its determination only from the scholarly man on scholarly grounds, not through some foreign precept or law lying outside scholarship, whereby constraint is done to the conviction of the teacher.

Who would first demand yet another proof that this freedom is necessary if any progress in knowledge is to take place, and who will not admit that doctrines which are not freely produced and inwardly grounded but externally prescribed have the nature of articles of faith rather than of scientific propositions?

Indeed, one may demand the independence of science from state and church just as fully as one demands the independence of the church from the state, although, frankly, with all the freedom I claim for science, I nevertheless do not consider its separation from the body of the state to be right; but to set aside this latter point for now, with respect both to science and to the church, the demand that science and teaching should be free is as simple as it is well supported; its application and execution, however, in relation to the state and the church, is subject to almost insurmountable difficulties, which in every age have in part manifested themselves in the most bizarre and the most horrifying manner, in that state or church authorities declared teachings to be sacrilegious or godless and threatened or punished them with the severest penalties—teachings which, in the further progress
of human and scholarly culture, came to be universally recognized not only as perfectly harmless and innocent but also as uniquely true: whereas, to be sure, it cannot be denied that truly pernicious teachings, undermining the foundations of morality and of civil society, can also emerge, regarding whose toleration—especially in the bosom of an academic body established or sanctioned by the state—at least great doubt may prevail.

Many branches of knowledge are, to be sure, entirely above suspicion: no one will expect a danger to Church or State from grammar or zoology or botany, from anatomy or chemistry or pure mathematics; but who would believe it, if it were not a matter of established fact, that statesmen of the Roman Republic already feared Greek rhetoric? Who does not know that the Church sought to set arbitrary limits to the teachings of astronomy, that the study of classical antiquity was viewed with suspicion on political and religious grounds, that political science, the writing of history, and philosophy have frequently come into collision with the power of the State and the Church?

And indeed, it cannot be a matter of indifference to the monarchy if republican principles are spread by the teachers of science, nor to the republic if monarchical principles are: a democratic state power will have to regard aristocratic teachings as dangerous, and an aristocratic state power democratic teachings; and every political community will regard those as its enemies whose theories put some other association in the place of the state, as a higher and supposedly more moral one.
Can one, further, from the Church's own standpoint, blame it if it takes no pleasure in teachings by which its dogmas are made to totter?
But again, should nothing be taught except what is agreeable to the ruling power? Should truth be different in every state and in every church community, and predetermined for all eternity?

In these few sentences, which can easily be extended and multiplied, the difficulties and contradictions lie plainly exposed into which the principle of free science—in itself a splendid one—is entangled; and in this respect too it should prove true which Tacitus
puts into Galba's mouth: that men not wholly enslaved can endure neither complete freedom nor complete servitude.

Should those difficulties be resolved by allowing every doctrine, however displeasing it may be to the ruling power, to go unmolested so long as it does not pass into deeds or call for or incite to deeds, on the well-known assumption that falsehood will collapse of itself and will at all times be overcome by invincible truth? Or should pernicious doctrines be subject to judicial and disciplinary punishment?

If the freedom of science—which, to be sure, cannot include an unconditional immunity from punishment—is to be compatible with such punishment, then liberal-minded state laws and legal customs, and judges of lofty spirit, deep insight into the innermost essence of science, and an unprejudiced, clear vision must be presupposed, if similar judgments are not to be pronounced as were pronounced against Socrates, Johannes Hus, Giordano Bruno, Galileo, and countless others—judgments that are not indeed bloody and cruel (which our advanced civilization no longer tolerates), but are nonetheless equally wrong and reprehensible in spirit.

Suppose one were to say that, in order that science may move wholly freely within itself, it should refrain from any contact with everything with which it might collide with the state or the church, just as Plato—who was the first to recognize, and to delineate with vigorous strokes, the conflict between the statecraft dominant in his day and philosophy—advises the philosopher not to concern himself with state administration at all; then it must be replied, on the contrary, that such an exercise of scientific freedom is rather a submission to servitude: science thereby renounces the treatment of the most important tasks of practical reason, a renunciation from which Plato himself was so far removed that he rather, in theory, openly set himself against the political views realized in his time; furthermore, science then exposes itself to the reproach so often heard, that it is dead and alienated from everything that moves the spirit of the people and of the age; finally, the universities in particular have been assigned, besides general education
in science, the special vocation of making their hearers fit to enter the various branches of the higher state and church service, and consequently cannot dispense with the scientific consideration of things political and ecclesiastical—of the latter at least not so long as positive religion also, as happens in Protestantism, is recognized as an object of science.

I now turn to external freedom, which consists in this: that the scholarly institutions, and especially therefore the universities, be established by their constitution as free communities as far as possible and be endowed with such powers that, subject to a supreme oversight by the superior state authority and to accountability toward it, they govern themselves—something that was intended especially in the year 1848, partly from above and partly within the bosom of the universities: the aim was to make the highest university authorities more independent of the state authority, to give the totality of teachers, in contrast to the privileged classes among them, a greater influence on administration according to the democratic principle of equal rights (isonomia and isegoria) and for the enhancement of the communal spirit, and to abolish—or at least make less perceptible—the distinctions among the various kinds of teachers, namely the ordinary and extraordinary professors and the Privatdozenten; and it could not fail that the students too would demand more freedom in relation to the teachers and even a participation in university affairs.

Although it can never have been misjudged that the power of the government over the universities must be upheld, and that the complete liberation of the latter would tend rather to their ruin than to their advantage, yet self-administration was nevertheless held to be appropriate and beneficial for the universities, and in particular most people expected a substantial improvement from the removal of that intermediate authority of the curators, placed between the superior minister and the universities, which, being in any case already a telling expression of the universities' lack of independence and immaturity, appeared all the more burdensome once, as extraordinary government commissioners, they had pressed upon
the universities with the full weight of the powers allotted to them under the federal resolutions, even if in some places, and notably at the university here, those federal laws had never attained full validity and had been substantially mitigated through the grace of our exalted king.

If we go back into the earlier history of the universities, we find among the authorities similar to the curators, first papal or princely conservators; but their appointment did not have the purpose of restricting the universities, which were rather governed by their rectors, invested with great prestige, and by the heads of the nations and of the faculties, but rather of coming to the aid of the weakness and helplessness of the universities, of protecting them against the powerful in their privileges and liberties, and of calling the violators of the same to account and punishing them; thus in the fourteenth century the provost of Paris, as conservator of the university, by royal ordinance, and likewise the papal conservator, had to swear that they would steadfastly defend the privileges of the University of Paris.
The old German universities had, as is believed, all from the beginning such or similar conservators of their rights.

Meanwhile, people did not stop at appointing protectors; it soon became apparent that the members of the universities did not always observe their laws, and that they had to be compelled to observe them, for which purpose visitators, chancellors, superintendents, directors, and the like were introduced. To what degree the authority of such visitators sometimes exceeded that of our government commissioners is shown by the example of the royal visitators of the University of Oxford from the year 1549, who had unlimited power to change, remove, or otherwise punish the university authorities, teachers, officials, members, and other affiliates of the university, to abolish and renew the colleges and other foundations and institutions, and to change the statutes.

The Archdukes of Austria were indeed obliged to uphold the privileges and statutes of their university in Vienna; but since they had not renounced their supreme authority over it, they very soon appointed, for the preservation of the laws, a so-called
superintendent of the prince, who held the third rank, namely after the Rector and Chancellor.
Later the university itself appointed one, and afterward two, guardians of the laws under the name of superintendents of the university.
Since the fifteenth century, the preservation of the laws was entrusted to chancellors, without this dignity having been introduced at all universities in the period that followed.

Meiners, who has carried out the most detailed investigations into the history of the academic chancellorship, describes it as something entirely new that the Emperor Leopold, at the founding of the University of Halle, left it to the Elector Frederick to decide whether he would reserve the dignity of a rector and chancellor for himself and his descendants, or whether he would transfer the power to appoint rectors and chancellors to the university, and indeed not only to the teachers but also to the students; the Emperor Charles VI granted the same to the founder of the University of Göttingen, and Charles VII to the Margrave Frederick at the founding of the University of Erlangen.

Undoubtedly every university would regard it as a piece of good fortune to have a curator in the sense of the original conservators; and in fact the most distinguished curators of German universities, whose memory will never fade, have been such guardians and protectors—a Münchhausen for Göttingen, a Fürstenberg for Münster, a Reizenstein for Heidelberg—full of love and enthusiasm for learning and for the institutions entrusted to them, yet also, by virtue of their high position as ministers, eminently suited to this protection, as formerly also several Prussian ministers who presided over universities in the same capacity; but whether subordinate curators afford universities the same advantages, and greater ones than the direct supervision of a liberal-minded and benevolent minister of education, and whether the safeguarding of the laws together with the administration of property is not just as well attainable through a well-ordered organism of university authorities and officials as through superiors who do not belong to the university—this I leave, although it has long since been decided in favor of the freer and at the same time more honorable position of the universities, at this point, with deliberate intent, to higher consideration.

Depending on the differing constitutions of the
individual universities, already until now more or fewer teachers have taken part in the direction or administration of the same; in the most recent efforts at improvement, as has already been remarked, work was done from various sides toward giving all teachers a certain influence on general affairs, and out of the deliberations of the conference of delegates held here the proposal has emerged that a narrower committee, which is usually called the senate, should be established uniformly at all Prussian universities, and alongside it a general council, in which all ordinary professors and also an elected number of the extraordinary ones would have seat and vote.

The few older members of this university who still remain from its first years will recall that here originally all the regular teachers formed the senate, but that this arrangement soon proved impractical and was abolished for that very reason; whereas, as we hope, the coexistence of a narrower and a broader assembly with different powers may well prove sound.

The participation of the extraordinary professors in these assemblies is, to be sure, contrary to strict conceptions in general, however varied the position of ordinary and extraordinary teachers may also have been at the oldest universities, especially at the Italian ones, where the latter, at least in some respects, by no means lagged behind the former; for the essential nature of extraordinary professors has been determined precisely to the effect that, as younger teachers, or as those for whom teaching at the university is only a secondary occupation alongside another principal office, they were not to be drawn into the representation of the university. But it has been asserted with full grounds, especially given the greatly increased number of extraordinary teachers at some universities and the impossibility arising therefrom of doing justice to their merits by early advancement into ordinary positions, that "circumstances had gradually so transformed themselves that the extraordinary professors could also make claims in this respect, so as not to stand too far behind the ordinary ones, particularly in
relation to the appointment of academic offices and these offices themselves"; and it has therefore seemed expedient, yielding to their natural desire, to grant them a proportionate share in the representation of the universities.

If the same thing had not been resolved for the Privatdozenten, the guiding idea in that case was that they are entirely freely connected with the university, that their activity depends wholly on their own will, and that they are not even under an obligation but merely have the right to teach, the exercise of which is left to their own discretion: moreover, their great importance for the universities, which owe their very origin to them and have in them the surest and most flourishing source of future teachers, has not been misjudged, and the removal of some unjustified or unreasonable restrictions on their teaching activity has been proposed.
As for the students, resolutions were indeed adopted and motions put forward by them at the Wartburg, the immoderateness of which soon became clear even to a large portion of them.

The students of the university here, far from demanding greater rights, have for the most part limited themselves to being willing to renounce their privileged jurisdiction; and the conference could not find itself moved to answer in the affirmative the question laid before it, namely whether the students should take part in the elections to academic offices, especially in the election of the rector, because no student, given the transience of his stay at a particular university and the absence of all accountability, could have a right to influence the administration.

If in the Middle Ages the students enjoyed far greater rights, then we, without wishing to offend our noble youth, must recall that at that time the students were for the most part mature men, even canons and officials of wealthy foundations.
Highly esteemed assembly!

From the rich material that the subject I have discussed offers, I have selected a few points, to the discussion of which I was led by the improvements in the university system intended in recent years: as I said, these attempts all proceeded from the striving for greater freedom, which had received its
impetus from the political movements of the time.

Just as at first the measure of political freedom was overstepped, so too were the plans of the reformers of the educational system, and especially of the universities, at first in part extravagant; but in time, with recovered composure, they found the right middle course. And there is just as little reason to fear that changes now will lead to destruction as that the movement which arose on the ground of the educational system will vanish without a trace.

Much else besides, concerning the greater freedom of the universities, has been brought up for discussion, namely the powers to be assigned to the various university authorities in their relation both to one another and to the superior supervisory authority: this and similar matters I pass over, because it seems to me inappropriate, in this place, to descend so far into particular details, even though some of them are not unimportant.

Furthermore, various abuses have been censured and their removal recommended, and various customs have been subjected to scrutiny which no longer are, or no longer appear to be, appropriate to the present stage of development of scholarship: it will suffice if, among the former, I mention the frivolous conferring of academic degrees, and among the latter the use of the Latin language, especially at public ceremonies—a use which, however, without prejudice to German national character, we by no means wish to see entirely abolished for very weighty reasons, but only restricted to strictly scholarly acts.

We may hope that, under the auspices and the sanction of the King and with the cooperation of the people's representatives, out of the manifold expert opinions on the most important questions relating to the university system there will emerge a wise and liberal education law and improvements of the statutes founded thereon; changes which would be brought about not only by a gentler path than those of the visitors at Oxford, but would even have arisen in a manner, if not equally free, yet similar, to the laws of the oldest universities, and in quite the same manner as the statutes of the university here and of its faculties hitherto in force, whose drafting proceeded from the midst of this academic body itself and was subjected by the state authority only
to a scrutinizing review.

May those improvements at the same time, through the larger community of teachers now in prospect, pave the way for an increase in the common spirit, which is the surest guarantee for the well-being of every association!

If the overthrow of all conditions, which a licentious and wild ochlocracy was capable of bringing about, would also have buried the sciences and the institutions established for their advancement in the whirlpool of destruction—since that kind of rule is even more averse to the nobler education, one not calculated merely for the common utility, than despotism itself, which at least gladly interweaves the blossoms of art and science into its victor's wreath—then, by contrast, on the path of a moderate and prudent reform we shall attain the advantages of liberty and of order at the same time, and thus most securely preserve the scientific spirit and a vigorous scientific life, which is presently all the more necessary since, on the one hand, serious studies and mature insight, apart from rare exceptions, along with the cultivation of the sense of true liberty, also curb the political passions with which the age is sick, and since, on the other hand, in this gloomy condition of our common fatherland, German scholarship must, as it often has, so also now once again assume the role of representing, by way of substitute, within itself the Germanic unity which could not be realized politically.
It is precisely on the restoration of order that the secure continuance of our universities depends, and thus on the establishment of the lawful power of the beloved King.
May we, the teachers, and may you, our dear listeners, never forget this, and, conscious of it, both in our own place now and in the future work in this spirit of order and moderation!

Finally, let us all who are gathered here unite once more in prayer to the almighty and all-good Father, that He may cover the King and the Royal House with His shield and buckler, and fill him and the counselors of the Crown wholly with wisdom and vigor in the governance of the state, and may unshakably confirm the loyalty of the people and the concord of the rulers and the ruled.
Hail to the King and to his House!

div.head: V. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1852.
Die Vorsehung, nicht der Zufall, regiert die Welt

p.s: On the annual celebration of the birth of a distinguished ruler, such as we commemorate today, highly esteemed listeners, there presses in upon the one appointed to speak a flood of the most varied feelings and thoughts, both cheering and grave, which exposes him to the danger of being swept away by it and of perishing in a chaotic mass of emotions or reflections, unless he knows how to ward off from himself the greater part of the surging material and, as it were, to cast anchor at a freely chosen point of view.

Before his gaze stands the whole life of the prince who is celebrated and to be celebrated, his distinctive nature, his successes and fortunes, and especially the last years of his reign, which whoever appears repeatedly as orator at this celebration will be moved first of all to fix his eyes upon; and if the ruler counts a long line of ancestors on the throne to which he is called by birth and hereditary right, then the observer will also be directed to the dynasty, to the earlier greatness and majesty of the house.

Moreover, if the ruling house is not estranged from the people, if it acts with them, through them, for them, how could one then forget the fatherland when one speaks of the father of the fatherland? How, at such a celebration, should there not also hover before our soul the life and essential character of the people and the state, its happiness and misfortune, its fortunes changing together with the fortunes of the princes—indeed, its whole position and destiny in the organization of peoples and tribes and in the great chain of the development of the human race?

Thus there opens before us an infinite field of contemplation for a time sparingly allotted, and indeed a contemplation that, especially in turbulent times and in an unclear or not on all sides consolidated state of
affairs, requires the most exact knowledge of the world's conditions, the highest maturity and prudence of judgment, and can worthily be undertaken only by one who, not absorbed in individual smaller branches of knowledge, has directed his whole attention to the course of world events in past and present.

If, although I am conscious that I cannot meet this demand, I nevertheless even now, with worn-out or exhausted strength, submit to the honorable commission to appear before you as orator on this day, then I venture to do so only on the assumption that it is permitted, as I have said, to adopt a freely chosen point of view which allows much to be left aside that would here find its proper place, and that we, removed from all the questions of the day and of the year and unconcerned whether we fall under the reproach and censure of a school wisdom that issues in generalities, may string together a few thoughts which, separated out from the mass of all the others that offer themselves to the thinking mind on such a solemn day, may join and shape themselves into the unity of a single contemplation.

For states in which the ruler is determined by hereditary succession, however much the constitution may extend or limit his rights, the birth of the heir to the throne is of decisive importance: for the whole life of the state in its entire development is more or less bound to the person of the ruler, who indeed can even break through the restrictions imposed upon him in order to make the state more independent of him; that life must run its course quite differently according as this or that personality ascends the throne, and the personality itself, even if it is more closely determined by upbringing and education, is nevertheless primarily and for the most part conditioned by natural and innate disposition.
This truth seems little comfort for the life of the state: for, according to this, the happiness and misfortune of the state seem to depend on the accident of birth.

This dependence on chance is heightened still further for our consideration when one gives oneself over to the notion—not inaccessible and supported by various experiences—that over the one and the other there presides, as it were, an innate favorable or unfavorable destiny, a lucky
star or an unlucky one; that for the one everything he undertakes succeeds, while for the other everything he attempts goes to ruin: for according as the ruler or his influential counselors have a good fortune or a demonic misfortune, under this notion the whole land and people would be drawn into the same.

Yet whoever followed such a view could not, for that matter, withdraw himself from another, more consoling view, one that was not devised in the school but flowed from the mouth of one of the greatest statesmen.

For if one wished to ascribe such a star or unlucky star to the individual human being, then one would have to presuppose the same also for states and peoples, even without having investigated whether there is anything true at the basis of this assumption: but the destiny of peoples is a higher one than that of the individual, and their fate, the mightier, will triumph over that of the individual.

Thus, when Aeschines warned the Athenians to beware of the demon, Fortune, that accompanied Demosthenes, since no state and no private individual had come off happily who had followed the counsel of Demosthenes, the latter replied to his opponent with roughly the following words: "I regard the fortune of the state as good, and I see that the Dodonaean Zeus and the Pythian Apollo prophesy this too, but the fortune of all mankind, which now prevails, I regard as heavy and hard; for who among the Greeks or who among the barbarians has not in the present time experienced many and great evils?"

That the state formed noble resolutions and came off better than most other Greeks, who believed that if they left us they would be happier — that I count to the good fortune of the state; but that we suffered a blow and not everything went as we wished — that I regard as the share falling to our state in the fate of all mankind.

But the opponent says that my own destiny is more effective than the common destiny of the state, the small and slight more effective than the good and great: how should this be possible?" But here a far more important question presses itself upon us: what, then, is this happiness or destiny?
Is it really chance, as we seem to say?

Does chance, then, direct the course of states and of all human events? "Fortune directs the life of men, not the wise counsel," says
an ancient poet; and the deeds and successes of the greatest men, and consequently also the greatness and significance of the states that have been raised up by them, have often been set down to the account of the accidental, or of fortune, which is synonymous with it—not to virtue and wisdom.

Yet people already inquired in antiquity whether the greatest man of that age, whether Alexander, the son of Philip, climbed to his height through fortune or through virtue; and to cite an example that lies very close to us, Frederick the Great calls the world the realm of chance. Like that messenger in Sophocles, he holds that chance raises up and chance destroys; and precisely in application to what we began from, he says: "A king dies, the son replaces him, and the political world takes on another shape; he lets himself be ruled by other passions, governs according to another plan; new errors drive out the old and change the motives of favor or hatred." Indeed he goes so far as to assert of himself that when he entered the world in his young years he owed everything to chance and nothing to reason; only under the protection of fortune had he learned, until fortune abandoned him.
But if both had from their father the, for them, accidental good fortune to possess a well-ordered army, this was only the means to their greatness, not its cause.

With good reason, in reference to Alexander, the spirited Plutarch poses the question: if a great statue cannot come into being without art merely because chance or fortune pours down and scatters gold and bronze and ivory and abundant and rich material, whether it is then possible that the great man, indeed the greatest of all who have lived, should have been perfected by fortune without virtue, in that fortune equipped him with weapons and horses and money and cities, which for one who does not know how to use them are a danger, not a power, and not an ornament but a reproach of weakness and smallness.

And the history of our own Frederick teaches that he was not raised up by fortune, whose withdrawal he himself laments; rather, misfortune pursued him to such a degree that the full greatness of his spirit was necessary to him if he was not to succumb to despair.

Furthermore, it is in itself contradictory that any being, whether man or state, should possess a determinate
happiness and that this should nevertheless be a contingent one: if it is determinate and original, then it is a necessary one, whether one describes this determination as a necessity of nature or as a gift of Providence.

If the great Frederick ascribes the empire of the world to chance, he by no means understood by the accidental anything arbitrary, which might just as well have been replaced by its opposite; for him chance is the consequence of secondary causes, which, wrapped in deep darkness, elude our insight: and when Demosthenes extols the good fortune of Athens, he is far from regarding it as accidental; on the contrary, though certainly not with philosophical dialectic, yet with sound understanding and the correct tact that is the organ of statesmanlike wisdom, he grasped and intimated the profound thought that a significant state has a peculiar destiny, which it is granted to it to attain in its historical development.

And herein lies the world-historical significance of a state: if it has no such purpose, it counts only as a satellite or vassal of another, which drags it along in its tow and uses it as a means to the attainment of its own end.
Or should even that which we recognize as the world-historical significance of a state, and the entire course of world history, likewise be merely accidental?

If one considers the unexpected inconstancy of fortunes, the unforeseen downfall of the greatest empires—empires that seemed founded on bedrock and to which one cannot deny a role in world history—then one might here too be inclined to plead the cause of chance.

Thus Demetrius of Phalerum said in his work on Tyche, foreknowing the future from the past: "If you take not, say, an infinite span of time nor yet many generations, but only these fifty years before us, you will recognize the harshness of Tyche: for do you think that fifty years ago the Persians, or the kings of the Persians, or the Macedonians, or the kings of the Macedonians, if one of the gods had foretold the future to them, would have believed that at this time not even the name of the Persians would remain, who ruled almost the whole inhabited earth, and that, by contrast, the Macedonians would hold power over the world, whose name
was formerly scarcely known?"

And yet the inconstant fortune that governs our life, which reshapes everything in opposition to our thinking and displays its power in unexpected things, shows all people that, in setting the Macedonians in the splendor of the Persians, it has only lent those goods to them as well, until it shall have formed another decree concerning them: a thought capable of awakening from their comfortable and confident dreams those who, I will not say on the eternal duration of a state, but even only on its continuance for a hundred or fifty years more, recklessly count with assurance.
Yet even this rapid turn of fortune must not convince us that human affairs are governed by chance.

However imperfect our insight into the course of world history may be—an insight whose comprehension a still young science, one that has scarcely come into possession of its first rudiments and that has been called the philosophy of history, sets itself as its task—we nonetheless have a presentiment of, and in part recognize, how nature, the realm of necessity, is subject to eternal and immutable laws; so too, then, is the spiritual realm of freedom, human history, not a realm of arbitrary will. What moved our race thousands of years ago, what was thought and created by it thousands of years ago, could not just as well have fallen into later ages, nor could the younger stage of development have become the earlier one, nor could the Oriental have been attained in the West and conversely: rather, in the great historical masses and epochs that we call peoples and ages, definite forms of development were stamped out and run through in a lawful sequence; in the facts there lies an ideal content of thought as the driving and formative cause, as the essence of the forms; history is the order of the rational spirit unfolded in the moral and cognitive life of humanity; the peoples or states of world history are the bearers of the various forms of this development.
Permit me, highly esteemed listeners, to offer a few remarks on this matter, which should lead me to the goal I have set before myself.

Whoever is capable of beholding the idea through the veil of appearances recognizes the opposition between the whole of
ancient life and the whole of modern life as the two highest and most universal forms of culture of the human race that have so far been unfolded.
