In antiquity, however, the earliest stage of culture appears as the Oriental or Asiatic stage, on which the spirit is still predominantly bound by a principle of nature, by virtue of which even the entire activity of individuals was unalterably determined by birth: from this bondage despotism too arose; there was no lack of art and sensibility, but rather of freedom, whereas the Western barbarians, who do not count for the development of the human spirit, were indeed free, or rather unbound, but lacked art and the formative sense.

With what peculiarities that first universal form of culture expressed itself in the various kingdoms or states—in the Assyrian and Chaldean empire, in rigid but, in its own obstinate fashion, highly cultivated Egypt, in the smaller Semitic states of the Phoenicians and Hebrews, which, like Phrygia and Lydia, admittedly already show a transition into another cultural sphere—I leave untouched here: the Medo-Persian empire, which is the summit of that development, ultimately swallowed them all, only, after attaining this world-purpose, to succumb to the Hellenic spirit.
I pass over the more distant lands of Asia, which, self-contained, exercised no significant influence on the West.

It was the Hellenic spirit that first strove upward out of that bondage toward individual consciousness and toward freedom, which it initially realized as political freedom: it succeeded in cultivating soul and body in noble harmony and beauty, in laying the foundation of the arts and sciences, especially of philosophy as the science of sciences, in perfecting these so far as its own peculiar character allowed and in accordance with that peculiar character—indeed, in part even unconditionally—in making the Hellenic people, for a long time and over almost the entire world then known, the normative people, and in leaving behind imperishable models for all ages to come as well.

Yet even in this culture the old spirit of nature has not yet lost its right; indeed, compared with the modern world, it has a one-sidedness and narrowness without which it could not even have been attained, and
even a lack of freedom that emerges on a mass scale, especially in the relation of slavery and in the great subordination of the weaker sex.

When the Hellenic world had fulfilled itself in its ideals, it too succumbed, as the Orient had earlier succumbed to it, to the practical spirit of the Romans; Italy became the center of a world dominion that cannot have been created by chance.

But this order too gave way to a new world order that was rooted in the old, because the ancient character itself, after the completion of its own essential nature, surpassing and overleaping itself and itself laboring at its own destruction, thrust forth the seeds of new forms of culture: thus that new order built itself upon the ruins of the old world, and while it buried in the rubble much that was noble and great, which was never again to come to appearance with equal power and clarity, it nevertheless found nourishment in the imperishable fruits of the older, dead time, which will still nourish our youth as well, so long as a barbarism, hardly to be feared, does not in foolish delusion contemptuously cast aside the treasures of antiquity, to be sufficient unto itself.

From small beginnings, among an enslaved and despised people that, after the destruction of its capital, was to fall prey to dispersion, there grew the world religion of Christianity, to which the Roman empires themselves became subservient, and later the Germanic peoples, who, softened by Christianity, were called to reshape world history, even though the Orient to this very day offers a resistance to the new principle that is hard to overcome.

Are we to regard the migration of peoples, the entire history of the Middle Ages, the Frankish monarchy of Charlemagne, the power and dominion of the papacy, the German Empire and the struggles of the two against each other, the new struggle between the West and the East, the formation of new kingdoms and states as the work or the play of blind chance?

Soon a new stirring and movement of the spirit was kindled in Europe—the restoration of the sciences, won from the remnants of antiquity, and in its train the Reformation, which sprang from the German spirit: together they cast down a ferment for many centuries, one that works on and on forever and
can be banished by no magic formula.

To some appeasement of the movements, a European system of states gradually took shape, into which the great Slavic empire in the East was also incorporated, and a so-called European balance of power, often disturbed by manifold fluctuations and preponderances, [took shape] to guarantee the continued existence of each and every one; and in the new continent discovered shortly before the Reformation, a new history is in the process of formation and promises a great future.

Only in the new system of states has the state to which we belong attained greater standing: its roots indeed reach back beyond the Reformation, but its growth was founded upon it, and it prepared the way for its entry into the states of world-historical significance.

Such an entrance is wont to be announced by a hero who knows how to seize the reins of destiny and who, with invincible courage and inflexible firmness, stakes his life for the idea: this hero was, for Prussia, Frederick, to whom the voice of the world has awarded the name of the Great.

But it requires continued adherence to lofty principles and resolutions if the splendor that radiates from the hero is not quickly to be extinguished again, just as Thebes, raised to hegemony by Pelopidas and Epaminondas, collapsed again with their deaths.

To be sure, even a state of enduring world-historical significance is subject to fluctuations and vicissitudes, indeed even to an internal decay that can bring it to the brink of ruin; yet these can also be a necessary remedy for it.

What the exiled Themistocles, endowed by the Persian king with the rich revenues of three cities, said to his own people — "O children, we would have been ruined if we had not been ruined" — proves to be a great truth in the case of states, as long as their vital force is not exhausted, which force lies in the strength of the people: for, having passed through the school of misfortune, they then raise themselves up again from humiliation, renewed like the phoenix from the ashes.
This realm too has stood this test.

But what the world-historical significance of any country may be can, to be sure, become more clearly apparent only when its destiny is fulfilled. Yet the hero who announced its entry into
the ranks, and the continued life in his spirit, already allow a faint glimpse of that destiny even during the development of the state; and thus the fairly general judgment of the discerning—and, as I believe, especially of the true friends of the state and of its royal house—has long since decided, as seems to me rightly, that it is Prussia's destiny to be, as through military power and a warlike spirit, so through the free power of the spirit, a shield and refuge of the German fatherland, whose world-historical position may be presupposed, and thus also of German intelligence—though we do not mean by this to say that this dwells among us alone, which would be mere foolish presumption.

May it not appear, highly esteemed listeners, as though with these fleeting and fragmentary hints I believed I had, as the saying goes, constructed the course of world history: I wished only to strike a few notes from the harmony of the history of humanity, into which, to be sure, many discords are also mixed that stand in need of resolution: however attentively the spiritual ear may listen to this work of art composed of the most manifold elements, we shall never fathom all the arrangements by which it has come into being and continues to come into being; but we may yet feel, from what has taken place, that neither chance nor fortune rules therein, but rather that a world plan runs through the destinies of nations, or, what is the same thing, that Providence is the guide of world history, and that nations and states serve it as instruments that accomplish its will, and above all the leaders of states, the princes.
Thus the disconsolate sentence that I mentioned at the beginning of this reflection is transformed into its comforting opposite.
This is not flattery, which is foreign to me; it is the truth of the matter, which forces itself upon feeling, and still more upon thought.
But, it will be said, is this conception really more consoling?

Have we been improved by the fact that we leap from one extreme to the other, putting Providence in the place of chance—a Providence which, even in milder expression, is nothing other than an unalterable fate?

Do not the actions of men thereby become entirely indifferent, since, however these may always be constituted, what has been decreed in
the council of Providence comes to pass?

What avail all our cares and efforts, if world history rolls on toward a predetermined goal according to the laws of a providential mechanics, and if, just as the origin and growth of the forms of culture and of states, so too their downfall is irrevocably fixed, and only one people and state may hand on the light of the spirit to another, while itself, after it has played out its role in the great drama, is to die away just as individuals die away one after another—all independently of their will and their ways of acting?
And are we also to accept the whole succession of human and political monsters, whether monarchical or ochlocratic, as gifts of Providence?

I have already suggested that I do not presume to be able to resolve the discords in the harmony of world history; if, however, belief in a providence which, while man thinks, guides the outcomes, without which, according to the word of Scripture, no hair falls from our head, appears fatalistic, then it is at least not a fatalism of irrational chance, but a fatalism of reason and of law, whether one conceives this with Leibniz as pre-established harmony or in whatever other form.
But it is altogether to be disputed that this view abolishes the freedom of human action and its accountability or imputability.

The highest necessity is at the same time the highest freedom—the necessity and freedom of reason and morality—and for their opposite, the being endowed with reason and consciousness is responsible before reason and morality.

If the world plan is a rational and moral one, then it cannot be realized through unreason and immorality, and therefore also not through unfreedom, but only through the free resolve of those who are the instruments of Providence — just as in the old tragedy, which conceals deep views of the world beneath its mask, fate does not compel the acting heroes to their deeds with magical powers, but the actors freely and of their own free deed go to meet their destiny. If, nevertheless, destructive powers bring heart-rending calamity upon humanity, then, until we have a better explanation, we may designate this as the retributive Nemesis for folly, arrogance,
and vice — a Nemesis who, by the traces impressed upon history, does indeed seem to walk among the nations, as even Tacitus recognized her at Rome.

Through reason and morality the nations lay the foundation of their happiness; through folly and vice, of their downfall. True statecraft consists in bringing about the happiness of nations through the rule of the former. "Art is wont to love happiness, and happiness art," said a quibbling poet, and not without justice.

But happiness does not consist in wealth and luxury, which is rather a diseased condition and the source of enervation and corruption; rather, prosperity and activity are its foundation, because idleness is the beginning of vice and poverty leads to wretchedness.
And above all, virtue is needful, as for the people so for those who rule—their wisdom, prudence, justice, and courage, which, acting freely, at the same time serve Providence.

The beginning of wisdom is a deep awe of the Divine—not, however, superstition, which dulls the mind; not deisidaimonia, which paralyzes the power to act; not fanaticism, which brings hatred and discord and persecution instead of divine peace.

Wisdom looks inward, so that the state does not lose its strength through internal disintegration and dissolution; outward, so that it does not forfeit its independence and self-determination. But the false statesman, the most dangerous of all sophists, seizes instead of wisdom the semblance, cunning, deception, and fraud, and works without foresight for momentary successes, even if, as they say, the Flood should break in after him.

Sober-mindedness raises the rulers of states above the passions of parties, moderates designs and resolutions through self-conquest, guards against arrogance and presumption, which plunge into ruin, and teaches gentleness, reconciliation, and forgiveness: from it springs the unity of mind between the rulers and the ruled, the surest guarantee of endurance in good and in bad times.

Furthermore, the fundamental condition of all rule is justice, whose realization the state itself is meant to be: its expression is the law; its opposite is arbitrariness and force, which press into the place of the law in the most diametrically opposed degenerations of the state, in ochlocracy as in despotism,
elevating the arbitrary decree or the plebiscite, as the so-called will of the people, above the law.

Indeed, as Aristotle says, the great man may be like a god among men, and there may be no law for such men, because they themselves are law; these men may indeed have to be measured by their own standard, not by our pygmy one: nevertheless, even these world-historical heroes will be able to rule only through justice and virtues, not through injustice and crimes.
In the end, what is all the excellence of mind and spirit without courage?

If servility among the governed, and the hypocrisy and flattery that spring from it, are the worst poison of states, then the high spirit of princes and peoples is the noblest spur to greatness: this inspires the worthiest resolutions and enables one to persevere in them; even when fortune veils itself, it defies dangers, does not shrink back before the horror of the moment, stakes goods and blood on true honor, while faint-heartedness and cowardly disposition surrender themselves to contempt and, out of fear of perishing, perish.
Highly esteemed assembly!

If I have taken the liberty of setting before you on this day, in all modesty, this view of the world such as I happen to hold, I know well that it will meet with no general assent, nor are those who share it with me likely to find this grounding of mine successful, since I am only repeating what is ordinary and often said.
But those who agree with me will also approve the conclusions for whose sake I have entered into these reflections, and which I now, without further circumlocution, summarize in brief words.

You will share with me the belief and the conviction that this land and realm have received a sublime and world-historical destiny, and that it was not chance that allotted this ruling house of the Hohenzollerns to this people, but that Providence assigned it to them, so that in the present and the future, through great virtues, it may fulfill the historical task which, in light of the deeds and fortunes of a great past, we recognize as the task of this land and realm.

You will join me in commemorating today's celebration as the celebration not of a chance occurrence, but of
a gift of Providence, which called the noble and magnanimous King to this throne.

They will hope and trust that under his rule the happiness of the state will be preserved and increased as a good, and that, as Demosthenes of Athens said, this will also be confirmed by the fact that this land, borne up by the wise and worthy resolutions of its ruler, comes to terms with the hard and heavy times at smaller sacrifices than others, who had believed they would be happier if they separated their advantage from ours.

May all parts of the people, in concord with the high-minded King and together with him, each in its own place, without self-interest and selfishness, go forward courageously and bravely on the path that our glorious forefathers have unambiguously marked out for us.
May God preserve and bless the King and his House!

div.head: VI. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1853.
Ueber die Wissenschaft, insbesondere ihr Verhältnifs zum Praktischen und Positiven

p.s: We are assembled here today, an association of men and youths, teachers and listeners, in order to give expression, among ourselves and before you, highly honored guests, who are attached to our affairs with benevolent sympathy, to a confession of reverence and love for the King our lord, of gratitude for the benefits which we, together with the whole country, have received from him as earlier from the princes his glorious forefathers, and of the joy with which we greet this day, on which the celebration of his entry into life returns.
Whatever the year that has just passed has each time brought out of the...

Whether the course of times and fortunes has brought us joy and sorrow, prosperity and benefit or cause for concern and the unwelcome, whatever hopes or fears it may have aroused: amid all the change of things, the irresistible revolution of events, one thing remains fixed and constant for us, like the heavenly pole within our inmost being—the feeling of homage for the father of the fatherland, proven in fortune and in sorrow.

Upon this immutable foundation we carry the thoughts that change with the years, because other circumstances and conditions produce other considerations—unless one would prefer precisely not to say what the immediate occasion has given cause to say.

To be sure, there are times when one may prefer this, so as not to be swept into the whirlpool of partisan views; but I do not count the present among these troubling times, and I would know of nothing that, from my standpoint, I could be moved to say and yet would not wish to say.

For today the inner calm and stillness that have come over me invite me to cast my gaze toward that from which the surging waves of a more agitated public life mostly draw away, toward that to which the spirit gladly flees from storm-tossed circles, in order to find in itself untroubled
calm and serenity—toward scholarship.

Since this subject lies closest to us in any case, the celebrated King's unselfish love of scholarship, independent of every secondary consideration, further directs me on this day to contemplate knowledge stripped of the constricting secondary considerations that are demanded of it from various quarters.

Should some thought here present itself to me again unconsciously and involuntarily, a thought that had also been expressed earlier from this orator's platform, then, far from regarding this as a fault, I find the repeated expression of certain principles fully justified by the position of the one who speaks here on this day.

For as I understand it, and as it is also described in the public announcement of our celebration, this orator is less dependent on speaking from his own person than he is meant to be an interpreter of the feeling and sense of the academic body: to be sure, with a good conscience he can say nothing that did not proceed from his own thinking, that was not his own conviction; but this conviction must at the same time be the conviction of the academic body; he must have lived himself into the latter, must be one heart and one soul with it, and speak out of it.

But what we call an academic body, or, in a foreign tongue, a university, indeed consists of the isolated component parts but not in them; its essence is the universality and unity that runs through the particular members and shapes them into a whole that is prior to the parts, not the parts prior to the whole; and this whole is something enduring, however much the members themselves may change, just as the organic body remains the same while it nevertheless constantly exchanges its substances and takes up new ones in place of those that have been expelled or are dying off, and transforms them into its own blood and flesh.

Just as the unity of the body lies in the soul, which from its origin dwells in it as a determinate soul and, notwithstanding its progressive development, remains one and the same, so the true academic body has as its constant unity and its vital principle a determinate spirit; its constancy gives the body itself stability, so that it does not, driven hither and thither by the shifting currents of the air like a reed, follow now this direction and now that, and in holding fast to that spirit
consists the preserving power which is ascribed to academic bodies.

For, formed together with the emergence of the community itself, it is propagated through inner tradition; not that something foreign to its essence could not also arise within it, but so long as it is vital, this will not take deep root.

Our academic body, of which I have the good fortune to be a member still with only a few almost from its first establishment onward, surely had such a spirit born with it at its founding, through the spirit of its magnanimous founders and of the immortal heroes of scholarship whom it then counted among its own; and this spirit has been strengthened and invigorated by it in continual exercise.

From him, whoever is to be her representative must have drawn his principles; and if I, as such, have been appointed for this celebration, I must indeed presume to be filled with this spirit in order to be able to give expression to it: but if this spirit is an old one, then its expression cannot lay claim to the charm of novelty.

To be sure, doubt remains as to whether I have grasped that spirit; but, to avail myself of a Demosthenic turn of phrase, I hold the conviction—perhaps from a lack of proper feeling, but I do hold the conviction, without which I could not appear here at all—that from the very beginning, and through a long series of years, I have striven to make my words correspond to that sense.
Cognition is a common possession of all human beings who are masters of their own spirit; through it, and through the will founded upon it, they distinguish themselves from the animals.

But in the measure that the bodily or the spiritual life predominates in man, and the latter has attained to a lesser or higher consciousness, the capacity for knowledge rises from a lowest point through countless degrees to an indeterminable height and depth.

Permit me, highly esteemed listeners, a few words necessary for the consideration, concerning the sources and the purpose of knowledge—only as a reminder of it, not for instruction or demonstration in the strictest form.

A great part of our knowledge springs from experience: impressions of the world standing over against the mind, mediated through the senses, give the soul perceptions, out of which representations of the individual are formed; induction leads to consciousness of the common
element and causes this to be recognized in the unity of the concept and of the law.

This is the course not of natural science alone, but also of historical and philological research, except that in the former perception comes through observation, in the latter mostly through tradition, for the examination of which it requires particular activities.

But everything universal and all unity come from the spirit; only the individual is perceived by the senses; so too, even in the knowledge mediated by experience, it is the spirit that, as thinking, carries out the act of knowing according to immutable laws.

Few, unless I am mistaken, still regard this experience as the sole source of knowledge: mathematical concepts, the pure determinations of thought, and moral ideas lie in the mind itself and are not formed from sensory perceptions.

Whether, then, cognition descends from pure concepts of reason to what is sensibly perceptible, or ascends from the latter to concepts, both paths, if followed correctly and insofar as each of them leads, must yield the same results from opposite starting points.

But as to what the purpose of cognition is, on this point once again not all are agreed: Aristotle, who, next after his teacher Plato, subjected cognition itself to examination with a genuinely scientific spirit of contemplation, declared cognition itself to be the aim and purpose of cognition.

All men, he says, strive by nature after knowledge: a proof of this is the love of perceptions; for these are loved for their own sake even without need or use, and above all perception through the eyes: not only in order to act, but even when we wish to do nothing, we prefer seeing to almost everything else, and indeed because this kind of perception makes something most known to us and reveals many differences.

In investigating to what causes and principles that which wisdom is relates, he explains that, of the sciences, the one that is taken up for its own sake, for the sake of knowledge, is more wisdom than the one sought for the sake of its consequences: the principles and causes are most worth knowing, because through them and from them the rest is known, but not conversely, and it belongs most of all to this knowledge that it
know and understand for its own sake.

People would have begun, and are still beginning, to philosophize because they were astonished at things and were uncertain; but those who are uncertain and astonished do not believe that they know. If, then, they philosophized in order to escape ignorance, it follows that they philosophized for the sake of knowledge, not on account of any use. And only when people were already in possession of what is necessary for a comfortable conduct of life did the higher science arise—consequently not for any other use of it, but just as that human being is free who exists for his own sake and not for another's, so too is the highest science alone free among the sciences, because it alone exists for its own sake.

This, he says, is also the most dominant of the sciences, because it knows for whose sake everything is to be done: this is namely the good in each thing, but in the whole it is the best in all of nature, and also the good and the "for whose sake" is one of the final causes.

Thus the philosopher establishes the freedom, self-sufficiency, and independence of knowledge—though only in relative terms—in that the purer and higher cognition is, the more it is an end in itself for him; and surely the purest and highest knowledge has no other purpose than in itself.
But if this is true, we are entitled to extend the intrinsic purpose of cognition to all knowledge.

For if some other purpose besides the purpose itself is ascribed even to a lower form of cognition, while to the highest only this latter belongs, then that other purpose can only originate in something that, in knowledge, is no longer knowledge.

Whether, then, the science thus defined is to be esteemed or despised, everyone will have to judge according to the disposition and direction of his own mind; we say only that the former will be done by the one who recognizes in the knowledge of nature and of spirit in themselves the unfolding of the conscious human spirit in general, or of reason, and in reason a divine element dwelling in man, and who finds the highest satisfaction in the being and life of the spirit within itself; but that there is also a cast of mind for which knowledge is merely a means to the attainment of other ends, a cast of mind that has been called banausic by the
more cultivated of all ages and is unworthy of the free-minded and highly gifted man: for which reason also that portion of the student youth which strives after knowledge for its own sake is regarded as the nobler, and to it alone is a scientific spirit attributed.

Those other purposes are indeed very diverse; but the most external and the most spirit-killing among them is the one by virtue of which scholarship becomes for the disciple a so-called bread-study, for which it must assume a more limited form and sometimes, according to circumstances, submits to an accommodation that promises more advantageous prospects.

Yet this way of thinking is also ancient; Aristophanes' comedy already presented its model in its boorish Strepsiades, when, over an object set before him for learning, it puts into his mouth the question of what use this was to him for bread. But even if one rejects this wholly unfree relation of science to the advantage and gain of the individual person, one has nevertheless often heard the demand, indeed even from the throne, that science should make itself practical; that theory, that is, cognition for its own sake, is useless. Theory and practice are two generally current words that everyone lightly carries on his lips, like coin in the pocket; such words wear down their stamp over the course of time to unrecognizability, and dark subsidiary notions attach themselves to them, which obscure the true sense and scarcely still permit any firm concept to be connected with them: to find the genuine meaning of the two words, we shall indeed have to go back to where they arose or were stamped and whence we have received them.

The same master of thought, whom I have just been following, distinguishes a threefold activity of the soul—the theoretical or cognitive, the practical or active, and the poetic or productive—each according to its own principle and end.

The principle of theoretical activity is, for him, the objects of knowledge—things themselves in their distinctness from the subject—and its purpose is knowledge, the theorem itself, or, what is the same thing, the true; practical activity has its principle in the subject, in its will, and its purpose is what is to be
done, the action apart from the work, the realization of the good, or eupraxia; productive activity has as its ground spirit, art, or a faculty of the subject, and as its purpose the work.
Accordingly, he decides in particular the question of where physics is to be classified, and declares it to be theoretical.

He does not, however, hold fast to this well-founded triad everywhere, but more often contents himself with the opposition between the theoretical and the practical, as it seems to me, with good reason.

For the productive activity, insofar as it as fine art relates precisely to the shaping of the beautiful, that is, of the idea embodied and absorbed in the sensible, shares with theory the ideal inner vision, and one principal branch of it, poetry, so called by way of preeminence, even presents in the very material that cognition must employ, namely language; and the fine arts again have no other purpose than the presentation of that inner vision, which, if not equal to cognition, is yet very similar to it as its image; so that this part of the arts is more closely related to cognition than to action: the remaining productive activity, by contrast, is more closely related to action, since it is almost wholly absorbed in doing and work and serves the purpose of use: for which reason the whole of productive activity can be divided between the theoretical and the practical.

But even this latter opposition is not an exclusive one: for cognition itself does not come about without will and intention, and is also a good, and a very high one; the theoretical activity is therefore not absolutely opposed to the practical. And conversely, if the will is a rational one, distinct from the blind impulse that the animal also has, then it is determined by cognition; and for this reason the profound Plato, less inclined to tear the theoretical and the practical apart, designated virtue as knowledge. Indeed, the entire practical activity of the soul is subordinate to the theoretical in that the goal of the former, the good, is a principle that can be perfectly grasped only through cognition, even if it is also given—though unconsciously—in feeling and faith. Thus the practical itself becomes the object of theory; and because the true and the good cannot contradict each other, a
contradiction between genuine theory and genuine practice is impossible.

Nevertheless, both directions remain two distinct ones, even in their demonstrated unity; and, not wishing to make the claim that almost the very same people who demand that science should make itself practical again wish, in complete contrast, to exclude the men of science from action, so that the practical circles might not be disturbed by their theories—the separation is already justified as a division of labor, because few can pursue both directions with equal strength; just as, to take examples only from antiquity, whose conditions were yet much simpler than ours, Pericles and Demosthenes would not have become the great statesmen if they had at the same time striven for the scholarly height of Plato and Aristotle, nor would the latter have become the great philosophers and rulers in the realm of theory if they had at the same time wished to win the laurels of those men.

Yet the demand is perhaps rather this: that science should relate not to the being and becoming of things in general, but to human purposes, as a theory of action itself—action taken in the opposition designated earlier—much as it was said of Socrates that he had called philosophy down from heaven to earth and introduced it into the cities and houses, and compelled it to undertake inquiries into life and morals, goods and evils.

Thus the true should no longer be the object of knowledge, but only the good: yet the good itself cannot be recognized without the knowledge of nature and of spirit, and with the extinction of the one side of the soul's activity the other also dies.

Finally, the demand that science should become practical is seldom even meant in such a way that it should recognize the good; rather, while there are various goods, spiritual and bodily, both desirable, because the full excellence of man consists in the health and excellence of body and soul, and because the more excellent part, the spirit, becomes the more independent the more the narrowness of bodily existence and the inconveniences and evils of physical life are removed—to which the possession of external goods contributes much—so the concept of the practical is mostly reduced to
the acquisition of bodily and sensual goods, the attainment of sensual eupraxy; and if it is indeed at the same time related to the moral and spiritual goods, these are grasped in the limited form of given or positive conditions, and the practical is found in the effect within them.

This cast of mind is above all averse to the speculative, and not merely as useless but in certain cases also as dangerous, because, independently of current opinions, it goes back to principles; indeed, moreover, it is also regarded as impossible, because absorption in this kind of practice usually has skepticism for its companion. Less hateful to such minds is empirical inquiry, but wrongly so, since a great part of it must seem to them equally useless and equally dangerous.
Moreover, if this tendency were consistently carried through with sole reference to what is capable of a so-called practical application, it would work against itself.

For if one sets aside the cases in which practice has preceded theory, and the latter first arose out of the former, then one cannot apply a piece of knowledge before it has been acquired in itself, without application; and it cannot be determined in advance whether something is applicable and to what, or not.

It has been aptly observed that Kepler could not have discovered that the planetary orbits are elliptical had not the Greek mathematicians, out of pure delight in theorems, which were worth more to them than application because they are more ideal and therefore more beautiful, developed the theory of conic sections; or if this example of application should not quite fit here, because it is a matter of indifference to our comfort in what orbits the heavenly bodies move, it will be conceded that the application of the doctrine of conic sections to artillery was just as little foreseen.
I pass over other examples, because they lie too close at hand.
Theory is the noble, ambrosially fragrant blossom; application is the slowly ripening fruit. Whoever wants the fruit must wait for the blossom.

If we persist, undistracted by this image that is not authoritative, in holding that cognition is an end in itself, then science cannot be determined by anything other than itself; by virtue of its ownmost essence it is free, like the spirit in which it is born.

I do not yet wish to say that herein is
at the same time contained the demand of progress upon it; for its freedom could also prove itself by its holding fast to the old or turning back to what is earlier: but it lies in its freedom that, when it itself presses onward within itself toward progress, it cannot endure any external hindrance of the same.

Meanwhile, even without further justification—which I may spare you—the task of science reveals itself as an infinite labor of the spirit; it is therefore indeed dependent upon an infinite progress, although for it, as for all of life, the opposite views prevail: that nothing new happens under the sun, and again that the foot does not twice pass through the same river.

The knowledge of the human race is a continuous chain of intellectual activities, in which old and new are inseparably interwoven; the new is rooted in the old, but from the old root new shoots spring forth, and so the same truth is at once old and new, and in the more developed reproduction lies a progress—only not exactly a straight-line one, but one comparable to a helical line, in which the movement, though it turns back in circular form, nevertheless never returns again to its starting point, but in a direction that cuts across all circles, often indeed amid manifold aberrations also from this path, advances further and further to other points.

Moreover, this progress is very different according to the nature of the objects; as I believe I have shown elsewhere, it is slower and more imperceptible in proportion as the things to which knowledge relates are more immaterial, more inward, and more spiritual, because the depth of spiritual intuition does not grow with the times, and precisely in the remote antiquity the highly gifted natures were filled with the creative supersensible power of mind with which they, not distracted by the multiplicity of impressions and relations that later grew to infinity, grasped and shaped the eternal ideas of the human race in mighty concentration and youthful freshness, so that later generations can warm themselves at these life-filled products, and from them can nourish and strengthen themselves: on the other hand, long time accumulates the sum of experiences, and since these are worked
over by the mind and referred back to the spiritual, those imperishable primal intuitions must at last also emerge in a purer light.
This progress of cognition, and every other, is hindered when its beginning and starting point, its purpose and goal, are determined for it by something other than itself.

This other is the positive, not that whose opposite is the negative: for science is not the negating, but the positive in its most original meaning, that is, in contrast to the natural, which is given in the nature of things and in rational cognition; for the principle of the positive is not the same as the sources of knowledge, but authority, which is without validity in science, and its goal is not free cognition, but subjection to what is posited.
In vain will one deny the existence of this opposition, even though it is not insoluble.

To be sure, the positive has been declared to be something objective—as the custom and tradition inherited from the ancestors, over against subjective opinion—and to be the constant and immutable; and since cognition seeks nothing other than the objective and the eternally self-same, because it seeks the true, it therefore seems that in the positive the goal of cognition has already been reached.
But that is by no means the case.

For even if we acknowledge that the positive is not something arbitrarily posited by the ruling power, not, as Plato's Thrasymachus teaches, the advantage of the stronger, but something better — that which the feeling or even the consciousness of each people, or of the more discerning among them, has recognized in each particular age as the more correct, and has therefore posited for the present and the future — it is nevertheless not for that reason objective, but often merely the petrified expression of an earlier subjectivity: it is unchangeable only to the extent that the spirit of a people is inclined to standstill, as with the Egyptians and the Chinese, and, in relation to the free inhabitants of the West, with the Orient in general, accustomed as it has been to servitude since time immemorial; moreover, since it often rests indeed only on the ruling power, it is at certain times posited and overturned and once again overturned in rapid succession, and even custom and tradition are not unchangeable, but rather move in the course of history together with the entire
state of culture.

Undeniably, however, the positive moves more slowly than science and thus remains behind it: if the former sets limits to the latter and demands that it take secondary considerations into account, then the conflict between the two comes to light—a conflict as old as science itself, but for the first time it was felt and expressed in full depth, in the most cultivated state of the world and at the height of that state's culture, by the most brilliant man of his time, when this state, having allowed itself to be seduced by demagogy into avenging with death the alleged violation of the positive by science—an eternally memorable example of blindness repented too late, and yet not sufficiently taken to heart by posterity!
Shall we not lay the whole blame for this conflict upon the positive element, if it does not abuse its power!

For if it is true that great and holy intuitions of deep content were given vigorous expression in early times, and if—what is equally little to be doubted—much of this has passed over into the positive [teachings] of civilized peoples, has been firmly established therein, and has become dear to hearts and minds, then one should not frivolously and presumptuously shake the positive: if one disdains authority, one has not thereby put truth in the place of an error; rather, the content of one's own opinion can be more incorrect or shallower than the content of belief in authority, while that opinion is often, into the bargain, bound up with vain arrogance.

If Aristotle says that the philosopher is a lover of myth, because philosophizing begins with wonder and myth consists of the wondrous, then it may be added that he loves myth also because in its wondrous and mystical shell it harbors a noble core or seed of knowledge; and even if they are only half-waking dreams, they are sacred and prophetic dreams.

In general, the man of science will show the positive, through teaching and life, the highest regard, respect, and conscientious reverence—with preeminent awe toward that which is most positive, the religious ordinances concerning the most holy divine things, insofar as these are founded upon a typical and symbolic revelation of the divine Spirit entering into the human race, even if this revelation appears clouded in
its human formulation.
But there is yet another way in which science is conducive to the positive.
We find a secular authority and a spiritual authority: the former establishes the political and legal conditions, the latter establishes belief, insofar as belief is formulated as dogma.

Both are, without further ado—the former for the public sphere, the latter for the ecclesiastical sphere as recognized by the state—positively valid and binding. But since, on the one hand, it is not beyond doubt what these authorities have actually established, and on the other hand, even in cases where no doubt prevails on this point, it is not yet immediately clear how much the statute contains and what follows from it or does not, the positive content—without subjecting its worth and validity, grounded in faith and obedience, to the judgment of cognition—becomes the object of historical research, artful interpretation, and conceptual analysis for the sciences which, because their ultimate source is authority, we call positive sciences—an expression that admittedly seems burdened with a contradiction, which for now we shall leave to itself.

These are the broad fields of positive political science and jurisprudence and of positive theology, preferably Protestant theology, which claims for itself a broader scope for investigation: even in their bound condition, these will be able to contribute much to the purification of the political and the religious along the path of cognition, in that they separate out whatever has accidentally and erroneously attached to the statute as content or consequence, lead it back to its essential determinations and constituent parts, and in possible cases even establish it, and thus take commandment and faith up into knowledge.

If science thus pays its tribute to authority, then it may fairly receive in return the requital that lies in this: that spirit is fought with spirit, not with force; that even the most extreme means of force, to say nothing of lesser ones — that extermination, burning, killing do not overcome thought and science; that even the revocation of alleged heresy, that expedient so popular in the Middle Ages and, amid the coarseness of the age, unquestionably mild and gentle and therefore praiseworthy, granted authority only an apparent victory over knowledge — all this is proved by a long series of experiences, since each time the better knowledge has nevertheless
rescued itself from the destruction of the bodily into the realm of truth, while the persecutors have fallen prey to the contempt and abhorrence of posterity; and when, out of timidity and weakness — which deserves excuse in the face of uncomprehending and cruel force — a revocation had been made with extorted hypocrisy, that revocation was itself revoked as soon as the fear had vanished.
In truth there is measure and prudence; persecution is the work of fanatical passion, which, once unleashed, knows no limit any longer.

I need not remind you that I do not include within science those wicked principles whose dissemination, inciting to deeds, by any reasonable standard falls under punishment; but if, beyond this, the free granting of latitude to science is under certain circumstances subject to great misgivings and difficulties, which I indicated earlier at this very place, then these may have their ground in a diseased condition of society, not in science, which against its own diseased excrescences and aberrations has its cure within itself through refutation, and whose excesses are entirely harmless, unless society has already previously been shaken in its foundations by other evils.

And without doubt the claim is justified, since state and church neither restrict the positive sciences in the scope that I have just now marked out for them, nor encroach upon the domains in which authority can have no validity.

If the statute and free cognition do not yet always go together, this is for a time to be borne as a human imperfection, until in further development, as is to be hoped, they will merge into unity, since the content of the two is not necessarily different: the beginning and end of both is God and the Good!
On the other hand, a substantial injury is done to science when categories are forced upon it that are taken from the positive [sciences].

It has already been pointed out that the latter is by no means something immutable and ever self-identical: rather, we find many mutually repelling and mutually exclusive forms of it not only in different ages but simultaneously.
Which of them, then, is to accommodate himself to knowledge and science?

Even if it
can get along with the most universal element of almost everyone, it will nonetheless agree less with particularities.

Should it recognize slavery in the slave states of North America, say, in the Aristotelian manner as a relation founded in nature, but in the other states as a disgrace to humanity? Should it be monarchical here, republican there, and again absolutist or constitutional, aristocratic or democratic, and all of this hypocritically and sophistically, now one way and again differently tomorrow?
Even their diversity according to national character and the most general religious differences is an imperfection: for the truth can only be one.

Yet if one insists on carrying still narrower categories into scholarship: people want, over against Protestantism, a Catholic philosophy, a Catholic history—and I do not see why, by the same logic, there should not also be a Catholic physics, which anyone acquainted with Leibniz's now-lost accommodations might even consider rather more justified.

But does another confession, then, supply other scientific grounds of knowledge? Are perception and the determinations of thought, the formation of concepts and the forms of judgment and inference, different according to it? Are observations of nature conducted differently under the one or the other presupposition? And does not historical truth remain the same for the unbiased and conscientious investigator, whatever faith he may hold?

Here too, people expect cognition to be guided by ulterior considerations: this is the most reprehensible confusion of the different domains, and it is not without danger where the presumption of ecclesiastical power, in remembrance of its former world dominion, threatens to raise itself above the state and scholarship.
There is also the further point that people pass off as something positive what it is not.

That the earth stands still and the sun and the universe revolve around it, and similar things with which physical science cannot reconcile itself, is no dogma of either Judaism or Christianity, and our religion does not concern itself with such things, which are indifferent to the salvation of the soul: only the lack of understanding of men has also stamped such things as articles of faith, and only with time does it recede, when it no longer finds its position tenable.

Let us count ourselves fortunate
to live in a state in which such secondary considerations are not demanded or encouraged from on high; let us count ourselves fortunate that we have a king who well knows how to keep separate the domains of which I speak: I would give decisive proofs of this if I did not consider it more respectful to leave this to your own consciousness.
I hasten to my conclusion, highly esteemed assembly!

The freedom and self-determination of scholarship will no more require justification than ecclesiastical freedom does, if the state is regarded merely as an institution for the protection of its members in their activity and their goods, but is otherwise to conduct itself indifferently toward this activity and these goods.

But if the state is the realization of the whole of the good through human activity, to which good cognition also belongs, then it does not remain indifferent to cognition either, but posits it within itself; yet it does not follow from this that the state thereby abolishes cognition's freedom and self-determination: rather, if it abolished these by means of its own positing, it would abolish cognition itself, whereas it intends to posit it.
He must therefore take it up into himself as something free, just as he recognizes the freedom of consciences in the religious communities encompassed by him.

Thus, I think, our state has placed science within itself: as proof, the statutes of the highest scientific institutions of this capital serve, of which one has as its aim the promotion and expansion of the general sciences without any particular teaching purpose, the other the general and particular scientific education of duly prepared young men, both without restrictive provisions—unless one were to find such a provision in the task added for the second, namely to prepare the young men "for entry into the various branches of the higher state and church service," to which I shall return at once.

Indeed, the freedom of science as of conscience is a fundamental principle of this state—a principle that Frederick the Great, who, however one may seek to diminish him, will always remain Prussia's hero, has engraved deep in the heart of the state with the indelible writing of the spirit.

Hereby both the one-sided relation to common practice and the hindrance caused by
the mixing of the various fields are removed.

And to return to the beginning of my speech and not repeat what I have already anticipated at the point last mentioned, who does not recognize that Frederick William IV, whose mind was as lofty as it was finely cultivated—in a word, ideal—loves and honors science for its own sake?
Who has ever heard from his throne that philistine admonition to practicality on their behalf?

If, then, the purpose of the universities just cited—to prepare students for entry into the various branches of the higher state and church service—is indeed rooted in the positive, this purpose is nevertheless set forth only as the second, not as the first; and I have already remarked how scholarship also takes part in the positive, in acknowledgment of it. In no case, surely, is a mere fitting or drilling understood by this preparation—something far beneath the proper measure of a preparation—though very great things can indeed be meant by it.

For it is not the one who knows how to move well within the given state of affairs who is the capable man, especially among higher officials, but rather the one who, filled with the divine idea of the good, strives to realize it as far as it seems attainable in each case, in order to bring about a better future, since the positive itself stands in need of manifold purification and improvement.

It is for this truly higher service that science trains those who are destined for action—that is, for translating riper knowledge into deed: thus theory works in itself, and through the rulers and servants of the commonwealth enlightened by it, permeating all its parts, gradually upon the circumstances of life; and though thousands and again thousands revile it, it is and remains nonetheless that which governs action and moves humanity forward, because spirit governs and moves the mass.

How this spirit, since the restoration of the sciences and the church reform that followed, though only slowly and not without the resistance and lingering influence of the old barbarism, has fruitfully worked upon public and social life—of that there would be much to say, were I not, driven on by the course of my thoughts, already to have spoken longer than I intended: I break off, in order to add
yet a few words about the German universities.

For a long time these counted as the bearers of scholarly freedom, and our university enjoyed this renown already in its early bloom; for that reason too—though not for that reason alone—they have been suspected, opposed, and assailed, especially in the time of an oppressive foreign rule that placed their very existence almost in question.

But now many speak of the decline of the universities: they are no longer vital, merely decayed academic bodies hastening toward their fall, because they would be surpassed by the free research standing outside them.

That abuses have crept into it is acknowledged by themselves, and the better has been wished for; but its vital force is not exhausted so long as it does not lose or surrender the freedom of which it has been the guardian: it will, so we hope, as mighty trunks still long raise its freshly leafed crowns and defy the storms, and whoever should lay the axe to its root will recognize too late that he has killed the science in order to revive it.

It is precisely its corporate association, so offensive to many, that guarantees its duration and its freedom, if—as I touched upon at the outset—it has been received and born in a genuine spirit and knows how to preserve that spirit.
And now just one more thing!
Science is by its nature cosmopolitan; but this quality is not incompatible with love of country, and therefore, since we are men of science, we do not cease to be citizens of a state.

Yet this bond with the state is felt more strongly and more intimately in the academic body to which we are joined, because this body is an organic member of the state, and its life is inseparable from the collective life of the state.

And so today, in the assembly of harmonious colleagues of this whole scholarly enterprise, with greater elevation and more solemnity than any one of us could in other circles close to him, we commemorate the festival of the King, who is our protector, and we beseech the King of Kings that He may preserve the gracious sovereign and his house for the blessing and prosperity of the fatherland and of science, and grant him to lead a long life in the fullness of unclouded happiness, of which his noble soul is worthy.

div.head: VII. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1854.
Von der Uebereinstimmung der Herrschenden und der Beherrschten

p.s: Among the manifold festivities by which homage is paid to the living, none is more significant than the one for which we, highly esteemed assembly, are gathered together today at this place.

None is more significant—not merely because the King, to whom this celebration is dedicated, towers unattainably high above all the other members and fellows of the state, but far more because, among all the festivals consecrated to mortals, this one rests on the most sublime and elevating of thoughts: the thought that millions of loyal hearts on this day direct their supplications to the Most High, that He may preserve and bless the Prince in whom all—whatever else might otherwise separate them from one another—have and feel their most intimate union and brotherhood.

Certainly this consciousness is elevating in the same measure in which it must be depressing if, at such a celebration—which then, to be sure, would be arranged only for flattering show or out of custom—the feeling prevails that the one honored is not the center of that concord of all, but that prince and people are rather in a deep discord of mind, outwardly linked with one another only by the bonds of coercion exercised by power and of a reluctant obedience, or at least only by the indisputable political duty of obeying the authority that rightfully exists.

Such a festival is celebrated with full dignity when the ruler to whom it is dedicated has taken up into himself the whole significance of the state, when his spirit is the living breath and the soul of the body politic, pervading all its members, and when his subjects come to meet the ruler not under compulsion but out of an inner necessity, which I equate with freedom, just as he comes to meet them, and for the most significant and decisive matters and situations, in joys and sorrows, hopes and fears, each in his own
place and within his own circle, which no one is entitled to overstep, feel themselves at one with him, insofar as personally separate natures, which never feel and think entirely the same, because each has its own particularity, are capable of such a harmony.

Even if it be true that strife is the father of things, that the most important formations and developments spring from the conflict of opposites, it is nevertheless not the opposition itself that is productive, but its sublation in a higher unity; and the state in particular is not instituted so that this or that part of it should be worn down in conflict and the others remain as victors, but for the mediation of peace between the various elements, to be sure mutually antagonistic, which are united within it.

This is the great blessing of monarchy: that it, if any state constitution is, is suited to mediate this peace, and indeed in the person of the prince, in whom the oppositions are resolved, insofar as they can be resolved at all; provided, that is, that his subjects stand in the harmony with him that I have just described.

A long time has proven that in our fatherland this concord has struck deep roots; if storms have moved the crown of this tree and shaken it, it has only been all the more surely confirmed that they are not able to tear it down.
This mighty oak has drawn its strength from the concord of which the present day is witness to us.

We commemorate him in this unwavering confidence, which alone in the confusion of the times can grant us reassurance; we commemorate him with the twofold prayer to the Governor of destinies: that He may continue to bestow upon this king, and through him upon the land, the blessings He has hitherto poured out upon the King our Lord; and further, that He may preserve and strengthen that which above all else is the foundation of the state's welfare—that unity of mind—so that king and people, walking the same path in mutual trust, may increase the flowering and growth of the realm, and the realm, for its part and with the means at its disposal, may at the same time promote the overall progress of the human race and, as far as its powers allow, lead it nearer and nearer to its goal, however distant or infinite that goal may be.

The harmony between rulers and ruled is a commonplace
that people utter and apply lightly; it is harder to say wherein it consists and how it is to be attained, since it is conceivable in multiple ways, has many very different degrees, and, according to levels of culture and circumstances, rests on very different foundations.

That I should today, before you, undertake a few reflections on this very matter is prompted in me precisely by the fundamental idea with which I began my speech, and in connection with this, by the fact that the speaker appointed for this day, although after appearing repeatedly on the same occasion he must be allowed some freedom in the choice of his subject, will nevertheless prefer to fix his eye on something lying closer to the celebration itself.

If we go back to the beginnings, it should be historically well founded that the very first dominion among small communities of human beings was the paternal; these followed nature in accordance with the eldest or the tribal head as herds do unconsciously; in these small communities, through the commonality of the tribal feeling, the harmony of those who command and those who obey was given by nature, as between parents and children; and since the tribal head was at the same time in possession of the sacred treasures, at the same time tribal priest, as in the family the father is, it was strengthened by the bonds of religious feeling.

This first and smallest state, if one may call it so, is a state of nature, a product of the natural impulse, because man is a political animal, not one governed by a freely chosen and pursued purpose, little different from a society of ants, bees, or beavers or other social animals; the harmony between rulers and ruled that is given in it is therefore an involuntary one, and, so far as unconsciousness is conceivable in man, an unconscious one.

An ancient sage called this dominion the most just kingship; and insofar as this paternal or patriarchal monarchy is the most original form of the state, we are entitled to assert that the state came into being neither through usurpation nor through contract.

This is likewise still evident in the origins of the small Hellenic kingdoms: the Pelopids, the most powerful of the Greek kings, are said to have obtained their rule not by force nor by means of a formal treaty, but certainly
with the will of those they governed; and far from the tyranny — that is, the despotic rule of a single individual — having been regarded by the Hellenes as the original form of the state, even the name of the tyrant arose among them only late, and could only arise late, because it presupposes a political consciousness that develops only at a higher stage of civilization.

On the other hand, already in the earliest times a notion had attached itself to that natural right of dominion which even now has not entirely disappeared, although the true founder of political science, Aristotle—otherwise anything but averse to kingship—no longer thought of it, because he strove to grasp the essence of things by stripping away all mythical belief.
What is established by nature is established by God, who has ordered nature: paternal authority is therefore in accordance both with the divine commandment and with the commandment of nature.

That paternal rule, and therefore even the tyrannical rule that had clothed itself in its mask, thus appeared—the former, at least at the outset, quite rightly—as founded on divine right: the monarchy was at the same time a theocracy.

The gods themselves gave power to kings; indeed, kings are descendants of the gods, sprung from Zeus and nurtured by him, and thus are gods among men and at the same time the born priests of their divine forefathers.

The most distinguished Greek royal families—the Pelopids, the Heraclids, the Cretan dynasty, and others—all alike descend from the gods, and above all from the king of the gods, Zeus; the kings of the barbarians too, the Achaemenids of the Persians, the older dynasty of the Lydians, and the Macedonian kings, are offspring of the highest god: Zeus himself, through Hermes, gave Pelops the scepter, which was passed down to his descendants; it is the scepter of Zeus himself, with which Minos rules in power.

Who does not recognize that through such faith the harmony of the governed with the ruler was promoted most effectively, that by this means even the most decided despotism received a justification, while every contradiction and every deviation from the will of the divine potentate was stifled in its very germ?

If such notions—which in the course of history lose their validity to the point
that only the general truth remains, that all authority as all power is from God—do not give the violent ruler a substitute for the real right he lacks, then under a tyranny something at least akin to it, if not agreement with the ruler, is possible only when the masses, recognizing that because of inner corruption and decay or because of the discord of the parties freedom has become impossible and violent rule necessary, patiently submit to a usurper who has, so to speak, sacrificed his own conscience to the salvation of the whole and grants the population peace and a certain comfort of life, which to them, to be sure, soon counts for more than the highest goods; or when the usurper or his ancestors by their own strength have shielded the land from without and rescued it from an even more shameful servitude and have continually shown it benefits: then the people, forgetting the origin of the rule, will reconcile themselves to it and acquire a certain attachment to it strengthened by habit.

Thus Octavian Augustus subjected the entire Roman Empire to his sole rule, after it had been exhausted by the civil wars, without the people or the provinces having been averse to the new state of affairs: indeed, by virtue of his tribunician power he even appeared as the protector of the people against an insolent oligarchy, which had earlier weighed oppressively on the common people and had even, like that Claudia, not been ashamed to wish that the people might perish in lost battles, so that the streets would be freer for her carriage; thus earlier Pisistratus, under the appearance of being a friend of the people, had obtained the tyranny and had not exercised it without measure, whereas the later aristocrats, in the time of the Thirty, did not shrink from calling the demos of Athens the accursed; thus Theron the Sicilian tyrant became the savior and benefactor of his state, and his usurpation did not prevent the people, having again become free, from honoring him after his death like a hero.

On the other hand, I could not conceive how a harmony between ruler and ruled, resting on any tolerable foundation, could be imagined in the monarchy of a Nebuchadnezzar or a Xerxes; even though the marks of
despotism—the lord's unbridled and passionate exercise of power on the one side, and slavish fear on the other—correspond in mutual accord; and there are indeed souls that seem made to be slaves, because they find a pleasure in servitude, at least when they are permitted in turn to oppress others, like the satrap; but in truth these seek only their own advantage, not the advantage of the lord, and the nobler ruler despises them, because he does not wish to command slaves.

Even the superiority of mind, through which a monarch can exert a powerful influence, produces not so much agreement as confidence—a confidence that swiftly vanishes when successes no longer correspond to expectations.
But even the kinds of agreement described just now are not the true ones for us, since the one is scarcely a conscious agreement, the other scarcely a moral one.

Our age presses everywhere toward consciousness, toward thought and knowledge—at least among the more educated, who wish to live in the light of thought; and dark and drifting feelings have a place nowhere less than in the relations of the state.

Let us also admit that not everyone can raise himself to clarity of thought, indeed that, as the poet says, what no understanding of the understanding sees, a childlike mind practices in simplicity; yet the content of this heartfelt feeling has its justification only when it can stand before the tribunal of the understanding and of reason: we must grasp feeling through thinking, and, to use a happy foreign expression, as it were set eyes into blind impulse through the concept.
The unity of the rulers and the ruled must therefore rest on something other than what has been said thus far, if it is to be the genuine and true unity, a moral and conscious one.

If the primordial state from which I began is a direct product of nature and thus something uncontrived, then the state, as it develops at the stage of a higher development of humanity, is a work of art of reason; the form of this work of art, the expression of state reason, is law.

Not as though an exclusive opposition existed between the two stages: for in that state of nature there is also a law, the ruler himself as the inspired, living law, reason
represented in one person; and the rational state, on the other hand, would be ill ordered if nature had perished within it: rather, just as the works of the plastic arts and all poetry are held to be perfect only when, without prejudice to their ideality, they are at the same time wholly natural, so the rational law of the state expresses only the true nature of moral things, which the genuine legislator alone has in view, while the false one lets himself be guided by secondary considerations or serves self-interest and party passions.

But the law assigns to each his own; the deep sense of the Greeks themselves gave expression to this in the word by which they designated the law, and our exalted royal house has chosen, with truly political sense, the motto: "To each his own."

Where the law—I mean the rational law, not the law dictated by passion—pervades the whole state, where therefore each receives what is his own, all parts of the state are necessarily in harmony, because no one reaches beyond what is his own; there too, between the two principal parts of the state, the rulers and the ruled, there will be the fullest concord.
Justice and legality are the surest foundation of concord.
This is so certain that even the most contradictory elements can be united through the law of reason and through justice.

It has often been said that nothing is more conducive to harmony between the ruler and the ruled than the unity of stock or the same national character in both, since only under this condition is a common feeling and a common consciousness concerning the most important matters possible; but the history of the newer states especially shows that people have often preferred to call a foreigner to the throne, because he stands outside the sphere of the parties, and that different stocks can be united under one ruler and live with one another in friendship, provided only that rational law and justice hold them together, and that no one stock is oppressed.

Even if it is natural that the ruler should be of the same stock as his subjects, that one people should form one state, that one state should have a single national character, yet foreign ruling families too, accommodating themselves to the law and custom of the people, soon grow so intimately together with that people that they
recognize only their new land as their fatherland; and almost all states of antiquity and of modern times, indeed the peoples themselves, have grown together out of various gradually mingled stocks and have thereby even become stronger and more capable, because the one strengthened and, as it were, fertilized the other.

If the various peoples obey one and the same supreme head, their growing together is thereby favored all the more, though to be sure one could not maintain that harmony with the ruler is, as some believe, itself already produced by the mere fact that different tribes are united into a single state only through the person of the common prince.

For if this agreement is not already present in the individual tribes, independently of such association, for some reasons or other, then it cannot arise directly from the fact that they are thrown together into one state; rather, it must be added that they find this association beneficial in itself.

For if they recognize an advantage in this union, then through this recognition—since this advantage accrues to them solely through the sharing of rule—a conscious inclination toward the ruling house, and thus agreement with it, is indeed established.
This leads me to the second foundation of true concord between rulers and the ruled: the common advantage.

If the advantage of the one and of the other is different, if perhaps even the law, as an incorrect one, is calculated only on what is expedient for the stronger, if the subjects are, as Galba disapprovingly expressed it, only, as it were, the inheritance of a family, then a genuine harmony of the subjects with the government is not conceivable: the power and honor of the ruling house must rest on the power and honor of the people, the spiritual and external welfare of the people must be bound up with the well-being of the ruling house in itself and in the consciousness of both, and both must support themselves exclusively on one another, not on different or even on foreign elements.

Admittedly, this presupposes that the people are at one among themselves: if the people are torn by parties, then the discord of these is easily carried over, on one side, to the person or the house of the rulers, if these themselves take sides.

Apart
from utterly corrupt empires, such as the Byzantine, where the circus factions, the Blues and the Greens, in league with dogmatic fanaticism and moral decay, shattered the state, the principal political parties will for all time remain aristocracy and democracy: where the nobility was overmighty, the monarchy tended to lean toward the people; where the people, overleaping the measure of its natural rights in a stormy urge, threatened to seize the reins of government for itself, it [the monarchy] supported itself on the nobility.

Undoubtedly, in perilous times it is difficult for the monarchy to hold to the proper middle course, and most difficult of all when the parties at the same time look outward and, as I said, rely on foreign elements; but it is the fairest prerogative of the monarchy, in unclouded and—we may say—godlike calm and serenity, to hover above the parties, to curb them, to mediate between them; and surely it thus succeeds, supported by an impartial and unadulterated public opinion, in hitting upon what is right and in the end uniting even the most extreme party differences under the banner of a conscious love of country shared by the prince and the subjects—provided that this love has not been utterly deadened by self-interest and self-will, which, so long as the state still has vital forces, cannot be presumed; thus it succeeds in leading the parties, divided among themselves, back to uniform agreement with the ruler, in preserving them in the subordination and obedience without which no political life is possible, indeed in inspiring them to devotion and self-sacrifice, not in slavish but in free service.
Only one thing is hard to overcome: the fraternization of political factions with religious ones.

It is therefore a great good of a state when no different religious confessions occur within it and when the ruling house and the people have one and the same confession; if the state does not enjoy this happiness, then it must as far as possible be replaced by toleration and equal rights of the confessions, and the ruler must find the means to hold down the instigators of religious discord and their influence on the state and to render them harmless.
As in all development, so in the life of the state, standstill is the beginning of decline.

If a people or a state is not, so
to speak, something accidental and indifferent, but has a vocation in world history, then the state must advance from stage to stage until that vocation is fulfilled.
Do only the rulers complete this progress, or only the peoples, or both—whether in agreement or in conflict?

One may, in the first place, ascribe to a people or a state a destiny which, like the destiny of unconscious creatures, fulfills itself out of a higher necessity, whatever the prince and every individual may do or leave undone; a conception that could receive great confirmation through that irony of world history whose artistic imitation is the irony of tragedy—namely, that precisely the intention, hope, and confidence of promoting and attaining something, or of avoiding and thwarting something, together with the means set in motion for that purpose, not seldom bring about or hasten the opposite of what was intended and expected.
All human prudence and strength founder on the final decision of Providence.
But not without the fault of mortals!

Those who have rightly taken their stand and recognized their destiny will not reach into the spokes of the world's wheel to check it, but will themselves help to move it along in its proper course: man accomplishes his destinies out of his own resolve; the progress of the development of peoples and states springs from their own activity, and more or less according to their will and with the consciousness of those who act.
