There must be something driving within them themselves, by which they are moved forward, just as their decline is caused by their own inertia, slackening, and lack of understanding: if proof of this is needed, it is supplied by the peoples and states of antiquity that are world-historical, whose history, because it lies complete before us and can be surveyed from beginning to end, permits a sure judgment—Persia and Hellas, the Macedonian dynasties, and the world-ruling Romans in their growth and in their gradual decline.

That driving force must now, to be sure, lie in large part with the people, since even the best leader can accomplish nothing with them if the people's impulse does not meet his own impulse and plan in a corresponding way; indeed, in states in which the ruler is significantly limited by the constitution, the driving force of
the people will so predominate that the government follows it more than it leads it.

Conversely, in others the most effective impulse proceeds from the ruler; but I have just observed that this nevertheless promises little success if the drive of the people does not have the same direction.
Only unity gives strength.

Thus we are again pointed to the harmony between ruler and people as the condition of progress for nations and states, without which an increase of prosperity is difficult or impossible; where, by contrast, that harmony exists, the whole driving force of the people is concentrated in its head and leader as rays are concentrated in a single focal point, and again from this point light and warmth stream forth to the whole people, enlightening and quickening them.

To be sure, the prince or the people may advance ahead of the other part, or even hasten far in front, and one of the two may fall behind: in other words, the government may be better than the people, or the people better than its government.

The genius always hastens ahead of lesser minds; and here too we find again a noble and sublime prerogative of monarchy: that the brilliant and great ruler can boldly—though for that very reason not always without danger—hasten far ahead of his people and, by the golden threads of the spirit, draw that same people up to the height of his own mind.

This advancing and falling behind occurs, finally, not only between those who rule and those who obey, but also between states and states in relation to the development of the whole human race, into which every significant state is interwoven.
Happy the people that does not lag behind on this path common to all peoples, and that advances along it together with its princes in unity and harmony!

In taking the floor, most esteemed assembly, to hold your attention for a few moments upon this great subject, which I by no means feel myself capable of discussing in a few words of my own, there rises unbidden before my mind the thought that today, a year ago, at this very place, I summoned up from the grave, as it were, as witnesses for my words, the great heroes of learning whom this university counted among its own from the time of its founding; for among them is one whose soul
was wholly fired with the burning zeal for the progress of the human race, a man such as this century has not seen again; he is among them—Johann Gottlieb Fichte, the second Rector of this university, whom only a few of us have known more closely.

I am by no means a follower of his doctrine, nor was I formed by it or by him: indeed, our particular studies touch more closely, almost only, in his high esteem for classical antiquity, since he, in keeping with the idealism of his mind and of his age—which in its pure and unprejudiced, youthfully fresh striving after the ideal seems to surpass the present age—held the conviction that it was more advisable for the budding mind to breathe in the serene atmosphere of the writers of antiquity than in the compressed air of the modern way of thinking, and that only through the study of the ancient languages does youth emerge from the fog-world of half-understood notions, never examined to the core, in which the ordinary consciousness even of the so-called educated lives: but who that still saw him at work, or knows his activity from tradition, or has read his writings—does he not know what influence he exerted on his time and especially on his immediate circle as a man and citizen, as a teacher and writer? and who knows this, how could he wonder if on this day and at this celebration, which is to be for us all a strengthening and an elevation, I strengthen and elevate myself by his example?

He was equally distinguished in life by his Catonian severity, his fidelity to duty, his straightforwardness, his unselfishness, his imperturbability, and his intrepidity even toward the most implacable enemy of the fatherland, as in scholarship by the unity, firmness, consistency, and objectivity of his thinking, which fixes the object sharply in its eye and, without the serpentine paths of sophistry, proceeds undeviatingly and undistracted by anything external or accidental, absorbed in itself alone, straight toward the goal.

In him pure morality and deep piety were united with the boldest freedom of spirit, which did not escape persecution either; the most abstract theory with a constant regard for moral action, through which he exerted a fruitful and quickening influence on distinguished statesmen of this country; indignation at the defects and failings of the present with a
rare foresight into the future; love of country, which he had tested through dangers, with cosmopolitanism; philosophical thought with the gift of general intelligibility, when it was a matter of instructing the people, at least the educated.
His tongue is a flaming sword; the power of his speech is compelling, its force crushing and pulverizing.
This man, equipped with these qualities, fought, as I said just now, with enthusiasm for the progress of the human race.
Let us hear what the final goal of this development is for him.

As I above, basing myself on facts and independently of him, called the first political life theocratic, he too says: "The world proceeds from a believed [order], and ends," he continues, "in a thoroughly understood theocracy."
God will truly rule universally, and he alone, without other forces setting the world in motion: no longer merely as a teacher, but as a living and life-giving power."
Truly the most sublime thought, and uttered by a man whom the state or church authority of the land in which Luther had arisen had accused of godlessness!
But by what means did he believe this would be achieved and brought to realization?

A time must come, he says, when the church ceases to be something for itself and is taken up into the state—something that may already have been begun by the Reformation; but the kingdom must consist in the moral law, and at some time or other the task must be set before Christians of founding a state according to the moral law.
To him it is a preparation for the perfect state that "our race unite into a single body, throughout all its parts thoroughly known to itself, and everywhere formed in the same manner".

"Once that first goal has been attained, once everything useful that has been found at one end of the earth is at once made known and communicated to all, then, without interruption, without standstill or retrogression, with united strength and in a single step, mankind will raise itself to a state of cultivation for which we lack the concepts." Through the establishment of a state truly one within itself, in which no estate is oppressed, internal peace would be firmly grounded; unfortunately he found himself compelled to say that
the progress toward this one true state could be left very calmly to the passions and the blindness of the ruling estates, even if they were warned.

Now if that true state has first come into being, then at the same time foreign war, at least with true states, is cut off as regards its possibility: only a state that is unjust in its internal affairs can set out to despoil its neighbors; and once only a few truly free states have arisen, these, for the sake of their own security, would have to transform everything around them likewise into free states, so that the domain of culture and of freedom, and with it of universal peace, would gradually encompass the entire globe.
That this condition of universal peace should be brought about by all, as one great free moral community, appears to him as the final purpose of the present world.

Thus he attached himself to Kant, whose philosophical sketch toward perpetual peace is by no means a sketch of a nonentity, but already contains, in its preliminaries, very substantial things worthy of being taken to heart, of which I will cite only the first article by way of example: that no treaty of peace should actually be regarded as valid which has been made with a secret reservation of the material for a future war.

However far in the distance the fulfillment of these prospects held out to humanity may lie, no other earthly goal of our race can be conceived than that designated by our champion for truth, right, and morality, if the race is to have any such final purpose or final goal at all.

Toward this realization of the highest good on earth, which is impossible without the union of spiritual freedom with political freedom, and thus toward the progress of humanity, science is also for him one of the most important means: for, as he said to his listeners in the memorable days shortly before the outbreak of the war, which he fell a victim to, in the speech with which he broke off his lectures, he was "pervaded by the conviction that the realm of the old hereditary enemy of humanity, evil in general, which enemy appears in different ages in the most varied forms, is nowhere more surely and greatly diminished than through the cultivation of science in the human race." The Prussian
people, although consisting of various tribes, nevertheless has a common and definite national spirit, which is rooted in the Germanic national spirit.

Its kings have grasped this national spirit, and this spirit has continually developed, exerting an influence on the various phases of the advancing formation of the human race—phases that are marked by the spirit of each particular age, insofar as that spirit represents progress at all.

If in this development there is a correspondence between the spirit of the people and the princes, then each of the longer reigns following one another will correspond to a stage of development; but what this stage is can be recognized with some certainty only after the lapse of not merely a single period of development, but of several, because the character of each will emerge in its difference from the others and from the earlier ones only long after its completion, from its consequences and through comparison with others, especially the later ones: future times are the wisest witnesses, and posterity judges most surely.
No one can presume to anticipate this: for even in their case, the comprehension and determination of those characters remains always a difficult task and is subject to many errors.

If we go back only a little more than a century in the history of our state, we find in this period two memorable long reigns which seem to have been of significance not only for Prussia and Germany, but, together with the strivings of other peoples, for the development of the educated world—the reigns of Frederick the Great and Frederick William III. But as to what their character was and their significance within the state and beyond it, even now judgment is not yet fully settled and concluded, but wavers according to the intellectual disposition of those judging, and we may say according to their party position.
How could one expect full understanding of the present on the part of all?

But it is certain that with the accession of Frederick William IV, the most gracious of kings, a new epoch of this state has begun, and its political development has since that point in time gained a different, forward-driving form, which, to be sure, especially in the unavoidable interconnection
with the other movements of the age, could not remain without storms and vacillations: in harmony with the progress of the whole more cultivated part of humanity, under the government of this king, who is surpassed by none in elevation of spirit and noble cultivation, the world position of the state has for that very reason essentially changed, because we are going ever nearer and nearer to that first goal of the race, that everything useful which has been found at one end of the earth is at once made known and communicated to all; in our ruler's exalted mind there dwells an ideality which gives us a guarantee that this will not be pushed into the background even among the people by the strongly emerging material endeavors; finally, his direction toward the arts of peace, to which he is devoted from a pure inner impulse for their own sake, not from external or self-interested grounds, and his mild sense of justice toward all classes of the people, stir our souls to the consoling foreboding of a better future for the race.

Besides the general love for the illustrious royal house and the general attachment to the person of the father of the country, which we share with the other members of the state, the masters and disciples of science—since precisely they are pointed to the ideal and its implantation in the state, or, in the words of my authority, to "the transformation of knowledge, of reason, of wisdom, into life itself and into its highest source and impulse"—are, if possible, even more intimately linked with our king and lord.
May we all always be mindful of it!

In this wish all the good is united that we ourselves might wish for; and all that we can implore for people and state is united in the voice of the people, which rises to heaven: God bless the King and his house!

div.head: VIII. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1855.
Ueber die Pflichten der Männer der Wissenschaft gemäfs der bisherigen Entwickelung und dem gegenwärtigen Standpunkt derselben

p.s: This day, a day of the most general and joyous festivity for this land, highly esteemed listeners, is dedicated to the noble feelings of reverence and gratitude that we owe to the one being honored.

Are the two feelings not necessarily bound up with one another, since even without benefits received we honor great qualities for their own sake, and since for benefits we must also be grateful to those who claim our veneration neither by virtue of a bond of nature nor through their exalted station nor on account of outstanding excellence; yet these feelings, inseparably interwoven, rise from our hearts to a prince to whom such a celebration is worthily devoted.

We are all children of one fatherland, which, according to ancient tradition, is entitled to demand from us the same gratitude and the same reverence as our parents; this duty passes from that impersonal community to the personal embodiment of the state as a whole, the King.

We all stand, without distinction, at a great distance beneath the consecrated head from which most of the benefits that the fatherland grants flow to us; for this reason too, reverence and gratitude toward the King converge as one.
And who does not clearly recognize, or deeply feel, that this king's heart, animated only by benevolence, and his lofty spirit exclude every separation of those feelings within us?

Both gratitude and reverence show themselves in word and deed; but everywhere the deed is to be preferred to the word, insofar as a deed can be performed at all by us, the teachers and students of science.

For our activity consists in knowing and in the communication and dissemination of that knowledge: it is for this that our place has been assigned to us in this association of human beings for the attainment of all the ends of the race, which we call the
state.

The king, however, is the state in a purer sense than that in which this word was spoken in former times; for in him, as the center, all the peripheral activities of the life of the state unite, which with his wisdom he embraces centrally, without himself entering into the periphery.

Now we honor the fatherland and are grateful to it when each person in the state does his part in his own place according to the best of his knowledge and conscience: precisely thereby, then, each person will actively show himself to the bearer of the whole, the prince, as a grateful admirer.

That the comprehensive mind of Frederick William IV has grown equal to the Atlantic burden of bearing the entire state cannot be set forth in all its relations without entering the domain of the panegyrical, which one seeks to avoid in the same measure in which one feels truly and deeply; and we are concerned first of all with his relation to scholarship, whose worth only few princes have recognized as he has.

Therefore I may harbor no scruple about lingering in this solemn hour upon that whereby, in my judgment, the men of science, in accordance with the previous development of science and its present state, do their part and thus, as toward the fatherland and the state, so toward the exalted prince, actively fulfill the duties that correspond to those united feelings of the heart.

In undertaking this, I feel very well that neither the form of speech to which I am bound nor the time allotted for its execution, conventionally measured out as it were, is favorable to the task, nor does my range of vision suffice for the great overview that is required here: may you, then, highly honored assembly, attend more to the endeavor than to the success.
We all strive toward a distant goal, and whoever does not reach it may at least take joy in the consciousness that he is unswervingly directed toward it.

Concerning the stages or phases in which human cognition and knowledge are supposed to have developed, but above all concerning their beginnings, the most varied views have been held—not only in recent times, but from ancient times onward.

Some attribute to the earliest human race a brutish coarseness and wildness, as the Greeks already imagined: that in Arcadia King Pelasgos first invented giving humans protection against
cold and rain and heat by means of huts, making clothes from pigskin, and eating good and palatable acorns instead of green leaves and grasses and barely edible roots. Others, by contrast, posit a paradisiacal state of the first humans, which is also represented in the myths of the Cronian or Saturnian life; and from this it is no great step to the thought that those first humans enjoyed not only a blessed innocence but also a clear and certain intuition or knowledge of eternal and supersensible truths—indeed, even of the most important scientific knowledge, which, on the contrary, demonstrably was discovered in the course of historically known times through slow progress. And they are supposed to have owed all this either to their own invention or to the beginnings of all culture and to language, as a direct revelation and guidance of the divine spirit, or to the instruction of earlier natures endowed with a higher reason: for even notable thinkers—not merely scholars caught in traditional prejudices—have regarded it as unthinkable or impossible that this race could have been capable, without higher aid, of raising itself above its animal nature to thought and to the communication of what is thought, which is the first condition of social and intellectual intercourse, to the moral formation of family and state, to right and law, religion and art—in short, to a life of reason.
All such views rest on an underestimation of human nature.

If we still see today, among the nations as among individual human beings, a very great diversity of natural endowment, then one is not entitled to assume that the original stocks of our race were altogether in a state of savagery and crudeness, like the wild and neglected tribes of America, from which people have drawn conclusions about the condition of the earliest human beings; rather, among these, nobler lineages stood out, and by the inherent inner power of their inborn nature they raised themselves above the animal impulse.
"Many are the mighty things, and nothing is mightier than man," the wise poet said already thousands of years ago.

This is precisely the force and power of man: that the natural drive or instinct with which the Creator has equipped him is an instinct of reason, which, before reason has grown
up and gained strength, has overcome the most difficult obstacles and, as it were, worked wonders. But because human beings have acquired their culture for themselves, it has been acquired slowly and by stages, in beginnings that lie beyond all history.

If we remain true to our purpose and keep to what is most immediately connected with the domain of knowledge, and pass over in silence the bold and mighty works of an astonishing technology supported by great labor forces, then from the oldest traces that reach across to us, appearing to our eyes as if in the dim light of dawn, we may form a view of what may be called the primeval knowledge of humanity.

In the oldest traditions we find a rich treasure of already finished conceptions of the divine as of all that is human, moral, and natural, among many peoples, chiefly of the East, to which I also reckon Egypt, but also of the West, whose peoples, insofar as they belong to the Indo-Germanic language family, share a common primeval origin with a great part of the Eastern peoples, and especially among the Greeks, who have attained the highest culture of all these peoples.

I mean the treasure of the so-called myths, which has probably grown over thousands of years out of the most varied components and has, as it were, been deposited out of various strata that settled and were laid one over another from several successive formative processes, not without the original core being often veiled to the point of unrecognizability by what later accrued, and the strata themselves being thrown together into an almost inseparable mixture.

It is common to all the principal manifestations of myth that they present the supratemporal in the form of the temporal, and the impersonal as personal, even states, properties, and qualities, sensations, feelings, and thoughts: thus the nonsensible is embodied in something sensible, as the idea is in appearance.

Certainly the invention of the higher forms of myth required great depth of intuition, powerful imagination, and a fullness of creative activity that sprang from religious feeling and spread abroad in a poetry closely allied to it: seized and inspired especially by the impressions of nature, the soul rose to ecstasy, to which
the earlier human race, and particularly the Orientals, but also the Greeks in earlier times, were very much inclined; for which reason, at this stage of culture, divination and the practice of oracles also play a great role and exert a significant influence.

Certainly, in these myths—even in those connected with nature religions—great and sublime presentiments of the divine are contained, and in the Hellenic development the myth was further ennobled by the fact that the original symbols of the nature religions received a more spiritual content, just as Apollo became the symbol of the spiritual from a symbol of natural light.

Early on, however, the myth lost its significance, and of the symbol only the image survived in popular belief; only the myths most full of presentiment preserved themselves far down into the mysteries, which, in connection with consecrations and purifications, opened—not, to be sure, through doctrine, but through sacred contemplations—a serene and joyful view out of this world and the finite into the beyond and the infinite, and, in Cicero's phrase, granted a better hope of dying: whoever has beheld them, says the poet, knows the end of life, knows its God-given beginning.

Indeed, however vehemently the hierophants and servants of the mysteries still resisted Christianity in the last times, it has nevertheless been conjectured, not without all reason, that the nobler and purer forms of the mythos that lived on in them were conducive to Christianity and made minds more receptive to it.

“Nature,” remarks a profound thinker, “has wisely provided, for human eyes, through its arrangement, that they pass over into full day only through twilight”; this twilight, and indeed one of very long duration, in which the inner light was, as it were, bound, is, for the cognition of humanity, the entire period in which the mythical mode of intuition predominates.

But even before the latest offshoots of the latter, the need for an image-less knowledge had arisen—not, to be sure, in the Orient, which is less inclined to clear scientific cognition and is the proper soil of myth, but among the Hellenes, among the bearers of intellectual life.

Gradually reflection had ripened, whose first strengthening coincides with the first use of unbound
speech instead of bound speech in works of literature; for in the same period and in essential connection with it there begins both historiography and philosophy: people now wished to recognize the facts in themselves, with the stripping away of the wonderful and the fantastic into which the earlier mode of perception had involuntarily drawn them, and to grasp the grounds of things in general determinations, not through and for the imagination, but through and for thought.

The common fundamental trait of all Hellenic philosophy, regardless of doctrine, from the Ionian physiologists onward, lies in the inquiry into the primal grounds or causes—given the small extent of the experience available to them, mostly according to concepts of their own making, and for the most part with a rejection of the judgment of the senses.

The Ionians almost universally found the primal ground of things in living matter, which, to be sure, some of them determined only empirically, according to an imperfect experience, while the more advanced among them also did not regard even the material primal ground as perceptible to the senses; only Anaxagoras separated spirit from matter and posited it as the ordering principle of unordered matter.

The Eleatics have the merit of having established the concept of the one and absolute being, which is identical with thought, in opposition to the non-being or becoming of the many and manifold, and of having carried it through dialectically.

The Pythagorean school sought to grasp the essence and form of things, even of moral things, in measure and number, as it were as new images of concepts—no longer such as were created by the poetic imagination like the myths, but by mathematical intuition and the mathematical understanding—and thereby laid the first foundation of the mathematical sciences: of arithmetic, including harmonics, of geometry, and in some respect also of astronomy, which, like all the particular but as yet undeveloped sciences, were included in philosophy.

These theories, with few exceptions, related to nature, although the Pythagoreans practically strove for the realization of a moral life in their society and in the states over which they had influence; only Socrates gave the philosophizing spirit its principal direction toward moral teaching and at the
same time toward the contemplation of one's own inner self, in that he directed man to self-knowledge.

To pass over the remaining schools, which sprang from the Socratic teaching as branches from a knot, the profound Plato overcame the one-sidedness of the earlier systems not through an external eclectic combination but by means of an inner fusion of the principles; he comprehended the natural and the moral, both in connection, though with a predominance of the moral; he traced all knowledge back to reason as its source and to the ideas of reason, yet brought the mathematical concepts into relation with this, regarding mathematics as a guide of the soul to the knowledge of that which is; on the other hand, he disdained the judgment of the senses to such a degree that he will trust neither the eye for astronomy nor the ear for music, and even mocks the musicians when they measure the tones and chords actually heard against one another and hold up their ears at the sounds as though they wanted to eavesdrop a note from their neighbor, instead of, esteeming reason higher than the ear, seeking which numbers are the harmonious ones and which are not, and why both.

Plato's great pupil Aristotle, who divided the whole domain of philosophy more precisely and embraced all its parts, indeed departed considerably from his teacher's idealism and gave experience more of its due; but nevertheless he too follows the path of conceptual, purely philosophical speculation concerning the ultimate grounds.
Even the next principal dogmatic schools remain alike in their speculative direction, for all their diversity of view.

But after the Hellenic philosophy in the stricter sense had run its course, the Neoplatonic philosophy arose under the influence of enthusiastic Oriental conceptions, and its summit is Plotinus. In that he, through the intellectual intuition that precedes thought, recognizes the absolute One, the ground and essence of all things, and sinks himself into it to the point of identity, the striving after the supersensible and the removal from the world of experience reached their peak in him; at the same time, however, this school, notwithstanding all its dialectic, falls back to the mythical level both by virtue of its ecstatic ground of
knowledge and through its connection with magic, telestics, and mantic: indeed Proclus went so far in this direction that, apart from the Timaeus and the oracular sayings, he would have wished to destroy all the old books, if it had been in his power, because they might harm many.
The scholastic philosophy of the Middle Ages, which lies further from my own studies, may be permitted to touch upon in a few words.

Its foundation is historical revelation together with Aristotelian philosophy, since Plato was known to only a few; the latter served partly merely as a handmaid for the logical or dialectical development of Christian dogma, and partly was placed more freely alongside the philosophy of revelation: yet the whole of Scholasticism moved precisely, again in the realm of speculation, which also in a few outstanding minds, not without falling prey to persecution, took a lofty flight: by contrast, experience, nature, and history, and the tasteful cultivation of eloquence, which the ancients had known how to combine with philosophical exposition, were utterly neglected.

Despite all the acumen and the great intellectual powers that were devoted to it, the dominion of Scholasticism over the universities held minds in the fetters of a barren formalism—one bound, moreover, by the Church—throughout the centuries of its duration.
After the restoration of the sciences, philosophical views largely divided once again between Aristotle and Plato, or the new Platonism; mystical and enthusiastic tendencies also joined them anew.
But soon there began a series of distinctive and independent great thinkers, of whom I shall name only Descartes, Malebranche, Spinoza, and Leibniz, whose profound philosophemes were by Chr.
were flattened out by Wolff: although several of these were equipped with great mathematical and empirical knowledge, the center and core of their teaching is nevertheless speculative.

And after the critical philosophy of the great and far-reaching Kant had, by means of a more exact investigation of the cognitive faculty, set narrower limits to the knowledge of mortals, these limits were nevertheless again widely overstepped in the period that immediately followed: with what boldness, and to what height and depth, speculation was developed by
all the now departed heroes of philosophy who taught precisely at this university—by Fichte, Hegel, and Schelling—I scarcely need to recall.

These forms of philosophizing have also had a powerful influence on the particular sciences that serve the needs and purposes of society—sciences which, being directed toward the more general, I do not draw into the circle of consideration—and on the overall formation of the age.

Yet every significant development of dogmatism has been accompanied, or followed close upon the heels, by a skepticism corresponding to the standpoint of that particular moment and calling into question the possibility of knowledge, counting from the Hellenic Sophists onward; and although in our time skepticism does not appear to have received a sharper scientific grounding, many nevertheless believe that speculation, exhausted by its utmost exertions, has proved by trial its incapacity to solve its tasks, and that a general weariness of it has set in, from which it can never recover.

Thus, it seems, we are left entirely dependent on experience, unless another ground of knowledge is introduced into science, one that lies outside the domain of ordinary experience as well as of the speculation of reason.
Experience extends to two domains: the history of human beings and nature.

In the former field the youthful spirit of man, once conscious of itself, made its first attempts somewhat earlier, after it had freed itself from the mythical view of things—a view that had originally governed this domain as well and had for the most part carried human history over into the marvelous, which is indispensable to the mythical.

Nature, by contrast, man early made subservient to himself and acquired for himself those experiences of it that were useful for the practical purposes of life; but in science this empirical knowledge found entry relatively later than one should have expected given the prevailing sensuousness of antiquity; for science strove after theory, which did not seem to be given in experience.

To pass over earlier matters, with the enumeration of which I do not wish to weary you, it was Aristotle who first practiced a more extensive scientific
empiricism in the field of nature, at a time when the genuine Hellenic spirit was already advancing strongly toward decline; and the following age of Alexandrian scholarship extended this empiricism both in the field of human history, to which language and literature also belong, and in that of nature—in the latter to a lesser degree, yet most significantly still in astronomy.

It is indisputable that, according to the counsel of Providence, which at times permits a decline in culture—though not without that very decline bearing fruitful seeds for the time that followed—the course of development that had begun was checked and interrupted by the Middle Ages, more so for experience than for speculation.
Science stood in need of renewal.

The organon of all empirical science is induction, which does not descend from concepts or ideas to the particular, but strives to arrive from sensibly observed facts at general laws; this method, although sufficiently known to antiquity, was first brought to the honor—only after the overcoming of medieval philosophy—by Francis Bacon, who in this matter had only a few and less significant predecessors, namely that by means of it the whole edifice of knowledge was to be erected.

One cannot maintain that this path is suited only to the natural sciences; on the contrary, historical and philological research proceeds in a similar manner. Nevertheless, it is preeminently the natural sciences that have been designated by the name of the inductive, and these, down to our own time, and especially in this very time, have made on this path an admirable progress that opens up almost boundless prospects and hopes for the future; and through an initially unforeseen dispensation, mathematics had to come to the aid of this empirical inquiry most effectively—mathematics, a pure invention of the mind, was originally set in direct opposition to empirical inquiry, and was therefore recommended and promoted by the most decided opponents of experience.

So that, however, this progress with respect to historical studies may not be overestimated, it must not go unnoticed that these too have gained significantly in extent and depth in a similar way, in that not only linguistic research—with regard both to the classical and Oriental languages and to general and
comparative linguistics—but also the knowledge of the literatures of all more cultivated peoples, of public and private life, of commerce, of religions, sciences, and arts and their monuments, have been brought, through collection, interpretation, and critical sifting, and finally through skillful combination, to a level with which the stock of knowledge inherited from earlier times cannot bear comparison: only that, to be sure, this branch of the empirical sciences lacks the mighty lever that natural science possesses in instrumentation and in experiment, which, guided by intelligent purpose and sometimes favored by chance, compels nature to reveal its hidden inner being.
Nothing can give historical research a substitute for the telescope and the microscope and the rest of the apparatus of the physical sciences.

Thus, it seems, if in our time speculation has lost its old prestige, experience, on the other hand, raised to the philosophical throne, celebrates its highest triumphs over its grave—triumphs all the more brilliant since the one side of the empirical sciences has invented the means for countless advantages, alleviations, and conveniences of the life of mortals, and has taught them, almost superhumanly, to overcome the barriers of space and time for movement and the communication of thought.

If I have permitted myself, highly esteemed listeners, to designate these principal directions of human cognition so far as seemed possible in a general survey, which necessarily suffers from indeterminacy, then the question forces itself upon us of its own accord and unsought: whether, after we have through experience brought it so gloriously far, we must now entirely renounce that cognition which speculation has arrogated to itself, as something wholly empty and unsatisfying, or not.

Indeed, the human race would be to be pitied if the exertions of the noblest and most gifted minds—among whom the ablest bearers of speculation are indisputably counted—had produced and accomplished nothing further than the final conviction that their strivings had led only to the proof of their own nullity.

If, to be sure, one proceeds from the assumption that only sensible things
are real, while our mind is nothing but that blank tablet on which external impressions are caught and copied, and that this mind is incapable of producing from itself concepts and ideas rooted in it, and that there is therefore for it no possibility of knowing, and so presumably also none of acting from within, with self-determination, self-activity, and freedom, then we shall have to resign ourselves to that commiseration of human weakness. But for my part I am convinced that this view is a superficial one, and even rests on a mode of thinking that moves in a circle.
Everything general and all unity is the work of the spirit or of thought, since the senses offer only individual things and multiplicity, and that cannot come into the spirit from outside.

Whoever casts away everything that speculation has drawn from the spirit over the course of millennia deprives the understanding of mortals of the fairest and most elevating views of the supersensible, which—though dimmed by the mists that surround even our inner eye—has nonetheless shone across to us from the most ancient times as if from an ideal world, and is the one constant and truly existent thing amid the change of things, an eternal, never-failing source of our limited knowledge.

To be sure, myth also contains such glimpses; yet science must regard it as overcome: for as presentiment it has its justification only for feeling, not for knowledge, unless as a stimulus and figurative embellishment or as an object of philosophical and historical research and explanation.

But so that the creative spirit of pure science may not presume too much and soar too high, experience stands at its side; experience must prove the thought, and in turn thought casts light on what experience offers.

Both, if they are correct, must meet in the middle from different starting points—the idea from the spiritual and universal, experience from the sensory and particular; both must live in one another, appearance and fact must be taken up into thought, and thought must be brought to appearance: thus the idea gives knowledge its soul-like element, experience gives it matter and body, and in the unity and interpenetration of the two, joined like soul and body, science has its organic
formation and its organic life, in which the opposition and conflict of speculation and experience is sublated.
This union at the same time brings about a purification of speculation and a refinement of empirical knowledge.

For speculation has often clung to superstition, and the deeper it sought or imagined it could penetrate into the secret of the supersensible, the more so; and the essence of superstition consists in this: that man ascribes to a supernatural effect what lies in the natural law and course of things, whether it be that of a good or of an evil personal principle, which was early posited in a dualistic worldview of the Orient; or that man derives as fact, from such influences, what is not fact at all; finally, that he believes he can even compel such supernatural effects by human means.

I have already reminded you, in three words, at the name of the sublime Plotinus, how speculation is polluted by such excrescences, and something similar recurs in almost all enthusiastic speculations: after all, even the immortal Kepler, to whom we owe the discovery of important laws of nature, could not free himself from astrological divination, which is likewise a product of the Orient, coming from the Chaldeans.

A time shows how sad the consequences of such aberrations of the human spirit are—a time in which these had also taken possession of the Church and the State, and jurisprudence invented the forms for the cruel punishment of misdeeds, which had their justification only in the fanatical delusion of crude and heartless zealots.

It is a great merit, above all of empirical natural science, to have destroyed the wild monstrosities of darkness; yet historical research also has its share in this, in that through criticism it lays bare what is credible and what is not credible in the transmitted tradition.

Broadly speaking, and put quite generally, speculation is purified by experience in that the false facts are withdrawn from it: for since it seeks to ground what is given through the idea and, starting from the idea, ends in what is given, it becomes impure when what is given is false.

Thus Plato and Aristotle directed their physical speculations toward geocentric
astronomy: those speculations would have turned out quite differently had other empirical facts about the world system been available to the philosophers.

On the other side, empirical knowledge is ennobled by speculation, or the Idea, because all isolated knowledge is unsatisfying to the mind, which itself strives only as one toward unity and wishes to grasp all multiplicity as part of a whole; taken up into that whole, even the smallest thing acquires a worth that it does not have on its own. This unity cannot be attained without the Idea, and the Idea is needed all the more, the more massively the material grows, so that the mind may not degenerate and perish in the sensory and the material.

The full reward for the laborious procurement of the material that science requires comes to us precisely through the consciousness that the building stones we gather together gradually join into a unified work of art and magnificent edifice of human knowledge, even though its completion lies in the far distance because of the infinity of science.

If for the erection of this edifice the division of labor is a necessary law, and even the individual of the greatest gifts cannot embrace the whole in its full extent, yet just as the purpose of the civil state is accomplished by the totality of its members, so is the purpose of science accomplished by the totality of the scholarly state: only, in accordance with the essence of science, all within it should be equals and none merely a hired hand; rather each, however much he may limit himself, should recognize microcosmically, in his bounded subject, the idea of the whole in its depth.

To practice and to teach science in the spirit of this interpenetration of idea and experience has, to be sure, been the calling of university teachers not merely since yesterday and today, but on the present level of culture it seems to be quite preeminently so.
I believe that in so doing I am giving expression not to my own particular view but to your general view, esteemed colleagues—your view, to which it is my task and my endeavor to give expression.

But you, the students of this university—you who, according to the old German custom that would have the constraint of school discipline removed from these institutions, have of your own free will chosen us as your teachers—I may remind you of this and
exhort you to take possession of knowledge along this path that we have tested, and to surrender neither to hollow speculation nor to mindless empiricism. At the same time, returning to the beginning of my speech, I may give expression to the conviction that we and you, if in this spirit we do our part, will show ourselves grateful admirers of the King, our lord, whose lofty mind is as surely directed toward the ideal side of knowledge as it is prudent and clear in appreciating the vast realm of scientific experience.

But starting points and end points other than those indicated do not exist for science, and universally valid for every free doctrine not bound by a positive [system] is the pronouncement that one of our excellent teachers recently made concerning natural science: "To seek to lead contemplation, on grounds foreign to it and not presenting themselves within the context of its own development, toward some goal desired from outside, is and remains an impotent endeavor." How far, furthermore, the knowledge thus gained is to be cultivated into the great circles of the state and the people—this question must first of all be answered by the statesman.

For the state he answered it long ago: we ourselves at this place are the living proof that the state recognizes science as one of its elements, and he does this, as I showed earlier on this same festive day, not merely for the bare minimum training of the servants who attend to his affairs, but also so that his own principles may be purified and ennobled: truly, no one recognizes this more clearly than our spirited King!
But even the great Frederick despaired of leading the people, down to the lowest strata, to knowledge, when he called the prejudices the reason of the people.
Nor is this our task.

Yet alongside the cultivation of feeling and of the mind, the spread of piety and of morality, which fall primarily to the teachers of religion, the man who does not seek his own advantage and his own elevation at the expense of others—the true friend of humanity will wish the greatest possible measure of knowledge spread through the whole people: the sun does not wish to shine only on the mountain peaks and the high summits; it wishes also to penetrate into the depths of
the valleys and the clefts. Let us not be frightened by the specters that a mostly selfish fear of popular education conjures up out of itself: man is not the most terrible thing in his knowing, but the most terrible thing in his delusion.
But who could be a truer friend of humanity than Frederick William IV?
Who could be less opposed to the light of knowledge penetrating and pervading as far as possible?
Highly esteemed assembly!

The science to which we devote ourselves has its worth in itself even apart from its application to state and people; in and of itself it is a need of the spirit, because it is of a spiritual nature: indeed, whoever regards it merely as a means for life has not received its consecration.

Not amid the noise of the world does the scholarly man form himself: he needs a withdrawal, so that the mind may expand more freely, a collectedness that he cannot gain in the distracting marketplace, in the benumbing din of life.
That is why states and princes have founded these quiet sanctuaries of learning, in which we, teachers and learners, are united.
Happy the people whose prince, himself capable of a noble collectedness of mind and of deepening into the sanctuary of the inner self, honors and cultivates science for its own sake!
We enjoy this happiness to the full.

Yet it would be selfish if we wished to praise the King only because he grants us this leisure: we praise him because we recognize in him the noblest of princes, and we love him for the sake of his whole excellence.

And therefore we beseech God that He may preserve him and his entire house for us, for the welfare of the state and people for which He has called him to the throne, and that He may guide and lead all his resolutions to the most beneficial goal of fulfillment.

div.head: IX. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1856.
Ueber den Sinn und Geist der Gründung der Berliner Universität

p.s: We are gathered here today in celebration, highly esteemed listeners, in order to commemorate within the circle of the university a festival that is shared by the whole land, but is all the more sacred to the academic bodies the more they have become partakers of the King's favor, whose birth we celebrate today, and above all to our university, which, dwelling in the capital of the realm and near the throne, draws particular attention to itself.

Such festal gatherings the Hellenes, the teachers of human cultivation, designated by the name of panegyris, because the whole people flowed together to them; in these same gatherings unfolded the flower of gymnastic and musical arts in the noblest contest, and the victors in these peaceful struggles were praised in songs in which, together with the praise of those victors, the praise of the fatherland was likewise proclaimed.

A not joyful, but for that very reason more sublime panegyris was occasioned by the pious custom of the Athenians of burying, at public expense, the ashes and bones of those fallen in war in their native soil; to honor their memory was the task no longer of the poet, but of the orator.
Thus arose the speech that we call the panegyric.

If the praise of those to whom it was in the first instance directed was inseparable from her, the orator could nevertheless no more than the poet otherwise, without renouncing higher demands, stop short at this or even place it in the foreground alone: for besides that the finer sense rejects it as vulgar to lay the praise on thick—a sense which has, to be sure, been lost to the panegyrists of the Roman imperial age and to many later ones—regard for the particular character of the assembly requires that something be offered to it that has a bearing on it as well.

It is not the first time today that I give expression to this view of
mine concerning my calling—that of speaking on the highly joyful birthday of our most gracious King—before this honored assembly; but I must indeed permit myself this repetition, since it would be presumptuous to believe that everything I said earlier in this place is still remembered by all who heard it, and since with each year the band of young men is renewed as it changes, those who are gathered here as for our scholarly lectures, so for this celebration.

Consciously and unconsciously, much else may be said again: new material could be expected here on this day only if our academic body followed the example of the Athenians, who for each of their panegyric assemblies every time appointed by special election an orator who stood out in insight and prestige, like that Pericles; and the more I know how to acknowledge the preference granted to me once and for all, the more convinced I am that the election would then choose worthier men and open the way to the expression of more varied and more many-sided views.

May it then not seem strange if today I speak of a subject that at an earlier time was at least not left untouched, one that lies far beyond the reign of Frederick William IV, if I lead you back to the time in which the great-hearted King grew up into a young man.

I mean the time of the founding of this university: I intend to recall the spirit and mind from which the latter sprang and in which it was founded; I hope that even without a more detailed demonstration it will emerge from the matter itself that this spirit and mind correspond to the spirit of the exalted prince for whose veneration we are assembled here today, to the same degree as if he himself had been its founder, and that we may found upon this the firm confidence that he will maintain it continually for the welfare and benefit of scholarship and of the land, just as his father, now resting in God, who called it into life, originally established it with the counsel of high-minded and scholarly highly cultivated men.
In choosing this subject for consideration, I at the same time partially attain what I had missed and desired—the ability to let worthier men speak in my place.

That here I must touch upon persons, matters, and principles which were mentioned at this place a short while
ago, and that on these I shall have to express myself in a similar manner to the esteemed orator of the last third of August, has not been able to deter me from the choice of this subject; rather, it will be a satisfaction to me if my present lecture should be regarded as a further elaboration and closer explanation of certain utterances and hints which that spirited speech laid before us.

In these days half a century is drawing to a close since the University of Halle—which, under the care of Frederick William III, held an honorable place alongside the neighboring foreign universities of Leipzig, Jena, and Göttingen, and towered beyond comparison over the remaining Prussian ones—was dissolved by the victor of Jena.

Even though it was shortly afterward restored by the foreign ruler to whom this part of the country had fallen, it was nevertheless lost to Prussia; the two universities that remained to the country could not suffice for it even in its diminished extent—the one at Königsberg already because of its remoteness, the other at Frankfurt an der Oder because it suffered from defects difficult to cure.

Scarcely had Halle, in July 1807, been formally ceded by the Peace of Tilsit when the voices of several teachers of the University of Halle loyal to their hereditary sovereign found a hearing; these, in August of that same year, in their own name and in that of other colleagues, petitioned for the founding of a university in Berlin. It must be acknowledged that Schmalz, the former Director of the University of Halle, who later alienated his colleagues here through a fateful indiscretion, was the first personally to bring this wish forward at Memel, supported by the written cooperation of Fr. Aug. Wolf and the oral cooperation of Hufeland.

Already on September 4, 1807, the King issued the cabinet order to establish a university in Berlin in appropriate connection with the Academy of Sciences, since in the new organization of the state one of the first concerns must be to replace the loss of the University of Halle, formerly the most important and most complete general institution of learning in Prussia.

I should be doing something superfluous if I wished here to set forth what spirit animated the government in the first years of the diminution of Prussian power, how, in the conviction that
even on the edge of the abyss one must not give up courage and hope, it strove in every direction to rebuild the state on sounder foundations without destroying what was good in the old order, but especially to awaken and strengthen the intellectual powers, and at the same time, in the realm that was though severely threatened, to secure for the rest of Germany, particularly Protestant Germany, a rallying point of German sentiment and German culture; the older among us also know from their own experience with what attention and joy Prussia's magnificent efforts toward rebirth were received and welcomed in the German fatherland.

Quite truthfully did the man—whom I shall continue to commemorate in greater detail—report in his official petition to the King for the establishment of this university, dated July 10, 1809: "Far from the confidence that all Germany formerly placed in Prussia's influence upon true enlightenment and intellectual cultivation having declined through the recent unfortunate events, it had rather increased; it had been seen what spirit prevailed in all the more recent state institutions of His Royal Majesty, and with what readiness, even amid great distress, scholarly institutions had been supported and improved."
His

His Royal Majesty could and would therefore continue to assert the first rank in Germany from this quarter and to exert the most decisive influence on its intellectual and moral direction." To this confidence, judges the same writer in the same report, the thought of establishing a general institution of learning in Berlin contributed very greatly, because only such higher institutes could extend their influence beyond the borders of the state; the King would thereby bind to himself anew, most firmly, all that in Germany partakes of culture and enlightenment.
Schleiermacher expressed himself similarly around the same time in his writing on the universities.

Thus Prussia, in spite of its humiliation, then became a refuge and a sanctuary, scarcely still hoped for, of the harshly enslaved German spirit, and in return won for itself the power of public opinion, whose value proves itself in dangerous times and even in times free from danger is not unrecognized with impunity.

But I will not dwell on this any
longer; it matters more to me to fix my eye on the scientific spirit of the age in which the idea of founding this university arose.
In the second half of the previous century, German education had changed substantially, chiefly through two deeply influential elements: poetry and philosophy.

The former, gradually freed since Lessing from the fetters of arbitrary and pedantic laws, and elevated by a study of antiquity that, though still very imperfect, was all the more inspired, had in Goethe and Schiller attained an ideal height and depth; the latter, from Kant onward, by casting off the old dogmatism, had grasped the faculty of knowledge itself at its root and had also exerted an influence on the particular sciences, above all on theology and jurisprudence.

Hereby the period of the so-called Enlightenment, to whose victory the government of Frederick the Great powerfully contributed, was in Germany, as it were, brought to completion; if this Enlightenment has fallen into disrepute through shallow minds who flattened it out, its consequences have nevertheless remained immeasurable, and only what was hollow and barren in it has withered away, while its living element has put forth noble shoots.
The poetry and the philosophy of that age are rooted in this living ground of the same, in the freedom of thought, and are imperishable monuments of it.

The philosophy of the beautiful, or of art, became a mediator between poetry and philosophy; the friendship of the two showed itself especially at the University of Jena, and in one and the same person pre-eminently in Schiller: under the protection of the Weimar princely house and in its seat, the blossom of poetry unfolded, and in the nearby small town philosophy, in free flight, swiftly overleapt the boundaries that had recently been set for it.
I need only recall Fichte, Hegel, and Schelling, who had their first significant activity there.

In that period, the two Schlegels exercised a very influential effect on the further development of the philosophical-poetic spirit; their deeper criticism, joined to a manifold knowledge of literature, fought down the outdated views. They and their closest kindred spirits at the same time wedded the Romantic and the medieval to that cultivation—a witty counterweight to the vulgar side of the Enlightenment, which soon even
produced a leaning toward Catholicism, to which several of the spokesmen of that time have also converted.

The University of Halle had at first remained rather a stranger to the new speculative-aesthetic direction, while in Berlin it was already very widespread among the educated, chiefly through Fichte and the brothers Schlegel; only in the last years before the university's dissolution had it been transplanted there with Schleiermacher and Steffens.

But wherever it appeared, it had an inspiring effect on the more gifted students of the universities; it pushed into the background the mechanical and craftsmanlike conduct of studies, the piling up of details that are merely material for knowledge without any awareness of the spiritual content, and thus also studying for merely practical ends, for which one used to acquire knowledge; and it directed learners toward the general and the spiritual, toward the unity for which all genuine science strives.
Knowledge was transfigured by the light of the ideal; from the soil of the free ideal it sought to send its tendrils heavenward.
I say it with full conviction: the youthful striving of the scholarship of that time had a higher character of ideality than the scholarship of the present.

One can say that under this direction the necessary investigation of particulars must have suffered considerably; but it was by no means unrecognized that there is a sound empirical practice which, even without philosophical or conceptual construction, by innate instinct and sure tact hits upon the right thing and comes halfway to meet philosophical knowledge; and the bearers of such an empirical practice, as in the philological and historical field F. A. Wolf and Johannes von Müller, also found the highest recognition among the philosophers and poets.

I scarcely venture to touch upon the relation of that direction to the natural sciences, which lie further from my own field; it seems, however, that even if the titanically bold undertaking to trace the real back to thought and concept, and nature back to spirit or to the identity of both, went astray along manifold paths, the ideality of contemplation, even in this domain, did not remain without some beneficial influence, and, as I believe I may assume, it also had at that time a
stimulating effect upon a great living man, to whom the extravagances of natural philosophy always remained foreign, but who stands out through greatness of ideas, all-sided mastery of the material, and artistic presentation.
In close association with the noblest minds, who gave the age that direction, stood the no longer living brother of the still living man to whom I have just alluded—I mean Wilhelm von Humboldt.

Poetry and art, philosophy, and above all the philosophy of the beautiful, nourished the purely human and ideal direction that was originally native to his sublime spirit, and they merged in him in the fullest harmony; but it was not a superficial aesthetic cultivation—rather, the finest taste was joined with the keenest judgment and with comprehensive and penetrating studies, especially of antiquity and of languages, the latter to an extent that went beyond the horizon of all earlier scholars: and again, the most thorough and most careful investigation of every detail was ennobled by the charm of expression poured over the content and by the thoughtful relation to the universal and the spiritual, entirely in keeping with the cultural period whose finest sides he combined, while the unclouded clarity of his understanding and freedom of his spirit preserved him from its faults.

At the same time, by his example he furnished proof that in outstanding natures neither official business weakens or even deadens the sense for science and art, nor does devotion to these detract from practical ability; rather, the latter is through knowledge assigned the worthiest goal and given the higher consecration. But the worthiest goal of practice is the stamping of the idea into reality; and if any man was suited to accomplish this as a true statesman or artist in statecraft—indeed, as a director of the highest internal and external affairs of state—as far as the circumstances and surroundings that everywhere impose limits would permit, it was Wilhelm von Humboldt, in his enthusiasm equally great for the fatherland and for nobler culture.

Calm, patient, persevering, true to his principles, he never lost sight of his goal; and with the most deliberate and most unprejudiced, indeed seemingly cold, appraisal of things, he combined heart and feeling for persons.
To this man, in the memorable time when the founding of the Berlin University, already decided upon earlier, was actually taken in hand, the supreme direction of the educational system was entrusted; from his hand came the already mentioned petition to the King of the year 1809, and under him there took part in the conduct of the scientific affairs of the state men distinguished by noble cultivation of mind and heart and by a free and ideal spirit, of whom I will name only Nicolovius and Süvern: but there was also needed a finance minister of like mind, in order, in the state's distressed situation, willingly to make ample funds available for the scientific institutions, and such a one was found in Altenstein, whose heartfelt love and veneration of the sciences was later to prove itself in his administration, to our highest gratitude.

With the counsel of such men, the wise and experienced King did not set for the new university the lesser purpose—one that could, to be sure, be achieved perhaps better through special schools, though not without the danger of losing the nobler cultivation—of schooling or even drilling servants for the necessary and merely indispensable business of the state and for the ordinary vocations of life: what was intended was a school of genuine science, whose influence extends beyond the borders of the land, because it is not calculated directly upon the needs of the particular state and is not conditioned and determined by them: as we have seen, a spiritual conquest was to be made.

It is well known that the thought also hovered in the air, as it were, of raising the University of Berlin to a higher institution of learning over against the other universities, at which the students would complete the close of so-called academic study and, as it were, receive the final consecration: yet this was not only scarcely practicable, but also involved in itself an arrogance and presumption that none of the German universities may allow itself toward others, since all of them, rather, free from conceit and self-seeking, must regard themselves as equal communities of the republic of scholars.

To be sure, this thought might seem to have a justification in the fact that a university in a capital city already equipped with manifold institutions and resources of art and science could offer more opportunity
for a more complete education; but although the institutions already existing in Berlin earlier, namely the Academy of Sciences, even then offered some distinguished men who at the outset worked voluntarily at the university, still their regular assistance could not be counted upon with certainty for the long term; and if the talk is of resources consisting in collections and in localities well appointed for specific scholarly purposes, then a highly placed former member of our university, highly deserving of science, has with great right publicly declared that even in very recent times universities with quite meager collections have called forth a vigorous intellectual life, while the richest collections afford no protection against instruction sinking into utter lifelessness, and that the opinion must not become fixed that without collections of the first rank a university could, as it were, be reckoned only to the second class of educational institutions.
If much depends on abundant resources, still more depends on the spirit that is not bound to the capitals, indeed often develops most freely in the seclusion of a small place.

Moreover, it depends solely on the generosity of the governments whether they wish to accumulate larger resources in smaller places and outside the capital; and we would be doing an injustice to other universities if we wished to regard our resources, without exception, as the richest and most perfect.

But I return to the fundamental idea that here a school of genuine science was to be established, in which, accordingly, the viewpoints of specialized scholarship and of teaching and learning for the individual profession were by no means to predominate.

Wilhelm von Humboldt himself emphasized it: the authority for public instruction must keep the promotion of general education in view; it must see to it that scholarly education not be fragmented piecemeal according to external purposes and conditions, but rather be gathered into one focal point for the attainment of the highest universally human.

Meanwhile, it could not be the intention to narrow the traditional circle of university teaching and to exclude from it the education of theologians
and pastors, of jurists and officials of law and administration, and of physicians, and thereby to diminish the practical influence of the university: the one-sided pursuit of universality would rather have been in contradiction with the realization of thought in life, with the interpenetration of theory and practice, which was a demand of the age in its development: only, all specialized study—even the striving of the less capable hangers-on, for whom the pattern must surely not be made—should be immersed in the ether of free, universal scientific spirit.
The freest, most comprehensive, most universal knowledge is philosophical knowledge.

If states have as a rule, from the earliest times onward, been disinclined toward philosophy—because, to say no more, the former wish to hold fast to what exists and what has been handed down, while the latter strives after what ought to be—then at that time this opposition was less powerful, because the state itself was in the process of shaping its conditions, as far as possible, as they ought to be, and because the freedom of thought was in harmony with the state's struggle to regain its own political freedom.

Thus the course of my reflections carries me involuntarily—indeed, against my will—back again today to philosophy, and first of all to the recognition it then enjoyed, as earlier in Prussia, with few exceptions, from Leibniz down to Kant; without my intending, in emphasizing this, thereby to speak a word on behalf of the exaggerated claims of certain philosophers and their encroachment upon fields in which they were not sufficiently versed.
Philosophy was planted in this university from the very beginning as the all-quickening element, and in Fichte, Schleiermacher, and Solger it had distinguished representatives.

What the two first-named wrote about the nature of universities around the time of the founding of our university, and in connection with it, is too indicative of the sense and spirit of that time for me to be permitted to pass over it in silence; only let no one accuse me of one-sidedness or injustice, or even of impropriety, as though I wished to set the part of the university to which I myself primarily belong above the others, or to revive a contest of rank among the equally entitled academic bodies of the university—a thing from which I am so far removed that I at
once, from the very outset, disapprove Schleiermacher's saying that the philosophical faculty, even as the last, is yet the first, because everyone must recognize its independence, and on the other hand I guard against having attributed to me, as my own, what I communicate as another's opinion, since I do not find it appropriate to explain myself in greater detail from my own person on every point.

Already in 1807, at the instigation of the Privy Cabinet Councillor Beyme—who loved and promoted the sciences, placed his trust in Fichte, and took an eager part in the founding of the university—Fichte wrote a "deduced plan for a higher educational institution to be established in Berlin," which was officially submitted at that time and appeared in print ten years later.

He was entirely free not to bind himself to the old and the traditional, and he made full use of this freedom all the more because it was the task of his whole life and philosophizing to promote the perfection of humanity and to lead it onward to progress along new paths.

Earlier he had held inspiring and far-reaching lectures at two universities, at Jena and Erlangen, on the purpose of the student and of the scholar; he held the highest and worthiest view of this purpose and set it forth without any regard for approval or disapproval.

In his view, the scholar is by vocation the teacher of the human race, but he must look not only to the present but also to the future, toward which the human race must at every stage advance further, if it is not to stand still on the path to its final goal or even turn back; and since he cannot carry it forward to the goal at a single stroke, but must lead it there gradually, the scholar becomes for him the educator of humanity.

But the ultimate purpose of this is the moral ennoblement of the whole human being, which can proceed only from what is moral; therefore the scholar must be the morally best of men and must embody in himself the highest level of moral cultivation possible up to his time—a demand of the highest ideality, behind which reality, alas, all too often lags.

Furthermore, in his view only that person is a scholar who has truly arrived at the knowledge of the Idea through the learned education of the age, or who at least strives livingly and
powerfully to arrive at it, although he does not deny that one may also arrive at the Idea by another path: whoever does not attain to the knowledge of the Idea is, in his view, a scholar only in appearance and in mere opinion.

It therefore had to be the vocation of the university teacher to cultivate in his students a receptivity to the idea by means of the idea that had been formed in him with clear consciousness, bringing that idea before them expressed and clothed in the most varied forms and turns, and testing it upon them—for which he requires an artistic talent.

The university appears to him as a school of formation in the art of the free exercise of the scientific understanding, and indeed, to pass over many secondary qualifications, in such a way that science is not a means to any other end for the learner, but rather that he, in whatever manner he may in the future apply his scientific education in life, has the root of his life in the idea alone, beholds reality only from it and shapes reality according to it, and not the idea according to reality.

Now, he says, that which scientifically comprehends the whole of intellectual activity, and consequently also all the particular and further expressions of it, is philosophy; from philosophical artistic formation, therefore, the particular sciences must be given their art, and what in them hitherto was a mere natural gift dependent on good fortune must be raised to deliberate capability: with the developed philosophical spirit the whole scientific material must be grasped and penetrated in its organic unity.
It suffices for me to have stated his fundamental view, and I shall add only a few incidental remarks.

With his peculiar, rigid consistency, Fichte drafts a plan by virtue of which he must exclude much from his higher scientific teaching institution, namely theology, unless it would solemnly renounce its claim to a mystery; he arrives at the point of demanding, with an almost naive exclusiveness, a single philosophical teacher for the beginning of the institution, besides whom no other should have any influence on the development of the pupil toward philosophizing; of tracing everything back to encyclopedias as the first foundations of every science; and of assigning examinations—though, as he says, not in the spirit
of knowledge but in the spirit of art—and conversatoria a very significant role, although the latter, even if they are very important, cannot count as the predominant form of instruction, given that the relations of teaching and learning have, after all, taken shape since Plato and Aristotle.

Thus the most liberal-minded man of his age recommended an organization for the highest scientific institution that would have degenerated into the crudest mechanism and compulsion for scholarship and even for the state, which was to fill its most important offices with those who had emerged from this school, and into a complete caste system; indeed, he even goes to the extreme of a common household, of a division of the students into regulars and irregulars and a middle thing between the two, the novices, and finally so far that he assigns the regulars a uniform that no one is to be entitled to wear except them and the ordinary teachers.

Now if the authorities rightly gave no hearing to such exaggerated counsels, Fichte's influence, and with it the influence of philosophy on the university, was nevertheless very significant from the very beginning.

Not long after him, in the year 1808, Schleiermacher wrote his "Occasional Thoughts on Universities in the German Sense, together with an Appendix on One Newly to Be Established"—as far as I know, without official occasion, but for the most part with a view to the founding of the university here and certainly in the spirit of those who shortly thereafter put their hands to the work, since he was closely connected with them; his judgment is all the more important because he exercised a far-reaching influence on the university not only as a teacher, but also worked for several years in the highest educational authority.

Those who, he says, freely unite for the sake of science are not so much concerned with the accumulated particulars of knowledge, which the state alone is wont to value and to promote for its own use, as with "the consciousness of the necessary unity of all knowledge, of the laws and conditions of its origin, of the form and the stamp whereby in truth every perception, every thought is genuine knowledge"; "so too every human being whom they wish to form in their own likeness, even if only moderately equipped, they lead straight to this principal point of scientific unity and
form, train him in this way of seeing, and only then, after he has thus firmly established himself, let him go deeper into particulars, because he is to know everything truly in the stricter sense, and otherwise all heaping up of individual items of knowledge would be but an uncertain groping about, which could always have only a provisional value with a view to a better treatment."
