In discussing the difference between schools, universities, and academies, he identifies as the business of the university "to awaken the idea of science in those nobler young men already equipped with knowledge of various kinds, to help it to mastery over them in that field of knowledge to which each wishes especially to devote himself, so that it becomes second nature to them to regard everything from the standpoint of science, to contemplate everything individual not for itself but in its nearest scientific connections, and to enter it into a great context in constant relation to the unity and totality of knowledge, so that they learn to become conscious in every act of thought of the fundamental laws of science, and precisely thereby gradually to work out within themselves the capacity to research, to discover, and to present."
"The idea of knowledge, the highest consciousness of reason, is to be awakened as a guiding principle in man."
According to our Schleiermacher, there is no scientifically productive faculty without a speculative spirit; this depends, consciously or unconsciously, on a speculative orientation of reason.

For the university, therefore, "philosophical instruction is the foundation of everything that is pursued there; and because it is precisely these highest views that are to be communicated above all, and indeed in the most individual manner, they must also be presented in their difference from everything of a like kind that exists alongside them; hence it is above all at and between universities that philosophical disputes have their place, and it is chiefly at them that the philosophical schools form."

But "the scientific spirit as the highest principle, the immediate unity of all knowledge, cannot, for instance, be set up and exhibited by itself in mere transcendental philosophy, ghost-like, as unfortunately some have attempted and have thereby carried on spookery and an eerie business": only in its
living influence upon all knowledge can philosophy be presented; only together with its body, with real knowledge at the same time, can this spirit be represented and comprehended.

Therefore, knowledge is also imparted at the university." The supposed opposition between reason and experience, speculation and empiricism, he too wishes to see abolished: a point of view that I discussed in greater detail a year ago at this place in my own person.

And since science also needs the subordinate talents as faithful and capable workers, but the state needs them even more, the universities should at the same time be higher special schools for everything that, among useful branches of knowledge, is connected with genuine scientific education, without their two purposes being outwardly distinguished.
But it would lead too far if I wished here to communicate even only the most important things from Schleiermacher's writing that stand in the closest connection with what has been said.

If, moreover, in these proposals the philosophical element, the universal, and free education are everywhere emphasized most strongly, I must recall once more that genuine and sound empirical study, and also training for the practical disciplines, was not for that reason held in low esteem; but as the highest goal of scientific knowledge there hovered before us the interpenetration of theory and practice, of speculation and empiricism, of the ideal and the real—a point to which I, who am no professional philosopher, as you will easily judge, attach greater weight than to that strong emphasis on philosophy itself at that time.

This is a magnificent and sublime goal, which must be held before the eyes of scholars for all time, and which, I am certain of it and have already said so earlier, is also held before the eyes of the present teachers of this university and is set before their listeners by them.

If a noble sense and spirit have been implanted in an institution at its founding, it is a great gain for it when this spirit is handed down from generation to generation through an unbroken tradition, and there is no reason whatever to fear that through the constancy of its principles it will grow old and decay.

From the very beginning, a vigorous spirit has dwelt in this university: holding fast to the old customs of the academic body and working in
the old spirit therefore appears to me to be the most beneficial course for it, even though new scientific developments must take shape and young forces must step into the place of the old.
For how many are still left who, as teachers, saw this university in its youthful freshness?
Soon death will have swept them all away.

It is not appropriate today to stir up feelings of grief; but when I speak of the earliest times of this university, you would rightly miss it if I did not commemorate the loss that we suffered quite recently.

The man who has most recently been torn from us was the oldest member of the university, a man of the old stamp, of solid learning and noble disposition, wholly imbued with the spirit that animated the youthful university, not pliant nor always agreeable to everyone, yet full of heart and feeling, yet in unshakable loyalty and firmness a model reaching over from the old days for the younger generation.
But back to our subject.

In the course of this century the universities have more often been attacked, and from various quarters, as superfluous at the present standpoint of science and learning, or even as harmful—as superfluous, to dwell here on this point alone, especially because the communication of thoughts, the diffusion of knowledge and the learning of it, which in earlier times depended chiefly on oral instruction, can in our time, now that the world of books has won an extraordinary extension, be sufficiently accomplished by means of printed writings, from which anyone somewhat prepared by schooling can instruct himself more reliably.

But if the purpose of the university is conceived as it was conceived at the founding of our institution of learning, then one can scarcely assert with any semblance of plausibility that universities are superfluous or that they have, as some say, outlived their time.

If external dangers once threatened the universities of the German fatherland, which recognized in them a noble possession, these have now disappeared, and it will depend only on them that they preserve their inner worth by not allowing the higher unity of knowledge to recede before narrow specialized study and regard for the isolated profession, which of course must
not be lacking, and not allowing the ideal to recede before the real and the material.
But if I say that it will depend on them alone, then it must still matter greatly to us whether this spirit is also in accord with the King's mind.

It does not lie directly in the nature of a good sovereign that he should recognize science as such; indeed, since the affairs of the state and especially also the material prosperity of the country must draw his attention to a high degree, it is a natural and pardonable one-sidedness if he values science according to its useful consequences for the civil service and for ordinary life.

So that he may love and promote them for their own sake, he must value the spirit above all things; but this belongs only to the one who is wholly pervaded by the idea, the divine primal source of knowledge, and strives for its realization in the people and the state.

As such a one we recognize our exalted lord, King Frederick William IV, and therefore I said at the opening of this address that this university was founded entirely in the sense that it might have been founded by him himself and sprung from his spirit.

Thus, most honored assembly, we celebrate in him the high-minded preserver of this great scholarly community according to its original purpose—for us and in our place, teachers and learners closely united, and with us the noble guests who take part in our affairs, but at the same time, like all the communities of the land, the gracious father of the fatherland.

May the divine Providence continue to bestow upon him and the entire Royal House the blessing which it has hitherto poured out upon them in rich measure, and may the Father of Light cause the light of knowledge to shine throughout the whole land, beside and above outward goods, and may true virtue and piety, with which knowledge is in harmony, spread more and more in him.

div.head: X. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1857.
Vom Beruf des Königthums die Einheit aller Glieder der Gesellschaft zu vermitteln

p.s: The King, whose birthday we solemnly commemorate today, most honorable assembly, stands—as in every healthy realm, so too in our Prussian one—at once as the bearer of majesty, separated from all the other members of the state, exalted above all; and at the same time he, and he alone, nevertheless stands in the closest relation to each and every one through a firm bond, as it were through a family bond, as parents and children are linked with one another.

That is why we call him the father of his country, or the father of the fatherland; the most eloquent expression of this is that love, the tenderest and mightiest stirring of the human heart, the begetter of all that is beautiful and good, is to bind princes and peoples together in an indissoluble embrace.

Strife and friendship are, as a wise man has said, the forces at work in the world; but strife, though necessary, since without it there would be no motion, only dissolves, and if love does not bring the dissolved and opposed elements into harmony, no form can come into being.

The union of the discordant into unity, through measure and mutual limitation, alone gives order and form in nature and in the life of human beings, and lets the natural and moral world order, the cosmos, grow out of the chaotic masses.
That person has the noblest and most beautiful calling in human life who is called to mediate, in the last and highest place, the unity of all members of society.

The crown confers this vocation: neither the splendor of the throne and the court, nor the power of money and of armies, nor the sense of a more or less unlimited authority within the state can grant the prince's spirit and heart such an elevation as the consciousness of this vocation.

May it then be permitted to me, in this hour which is dedicated to the veneration of a king filled with love for his people, to
speak of this vocation of kingship, which in my judgment is suited, before all other forms of social life together, to establishing that unity.

What I venture to offer makes no claim to a rigorous and scholarly discussion of this most important subject, which, even if I were equal to it, would not be appropriate to the celebration: it is the orator's privilege to link thoughts together lightly, so as to meet a mood that he may presume, and to intervene in it in a stimulating way: I shall consider myself satisfied if only a few of my suggestions, which others serve in their connection, should correspond somewhat to the mood of this highly honored assembly.
Unfortunately, at today's birthday celebration this mood is not one of unclouded joy and cheerfulness.
By the counsel of God, a hard trial has come upon us a few days ago: anxious fears for the life of the most loving King have filled the august princely house and all loyal subjects with grief.

If the Lord's grace, through the more favorable turn of His Majesty's illness, has poured a drop of balm into our wounded heart, yet the discordant note of the danger that came upon us suddenly and has only just vanished still echoes in our mind, and into the joy over the new ray of hope there mingles the feeling of melancholy and the thought of the instability of all earthly things.

"Boast not thyself of the morrow," says the royal sage, "for thou knowest not what today may bring forth." And another: "Man that is born of woman is of few days, and full of trouble; he cometh forth like a flower and is cut down, he fleeth as a shadow and continueth not." Moved in my inmost being by such feelings, I cannot presume that you, highly esteemed assembly here present, will today follow my train of thought with undivided attention; but while I live in the comfort that the Almighty will grant the best of kings a longer beneficent activity and a longer duration of his life—which, like that of the other mortals, has been full of trouble—I nevertheless venture not to let myself be overcome by the momentary anxiety, which ever more gives way to a joyful hope, and to attempt that insight into the blessing-laden vocation of kingship, whose
fulfillment Frederick William the Fourth has ever kept before his eyes.

It may also be permitted now, as on other occasions, on this day, with composure and self-possession, to direct our attention to such a general matter, closely bound up with the exalted person of the King, whose contemplation falls to the men of science: the inestimable value of kingship for the state and for humanity, of which I intend to speak, may also, in this time of anxiety for a beloved royal head—especially now that the fear of the utmost has vanished—not appear as a subject foreign to our celebration.

For the darker or more definite feeling, and still more the clear and assured consciousness, of this worth—toward which I intend to lead you—is the first and firm foundation of love for the King and at the same time of the grief we feel at a danger threatening him, even if this love and this grief are heightened by the noble personal qualities of the ruler, especially by his loving disposition, the deep fundamental trait of his wonderfully gifted soul.

Permit me, then, a reflection which, although originally grounded in a serener mood, retains its significance even for the time of suddenly arrived affliction—indeed, whose significance is perhaps felt still more deeply in darkened days, in which the bearer of majesty, the unifying center around which the various circles of society move, the sun of the land, has been veiled by the shadow cast by earthly frailty.

Human society has from time immemorial consisted of diverse masses of people who are separated by their abilities, occupations, and the situations and circumstances arising from these, as well as by inclinations, habits, needs, and enjoyments—in short, by everything they possess, lack, and strive for—and who, although they indeed complement one another, nevertheless have different advantages.

It has therefore early been the task of thinking statesmen and of thinkers directed toward the state to consider how unity and concord might be brought about in society; but this task becomes ever more difficult the further a people advances: for even if precisely at the lowest stage of development the
separation of occupations and conditions of life is strongest, as in the caste constitution of the Orient, those distinctions rested on a natural necessity that did not let them feel any compulsion or constraint, and by virtue of the low degree or the entire lack of political consciousness in that dream-life or plant-life of humanity, the lower classes made no claim to the advantages of the privileged.
Only when such fetters have been burst asunder, when that consciousness and with it those claims have awakened, can a clash of the various advantages, and from that discord in society, arise.

Furthermore, with advanced education there is bound up an increase of labor, an augmentation of wealth, and a growth of the needs of individuals and still more of the community as a whole, together with an increased population; and since not all can earn in equal measure and consequently cannot consume in equal measure either, the difference between rich and poor grows ever greater and greater, and with it the difference in manner of living: there thus arises a division hard to reconcile, especially when luxury reaches a high degree and, as is almost inevitable, misery increases in equal measure; there arises, since both parties do not easily restrain themselves, envy and bitterness toward the higher in the lower, contempt of the former for the latter, and when the lower strive upward, harshness of the more powerful toward them, in order to hold them down the more surely, or when the lower are victorious, equal arrogance and brutality toward the former.

If, as is indeed fortunate, a middle class forms between the two extremes that could fill this gulf, then this class too is easily drawn into the quarrel, since it can be counted by both parties as belonging to the opposing side—by the higher party all the more so if it reaches close to them and thus threatens to endanger their standing.

In the most memorable times and states, this struggle appears as the struggle of the nobility, which forms a ruling aristocracy of lineage, and of the commoners, or of the rich, who as moneyed oligarchs have attained a plutocratic power, and of the poor, who strive for democracy; both—the aristocracy of nobility and the oligarchy of the rich—were originally and frequently united in the same persons, but
often separate in the course of development and then form a new opposition.
And these are not yet the only contrasts.

At a higher stage of development the state requires a standing army, whether that army be raised by recruitment or formed from the citizens by means of the obligation of all or of most of them to serve; and the military class, which even in states ordered by caste had held a preponderance either alone or alongside the priesthood, readily sets itself against the rest and acquires a power and might that made themselves felt most completely in the Roman Empire.

The state requires a large number of servants or officials, who must acquire a special education, special knowledge, and special skills; these too frequently separate themselves from the rest of society as eminently insightful persons, or as persons who attribute insight to themselves and are privileged.
If they are truly capable, they form a spiritual aristocracy.

This intellectual aristocracy is sometimes pursued in even higher measure by the administrators of divine things in the state: if they prevail completely, a hierarchy takes shape, a term that an inept usage of language has also transferred to public officials; and this hierarchy strives not merely for dominion over the less discerning, a dominion it exercised beneficially at a lower stage of development, especially since its representatives were also in preferential possession of knowledge, but at its summit it also wants to command all knowledge, after knowledge has taken shape independently for itself, and to give it laws and set it limits, while at the same time it wants to order civil relations and institutions according to its own views.

Only the bearers of the sciences and arts, in their corporate union, appear not to strive after state power—rare exceptions aside, of which the Pythagorean League in antiquity may be the most memorable example. For although even Plato expected the salvation of humanity only when philosophers would become rulers or rulers philosophers, science, by its very nature—since it has its purpose in itself and can neither seize hold of the masses nor possesses any other means of dominion—has had to confine itself to improving and ennobling the
life of society through the spread of knowledge, and especially of purer and gentler principles.
Finally, beyond all those oppositions, new divisions again arise even within the particular domains themselves.

The acquisitive class, when its activity has raised itself significantly, as in our days, splits—even apart from the distinction between rich and poor or master and worker—into hostile camps: the landowners, the owners of money, the factory and merchant lords.

Moreover, concerning divine things, not only do different peoples hold different conceptions, but so do parts of one and the same people or state; particular confessions and sects form, mostly under enthusiastic leaders, whereby even an existing hierarchy is dissolved or fragmented, and wholly contrary to the essence of religion, which is pre-eminently suited to produce brotherly love and concord in the veneration of the one God, strife and hatred are sown over faith, dogmas, and customs and are nourished and strengthened by worldly advantages and endeavors: this fanatical zeal has unfortunately, precisely in times when religious feeling was more awakened, visited society with evils equal in magnitude or far more horrifying than the political party struggles.
In some states there is also the additional diversity of peoples and tribes that have been joined together against nature, and their natural antagonism is difficult to overcome.
But enough of examples of how many contrasts the society is torn by.

How much, then, is to be reconciled and united within it, if this very discord is not to form its law, but rather concord, through which, as an old saying has it, the small grows, while through discord even the great falls apart.

Even when the whole sum of these oppositions had not yet accumulated, and especially in the present century, in which they have emerged more completely and with greater influence, theory—taking as its starting point given phenomena or the evils that had come to light—has sought a way by which this calamity might be eradicated from the root.

I mean the theories of socialism and communism, under which name I, with a distinguished master,
comprehend all endeavors "which seek essentially to reform the foundations of civil society, property and family, or to replace them with entirely different ones."
For "with wholly unrestrained development they all, consciously or unconsciously, come close to the ideal of community of goods and of women".

If engaging with these views seems to divert me from the immediate purpose of my present address—namely, to set forth the beneficent vocation of kingship—then their removal is all the more justified, the more hostilely they have been directed, precisely in our times, against royal rule, whose blessings we joyfully acknowledge, insofar as it is possible to rejoice today.

That ideal was first sketched by Plato, in his perfect state, for a particular part of society; but as a man of the finest culture and taste he surely felt that the subject was very well suited to have jest and mockery attached to it, as Aristophanes had already done: the philosopher has therefore, it seems, although he means the matter seriously, struck up a cheerful tone, and at once mingled in some self-mockery by way of anticipation; moreover he also raised considerable doubt as to the practicability of the ideal; only he holds that the fashioner of a state ideal need no more demonstrate its possibility than a painter, who had drawn a perfect archetype of a man, would have to show that such a man could also exist; and he remarks that he does not see why one of the two fundamental conditions he laid down for the realization of this state—which I pass over—or even both of them, should not be possible; the best is what he says, if only it be possible; he admits that it is difficult for it to be put into effect, yet it is not impossible.

Plato wishes to make the citizens of his state believe that they are indeed all brothers, but that the god who formed them, at their birth, mixed gold into those who are fitted to rule, silver into the remaining guardians of the state—or whatever he wishes to call them, the auxiliaries, that is, his separate, fully educated fighting force—and iron and bronze into the farmers and the other workers; and that the god commands them to take thought for nothing more than that these different classes of citizens not be mixed together, except that if one from the
higher class is born with any admixture of bronze or iron, he is to be cast without pity among the farmers and the other workers, while if one from the lower class is born with gold or silver in him, he is to be raised to the higher class.

Now, of this higher class, whose women were also to be educated for fighting and ruling equally with the men, no one may possess immovable or movable property; like armies in the field, they are to eat in common and also live together, and from the lower class they are to be supplied with what is necessary as a reward for protection; and so that no kind of separation may take place within this higher class, besides the lack of possessions, which—since this class is maintained in common by the rest—amounts to a community of goods, those men are to have women and children in common, far removed, however, from every licentiousness, since this commonality is regulated in manifold ways by the superiors, both in other respects and in order always to maintain the same measure of population, to which the ancients attached very great weight.
If the higher estate is thus wholly at unity within itself, the philosopher hopes, the remaining citizens would fall into discord neither with that estate nor among themselves.

It is a curious peculiarity of this perfected communism that it is calculated only for an aristocratic element of the state, so that the heads might not fall into discord; for from their unity—though hardly with justice—the unity of the lesser sort as well is expected. For the latter, as the beginning of the fourth book shows, possess lands as their own, build themselves fine and large houses and furnish them fittingly, bring their own sacrifices to the gods, receive guest-friends, and possess gold and silver and everything else that is commonly counted toward the happiness of life: all this points to separate personal property on the part of the lesser sort, and one must wonder at Aristotle when he asserts that Plato determined nothing as to whether the lesser sort should have common property and women and children in common or not.
It cannot be denied that some fundamental features of Plato's design were fully or nearly realized in the life of certain Greek states and barbarian tribes.

That ideal already had a model in the
ancient Dorian life, which appears ennobled in the Pythagorean society; and it was not unknown to the Hellenes that something similar was realized among various barbarian peoples.

I would enumerate these phenomena—not unworthy of note when compared with the newer systems of communism, and even later ones of the same kind, within Christianity itself—more precisely here, were I not called back from doing so by the seriousness of the moment.
Aristotle has the merit of having, with his clear mind, thoroughly eliminated the Platonic communism that does not wish to abolish the state itself.

To repeat only a little of what he says, he remarks that the state, the further it advances toward unity, would the less remain a state, in that the family is more a unity than the state, and the individual more than the family, while the state consists of different, not entirely equal, parts; what is regarded as the highest good for the state, that perfect unity, therefore rather abolishes the state: the state should not be a homophony of equal tones, but a symphony of different ones.

Furthermore, if everything were held in common, no one would much concern himself about it, since people ordinarily concern themselves only with what is their own; nor would a close friendship and love unite those for whom the family bond was not a particular bond but a wholly general one embracing all.
Hereby, moreover, many virtues would be destroyed, and common possession and use would divide those joined together for that purpose far more than it divides those whose possession is separate.

Incidentally, with regard to the common ownership of property—by which landownership is meant—Aristotle distinguishes three kinds: the common ownership of the land and its produce; the common ownership of the produce while property is separate, which is said to occur among some peoples; and the common ownership of the land and its cultivation, with a distribution of the fruits for the separate use of individuals, which is likewise said to occur among some of the barbarians. He holds, however, that the existing arrangement of separation is the best: property should be one's own, but through virtue it should be brought about that it be shared with others for their use, and the lawgiver should
strive toward this; this too has already been partly realized in some states and might be realized still more.
With this sound judgment I conclude my examination of ancient communism.

The one that has come into vogue in our century is in many respects different from that one; for it was chiefly the distressed condition of the working class and the higher recognition of every human personality and of its free development that gave rise to this one—points of view that lay further off from the ancients, because the.
Labor fell for the most part to a class of people without a state, to the slaves, to whom a free individuality was not granted.

In accordance with this origin, modern communism is democratic in nature, whereas ancient communism was aristocratic in its principal manifestations; it seeks above all to break the dominion of capital over labor and to eradicate the distinction between rich and poor. Yet this new communism too, starting from more moderate socialist views, has in the course of its development been driven toward the principles of the old communism—toward the dissolution of property and of the family, in conjunction with a so-called emancipation of women and all manner of religious and philosophical notions that incline strongly toward materialism. Even the more modest demand that property should indeed not cease to exist, but should be transferred not by virtue of a right of birth but rather by virtue of a right of capacity according to labor, stands very close to an annihilation of property.

These systems, into whose details I find neither occasion nor calling to enter, have, notwithstanding the most extravagant oddities, attained such importance that some of them have hoped, or still hope, for the healing of all the ills of the present and the future redemption of the human race, and awaken the same hopes, not without danger, in the propertyless class.

In our assembly, highly honored listeners, I may take it as granted that even the most moderate execution of a community of this kind, free from any morality-destroying exaggeration, would be possible only in a small congregation; but that in such subordinate forms, to use an expression of Schleiermacher's, the destinies of the human race cannot be fulfilled, but only through large civic associations; further, that a more extensive realization
of such principles, if possible at all, would not be possible without the most terrible upheavals and misdeeds; as indeed the spread of these principles was calculated first and foremost upon the overthrow of kingship, indeed upon the extermination of the princely houses; finally, that this realization would produce only the opposite of what was intended by it: instead of freedom, a boundless despotism, through the interference of superiors—of whom even such a community cannot be devoid—in all and every act of each individual; instead of the elevation of the lower class, general impoverishment and the debasement of all; instead of greater morality, rather demoralization, heartlessness, and the loss of the highest goods of knowledge, since with such complete equalization no one could raise himself spiritually to any significant degree above the others—a disadvantage which Plato's communism has after all happily avoided.
We shall therefore refuse to seek the unity of society in such an undifferentiated community, whereby no state at all would any longer be posited, but the state itself would be negated.
Rather, we remain dependent on finding the union or mediation of opposites in the state itself, which humanity has built up for itself as the greatest work of art and the highest form of society.
In this, the reconciliation of the opposing elements is to be accomplished.
In which form of state, then, can this reconciliation most surely be achieved?

Evidently in such a one, in which the bearer of the highest state power is separated from all the mutually contending parts of society, and is not so preferentially bound to any one of them through shared advantage and disadvantage that he himself becomes entangled in the strivings of parties, whereby the rift between the different classes of the population would only become more decided: rather must the bearer of state power, raised above the oppositions, have his existence in the existence of the whole, feel himself as one with the whole, be not any estate of the state, nor belong to such an estate or have its direction: he must be, in relation to the great number of distinctions, the undistinguished center and the only one
of his kind in the state.

This holds true neither in aristocracy—whether it be an aristocracy of nobility, of landowners, or of moneyed oligarchs—nor in democracy: for in these forms of government the ruling power stands within the antagonism, and so, in order to maintain its own advantage, it will oppress the others; and as soon as these others become conscious of this, their endeavor will in turn be to rid themselves of the rulers and to put themselves in their place: thus a constant struggle of parties and a government by whichever party prevails at the moment will arise, which can even degenerate into a government of hetaeriae, in which again individual over-powerful leaders seize the reins.

For aristocracy will seldom be an ideal of the most just and the wisest, and democracy will seldom be the rule of a single man who towers above all others through the loftiness of his spirit, as at Athens under Pericles—though through such ideality of the ruler the pressure on the ruled would admittedly be alleviated—but ordinarily aristocracy is harsh and strict, and loves to make the common people into wholly dependent serfs; and only the money oligarchy has often found it expedient, through largesses, as they became customary in Rome, to feed the urban people so that it might more easily endure the rule—a means of making the oligarchy appear milder, which is not so much political as dynasteutic; democracy, however, at its height is ruthless toward the propertied in overburdening them with burdens, and even resorts, as we see at Athens, to frequent confiscations of property in order to feed the masses, so that it approaches community of goods.

Even within the hierarchy, the ruling power is one of the opposites, and thus incapable of reconciling them, so long as state and church are separate spheres: that the two should merge into one another has to this day remained among pious wishes.

Only the monarchy of the crown is suited, above all the oppositions of society, untouched by them and removed from their strife, to hover independently in blessed repose, if it recognizes its calling as the representative of the undivided idea of the state.

So that it may remain untouched by those antagonisms, it is not only lifelong but also hereditary, independent, after its single original establishment, of election, from
which partisan endeavors are difficult to keep away; it is maintained and preserved not through the ruler's force and cunning, but through the loyalty and love of the people, who grow accustomed to and become attached to a family in which the sovereignty is hereditary.

In the healthy condition of the state, all parties accord it that reverence which is its due as the bearer of the state, in its elevation above every class of the people; and so that the outward appearance may also correspond to this reverence, the throne surrounds itself with its splendor.
All parties are united in loyalty and attachment to the bearer of the idea of the state, and their particular sympathies and antipathies are absorbed in love for him.

Aristocracy and democracy are strangers to any general enthusiasm for the head of the state, and envy and strife prevail in them; they know nothing of the heartfelt sympathy for his welfare or woe, nothing of that compassion for the prince which works wonders in times of the state's distress or danger, and which now, at a danger personally threatening him, breaks forth vividly.

To be sure, monarchy itself is of very various kinds, and I do not mean every kind of it: I do not mean despotic monarchy, which is chiefly peculiar to the Orient, where the monarch is the only free man, all the rest are slaves, and slaves of slaves, whom one calls satraps; a form of rule that can subsist only if and so long as the people itself is of a slavish nature: I mean a monarchy like that of our much-beloved King, a monarchy moderated by a constitution over free men, who are to have in the monarch precisely the guarantee of their freedom against one another.

For that despotic monarchy, again, rules only for its own advantage; it does not see its purpose in the representation of the idea of the state, does not relate the ruler to the state, but rather the state—if it can still be called that—to the ruling person; it is therefore selfish and lacks love for people and state.

But as for autocracy over free men, this cannot—except in the most dangerous times, in which the state requires the absolute power of the great man—be a purely personal rule, still less a self-willed and arbitrary one, precisely because it is a rule over free men: it must be a rule of wisdom
and according to law, through the exercise of justice, which gives each man his own.

How this law is to be found or made, and how by that very law it is to be made possible for the monarchy to bring about and preserve the unity of society without prejudice to the civil, political, and religious freedom of the subjects—that is the business of statecraft, which I do not intend to teach. It is enough for me to have been led or pointed to the fact that this is the purpose of the monarchy; and if one denies it this calling, or renders it incapable of fulfilling it, then it is only a sham monarchy and no longer a truth.

One may object to this that the monarchy, depending on circumstances, supports itself now on individual classes of the people, now on the commoners against the great men of the realm, now on the nobility against the commoners, now on an army against the unarmed multitude, now on a host of officials against the governed, now on church and clergy against the secular, or on the latter against a threatening hierarchy, and the like besides; indeed, it must even be conceded that the monarchy, for its own preservation and that of the state, temporarily and for a time requires a closer attachment to an effective part of society—in times of immoderate agitation and unbridled desire for innovations, attachment to a steady and conserving element, which is in any case necessary to the state even in quiet times, and conversely, in times of stagnation and decay, attachment to a more mobile element, which the state likewise continually requires; when disobedience and moral laxity break in, attachment to the armed power, the officialdom, the clergy: but precisely from the fact that the kingship has in practice had to make use of, or has made use of, now one and now the other side of the opposition, it follows that by its nature none of these sides is more closely bound to it or is the support of the throne before the others, but only an unhealthy condition of the state leads to or compels such a party alliance.

Even the fact that the monarchy, in accordance with the origin and the level of culture of its bearers and therefore also in its views or judgments and prejudices, stands closest to the highest class of the governed, and that the king, as
commander-in-chief, will if not necessarily then as a rule possess a martial spirit, cannot be decisive for an inclination toward particular directions that is to be placed in the essence of the monarchy, since history teaches that the elements which come into consideration here are by no means unconditionally and under all circumstances devoted to the existing government, and are even easily inclined by the highest class to curtail the rights of the crown or to seize them for themselves, in order to acquire a separate dominion of their own within the state.

In its idea, kingship is free from all such one-sided and exclusive directions; rather, in it all the threads of society converge in one center, and are gathered into one by it with a strong hand for the welfare of the whole.

The monarchy has founded the prosperity and glory of this land: its princes have indeed taken up the reins with this strong hand, and have not merely cared, labored, and fought for the dynasty, but for the people, with the people; from small beginnings they have gradually raised the realm to its present height through wisdom of government and administration, through the development of all the forces of the land and people, with the timely removal of long-established obstacles, and through a well-ordered and valiant military power, by virtue of which it occupies an honorable place among the most significant states of Europe.

You have done this—apart from a few exceptions grounded in the circumstances of the time and in the spirit of the age—not by favoring any one estate or any particular tendency, but by reconciling and merging the differences, which in this country seem to me to have advanced not a little, even if not all partisan endeavors have disappeared.

You have sought, in particular, by abolishing the unfreedom that held down a great mass of the people, and through popular education and the generalization of learning, to raise the lower class, whose outward condition must be improved by upbringing and instruction, since it is most surely worsened by ignorance and benightedness, although it cannot be said that these measures fully remedy poverty and misery; but these must be alleviated
through the virtue of others, as Aristotle already intimated, through the communication that springs from it and the spirit of benevolence, which seems to me likewise not insignificant in this land and is nourished from the throne by the most effective example.

The princes of this land have not promoted individual branches of enterprise one-sidedly, but have let their right be done equally to all: to agriculture, to the industry of the trades, to manufacturing activity, to commerce and free intercourse.
In the latest development, when the time for it had come, you united the civil and military estates as brothers through the most just and wisest ordering of the military system.

You have cultivated outward, or so-called material, prosperity and intellectual cultivation in equal measure; and even if individual voices are raised against industry, and individual voices against the spread of knowledge, it seems to me—not without the influence of our royal lord—that nowhere more than in this land is the conviction firmly established that the two directions do not contradict each other, but rather that industry, through the subjugation of matter, increasingly frees the mind from the fetters of the material, and that again it is the mind itself that governs, promotes, facilitates, and ennobles material labor.

The government of His Majesty Frederick William IV—to whom we are gathered today in our circle, as other parts of society are in theirs, with heartfelt love and attachment to the person of the sovereign—has, through the concurrence of many salutary and many pernicious things, become one of the most memorable; with God's assistance and with fatherly mildness it has happily overcome the unfortunate circumstances of the time, and has used the more favorable conditions that have arisen, with moderation, for the calming and internal consolidation of the state.

May it please divine Providence to guard and preserve the blossom of the realm, under the guidance of the prince who is equally distinguished by the goodness of his heart and by the sublime direction of his spirit, from every sickness and withering and from every storm, whether from without or from within!

Our constant supplication is: "God bless and preserve the King and his house!" But this prayer, which is so often sounded
publicly in solemn hours and echoes in the breast of the faithful and is the common prayer of all at all times, is felt today more fervently and rises like a blazing sacrificial flame more fiery toward heaven, now that the Almighty has rescued our benefactor from the near danger and has granted us to commemorate this day with new hope.
Hear, O Lord over life and death, this our supplication: "God bless and preserve the King and his house!"

div.head: XI. Festrede gehalten auf der Universität zu Berlin am 15. October 1858.
Ueber den Werth der Verbindung des Dynastischen mit dem Volksthümlichen, besonders im Hinblick auf die Bestrebungen zu einer Gesammtherrschaft

p.s: Universally valid for the monarchy, highly esteemed assembly, is the principle that you will all acknowledge with me: The king does not die.

All the less does his rule lapse if, during his lifetime, he is compelled or moved by illness or by the necessity of recuperation to entrust the safeguarding of royal affairs to a member of his high house.

If both cases are distressing to a loyal people—the one, that the personal bearer of the crown is torn from it by death; the other, that in his lifetime he can no longer exercise the sovereignty in his own person—then in both the thought consoles it: in the unity of the dynasty the king lives and reigns on.

Happy the people that can revere the living ruler with its whole soul, without having to bear anxiety about the successor and, for his sake, about its own future, and that, when a natural misfortune does not permit the living ruler himself to hold the reins of government, sees them in the hands of a worthy and beloved prince!

Even today we are still in a position to lament the state of health of our beloved King, for whose otherwise so joyful and serene birthday celebration we are assembled, and to be able to give ourselves over to the festivity only with half a heart and troubled feeling: but we revere His Majesty no less deeply even when, withdrawn and cut off from the unrest and confusion of public life, he does not shine down upon us through his own activity; indeed, we must acknowledge it in reverence and gratitude that the King, for the good of the country and for the calming of minds, for the time until he himself shall again be able to fulfill the duties of his royal office, has transferred the full royal authority to the heir to the throne next in right, worthy of his great ancestors and nobly minded,
as regent according to the constitution.

At the same time, especially on such an occasion, we recognize the value that the dynasty has for the state, in that in it, as an indivisible and closed unity, the government gains firm permanence, love for the king spreads to the entire ruling house, and the hopes for it and from it extend far into the distant future.

In the course of this very year, the country, and above all our capital, has given a proof as touching as it is brilliant of an attachment to the dynasty most intimately bound up with attachment to the person of the King; not contrived, not called forth by familiar means frequently employed, not sprung from a servile spirit or from venal flattery and dissimulation, but unfeigned, sincere, and free was the general sympathy of the Prussian people, and in particular of all the academic bodies and associations of this city, with the marriage of the exalted pair on whom the later future of this land is founded, and with the joy that the august parents—not untried—of the newly wedded, universally beloved Prince feel in this happy union; and we have been witnesses that the homage sprung from the heart of the people found a response, welcome to themselves and to the people, in the hearts of those to whom it was offered.
If such a harmony of feelings does not unite the ruling house and the people, what then is even the most powerful monarchy?

In the most radiant splendor of the throne, dominion then stands desolate, not refreshed by the warming sun of love—the love that is a need of all noble hearts; desolate, despite its great number, the subject people also stands, because it does not feel itself joined with its other half, which is to form the state together with it.

May that lucky star, which after the storm-tossed surge of a past overcome shines upon the ship of this state like the light of the Dioscuri at the masthead, constantly accompany it on its voyage wrapped in danger, and never be extinguished or fade away and grow pale!

Whoever is to speak before you on this day, highly honored assembly, finds manifold thoughts pressing in upon
him—especially if, like me, he is the ordinary and officially appointed ceremonial orator—not always the same ones in the different years, yet often closely related, many of which he must reject so as not to say once more what has been said before, though often also entirely different ones, because circumstances have become different; and the position of the ceremonial orator in this place has the particular inconvenience that a member of the academic body is to speak before an assembly of patrons, masters, and students of science, but not about learned matters of his own field: for who would not find it inappropriate to deliver a specialized scholarly lecture here today? but rather about the great circumstances of the state that concern everyone, to which the person of the celebrated prince himself directs us.

From such a union there arises something hybrid, half scholarly and half political; and whoever does not love half-measures might therefore shrink back from such a task, were he not to remind himself in good time that ancient primeval wisdom declared the half to be more than the whole.

Thus, in connection with the words with which I have just now given expression, from a deeply moved soul, to my feelings and yours for the Royal House—an expression, though a weak one—there presses upon me today, for this half-political reflection, the value of the union of the dynastic with the national-popular element, which I have indeed already touched upon elsewhere as well; only I do not intend now to consider it in its full extent, but in its limited relation to the masses and the extent of states, especially with a view to the strivings, often recurring in world history, toward a universal dominion that oversteps the bounds of the national-popular, which at all times is the enemy of national-popular character and of the dynasties standing in closer intercourse with the people, and which threatens now nearer and more strongly, now only in the far distance and more in words and claims than in deeds.
And even within this limitation, since the material is not slight, I shall often have to content myself with light hints.
The union of the dynasties with the people appears in two distinct stages.

Apart from the great empires of the Orient that arose early, most peoples were originally
divided into smaller tribes, each of which followed its own particular ruler, if indeed and as long as they had a constitution equal or similar to monarchical government.

How far this fragmentation went is shown by the example of the small country that became decisive for humanity not only through external power but also through intellectual cultivation—I mean Attica, which was originally divided into twelve small communities that had their own authorities and deliberated separately for themselves; outside times of danger they did not consult with the indeed common king, and even waged war against one another.
This relationship, which we find among the most cultivated people of antiquity, was the usual one among the less cultivated.
The further back one goes, the greater the isolation, even within one and the same people.

If certain circumstances are added, into which I shall not enter more closely here, then in this way many small patrimonial states arise, in which, without a precise or correct separation of what belongs to private law and what belongs to public law, the dynast is like a landed proprietor and the whole state appears as a family inheritance, which can also, as has happened in Germany, be divided by the father among several sons, whereas the true state is indivisible and in it the highest power passes only from one to one: the old fragmentation is made still greater by such divisions, and if nevertheless, through the preponderance of one of the dynasts, a larger state arises, this too often remains for a long time afflicted with the character of the patrimonial.

Although this now appears to be a noble, paternal relation that, under high-minded lords, is also agreeable to the subjects, yet the higher needs of the human race cannot be satisfied in it; on the contrary, these smaller states are for the most part without vitality and are not even in a position to protect themselves and their own adequately: and since the one side of these states is not a people, not a full unity, usually scarcely a tribe separated by perceptible differences from closely related tribes, but only an accidental small fragment of a people, separated from the other fragments merely by the diversity of the dynasties, so in such states no true
correspondence of the national and the dynastic takes place: the national extends far beyond the boundaries of the dynasty, and what is dynastically divided feels itself nationally one.

This encroachment of the national element, together with the necessity of protecting oneself against more powerful parties, leads first to a federal community, in which the small states, equal in national terms, unite into a whole; but since this union rests on the unity of the national character and not on dynastic unity, a federal constitution—or, more precisely, a federal state—is better suited to republics than to monarchical states, because in the former the divisive element, the dynasties, is not present at all, but only the unifying element, the common national character.

When dynasties enter into such a union resting on the shared national character of their subjects, then at the very least the purpose of the union must be to preserve and strengthen that on which it rests—the unity of the entire people—to do justice to its needs and rights, and not, however, to let dynastic advantages come to the fore and to protect the dynasties alone, not the peoples.

Yet, as history teaches, these federal arrangements generally prove ineffective when they are not held together by an overwhelmingly powerful hegemony—that is, by the very thing that makes a deception of the federation itself, which is supposed to consist of parties with equal rights; and hegemony, if it is to be effective, will seldom be able to dispense with force and pressure, whereby the weaker members are injured and embittered.

Incidentally, the course of historical development presses more and more toward the dissolution, or more correctly the merging, of the small state communities into larger national masses, or rather organisms, under a single dynasty—a merging that has long since been achieved in most European states, namely in France, England, and Spain; Italy and Germany have lagged furthest behind in this, the latter despite the Empire, under which, in the phrase of earlier political writers, it seemed united into a Germanic republic.
The nations are drawing ever closer to one another, and the lesser differences are evening out to a certain degree.

This urge corresponds to the spirit of
the comprehensive culture of modern times: I venture to set it forth as a principal contrast between ancient and modern culture—that the former, at its height and among the peoples in which it expresses itself completely, works toward shaping the separate particular and individual, and therefore in antiquity the political idea was realized in the phenomenon of the city, or the state was the same as the city, and even the greatest empire, the Roman, was absorbed into the concept of the eternal city; that, by contrast, the new age in which we live—we do not know precisely at what stage of it, but probably still far from its close—strives to sublate the particular distinctions in a culture that is relatively universal compared with the ancient, and thus also in political life forms larger wholes, more general and more comprehensive commonwealths, whose conceivable extreme, lying in an infinitely distant future, appears as the unity of the entire human race—unless it should lie in the world plan that here, as everywhere, the correct mean, that is, the fusion of the individual and the universal as of the real and the ideal in a higher unity that does not sublate the particular distinctions, is to be the true and enduring one.

Permit me, highly honored assembly, to dwell first upon that outermost extreme—or rather, since even those who accept it will find a future arrival of it possible only after the passage of many millennia, therefore rather, I say, upon the approximations to it or the attempts to establish the greatest and most comprehensive universality of the state; a consideration that fifty years ago may indeed have been more timely, while at that time it was at the same time dangerous, but which even now, though free of danger, does not come entirely too late.

An approximation such as I mean lies theoretically already in the thought of the cosmopolitan. To be sure, the framers of this word and concept did not wish by its adoption to separate themselves from the association of their particular state, but knew how to unite both: "State and fatherland are Rome to me," says M. Antoninus, "insofar as I am Antoninus; but both are the world to me, insofar as I am a human being." Still, however, therein lies the reference to a general
civic brotherhood of the human race, to a universally human state; and if the feeling of a shared human citizenship should gradually gain the upper hand over politism, and the theory hinted at in that word should be realized—as theory often long precedes reality, and the latter must yet at last follow despite all resistance—then humanity would truly arrive at an all-embracing human community, whose articulation is, to be sure, hard to comprehend.

Yet the man to whom this ideal was most clearly present before his mind conceived of it only as a sum of separate free communities, but bound to one another in eternal paradisiacal peace, in which dynasties seem to find no place.
But every attempt at a universal monarchy is a not theoretical but actual approximation to that outermost extreme.

To be sure, none of these attempts has so far been able to extend to all the peoples of the earth; but even dominion over a significant portion of the peoples of one or more continents—especially over a large number of civilized peoples, each already powerful when taken individually—is customarily designated by this name.

Almost all attempts of this kind have been the work of passionate, ambitious, warlike, conquest-hungry rulers and world-stormers who, unable to master themselves, wished to rule over all others; and once they had opened their career, one conquest pressed on toward the next, and their instrument, the army, compelled the leaders, in order to keep it occupied and satisfied, to go on and on ever further.

The earliest endeavors of this kind are found in Asia, which, alongside Egypt, was the primeval land of human civilization and at the same time the seat of the oldest despotisms, so far as our eye can reach: through the concentration of the power of the land in a single hand and the unconditional obedience of a servile population, distinguished despots were enabled, as conquerors, to unite formerly separate tribes and kingdoms into great wholes.

Even to the mythical Ninus is ascribed the subjugation of the peoples from the Nile to the Tanais, but to his Semiramis campaigns and subjugations as far as Libya and India, so far as the earth was known in both directions; in the succeeding Assyrian monarchies the same endeavors appear: but after this dominion
had fallen apart into several empires, among which the Babylonian received a wide extent through Nebuchadnezzar, a figure of world-historical significance despite his madness, the Persian monarchy unites Upper and Lower Asia together with Hither Asia and Egypt, from the Indus to the Mediterranean, from the Iaxartes to the desert of Libya, into one empire, which was to mirror the heavenly order in earthly life, especially in the court.

Further plans were thwarted already under Cyrus by the resistance of the northern peoples; under Cambyses, who likewise wished to subjugate the Ethiopians, the Ammonians, and the Carthaginians, by hunger, by sand, and by the steadfastness of the Phoenicians' oaths toward their descendants; under Darius, by the Scythians; and under the same king and his son Xerxes, by the heroic courage of the Greeks, who became a bulwark for Europe. But the thwarted attempts themselves prove that the King of Kings aimed at the subjugation of the whole earth known to him.

Soon the same attempt was also to be undertaken from Europe: Alexander the Great, with initially slight power, subjugated the decayed Persian Empire, while at the same time he held the actual supreme authority over the most cultivated people on earth and dominion over his ancestral land and the neighboring barbarians, and he also carried his victorious arms eastward beyond the borders of the Persian Empire.
It was reserved for him to win worldwide political dominion, just as his teacher Aristotle won intellectual dominion for a far longer time.

In the bold spirit of the youth there developed, after the great successes of arms, the thought of reconciling and uniting the European and the Asiatic humanity through a common military order and the intermingling of peoples and customs; and it can scarcely be doubted that he, dissatisfied with the territory he had won, wished to sail around Africa, to subjugate Arabia, Libya, and Carthage, to press on as far as the Pillars of Hercules and Gadeira, and to establish himself in Sicily and Italy, but to turn northward against the Scythians and neighboring peoples: he had also already received in Babylon embassies of the most distant peoples—of the Italians, probably also of the Romans, and of the Celts and Iberians.
Here, therefore, we have the draft of a far-reaching universal empire.

After the fragmentation of Macedonian
rule, Rome, appearing next as a conquering state, formed a more westerly European center for a world empire likewise shifted further west—first the free Rome under powerful, mostly oligarchic leaders, then the imperial rule, which from the Atlantic Ocean to the Euphrates held sway throughout the entire circuit of the Mediterranean over the most flourishing lands of Europe, including the British island, North Africa, and western Asia.
The Roman people, and later the Roman emperor, regarded itself as the lord of the earth, who had the crowns to bestow.

After this great empire had divided into two imperial realms, the Western one first became a prey to the northern peoples; the Eastern one sought for a time still to assert its claim to world dominion; and when Pope Leo III, in Rome, placed the imperial crown upon the Frankish king Charles, who as Roman Patricius was protector of the Church, for his own pious benefit and amid the jubilation of the Roman people, and himself bowing down before him, this man became the heir to the former Roman imperial dignity in the West.

This renewed empire was bound up with a territory that more or less corresponded to the extent of the former Western Roman Empire; the dignity of the ancient Roman emperors attached to this crown then passed over to the German throne, insofar as the German king had himself crowned in Rome; and as the Western Christian world formed a whole under one religious head, the Roman emperor was regarded, in common opinion, as sacred imperial majesty, the secular protector of that same whole.

Even if the power did not always correspond to this splendor, there nevertheless lay in it the ideal claim to a political preponderance that comes very close to the claim to universal dominion over Western Christendom.

I pass over similar dominions, widely extended and for a time not unsuccessful—such as, to name only one, that of the Caliphs, which stretched from Asia through Africa as far as Spain—and note only further that, after the East Roman Empire had been destroyed by the Ottomans, a certain claim to the Greek imperial throne was later carried over, quite naturally, to the powerful ruling house of kindred confession, to which a great part of the
East of Europe, right up to our own borders, and a part of Asia is subject.

In the sixteenth century, moreover, Emperor Charles V, in whose realm the sun never set, seemed, as holder of the German crown, to threaten the independence of the individual peoples and states from Spain, Naples and Sicily, Austria and Burgundy, Mexico and Peru.

Later, besides the House of Habsburg, strengthened by the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary, it was chiefly England and France that determined the destinies of Europe—the former at the same time in possession of an immense Asiatic territory and numerous colonies, the latter through the development of great military forces, with which at the beginning of this century Napoleon finally overwhelmed almost all of Europe and in fact seemed to be establishing a new world dominion.

Thus the striving for a universal power, in which the dynasty ruthlessly oversteps the bounds of what is national, has repeated itself from the earliest times into our own century, and Europe, in its supposed balance, still has no secure guarantee that a new attempt of this kind will not be taken up by one side or the other.
But besides political world dominion, another has also emerged, which has in part gone hand in hand with that one and in part fallen out with it: the dominion of a religious system.
For the most part the two went hand in hand in Islam; in Christianity, which more than any other religion is the religion of love, the unity soon turned into discord.
All Christendom was to be spiritually united under the supreme authority of the Pope in Rome, in the ancient seat of outward world dominion; its protector was the Emperor.
But soon the pope wanted to be above the emperor.
The Roman bishop claimed and won sole dominion over consciences, over minds, over spirits and their faith and their understanding, and this dominion was very well ordered and mightily founded.
It intervened in worldly affairs in many ways and with great force: for whoever holds the spirits in his power will also determine and limit worldly power.

Yet even today the boundaries and powers of the secular authority and of a foreign ecclesiastical power must still be regulated by so-called concordats, and even today the differences
of confession in individual states still press so far into the political sphere that political so-called factions are even named after them; and if this intrusion of confessional matters into politics is practiced quite artfully, and under the form of religion hatred and discord are sown and inflamed, we can be transported back into the conditions of the Thirty Years' War, which brought the greatest calamity upon the German fatherland.

That spiritual, or rather ecclesiastical, universal monarchy now suffered an early fracture through the separation of the Roman and the Greek Church, and into the more significant half, the Roman hierarchy, the Reformation broke a new rift.

Nevertheless, the hierarchical universal dominion has never abandoned its principles and aspirations, but has continually pursued them—at times, indeed, with a prudent assessment of circumstances and of the possibilities available on each occasion, and thus occasionally receding—yet all the while with its traditional tenacity, steadily pursuing them, and it pursues them still.

Although there must be a developing movement within states, they are nevertheless calculated, for the security, protection, and repose of human society—and thus, in terms of their ultimate purpose, for the state of peace—and the friend of humanity must therefore wish for their unity, and where possible the unity of the entire human race.
But universal monarchy is not the right means to that end.

The attempts to attain it can be fruitful if from them arises the civilization of crude and uneducated peoples, if in this way a superior culture is brought to them and instilled into them, as by the Hellenes to the so-called barbarians, and along with that culture a greater civil liberty, although as a rule it brings with it, through increased despotism, precisely a harsher servitude, and only by chance and incidentally are individual freer institutions introduced through it, such as even Napoleonic rule spread in some countries; moreover, it can for the most part exist only in the form of arbitrary rule, through satrapies or Roman governorships or pashaliks.

Furthermore, it can serve the spread of gentler religious principles, the broadening of the circle of thought, the increased exchange of all that every people needs—thus the promotion
and invigoration of trade and commerce and of the arts of industry, and also of scholarly communication.

But it weakens the vital energy of the individual peoples by destroying the distinctions that are well grounded in nature itself, and dissolves their life-giving particularities into a flat generality—unless, as has often happened before, it fails precisely on that account.
It is not this universal that is the ideal of education, but the balance of the universal and the particular; the latter should not be annihilated by the former, but raised, purified, idealized.
For this, the right middle course in the formation of states is required.
The consciousness of a particular national character should not perish, without prejudice to the growing friendship among the various peoples.
If, then, this national spirit and a dynasty come to an understanding, both are most securely protected with one another and through one another.
I shall define the national spirit somewhat more closely.
This proves itself in customs generally, in law, in religion, and finally quite pre-eminently in language.

To pass over morals and law, it certainly seems, from the Christian standpoint, that religion is capable of no national character, since it is indeed supposed to be precisely a universal one; and I myself, many years ago, in this very place, showed that the correspondence, assumed by some, of Catholicism with the southern and of Protestantism with the northern national character rests on delusion, at least for Germany.

Meanwhile, a confession may for a long time have grown so intertwined with a particular people that it has become fused with the national consciousness; and yet if religious dissensions arise within a state or a people, these are surely a great obstacle to its internal unity and even to its stability and security abroad. The only remedy for this evil consists in keeping the confession away from any influence on public life, in leaving faith—insofar as it is not contrary to the state—and consciences free, and in not favoring or inflaming religious passions or fanaticism, but rather moderating them and removing them as far as possible, as the religion of love itself commands.

Language, by contrast, is the surest mark of the spirit of a people, the expression of its innermost essence and of its knowledge; the preservation of language is therefore a
fundamental condition for the continued existence of a people and of a truly national state.
But in the history of language, too, those two extremes come into consideration which we have weighed with reference to political life.

Originally we find a great multiplicity of different languages, as of different small political communities; in the course of great periods of time those languages are gradually swallowed up by a few predominant languages and consigned almost to oblivion: after all, even the language of the .
of the people from which this empire takes its name, has died out.

What is more: if in a small country an older language, formerly more widely diffused, has still barely survived, then a mummy-like preservation of it is scarcely successful and equally unprofitable, and it places obstacles in the way of the little people's education rather than promoting it.

Just as the small political communities gradually passed over, for the most part, into larger ones—or, I should rather say, medium-sized ones—so too a transition had to take place from languages no longer viable into those full of life, and the small tribe had to attach itself to the firm core of a larger one.
It is conceivable, however, that the urge toward the universal might so take hold of language that even the larger linguistic individualities would be obscured or abolished.
What the cosmopolitan is in the sphere of the state, that the idea of a universal language is in the sphere of language.

Such a language, which, as has indeed been supposed, is to be formed on scientific lines, will scarcely ever succeed; and even if it did succeed, this universal language would be nothing but a sum of algebraic signs, in which no expression could be found for the noblest creations of language, the oratorical and the poetic.

By contrast, however, one of the living languages could indeed gain universal dominion, as Greek did through the Macedonian world empire and Latin through Rome's secular and spiritual power; and it would not be precisely the most perfect languages that could lay claim to this, but the decayed, inorganic, mixed languages, the most worn-down and least sonorous, in which the least that is distinctive is still preserved—languages which, to be sure, some even regard as themselves the most perfect.

“Which languages,” says a not contemptible researcher, “are the ones that seem destined, in the bonds of Böckh’s Speeches, Il. Verbrüderung,
to unite all the peoples of the earth?”

They are English and French." These he finds wonderfully formed to express all the new ideas that industry and science daily cause to blossom forth, which one should learn and speak by preference and with the greatest ease: these would have the greatest future; Spanish and Portuguese, for the moment, take only third rank; the Slavic dialects too would have a great future; German and Italian are perhaps most exposed to being swallowed up by the languages spoken by stronger peoples, between which they are enclosed.

Such prophecies can be pointers for our people, so that it holds its language in honor, cultivates it, and also purifies it of dispensable foreign intruders: enough has already been done amiss in that French has become the court language and, in place of the Latin that was harmless to all peoples, the language of diplomacy; an advantage that substantially promotes the claims of the people to a preponderance due to it.

Let us hope that the unfavorable horoscope set for the German language—which in its plasticity is eminently suited to give expression to all new ideas—and, with it, for the German people, does not come true: in our language lies the guarantee of our still living and vigorous national character, by no means narrowly bounded even in extent, and thus at the same time the guarantee of a Germanic state.
Before I leave this subject, let me be permitted to say a few words about the relation of science and its representatives to the spirit of the people.

The sciences are a common possession of educated humanity, and even if the various national spirits involuntarily introduce a certain difference into them, as one can see especially in philosophy, yet here too a leveling soon sets in more and more, and nowhere does national division have less justification than in science.

The exchange of ideas unites people even more than the exchange of goods; genuine scholarship, to which it is a matter of indifference from which people its advancement comes, must most especially pave the way for the reconciliation of nations.

This is also evident in the
mutual recognition shown by scholars, and above all by learned societies, among the various nations, even during political dissensions.
Are the men of science, then, the most indifferent to the particular character of a people and the readiest to favor a universal power?
Do they undermine the national character instead of supporting it?
I do not think.

On the contrary, the man of truly scientific spirit gathers together within himself, with full consciousness, the distinctive character of his people—that which lives and works almost unconsciously within them—and he feels more deeply and recognizes more clearly his people's virtues and excellences, their deficiencies and failings, their exaltation and their humiliation.
Thus, in dangerous times, the men of science, together with the youth they have educated and inspired, become the champions of the national character and of the state against subjugation.

This proved itself brilliantly among us some half a century ago: German scholarship and its representatives appeared to the foreign ruler as adversaries who must be fought just as much as the armies in the field.

At that time it was their duty and mission to nourish and quicken the noble feelings of love of country against a tyranny that threatened fatherland and freedom, including the freedom of thought: other times require a different conduct.

It must be a source of satisfaction to German scholarship, and in particular to the German universities, which found less recognition at home than they deserved, that still in April of the current year a distinguished French scholar says in one of the most respected Paris daily papers: “Struck down on twenty battlefields, trampled underfoot by conquest, Germany has steeled itself anew at the universities and learned to rise again beneath the hand that sought to stifle it.”

From 1804 to 1813 it was the professors and the scholars who reawakened the Germanic spirit, and who, without always being conscious of it, undertook this struggle of the idea against force, whose success no one at that time would have suspected." I have said that when a dynasty unites with the spirit of the people, the two are most securely protected with each other and through each other.

In considering this further, highly esteemed
assembly, I return to the beginning of my address and at the same time arrive at its end.
History gives magnificent examples of what the spirit of a people can accomplish even without a dynasty; but I leave these aside, since in this inquiry I presuppose a monarchy.

If in a popular state, not too small, a dynasty is at the same time present, this dynasty heightens the national strength: how could Macedonia ever have become a significant power without a dynasty, how could Brandenburg or Prussia ever have risen to this height without a dynasty?
Truly, neither through the cities nor through the landed nobility.
Admiration for a great prince, enthusiasm for him, works wonders of enthusiasm.
Indeed, even a national spirit the ruler can, if not create it entirely from nothing, at least awaken from the slumber into which it had sunk, and quicken and raise it up.
