Thus Frederick the Great awakened, or perhaps even created, a Prussian national spirit, and despite his personal inclination toward French culture he recognized this spirit as German; as such, this national spirit came increasingly to the fore, though not without the resistance of a particularism that could only gradually be entirely overcome.

To be sure, here we come upon a point at which much of what has been said so far may fail and our consistency may suffer a setback: for the Prussian dynasty reaches beyond what is national, in that—to pass over smaller matters—it also embraces Slavic elements; and the German national character, which is the foundation of the Prussian state, reaches far beyond the Prussian dynasty.

These contradictions I must leave to themselves; the second is to some extent resolved by the federal relationship in which, to be sure, through the attachment of German federal territories to foreign—though small, yet presumptuous—empires, other contradictions again emerge, whose resolution Germany has until now hoped for in vain.

But to return again to the advantages that a dynasty confers: peoples that are linked to such a dynasty are more secure against being partitioned or allotted to other states. Hereditary dynasties are as a rule respected and spared by the other hereditary dynasts, and along with them the people's national character, whereas
men have been less reluctant to partition an elective kingdom and to toss republics and ecclesiastical principalities to dynasties as compensation.
Moreover, through their family connections the dynasties are dependent on mutually protecting and preserving themselves and their state entities.

And again the dynasty is borne by the spirit of the people; but if it is not—which, to be sure, also occurs—then it is subject to changes and to the claims of pretenders, whereby the peace and welfare of the state are shaken and undermined; and where such change occurs frequently, the population grows accustomed to following indifferently now this ruler and now that one, and to regarding the state as the spoil of the boldest and most powerful.
Only when the popular element and the dynasty are intimately interwoven does a secure guarantee exist for the duration of both against an overweening lust for conquest.
Yet both, the people and the dynasty, if they are to withstand a foreign superior power, must be strong, courageous, brave, and capable of self-sacrifice.

But strength does not rest merely on military power, which by consuming its forces can even weaken the country: it also rests on the personal strength of the leaders of the state, on their not recoiling before every threatening danger, on their committing the whole power of the country in such a danger, not out of faint-heartedness sacrificing the prestige and dignity of the state and the dynasty, and letting state and dynasty sink into a subordinate position; it also rests on wisdom and intelligence, on the spirit that must be spread and preferred, and on the free-minded ordering of all the state's relations.

That is why the state also needs science, and indeed not the soporific and dead science, but the fresh and living science, through which Prussia in the worst of times made up for much and acquired a splendor that at the same time won for it the hearts of the Germans.
May this land never allow itself to be outdone in this either!
May Prussia always embody that cooperation of the national spirit and the dynasty which, apart from the temporary obscuring of its fundamental ideas, it has embodied until now!

For do we not recognize in this cooperation the full worth of a noble dynasty for the fatherland, recognize
what we owe to the exalted House of Hohenzollern, the courageous, the brave, the wise?

May the All-Gracious One at last grant full recovery to the sorely tried bearer of the Majesty, preserve him, and preserve the exalted Prince Regent, on whom the next hope of the people, faithfully devoted to him in reverence and love, surely rests—preserve the entire flourishing House of the Royal Dynasty of the Hohenzollern for our present and for the nearer and more distant future of the fatherland; may He pour out His grace abundantly over the ruling house and the people, without which all that is human is a weak reed swaying in the storm of the times, and thus bestow on the state its best good: justice and concord within, and firmness without!

div.head: XII. Rede zur Eröffnung der eilften Versammlung Deutscher Philologen, Schulmänner und Orientalisten, gehalten zu Berlin am 30. September 1850.
Von der Philologie, besonders der klassischen in Beziehung zur morgenländischen, zum Unterricht und zur Gegenwart

p.s: Highly esteemed gentlemen!

Three years have now passed since, near the border of Germanic culture and beyond the borders of the German confederation of states, but in a city to which German popular education and the German scholarship intimately connected with it—German philology in particular—owe much and great things, in Basel, our Society resolved that it would meet here in Berlin the following year.

If Basel's claims were founded, besides the zealous cultivation of our studies in the present, on a glorious past reaching back to the ancestors in the times of the restoration of the sciences, indeed even on its Roman origin, then Berlin, by contrast, is a relatively new creation; it cannot boast of having exerted, in the age of the reawakening of more vigorous scholarly activity, a powerful and salutary influence—as Basel did through an association of rare talents and through the extensive operation of the then still young art of printing—on general education and especially on the study of antiquity. But nowadays especially, when the new makes itself felt above all against the old, we may without hesitation place the younger flowering of scholarship in our city into the scales against the weight of the ancestors.

If, however, it could seem a matter for concern to summon this assembly into the turmoil of a great capital city, in which congenial togetherness might, if not impossible, still be subject to manifold disturbance, then we owe you thanks for having overcome this concern—a concern that presents itself to me, to be sure, as less significant than it does to many, since after all it lies entirely with us whether we wish to let ourselves be disturbed and distracted
or not. Unfortunately, the resolution adopted at Basel has been destroyed for the coming years by the unfavorableness of the times, by fateful storms which, despite all signs and forebodings, had nevertheless not been possible to foresee in their full extent.

The necessary preparations for receiving the assembly toward the end of September 1848 had already been made when the March events made the men entrusted with the direction of the affair recognize that the meeting of the association in Berlin at the said time would be impossible; the year 1849 brought new dissensions, less within this country than in the common German fatherland, and we were only following the wishes that had come to us from outside in many quarters when we also postponed the assembly for the last-named year and adjourned it for the time being in hope of better times.

Not without deep pain must I declare that even in the current year German conditions have by no means taken such a shape as, by my feeling and my insight, a gathering of German scholars was bound to wish for—a gathering that is essentially rooted in the consciousness of the unity of the German national spirit as of German science and learning, is borne up by this unity, and has long since realized this very unity together with the other men of science, each in his own place and in his own field, that is, without any political reference: for in German science the spiritual bond and the inner unity of the people have long been given, and every separate striving has been abolished; indeed, the German spirit has had to take refuge in it, to withdraw into this safe and inviolable asylum and to hide itself in it, when external power had sworn its destruction.

But even if our hopes have not been granted that fulfillment which could have afforded a compensation for the sufferings of the past, and if the enthusiasm is thereby somewhat dampened with which we had hoped to be able to receive you under more favorable circumstances, yet tranquility has returned once more, which is the first prerequisite for the existence and especially for the social activity of a scholarly association: hereby the obstacle had fallen away which stood in
the way of the earlier summons of the honored assembly to this capital, and the Royal Government has, with the greatest readiness and sympathy, in accord with the universally acknowledged love of His Majesty the King for the sciences, bestowed upon us the requisite support.
Welcome, then, within these walls, honored comrades of our society!

Receive our most heartfelt thanks for the trust that you have shown me and the other members of the board through your election—a trust which, insofar as it lies within our powers, to justify is our most earnest wish and will be our eager endeavor.

Undeterred by the confusions of the age, we wish joyfully to begin our work, whose immediate purpose will be attained if this assembly too, like earlier ones, helps to draw more tightly the bond of commonality by discussing the general conditions of our science and of instruction and by deliberating particular subjects.
This common bond rests, as the very name of the association teaches, on a twofold fact: that we are philologists and that we are Germans.

If I merely mention the latter without dwelling on it—since, without prejudice to our heartfelt sympathy for the fortunes of the fatherland, I deliberately keep every political reference at a distance—then let it be permitted to devote a few words to the other side of this commonality, without any oratorical ornament or pomp, which, although properly belonging to the panegyris, is yet little suited to the opening of this scholarly ceremonial assembly and to my subject.
Our society calls itself "Association of German Philologists, Schoolmen, and Orientalists."

If this union is a well-considered one, then, since schoolmen form the second member of this triad, we must assume in doing so that the direction of the latter is predominantly the philological; and so this combination, which in earlier centuries no one could have contested, rests upon a foundation that is no longer entirely fully valid. But even if schoolmen whose field is alien to philology are, according to the letter and spirit of the original foundation of our union, supposed to belong to it, the relationship has in fact, and in the nature of the thing, taken such a shape that schoolmen who occupy
themselves exclusively, say, with mathematics and the natural sciences, without any connection with philological studies, do not readily join us or appear actively among us; rather, the true point of union of this society has become classical and Oriental philology, and indeed both its scholarly or theoretical pursuit and the practical application of philology to instruction, and the methodology bearing upon that.

These, together with philosophy, which comprehends everything within itself, with the philology of the Middle Ages and of the more recent European peoples, as well as with the study of history, which is scarcely separable from philology, and finally with mathematics and the natural sciences, embrace the entire domain of scientific knowledge; and the so-called faculty sciences—theology, jurisprudence, and medicine—are in truth only applications of these in manifold combination.

Surely philosophy was with good deliberation not drawn into the association when it was formed; medieval and modern philology, together with history, are indeed not expressly excluded—on the contrary, the latter, at least with respect to schoolmasters, is explicitly admitted: but apart from this practical application of the study of history as a branch of instruction, the historical researchers and historians, insofar as they do not treat ancient history, are certainly not to be regarded as members of the association; and since medieval and modern philology is not particularly mentioned in the statute, it can at least appear doubtful whether their admission into our circle was intended, since by philology one mostly understands only the study of classical antiquity.

However one may judge of this, and of the correctness of these separations, the point is — although for science, yet truly not for the formation of such an association — not on thoroughly conceptual distinctions and combinations, but on which masses have in reality attracted one another and been historically formed; which too will not have arisen purely by chance, but from causes lying in the nature of the sciences, and the same causes have unquestionably produced the delimitation which the association has partly given itself from the beginning,
partly adopted in its development.

Now even if within these limits there still lies a twofold opposition—the one between the Oriental and the Classical, the other between the scientific or theoretical and the methodical or practical—it is admittedly to be granted that this justifies the formation of separate divisions, as indeed such divisions already exist; but the affinity of those opposed members is so great that it would be a matter for regret if they did not rather attract than repel one another, and if—as all harmony arises from the union of things that differ—these oppositions were not sublated into a higher unity.
One of these contrasts—I mean that between the theoretical and the practical—on closer examination even disappears entirely.

For although theoretical philology comes to a definite application in school instruction, in that it is to give the pupils a general education, yet here the distinction between scientific knowledge and its practical use is of an entirely different kind from that in the fields in which what has been theoretically established is transferred to the needs of life: for the application of the sciences in general, and hence also of philological knowledge, to instruction or to general education consists precisely only in this, that the rudiments of knowledge itself are taught, which, while they serve the purpose of producing that education, are at the same time the preparatory exercises of knowledge itself, so that the methodology of teaching, so important for school instruction, is at the same time the methodology of learning the first scientific principles themselves, or practice here is nothing other than the beginning of theory, and the methodology of instruction nothing other than the methodology of knowledge itself in its first elements; by contrast, in the application of particular sciences to life outside instruction, practice is by no means one and the same as the beginnings of theory, but follows after it.
What we have called the practical side of philology is therefore properly its elementary part, and since this cannot be separated from the rest, that opposition cancels itself out entirely.

It cannot be maintained even to this extent—that the foundational treatment of the elements required a lesser capacity; for, as
Quintilian already remarks, even the beginnings of grammar, once one has penetrated into its sanctuary, are suited not merely to sharpen the mind of boys but to occupy the deepest learning and science (altissimam eruditionem ac scientiam): true insight into scientific subjects rests precisely in the reduction to the simplest grounds (the ἀρχάς), in the resolution of the entire material into its simplest components, and it is not unworthy of the greatest master to devote himself to the first elements, just as, conversely, nothing is more detrimental than when not seldom men who are not masters of the science set themselves up, with great presumption and arrogance, as reformers of method.
The other of the contrasts I mentioned is that between the Oriental and the Classical.

The time is long past when the study of Oriental languages and Oriental literature attached itself merely to our sacred books and thus to theology; gradually the whole Orient has unfolded before our eyes: alongside the Semitic and other Oriental languages more remote from our own linguistic formation, we have come to know, as more closely related to the Classical and Germanic, a richly articulated language family, whose noblest branch is Sanskrit, and it was especially on the latter, in connection with the languages of classical antiquity and with our mother tongue, that comparative linguistics developed.

At the same time we have penetrated more deeply into Phoenician, and at last the key has also been found to the mysterious characters of the Egyptians, as well as to their language, together with a closer acquaintance with their monuments of art, even if it does not yet always fit easily and perfectly.

However different the Oriental and the classical may be, at the present standpoint of linguistic research the grammar of the classical languages can no longer dispense with the connection to the comparative grammar of the Indo-Germanic languages: already in this the community of Oriental philology with classical philology is sufficiently grounded; and, to set aside the disputed question of what influence the Orient and especially Egypt had upon the classical peoples of
antiquity, it must in any case be conceded that not only is the later history of the Orient, particularly since the rule of the Persians in the eastern coastal lands of the Mediterranean, interwoven with the history of the classical peoples, but also that, just as the languages, so the oldest conceptions of the aforementioned Oriental and of the classical peoples have, without prejudice to the strictly developed Hellenic peculiarity, manifold points of contact, most clearly in religion and mythology, and that the history of classical art, which we claim as a part of philology, cannot be separated from knowledge of Oriental artistic monuments: indeed I would maintain that, just as comparative linguistics has taken shape, so too a comparative cultural history of the whole of antiquity may in time emerge as a principal task of philological science.
So then, instead of wishing to posit an opposition between Oriental and classical studies, let us rather joyfully welcome the bond between them that is displayed in our association.

Each of these two fields is, to be sure, again very broad and in itself highly manifold, and the Oriental field especially falls into many branches separated according to peoples and language families, of which almost every one offers abundant material for the undivided activity of a single scholar.

Classical philology too—to linger a moment on this field, which lies closest to me—if philology, as I understand it along with most others, is to be the historical construction of the whole of life, that is, of all the circles of culture and the products of a people in its practical and intellectual directions, then it encompasses an infinity of subjects that no single individual will be able to fathom all of with equal depth, even if he had the spirit of an Aristotle or a Leibniz and the leisure that most of us lack.

But this infinity, which philology shares with all knowledge, is precisely the condition and the most powerful spur of the courageous striving after knowledge, which would slacken and finally cease if, beyond every goal attained, a new and more distant one were not set: and what Socrates says of Eros, that he is a philosopher because, being a son of Poros and Penia,
he does not yet partake of the wealth of knowledge but strives after knowledge, admits of application to the philologist as well; indeed, just as the philosopher is named precisely from the love of wisdom, and, in the view of him who invented this word—though certainly not with the full agreement of those who believe they have made all knowledge ready and possess it completely—is to strive after Sophia continually, without ever being satisfied, so too in the corresponding name of philology, with fine sense, it is not complete possession but the striving after the Logos, in never-failing love for it, that is expressed.

Thus our philology is an infinite task, whose solution we approach by approximation; and if for no other reasons, for this one alone it will never cease and never perish, because it can never be exhausted and brought to a close.

Precisely for that reason it also cannot be brought to completion in the spirit of a single individual in its full extent; in its full meaning it is only ideally realized in the totality of its adherents, variously distributed among countless spirits and represented more or less perfectly, and yet in all who are called to it it is the very same, just as the idea of humanity repeats itself in countless individuals.

This distribution and fragmentation has indisputably grown greatly prevalent in our age, in which the celebrated principle of the division of labor has also asserted itself in scholarship to a high degree: hence a multitude—indeed, we may say a flood—of monographic writings has arisen, all of which it is difficult to become acquainted with, but which certainly contribute very much to the expansion of our knowledge; and if the micrological cannot be kept entirely away from this tendency, then this very thing has its justification in the fact that, provided only the larger matters are not neglected on that account, nothing in scholarship is so small as to be overlooked without harm, and one may no more begrudge philology its micrology—philology, which can see only with the unaided eye of the mind—than one may begrudge natural science its microscopy, even if the latter brings more important things to light than the former.

Nevertheless, for all the necessary articulation, our knowledge can be endangered by too great a division
of labor extending down into too small masses, because every detail first gains its correct illumination in the context of a larger whole, and for the investigation of each particular a knowledge of very many other things is required; just as in the division of mechanical labor the part that falls to each worker has a correspondence fixed in advance with each of the other parts—as, for example, among the Egyptians the individual limbs of larger sculptures, though made by different persons, were yet fashioned according to a given canon—so the monographic worker must look toward, not a law given to him from outside, which can serve only for mechanical labor, but rather the idea of the whole dwelling within him himself, and must never lose sight of it.

But in order that this idea may be kept alive, it would be especially serviceable if, following each successive advance of the science, one person and another, in a philosophical spirit, would construct the whole or large parts of it and thereby show how everything individual within it is necessary; only not without his having first tested and proved himself in the individual details, since otherwise he runs the danger of setting up empty compartments and schematisms instead of living forms.

If that organic unity of all parts is recognized in a living way, then the hostile conflicts among the various directions within the field of classical philology—such as the grammatical, the so-called substantive, the art-archaeological, and the like—also disappear of their own accord, because all of these appear as equally entitled and, for philology, as equally substantive.
Although we together form a close community of scholarly life, it still cannot occur to us to shut ourselves off from the rest of scholarship or to isolate ourselves from it.

The intimate connection among all branches of knowledge, and the common advantage which, for every association—be it political or of another kind—is the surest guarantee of concord, impose upon all scholarly men the duty to feel themselves members of the great and single republic of letters, in which the particular societies stand only as the individual states of a confederation of nations.

Even if one is
willing to make allowances for the philological arrogance that has often raised our knowledge above everything else, that has even attributed a peculiar divinity to philology in one of its principal activities, in criticism, through the honorific title "diva critica"—a title, to be sure, very seldom justified—even if, I say, one is willing to make allowances for this arrogance on behalf of the enthusiasm that everyone feels for his own field, an enthusiasm that is not only beneficial but necessary: still, the truly moral standpoint of scholars in every field is that of mutual recognition and approach, with the consciousness that however different the paths of the various sciences may be, each has its justification and each does its part.
This moral demand will always carry the day: philology therefore has no enemy in the camps of scholarship, and from this quarter it has nothing to fear.

To be sure, philology and philosophy, already by virtue of their far-embracing names, are in the first instance, and as the most general directions of knowing, set side by side with one another, and thereby at the same time distinguished and opposed, as Plotinus and his pupils already declared; yet in spite of this, in fact the two have for the most part remained on friendly terms, and far from that opposition being an insoluble one, I venture rather to assert that both, in the realm of the spirit and apart from the philosophy of nature, which does not come into consideration here, must lead from an opposite starting point to the same result, if both follow the right path, and if philology, as in my opinion it ought, raises itself from the individual and through the individual to the idea and beyond a crude polyhistory, and philosophy, not lost in mere abstractions, pervades the individual with the idea.

If a great philosopher has done us the disgrace of calling philology an aggregate, then in many respects he has not done it wrong; instead of being angry at this, it is more fitting for us to bring about that this aggregate state be abolished through a more scientific treatment of the whole.

Just as little can philology as a science ever be impaired by the natural sciences: for these lie in an entirely different field, and it is inconceivable that philology, whose task is the history of the mind, could ever be displaced by
the contemplation of nature, since the mind will never renounce the endeavor to come to know itself in its own earlier developments.

I do not wish to weary you by also considering the other branches of knowledge in the same connection; but I believe I find no contradiction in saying that almost every science can and must seek counsel from philology, and philology from every science. And to dwell only on the second of these propositions, it seems to me that the philologist is quite properly called upon to go about among the masters of every discipline, as Socrates did—not, like him, to see whether they were wiser than he or not, but to learn from them what he must know as material for his own great work.
If, then, no impairment of philology is to be feared from any scholarly quarter, how does it come about that nevertheless not a few of the philologists themselves harbor apprehensions for it?

The answer is quite simple: if there is any well-founded apprehension of a power hostile to philology, that power can only be an unscientific one, for the designation of which the word "barbarism" is the most comprehensive and the most weighty.

However dark the powers that weigh upon our time, I confess that I was not frightened by them, either twenty years ago, when a gloomy prophecy of threatening universal barbarism first arose, or in the years just past; and in both cases the immediate future soon gave the lie to the prophetic voices.

But there are indisputably individual elements lying outside science that are directed especially against philological studies, and indeed primarily against the classical ones—against these more only because they have a greater influence on the education of youth—while in principle they must equally be hostile to Oriental philology and have in fact been hostile to it in the cases where they encountered it and it came within their field of view.

As the dangerous bearers of these hostile elements, we must regard not so much the great mass of the wholly uneducated and unscientific, who entirely lack the intellectual weapons with which they might assail and combat science and learning, as rather the by no means untalented and
even highly eloquent half-learned and half-scholarly, who, without having immersed themselves in any one science and without esteeming and loving it for its own sake, make it their business to determine the relations of science to the state, to national life, to the so-called spirit of the age and its requirements and needs, each according to his own particular bent, in order then to measure the worth or worthlessness of the sciences by that standard—hybrid beings between scholars and politicians, filled with the urge to transform the whole life of humanity and to build up a new culture on new foundations.

From here proceed almost all attacks on philology; I would say "all" without qualification, were there not one coming from a wholly opposite quarter, namely, that the study of classical antiquity does injury to Christianity.

Those other missiles, seemingly more effective nowadays, which are dispatched against philology, may be reduced to the following three: first, that all education must be popular in character and therefore calculated quite especially for the lower classes, for which this pedantic and dead erudition is not suited; second, that the welfare of the people rests in the so-called material interests, to which our erudition contributes nothing and adds nothing; third, that the education of our age and people already stands on firm feet by itself and can dispense with the means of ancient education, since these have already been surpassed, and that in general a free education, hitherto unprecedented and exalted above all antiquity, must be won.

Although I do not presume to be able to offer this enlightened assembly anything that every one of you does not know as well as or better than I, may it be permitted me to attach a few briefly drawn remarks to these points, without intending to tax your patience too long.

The charge of being anti-Christian, which was cited first, springs less from the temper of this age than from a zeal for the faith that oversteps its bounds—a zeal that is by no means exclusively peculiar to Christianity, since it already stirred up Anytos and Meletos against Socrates, as it stirred up many others in antiquity against the teachings of science. But few of the
scholarly theologians will be found to have had a share in this charge; on the contrary, we owe thanks both to the Church of the Middle Ages for preserving and handing down to us the noble treasures of antiquity, and to the church reform of the sixteenth century for having promoted and cultivated these studies in a quite pre-eminent way and introduced them into the schools.
To be sure, I think, these studies nourish the freedom of the spirit; but a church that could not endure this would not be the church in spirit and in truth.

On the other hand, the whole of antiquity, notwithstanding all its aberrations, is so filled with religious feelings, thoughts, and perceptions, and felt so deep a religious need, that it was this far more than the deadness and weariness of polytheism that made the ancients themselves receptive to the purer and more inward doctrines of Christianity.

Furthermore, who could be more ardently inspired by a truly national education than the devotees of classical philology, since they in particular have daily, as it were, before their eyes a people in which a purely national education, as independent as possible of foreign influence, had reached perfection, and which at once transformed everything foreign that it had taken up into its own being and its own flesh and blood?

Admittedly, one must concede that from the principle that education should be national, the use of classical studies of antiquity for the attainment of that end cannot be derived, and consequently, if this use is to be justified, other grounds for it must exist. If, however, for any purpose whatsoever, besides what is native, another linguistic, literary, historical—in short, in the widest sense of the word, philological—means of education is found to be appropriate, then certainly none is less dangerous to national character than the classical, because through it the education of another contemporary people is not consciously, or—what is still worse—unconsciously, transferred, as French education was for a long time insinuated into the German, but the classical is simply the common root and foundation of all European education.

That our studies are in no way suited to elementary popular instruction is a point on which I scarcely need to dwell; for however important such instruction
is, and however greatly it must be promoted with all our powers and by every possible means—which is why we ourselves would gladly have drawn all who carry it on into our circle—the state of the sciences would nonetheless be very bad indeed if they were to be valued according to the measure of their applicability to such instruction.

That widespread tendency of the age toward whatever is useful to practical life, to commerce and acquisition and private prosperity, is excellent: for it lightens, promotes, and adorns earthly life; yet if it seeks to stunt, banish, and deaden in us the more spiritual element, it is banausic and repels nobler souls all the more from itself, in that it even prides itself on its aphilokalia; it then necessarily becomes misological and thus, to be sure, can tolerate no philology, least of all that of classical antiquity, which has long since stamped that banausic disposition with the mark it deserves.
Let those exclusive praisers of the so-called useful nevertheless consider that there are also ideal goods, and that with their loss the others at the same time lose their value!
And should we perhaps be presumptuous if we claim to occupy ourselves with a great part of this?

As for, finally, those propositions and demands which I have summarized under the last of the points touched upon above: I am indeed far from believing that all the periods of human development have already run their course and that the human race has no new phase of that development still to enter; but just as the great Plato, even while he is on the point of sketching a wholly new ideal of the political community, is yet modest enough to confess that it is hard to discover a better education than the one that has long since been found, so I regard it as a titanic rebellion against world history if even the wisest man or the most cultivated people or age should wish to cast down everything old at the storming pace of an emancipation frenzy and, disdaining all the teachings of the ancient world, to build up a new world of knowledge and action out of itself alone. Rather, if it is not too presumptuous to prophesy about the future course of human history, then according to what is somewhat boldly called the
dialectic of world history, the third great world period would presumably be one in which the genuine elements of the ancient and the modern had been most intimately fused into a higher unity.

But leaving this undecided (for I do not claim any gift of prophecy), it remains that, by virtue of the course of development which European humanity has taken not without Providence, our whole body of knowledge is so interwoven and grown together with antiquity by a thousand and yet a thousand threads that one cannot arbitrarily cut out this one without destroying the whole fabric; and if we once began to neglect the older half of human history and everything that antiquity has done in advance for us, then, in order to stand on our own feet, we would withdraw the ground from under the feet that have learned to walk on it, or destroy the foundations after we imagine we have reached the building of the roof.

Whether, moreover, antiquity has really been surpassed by us to such an extent, as many believe, that we could be released from this means of education, I take the liberty, without prejudice to the veneration for all that is noble and beautiful and great which the modern world has produced, modestly to deny, and only to recall that it is not so very long ago since our poetry, philosophy, and sculpture renewed themselves upon antiquity and gave themselves a higher consecration, and that it would be folly to believe that with this the wellspring of fresh life is exhausted, which flows over to us from antiquity and has watered and refreshed all succeeding ages down to us.

If we ask ourselves wherein the great advances of our age lie, we shall, unprejudiced, hardly be able to give any other answer than the one I recently attempted to develop on another occasion: that we have become great through empirical inquiry, but that the fundamental ideas of the creative spirit and the primal forms of the beautiful are an ancient Promethean endowment for humanity, and that antiquity, because it brought these forth with youthful enthusiasm and shaped them with vigor, retains an imperishable value for all posterity.

Our forebears recognized this, and things akin to it that are
connected with it—the most cultivated among our older contemporaries, the creators of our national literature, even those whose own character stands furthest removed from antiquity.
Who could be less classical than Jean Paul?

All the more weighty is it when this sensitive humorist says: “the present world would sink unfathomably deep, if youth did not first, through the silent temple of the great old times and men, take the passage to the fair of later life.”

And if we too had not had statesmen—and if we did not still have them—who recognized the high significance of classical education for us, who took it up into themselves and wished for its spread through instruction, then we would have to step back in shame when a French statesman, when Thiers, instructs us: it is not merely words that are taught to the young with Latin and Greek; they are noble and sublime things, it is the history of humanity in simple, great, and indelible images; and in our century, to remove the young from the source of the simple beauty of antiquity is nothing other than to hasten our moral degradation.

“Let us leave youth in antiquity, as in a stormless, peaceful, and healthy refuge, which is destined to keep it fresh and pure!” As long as such voices still sound (and they are not so isolated, and will increase the more calm returns to people’s minds), as long, further, as the philologists themselves do their part, and the great leaders of scholarship—among whom, since the time of the last gathering, we have to mourn the death of the noble Gottfried Hermann—are replaced by kindred vigorous spirits, I trust—not especially sharing the anxieties for our studies—in that primal power of antiquity as surely as Ovid trusted in the immortality of Aratus, which, although he is no star of the first magnitude in the heaven of ancient culture, has nevertheless proved itself brilliantly.

If these studies have outlasted far worse times—if they have outlasted the migration of peoples and the whole Middle Ages, if they have outlasted the Thirty Years' War, in which they were almost entirely extinguished, and yet soon rose again to
beautiful bloom—then they will also outlast the time of the most recent troubles, to which they themselves, especially for the torn German fatherland, can offer a salutary antidote in the political wisdom of antiquity that is, alas, too often ignored.
Gentlemen, if you share this confidence and these hopes with me, then the mood of our assembly, insofar as it is determined by the prospects for our studies, can only be cheerful and joyful!

div.head: XIII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 9. Juli 1835.
Ueber Leibniz und die Deutschen Akademien

p.s: The commemoration of memorial days for deserving men—the most vivid expression of the gratitude dwelling in every noble and receptive mind toward those who have departed, who sowed what we reap—has, according to the difference between those commemorated and the legacy they have left us, a very different meaning.

Larger or smaller communities, corporate bodies, and institutions have received gifts and benefactions whose enjoyment benefits succeeding generations; but however lasting the effectiveness of the useful foundation may be, little nevertheless passes from the founder to posterity beyond his name and good intent, because neither does a great personality of the founder shine forth from the work he established, nor has any other influence surpassing the ordinary measure secured for him a historical significance in the shaping of things.

To such people memorial days will be dedicated, not only to satisfy one's own feeling of gratitude, but so that a well-deserved memory may not be extinguished—a memory that would not yet be preserved merely by the name of its founder continuing, perhaps, in the name of the foundation.

Others, by their independent intellectual power, have established themselves as necessary links in that chain of developments in which the human spirit progressively reveals itself; their own innermost being has passed directly into the formation of the age that follows: they live on in world history and cannot be forgotten, even if their memory were proscribed; rather, to celebrate them is the very need of the later generation, which basks in their rays, and strengthens and elevates itself by their example.
Leibniz belongs among the latter.

Just as it did
not diminish his fame that no one followed his corpse but his faithful Eckhart, just as his fame would not have grown by a single inch if the entire court invited for the purpose had paid him a final homage, so he could become neither greater nor lesser by anything whether our Academy established this day of honor for Leibniz or did not establish it: indeed, by the very fact that it has only now begun to commemorate this day after more than a full century had acknowledged the greatness of the one honored, it has itself declared that it honors itself in a name to whose honor nothing more remained to be added, and has given expression to a confession of intent to work in his spirit—at that time perhaps not without a tacit reference also to the fact that the Academy should again, in accordance with his original intention, be a German-minded society of sciences; though to be sure not with a hostile stance toward foreign merit, since Leibniz, belonging to the entire scholarly world, united within himself the whole culture of Europe, and had to be all the more averse to a partiality springing from false patriotism the more painfully it, or the appearance of it, had been visited upon him himself.

And truly, even without his having been the first head of the scholarly association out of which the Academy developed, it could not have chosen a worthier man, one whom it revered—just as almost every corporate body of antiquity revered a heroic ancestor—as its own peculiar hero, in whom the unity of those bound together and the essence of their union, fused into a single person, portrayed itself, and whom it thus set forth as the hero who exhausted its concept in an undivided personality and living movement.

For Leibniz was not, as Herder says, merely a collaborator and president of the universal academy of all European sciences, but rather he alone was, in himself, an entire academy—and indeed one that, with the richest abundance of scientific life, intervened in the formation of his contemporaries and of posterity: such an academy he presents both in his Aristotelian comprehensiveness—which does not merely range over the general but is deepened into the minutest details of every branch of knowledge—and in the manner of his occupation and activity.

Simultaneously with a great rival, an inventor of mathematical forms on which those
earlier undreamed-of extensions and advances of this science rest, at the height in physics, chemistry, and geology that was attainable at that time, he developed at the same time, to be sure, no school-orthodox philosophical system, but distinctive philosophemes that contain a system within themselves; and even if the particular determinations in which he sought to grasp the eternally true, even if his monads and his pre-established harmony have not remained absolutely valid in this form, yet every deeper philosophizing feels itself as closely akin to his cognition as to Plato's, because in it, despite later flattening and disfigurement, it discovers a higher and genuinely speculative direction: for he sought, in his own phrase, raised above the senses and the imagination, the origin of appearances in the intellectual realm.

"I flatter myself," he says somewhere, "to have some ideas of this, but this age is not made to receive them"; a remark that applies equally well to his historical and linguistic plans and to his religious and ecclesiastical convictions and projects, some of which only our own time is beginning to realize in their full scope, while others, after small beginnings, remain reserved for the future.

He had read Plato and Aristotle in the original language and early set himself the goal of uniting them; his extensive knowledge of the rest of classical philology, although its fruits are not before us, can be gauged from his youthful attempts—partly left unfinished, partly lost—at editions of Petronius and Martianus Capella; his intention to write on the imitators of Lipsius shows a genuinely philological attention to the forms of presentation, and his poetic description of the newly discovered phosphorus is not unworthy of Lucretius.
He even occupied himself with Roman coins and Greek inscriptions, and at least in the latter solved more difficult problems that were scarcely penetrable by the men of the profession.
Etymology, both in itself and in relation to the origin and connection of the peoples, and especially the antiquities of the mother tongue, occupied him in many ways.

Along with those grand undertakings in history and the study of
documents, he combined jurisprudence and the activity of the publicist, and, along with the highest theological and philosophical reflections, as later Lessing did, a librarianship; and from the investigation of the divine plan of the world his gaze descended even to the improvement of carriages, to mechanical engineering, to mining and the cultivation of silkworms, which he carried on in his garden.

Wholly academic in character, he never taught publicly; rather, only his patronesses, those high-minded and intellectually brilliant princesses, were directly formed in his school. He took part in all the learned endeavors of the age as a full academy would, and maintained a larger correspondence than such an academy with every person of scholarly significance. Even the courtier's coloring, which has often served as an object of mockery, at least corresponded to the earlier position of the academies and removed him from the pedantry of the scholars of his time, whom no one will regard as academic.

He was always forming great designs, some of them impracticable for himself and for others alike; many required a union of forces and the sustained efforts of many, such as precisely an academy could supply: he discovered the gaps in the sciences, gave encouragement and counsel toward filling them, and sketched out the plans.

Devoted to shared studies, he longed for a stay in a great capital city such as London or Paris, in order to help and to let himself be helped; for many things, he says, cannot be accomplished by a single individual.

Therefore the thought of founding comprehensive scholarly associations, in which many working together accomplished what is denied to one individual to bring about, and which at the same time, through correspondence, promoted the general connection of all scholarly nations and, as it were, prepared the way for a single universal empire of knowledge—this thought continually spurred him, in various capitals of Germany—in Berlin, Dresden, and Vienna—to pursue the founding of academies; and he succeeded in Berlin.

Although more significant products of the mind have sides which at first lie hidden and only emerge in the course of further development—as a poem and every genuine work of art contain many a meaning that the artist did not consciously put
into it—nevertheless the human work, after its first birth, as it were, still naked and more transparent, and stripped of all ornament and accessory with which it is later decked out, usually lets its inner essence shine through more clearly.
This also holds true of the academies, especially of the one that owes its existence to Leibniz.

The honorable endeavor of our age, which demands a reason for everything and will not acknowledge what exists merely because it exists, made it natural to raise the vital question of what these academies, especially in Germany, were actually for, and why they were established and maintained by the state; they had brought little of benefit to scholarship—the Berlin Academy, says a once widely read writer on the Prussian monarchy under Frederick the Great, even less than many others; and indeed the French Academy attained a dominion such as no German academy could win, because it united many and almost all the lights of learning in the one great capital, and the universities of France gradually became subordinate institutions, whereas in Germany the latter, scattered across many separate regions, with great vigor and freshness of life took possession of scholarly influence.

If one did not wish to regard the academies as objects of vain splendor, as a more distant appendage of the court retinue, then one preserved them as representatives of learning in the capitals, from which the restless universities were kept at a distance.
Yet the difficulty of assigning them a significant place in the realm of science had to grow with the transplantation of the universities into capital cities, where they shone forth even more.
What matters is to assign to each of the two institutions a distinct and valid value.

The view that first presents itself—that the state maintains the universities as institutions of learning for the education of its servants, while in the Academy it recognizes, and rightly so, pure science without any purposes of the state—lends the state, in regard to the Academy, that liberality of mind which is worthy of it, but takes it away from the state in its relation to the universities.

The state should also maintain these [universities] for the sake of pure science, because science itself, even without particular
purposes, is already the light of life for the human race, and this light, proceeding from the lower and higher schools, must also permeate the state. If much that is practical is taught at universities, academies of sciences likewise pursue such things, and for neither the former nor the latter is the merely practical the main thing, but only for special and lesser schools, in which servants are to be trained and trimmed up.

That at least the German universities themselves, which surely wish to understand their purpose better than anyone, have been understood by discerning statesmen, without dispute, as a purely scholarly institution—for this the purest proof is given by pure scholarship itself, philosophy, which, following Leibniz's impulse, developed through all its stages, from Christian Wolf down to our own times, exclusively at the universities; not to mention that the universities have from the beginning existed only within the state, yet wholly independent of its particular purposes.

Moreover, that view—that the Academy is merely the recognition of pure science within the state—is not very different from the one that Frederick the Great wished to eliminate when he said "that the Academy should exist not for parade but for instruction"; for the establishment of an academic body as mere recognition, without the demand for a distinctive achievement such as is directed at the universities—namely, that they should spread abroad through teaching the entire body of science which they share with the Academy—comes very close indeed to a parade formation.

The view just mentioned likewise readily produces a negative, more or less inactive attitude and a lofty aloofness; and if, in the present state of the realm of science, the various critical journals represent what public opinion and a free press are in the life of the state, while the universities are comparable to that state power which arises out of the restless element of the people, then one of those living academics of lofty conviction might well believe that he is settling himself into the comfortable armchair of a scientific peerage.
Leibniz was far removed from such notions.

To be sure, he and the founder of the Prussian Academy of Sciences
did not subscribe to the principles of a common utility, and it seems almost significant that this foundation, which soon fell into decline and from which he had, however, long since withdrawn, was nevertheless obliged, only in the year after his death, in order to escape complete ruin, to establish a medico-surgical college for field surgeons: yet there did hover before him a positive character of an academy, with a specifically determined scientific activity, and indeed his own, which he realized durably outside himself in a society of many: and herein lies what distinguishes an academy, or public learned society, from other scientific institutions, and in the first instance from the universities.

The academies and universities jointly pursue the expansion and diffusion of the whole of science through living community and communication, free of restrictive relations; the state establishes and maintains both, because the attainment of all the moral ends of man, and thus also of the highest, knowledge, is its task, and the most comprehensive scientific institutions, under the given circumstances, cannot fully achieve their purpose without its assistance; in return it takes from both that practical benefit, esteemed by Leibniz as no small matter, which genuine science abundantly yields for all branches and spheres of human life.

But the manner of community and communication is different: the universities comprise a community of masters with pupils, the academies a community of masters with masters. The latter, as a distinctive form of the highest scientific life, has its justification within itself just as much as the former, and consequently lays claim to validity independently of the greater or lesser need of the ages, as soon as that need has once awakened at all and remains alive.
But this will never die out.

Just as an encyclopedia of all the sciences, and again of each particular principal discipline, is necessary, so the scholarly life requires a comprehensive society of masters, so that the individual members may remain in living connection; for only to few minds is it granted, like Leibniz, to bear and to master the entire body of human knowledge.

Furthermore,
to be sure, as one hears every day, the division of labor also promotes [progress] in science—a division that Leibniz too intended; but the greater the division becomes (and it is beginning to become almost alarmingly great), the more necessary it is for the individual workers to have common deliberation and the most many-sided contact, so that amid their specialities they do not lose sight of the general and the whole.

In a select community the master measures himself against the master; it holds up a mirror of self-knowledge so that even the greatest, not overestimating himself, may always keep the awareness present that his knowledge is only a limited part of the learned wealth of the people.

Profound insights and inventions are indeed the fruit of the solitary, secret conception of the mind; but the most extreme scientific aberrations, too, are hatched in seclusion, and have never originated with scientific societies.

Shared study diminishes and cures error; and that in this shared endeavor of the master the academic element precisely lies, those have shown by their own example who, like several of our departed colleagues whom we sorrowfully miss, were active as academics above all and with predilection.

But academies are especially dependent on those things which, as Leibniz says, cannot be carried out by a single individual, whether because various kinds of knowledge and abilities are required for them, or because of the collection of material and the procurement of the aids themselves.

Travels, such as Leibniz himself likewise undertook again, exceed the powers of individuals, or the leisure of a single person is not equal to the treatment of the subject: and precisely nowadays great and costly undertakings stand all the more in need of support, the more literature fragments itself in endless petty trade.

To be sure, since its last restoration our Academy has fulfilled its purpose to the best of its powers in all these respects and in the most diverse branches of knowledge; if it has not as yet delivered another common work, which according to its statutes likewise lies within its purpose—a continuous survey of the state and progress of the sciences, to be compiled from the reports of its members—then the
cause of this lies in its insufficient means.

Finally, the stated purpose of the academies proves itself in particular, in contrast to the universities, in that they extend the community of masters beyond the limits of their particular places of residence, partly by spurring and encouraging all scholars to the solution of significant problems—to which belong, among us, the academic prize questions that we are accustomed to announce on this day, not without our intention having often already been crowned with the most favorable success in filling significant gaps in scholarship—partly by maintaining, through external members and mutual communications, a friendly connection among themselves and a general scholarly world-intercourse.

If all the academic societies founded by states or princes, from the Platonic Academy at Florence onward, and further back from the Alexandrian Museum onward—to which the prize essays that we must consider later refer—pursued the same purpose, variously modified according to circumstances and the spirit of the ages, then at the founding of the Society of Sciences as well, which Leibniz brought about through the advocacy of the discerning Queen Charlotte, that purpose was given expression in a manner peculiar to the age, in part with uncommon naivety.

The King, it is said among other things, wished to establish a common workshop where the work of science might be carried on with a united hand; for to attain its further growth, societies served better than individuals, since the deficiency of one is supplied by another: indeed, one might wish for a society not only of persons but also of peoples, so that their various qualities and intellectual powers might complement one another.

Although, in accordance with the King's patriotic and pious disposition, the principal purposes are stated to be, first, the cultivation and preservation of the German language in its proper purity, to the honor and adornment of the German people — which even from that mixture of German and Latin in which this is presented proves itself to be a demand of the age — then the treatment of German, and in particular of Prussian, secular and ecclesiastical
history, and finally the pursuit of the Oriental languages for the propagation of the Gospel among the unbelievers; nevertheless the Society already embraced the greater part of knowledge in four divisions, one for physics, chemistry, medicine, and the like, one for mathematics and its applications, a third for the national language and history, and a fourth for literature, especially Oriental literature: whether Leibniz excluded philosophy because he presupposed no effective participation in it, or because he did not expect its advancement from a commonality of studies, or whether external reasons prevailed in this exclusion, is uncertain.

In any case, Frederick the Great deserves thanks for having added those as well, since—however powerfully the obstacles to common understanding in philosophy may have grown—within every scholarly society it exerts a beneficent influence through its unperceived effect on all the other endeavors; if, by contrast, he excluded poetry and eloquence, then a later age will perhaps admit these as well.

Nor were the acquisition of manifold aids and the establishment of connections with foreign countries forgotten already under Frederick the First; attention was directed in particular to great scholarly undertakings in the East—ideas that do honor to that age, which was animated by the highest thirst for knowledge, and that attained their realization in the following ages and in the present one, even if in a different manner.

It is well known, says the King, in what a particularly good understanding we stand with the Muscovite Tsar, and how this prince shows a great fondness for the works of nature and of art, but especially for navigation; since, now, by reason of his great power and extensive lands, he could contribute greatly to the common purpose achieved through the establishment of the Society, negotiations should be conducted with him on occasion, so that useful astronomical and geographical observations might be undertaken from the Prussian frontiers as far as China, and remarks concerning peoples, languages, customs, and unknown objects of nature and art might be made and sent to the Society.

In particular, attention is here drawn to the variation in the magnetic needle's declination according to place and time; this point, it was said, could be
investigated from the Rhine all the way to the Memel and farther in the north and east of the earth, and on this occasion the light of Christianity could be kindled among the barbarous peoples as far as China, for which purpose the King, beyond other princes, has the advantage of possessing amber, which of all European wares is almost alone highly prized and sought after in China.

Leibniz's attention to the variation of the magnetic needle, about which he later conversed with the Czar at Torgau, and also his Chinese studies make it probable, despite the seemingly strange combination of very dissimilar things, that this plan too rested on his inspiration; and in this one likewise recognizes his spirit, ever striving into the distant and scarcely attainable by the present.

Truly, no fairer dispensation, no more favorable omen of future flourishing could fall to the Academy's lot than that it should have been received in this spirit; and as long as it remains worthy of this model and faithful to the sense which, at its last restoration, it gave expression to by nothing more definitely than by the institution of our present celebration, it will—even after the most lamentable loss of its fairest ornaments and those most closely akin to them, a loss in which the pursuit of knowledge too pays the due tribute to the transitoriness of all finite things—under the protection of a noble royal house, in ever-renewed youthful vigor, put forth fresh branches and blossoms from a healthy stock, and bear fruit for the enjoyment of its contemporaries and for a later sowing.

div.head: XIV. Etwas über Wilhelm von Humboldt, gesprochen in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 9. Juli 1835.
Etwas über Wilhelm von Humboldt

p.s: Literature and scholarship have in recent times suffered so many and such irreplaceable losses in rapid succession that the observation, often voiced, must involuntarily have forced itself upon the leaders of public opinion in this field: that those glorious spirits who were chiefly responsible for calling forth and consolidating the present state of our culture, and upon whose mighty power our age has raised itself up, would all be summoned so suddenly from the scene of their activity that, while the younger generation has not yet grown strong enough for similar might—or at least for the hope of it—a gulf would remain between the past and the future.

Baron Wilhelm von Humboldt, who was torn from our Academy, our State, and the entire educated world scarcely three months ago, had won among those heroes in the field of scholarship and of the whole intellectual life no lesser a place than in the State; at his grave that lamentable gulf opened anew: who among us living could already now claim the right, or give reason to hope, to be regarded as his successor and substitute for the present or the coming generation?

Granted also that the manifold directions which he united in his person could be pursued individually with the same or similar success, and that what he set before himself as his goal could thus be continued and perhaps even more completely attained in small details, because the new workers each confined themselves to a smaller part of the intellectual domain and sought to perfect it down to the most particular point: although Humboldt descended from the most
comprehensive and general views, with rare devotion and patience, into the smallest and finest details, and precisely this was part of his peculiar character, that out of the totality of the countless manifold he shaped the general thought, and likewise articulated this again organically down to the most particular, penetrating, fertilizing, and animating the entire material, which lay dead for others, with life and spirit: yet granted also, I say, that the directions which he combined would be pursued not without success in their separation, still the great personality will not be restored, which gave unity to the many-sided movements, the unity in which at the same time the most fruitful interaction of different and in a certain sense opposed activities upon one another became possible.

If one man treats logic excellently and advances it further, another poetics or rhetoric, a third politics or the theory of education, a fourth zoology or anatomy or meteorology, then the sciences indeed advance on their own, but all these individual scientific men do not give us back the spirit of the Stagirite, in which the whole of human knowledge, shaped in conceptual form, had found its center, whereas the most eminent representatives of individual doctrines always stand only as points on the periphery: here there is lacking the mutual illumination which one part of cognition casts upon another, and the grandeur which lies precisely in this, that in this one spirit infinitely many rays of knowledge are gathered as in a single focal point into the strongest light and, as it were, compressed into the monad of a single soul to infinite density.

The same point applies, without further elaboration, of itself to the union of the activities of the statesman and the scholar—a union whose importance is all the more evident the more ordinary business activity dulls the capacity for more ideal contemplation, and a scholarly life dulls the capacity for conducting public affairs.

If, then, that latter union nowadays no longer seems impermissible to the same degree as formerly, because scientific knowledge has emerged from its earlier seclusion and has drawn near to the battlefield of
life, while the states have become more receptive to the dominion of thought — in which we believe we may discern an essential advance of the human race — yet in more recent times scarcely anyone has handled public affairs and science at once with such greatness of mind and such skill as Wilhelm von Humboldt.

He was, as we all know, not merely what one calls a capable man of business, who is regarded as a statesman of only a very subordinate understanding: although, as in science, so too in his public activity he devoted accuracy and care even to the small and the particular: he was a true statesman, imbued with and guided by ideas, and we venture to say it, and it will be understood in the various senses that lie in the word, he was a statesman of Periclean loftiness of mind.

In scholarship he showed, however many sides and parts of it he might unite within himself, nowhere did he appear merely as a distinguished amateur, nor did one find in him merely the ordinary specialist; rather, one found the freedom, ease, and unconstraint of the former, who occupies himself with scholarship only for his own delight, together with the thoroughness and perseverance of the latter; and everywhere his gaze was fixed unwaveringly on what is nobler and truly human, and thereby his whole understanding was purified and raised to the ideal.

Philosophy and poetry, oratory, historical, philological, and linguistic scholarship were fused in him into a harmony disturbed by no discordant note, and into that wondrous symmetry which is the stamp of the most deliberate mastery.

Clarity and depth, a lofty intellect and penetrating acumen and lively imagination, dignity and grace, the mastery of an immense body of material gathered together with untiring diligence, which has been worked up for thought with rigorous technique, and again the finest taste and a delicate sense for consummate artistic form, together with facility and the antique plasticity of presentation, give his works lasting value in equal measure as a distinctive charm.

Nourished by classical antiquity, he remained ever turned toward it with the same love and admiration; his more mature youth entered into the poetic, aesthetic, and speculative currents that animated
everything at that time, the currents of the great shapers of our literature and philosophy: but just as Plato's earlier poetic studies also spread a wonderful splendor over his later philosophical works, so Humboldt's subsequent researches into the languages of all mankind—in which, encompassing the entire globe in this respect, he accomplished what had scarcely been surmised before, to a degree that seems to surpass the power of the individual—cast the glory of a soul originally filled with the archetype of beauty over them.

He devoted himself to these studies, alongside delightful poetry, until the end of his life, with a creative power that could not be overcome even by great bodily weakness; and his last work he left behind to the Academy, to which he always granted his most active participation, as a cherished legacy.

I speak these words only as an introduction to what is to be communicated here today on this subject; it remains reserved for a later assembly to fulfill the academic duty toward the memory of the great man in a more detailed presentation.
The work of which I speak, and the preparation of which for the press the late lamented entrusted to Dr. Buschmann, bears the title: On the Kawi Language on the Island of Java.
It consists of three books and an introduction, which will form the second volume of the Academy's writings from the year 1832; at the same time, the introduction will also appear separately.

The first book, already printed, thirty-nine sheets in length, treats of the connections between India and Java and contains a large number of investigations into the origin, history, language, religion, mythology, sacred books, architecture and sculpture, inscriptions, customs, and conditions of the Javanese, and into the Indian influence upon them, particularly also in relation to Buddhism.

The second book gives the grammar of the Kawi language, taken from the portion of the Kawi poem Brata-Yuddha printed in Raffles' History of Java, everywhere in comparison with the grammar of the remaining languages of the Malay stock, under which name the inhabitants of all the islands of the great southern ocean are comprehended together with the population of Malacca, whose languages, together with that called Malay in the narrower sense, on Malacca, belong to
one and the same stock.
This book will take up about forty printed sheets.

The third, roughly twenty sheets in length, goes more closely into the grammar of several Malay languages—Madagascan, Tagalog, Tongan, Tahitian, New Zealand, and others—and finally into the languages of the Australian Negroes.

The introduction, projected at about fifty printed sheets, examines the diversity of human language structure and its influence on the intellectual development of the human race: here the departed one has summarized the fundamental features of his views on language.
With the reading of a fragment from this introduction, today's session will be brought to a worthy close.

Wilhelm von Humboldt was, among his contemporaries, the one who had studied the most languages grammatically; and he fathomed the structure of each one as though it were the sole object of his researches, devoting to each the attention that was formerly bestowed only on languages upon which the splendor of a perfected literature descends.
He was at the same time the man who most profoundly and most lucidly defined the interconnection of all language forms and their influence on the intellectual cultivation of humanity.

The posthumous work will show his contemporaries and posterity how, after a long life devoted to knowledge, a powerful mind can gather together the scattered sources of knowledge, draw from them new and far-reaching views, and, with mastery, subject the varied structure of manifold tongues to the eternal laws of intelligence.

div.head: XV. Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Steffens als neu eingetretenen Mitgliedes der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 9. Juli 1835.
Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Steffens in der Akademie

p.s: If it is precisely I, esteemed Sir, who greet you in the name of the Academy as a newly admitted member, then I owe this honor solely to my official position in relation to you, insofar as we both belong to the philosophical-historical class—not, like the speaker who welcomed our new colleagues before me, to any insight into the field in which the one elected is chiefly engaged.

You, esteemed sir, have devoted the greatest part of your studies to the investigation of nature—of nature in its individual phenomena, which reveal themselves to observation and experiment, and of nature in its wholeness, which you grasp as a philosopher with magnificent intuition and understanding.

At the same time, stepping forth from this realm of necessity, you have subjected to your consideration the intellectual and historical life of humanity, which takes shape through freedom and feeling; here too you have developed the same grand conception of the world, have followed with a sage's eye the sound and the diseased tendencies of our own age, and have forcefully pointed the way toward what is better.
Beyond the boundaries of those sciences to which our Academy is devoted, you have also unfolded in free play the poetic spirit that pervades and elevates your whole being.
In all these respects I must appear a stranger to your activity.
But there is a secret accord of spirits that permits even men who seldom or never meet on their scholarly paths a mutual contact of the inner self.

While you stand closer to some among us through a more exact kinship of studies and
may be more highly esteemed by them, I feel myself near enough to you in spirit and in disposition to wish the Academy joy that we may count you among our own; I feel myself the less removed from you in that I myself in my youth was filled by you with that enthusiasm which, welling up from the depths of your soul, seizes the receptive listener with magical power; and with most of our own I have recognized your spirit, glowing for all that is noble, good, and beautiful, in other circumstances too surely for us not all to be glad to be bound yet more closely to you by the academic bond.
Whatever value you for your part also place on this new connection, we all have certainly just now heard of it with satisfaction.
To be sure, we strive for solid achievements: but the hope of perfection in scholarship is a youthful dream.
Every day new research produces something new; the colossal edifice of human knowledge rises ever higher and higher through the tireless labor of the mind.

The work of art springs from the spirit of the sculptor as Pallas sprang from the head of Zeus, in one immediate act of creation, so far finished that the artist need only make the conceived image perceptible to the eye with his shaping hand, and it possesses within itself its unalterable perfection, requiring no further assistance; science, on the other hand, is conditioned by so many particulars that it remains capable of ever further perfection.
But what can be perfected in science—the spirit that breathes through it—that the genius perfects, the genius that also gives the consecration to the work of art: and in you the genius stirs.

div.head: XVI. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Geburtsfestes Seiner Majestät des Königs Friedrich Wilhelms III. am 4. August 1836.
Die von der philosophisch-historischen Klasse veranlafsten Unternehmungen der Berliner Akademie

p.s: Among the sessions which our Academy formally designates as public—although access is not denied even to strangers admitted to its ordinary lectures—the present one is, if we consider the occasion and the significance of the celebration, indisputably the most important.

Leibniz, to be sure, and Frederick the Great—to whom the two other ceremonial assemblies of the Academy are dedicated—the former wrought such extraordinary things for the whole of science and again for most of its parts, the latter for our country and indirectly for the entire European system of states, but especially for the free upward striving of the mind, that few can be compared with them; yet even though we still harvest the fruits of their sowing, the influence of the present nevertheless prevails.

For just as in the realm of knowledge contemporaries, standing as they do at roughly the same point of view and resting upon the foundation of the stock of thought common to all that is already at hand, stimulate one another more powerfully through new scientific discoveries and views, without the effect of the past being lost, because whatever in it was immortal has passed over into the knowledge of those who follow: so too do we feel the blessings of the present government most directly and most vividly, although no small part of them is also the work of our predecessors, through whose mighty strength the realm grew strong and was brought into the ranks of the significant powers, and through whose spirit it was given its direction toward the noble and the beautiful.
