Nor would it hardly be in keeping with the truth to say that the Academy owed its foundation to Frederick the First, or to Leibniz as the executor of his will, and later again
to Frederick the Second, and that Frederick William the Third was therefore to be honored only as its preserver; rather it is, in its present...

in its organization and its activity, and because during the unhappiest years of the Prussian state it had been close to dissolution, it is to be regarded as a new creation; indeed, we may confidently assert that in that time, when the King had resolved to raise the intellectual powers of the state by all the means at his disposal and in all directions, among which the academic is an essential and peculiar one, an Academy of Sciences would have been founded at the same time as the university, had such an academy not already been found in existence from Frederick's time, which needed only to be reshaped through a more timely constitution.

Never was anyone further removed from the principle of common utility, which science is supposed to serve—a demand that an academy, even in the most vigorous activity in the manner of working that is proper to it, would be less able to satisfy than any other scholarly institution, because, devoted to science alone, it does not even intervene in ordinary life through the instruction of youth; on the other hand, certainly no one intended to found merely such educational institutions as could serve the political purposes of that time, for which the academies of sciences are without doubt the most useless instruments at any time, especially when they, like ours, concern themselves with all things more than with political science, unless in a purely historical respect; rather, the King and his advisers were imbued with the purest zeal for genuine intellectual cultivation and its promotion in every direction, without any regard for this or that concern foreign to knowledge, by which the appreciation of scholarly life would have been just as much clouded and the scholarly institutions given a false direction, as religious and ecclesiastical conditions would necessarily be confused and perverted if one wanted to use them for state purposes and to order and model them according to these.

It was from this spirit—which, though more awakened at that time than shortly before, has not since been extinguished again but continues to work on livingly under more favorable circumstances of the age—that
there also arose the new establishment of the Academy of Sciences, which, had one not recognized in its particular scientific life a necessary stage of intellectual cultivation, could easily have been entirely abolished amid the then almost total transformation of the conditions most closely related to it, as something superfluous and unsuited to the more agitated age.

If, however, this new foundation—as we believe we may be permitted to call it—secured for the Academy a purely scholarly position, then at the same time an all the more effective influence upon scholarship itself was at least tacitly presupposed as necessary; an influence, however, that was not to be gained through business affairs foreign to academic activity—under which we count teaching as well as every kind of administration that fell to the older Academy—but through the direct promotion and extension of the branches of knowledge and learning lying within its sphere.

If this were now to be achieved solely through the activity of the members, then the Academy, for the greater part of its composition, would have had to be made up of scholars who, like many of the earlier academicians, were assigned solely to this position and were not significantly claimed by either teaching or state offices, but could devote their entire leisure to scholarly research.

But if, for reasons whose discussion is not to be given here, this lot—which for anyone who knows how to use it is indeed very enviable—has now, precisely in the reverse of former times, fallen to very few, while on the contrary a large part of those who form this learned community are so overwhelmed with manifold business that the fulfillment of their academic duties is possible for them only with exertion and effort; then the Academy, if it was nevertheless to maintain that influence, had to be regarded as a center for scholarly undertakings which would be begun and carried through by it or with its cooperation—by no means necessarily and exclusively by its own members—and it had to have means at its disposal to come effectively to the aid of such undertakings.

It has therefore been legally established by the Academy itself, as one of its purposes—though not indeed at the very beginning, yet in the further development of the
new foundation—that scholarly works and undertakings should proceed from it, whereby the present Academy differs essentially from the earlier one, apart from a few not very significant achievements of the latter; and a portion of its income has been set aside which is intended solely for this purpose.

What the Academy accomplishes hereby, according to the measure of its means, it cannot count to its own credit, nor do those to whom it benefits have the Academy to thank for it, but rather our exalted protector; the Academy regards itself as the administrator and dispenser of what the King's favor has bestowed upon it, in order to employ it according to its best understanding.

Therefore it has laid upon itself the obligation, precisely on this solemn day, to have a yearly report given alternately by a secretary of the one or the other class—a report not merely on the achievements proper to that particular class, but above all on the scholarly works and undertakings occasioned and supported by it, with the exclusion of the prize questions.

And indeed, if this day invites the capable man also to praise the prince whose many years of wise and mild rule have happily guided the state through the most fateful of times and have won and secured for him himself the universal love of the people — to praise him not merely in some limited respect, but in the full extent of what has been accomplished by him or under him — yet even so, if every individual community or academic body were to give an account, on each recurring anniversary of his birth, of the benefits that had flowed to it from the throne in the course of the preceding year, the sum of these accounts, without any expenditure of brilliant eloquence — which is far removed from the simplicity and unpretentiousness at least of this academic introductory address — would be the finest eulogy for the prince and his government.

As I have just remarked, the present reporter is to confine himself to what relates to the class to which he belongs, and to speak partly of its academic achievements in the narrower sense, by which only the lectures delivered are understood, and partly of the works which have been occasioned primarily by this class with the agreement of the whole Academy.

Recently, however, the Academy
has made an arrangement that renders it superfluous to supply the prescribed overview of its achievements, in that it now regularly makes known monthly reports which, serving only the need for a rapid dissemination of what has been established, give condensed extracts from the lectures delivered, without any pomp, but rather in a very modest form.

But the scholarly undertakings that a university is to call forth and to support are, as a rule, such as cannot be completed in the course of one or two years; larger works that require extraordinary preparations, the costly procurement of a substantial and widely scattered body of material, and laborious processing of that material that advances slowly even with unusual perseverance, and finally even require assistance for their publication, because this too produces a great expense whose early recovery, under the given circumstances, can scarcely be expected—such far-reaching plans, whose gradual execution perhaps does not even in the first years yield a fully mature result that could be exhibited at once in complete form—it is these, properly speaking, for which the support of a university may be claimed with full right, whereby the attainment of the purpose is at the same time made independent of the personality of an individual and secured.

Precisely because the Academy has grasped this point of view with a correct sense, a reporter cannot confine himself to the current year of each occasion, but must reach back into the past and forward into the future.
The earliest undertaking of the class to which I have the honor to belong was the Corpus Inscriptionum Graecarum.

If this work, even at the time it was begun, was not regarded as a transient undertaking—since its material, ever growing anew from the earth, can never be exhausted—then the unexpected restoration of a Greek state has, in a manner that is certainly only cause for rejoicing, set the completion of the work yet a further goal, whose full attainment requires a younger swift runner than the speaker of these words is.
The importance and timeliness of the undertaking have been generally recognized.

Yet, as is well known, several distinguished Dutch philologists who had resolved to produce major works
never got around to these works themselves, because they did not, in Homeric fashion, immediately place themselves in the midst of the action, but first made more distant preparations—indeed, preparations for the preparations—of which Ruhnken gave the most evident example, when, in order to publish Plato, he first worked on the meager dictionary of Timaeus, and then again on the scholia, without however bringing even the commentary on these to completion; so too a Dutchman was of the opinion that the Academy should not at once produce a complete work, but should publish the inscriptions separately as broadsheets by way of preparation, because the liberation of Greece, which had meanwhile occurred, would allow one to expect a significant increase in the material.

But setting aside the fact that a political prophetic vision was indeed lacking to recognize, several years beforehand, the transformation of that land—which, moreover, has only recently begun to accomplish something more significant for the discovery of new monuments—the outcome would have been simply this: the work would not merely have appeared later, but would not have appeared at all for the present age, and one principal advantage that it has brought would have been lost—namely, that after the Academy has provided a firm and systematically ordered foundation, everything that is now newly discovered can easily be attached to what already exists and, from the compilation and explanation of the latter that has been accomplished, can be judged and understood with greater certainty.

To this enterprise, not yet completed (for I am not speaking of earlier, fully finished ones, among which the recovery of that treasure of Roman jurisprudence, the Institutions of Gaius, will always hold an honorable place), there attaches itself, at least in conception and purpose, the bold undertaking of bringing together a great Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum, which Mr. Dr. Kellermann, chiefly known for his excellent edition of the highly instructive inscriptions concerning the Roman Vigiles, promises to accomplish in association with Professor Sarti at Rome, and with the special assistance of Count Borghesi at San Marino, a recognized master in these and related fields.

Now, even if the preparation of this work should not be as laborious as that of the Greek inscriptions work, yet on the other hand the quantity of material surpasses
that other one perhaps fivefold; and since, in order to remedy thoroughly the deficiencies with which epigraphy still suffers, the editors intend to copy as many inscriptions as possible with their own hand or to have new copies of them procured by reliable scholars, and moreover to add the pictorial monuments connected with the written ones, which in the academic work are not included chiefly on account of the cost, the execution of this plan, for which, besides, the undertakers lack no vigor, is certainly not to be achieved without public support.

Just as it is now to be hoped that the Papal government will not leave a work which so closely concerns the honor of Rome without active support, and as the Royal Danish Society of Sciences at Copenhagen and the Academy of Fine Arts there, with that zeal for the promotion of the study of antiquity which is peculiar to the Danish government, have already promised contributions toward the considerable costs, so our Academy could the less withdraw itself from the encouragement of the editors, the more the philosophical-historical class felt the need of such a work, to which through Joh.
Casp.

that Orelli's industrious collection has not been fully remedied, has long been felt, and it must even be acknowledged that Mr. Kellermann meets the frequently expressed wish of several of its members, who would themselves already have proposed an undertaking of this kind if they had been able to name scholars from whom a suitable execution might be expected.

If comprehensive collections of inscriptions bring fruitful results not merely for some particular branch of the study of antiquity, but for a deeper insight into the whole life of the ancients and thus at the same time for the understanding of the writers, for knowledge of the language and script, and for nearly all the individual branches of the study of antiquity, then we can assert the same of the publication of Aristotle, which likewise belongs among the Academy's undertakings still in progress: for Aristotle too, since he embraced almost the entire domain of knowledge, casts light in every direction upon the most diverse fields of the study of antiquity.

This resolution too—to have a new edition of the collected works of this mighty spirit prepared—arose quite
as much from the difficulty of bringing together the collations of the manuscripts and the commentaries of the old interpreters required for the purpose, as from the need of the age, which, after Plato's writings and doctrines had found many admirers and fortunate expositors, began at last, through the new turn taken by philosophy, once more to devote to Aristotle that attention which had been fastened upon him for more than a thousand years.

Into this, in a sense, new direction of philology and philosophy, this Society has intervened in a worthy manner; even if its edition contains no commentaries of its own, and we had to leave these to the editors of individual writings, because those scholars who encompassed the whole could not at the same time bestow upon every detail the care that is required for the composition of detailed commentaries, the undertaking has nevertheless contributed essentially to the revival and establishment of Aristotelian studies, and has offered abundant material for the criticism of all Aristotle's writings, material which has been widely used, even if it has not always been acknowledged according to its merit.

In an appendix, as soon as circumstances permit, we shall also supply further unpublished Greek commentators besides those which, like much from the writings of Alexander of Aphrodisias, are already contained in the fourth volume now in the press—namely, the original text of Syrianus's commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics.

Niebuhr, too early torn from his friends and from scholarship, once an ornament of our association, in which, as long as he resided here, he urged on with his characteristic zeal larger works that could be carried out only with united efforts, and had also initiated the first undertakings of this kind, namely the Corpus Inscriptionum Graecarum and the edition of Gaius, partly with others and partly alone—later, after he had chosen Bonn as his residence, he undertook independently of the Academy the new Corpus scriptorum historiae Byzantinae, which is not yet completed.

After his passing, which we all felt deeply, the necessity of public support emerged here once again; the work, now as it were orphaned and whose continuation seemed endangered, was therefore taken over by the Academy; several
members themselves set their hands to it, and the money required for the necessary collation of the manuscripts was allocated.
Far from any one-sided preference for this or that discipline, which is least becoming to an academy, we by no means limit ourselves to the advancement of Greek and Roman philology.

The Old High German vocabulary, which one of our members is handing over to the press after many years of great preparatory work, had already attracted the Academy's attention even before its editor belonged to our association, and the Academy did its part to make its publication possible.

Egyptian philology is a still young discipline, scarcely yet ripening; distinguished scholars of England, France, and Italy have meanwhile made important contributions to its elucidation; the achievements of some Germans, once announced with great pomp, have on the other hand remained of very doubtful worth and success.

The Academy could therefore not scruple to support on his travels a young man who aroused many hopes, Dr. Lepsius, who devotes himself especially to the cultivation of this wide field—travels which he undertook last year in order to acquire possession of a rich treasure of aids.

Already at this time he alone has brought together in Paris impressions of nearly four thousand hieroglyphic inscriptions not yet published; next, in Turin, he has likewise taken careful impressions of the colossal statues, of which the collection there is especially rich, of the figures and inscriptions, which, with the exception of those used by Champollion for the history of the eighteenth dynasty under unfavorable circumstances and therefore inaccurately, are until now still entirely unknown; he has likewise established a very considerable collection of copies of all the other Egyptian monuments located there, and notably of the painted ones and of the papyrus rolls, in whose number the Turin collection far surpasses all similar ones in London, Paris, Leiden, and elsewhere: among others he has drawn the great complete Book of the Dead, filling more than a hundred half-folio leaves, and a quantity of historical demotic and hieratic inscriptions.

At Pisa, from Professor Rosellini—the most comprehensive connoisseur of Egyptian antiquity since Champollion's death—he received, with the most selfless love
of scholarship, the entire apparatus of Egyptian studies collected by the latter, communicated to him for the freest possible use; furthermore, he exploited for his purpose the two small but select collections at Florence and at Livorno, and three others temporarily present at Rome.

Passing over most of what he intends besides, I note only that, after he has made use of the numerous Coptic manuscripts in Rome and Naples in order to extend his knowledge of the Egyptian language, he then intends in the coming years to work out a Coptic grammar, such as must be laid as the foundation for hieroglyphic studies and in turn be completed by these into a general Egyptian grammar.

Finally, almost more than anything else, and without doubt, art archaeology—especially in Germany—stands in need of support from public institutions, because the publication of monuments requires an extraordinary expenditure of money.

The King's generous spirit, open to all that is beautiful, has here given this study a new stimulus through the founding of the art museum; but in order to follow it, reproductions must also be at hand of those works of art that cannot be acquired.

The soil of Etruria has in recent times been especially productive in important and remarkable remains of ancient art, namely burial chests, painted vessels, and the metal mirrors that are of very considerable importance for art history; Mr. Gerhard, whom we now count among our members, has, with the Academy's support, over the course of several years brought about a very significant collection of Tuscan monuments, whose early completion and publication we look forward to.

If we add to all this the fact that the Academy, with considerable expense, has procured a quantity of type for its printing press—established not for the sake of profit but rather at great sacrifice for the promotion of scholarly purposes—type in which the capital of the realm formerly suffered a shortage not merely distressing but, one may say, indecent, and indeed especially for Greek inscriptions, for Etruscan, Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Coptic, Old Slavonic and Russian, Sanskrit and Zend; and if we add to this the no small achievements of the physical-mathematical class, to report on
which is the duty of one more knowledgeable; then we may assert that, in proportion to our means, even beyond the circle of the researches undertaken by individual members, we have had far more effect than is ordinarily expected of German academies, to which nowadays much less influence on scholarship is generally attributed than they actually exert, because their peculiar character and their particular position in the scholarly life of the fatherland have assigned them a certain retirement in relation to other institutions.

Thus we have a share in the glory of the widespread science and learning which Prussia at present, under the best of rulers, has by general judgment attained to a greater degree than ever before—not merely the share that this man or that may have won by his own intellectual power, but, through special favor, the still finer share of cooperating as instruments of the royal liberality in the advancement of knowledge, insofar as it can be achieved by external means and active encouragement: a share which, even if the duty of gratitude toward the generous patron of our association did not require it, would all the more have to be emphasized the less highly each individual, as befits the nobler man, is inclined to measure his personal achievements and merits, which vanish within the whole.

div.head: XVII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Jahrestages Friedrichs des Grofsen, am 25. Januar 1838.
Von d'Alembert's Ansicht über das Verhältnifs der Wissenschaften zur Gesellschaft, und von Friedrichs des Grofsen Verhältnifs zur Wissenschaft

p.s: One of the distinguished minds whom Frederick revered, and with whom he carried on that wonderful correspondence which had become a necessity to him, in order to pour out from an inner impulse, and for his own satisfaction, everything that filled his great soul and his easily stirred heart, and to share it with like-minded friends in common enjoyment or pain—d'Alembert says in his Essay on the Learned: Charles the Fifth, King of France, one of the wisest and consequently best princes who ever ruled, though less renowned in history than many kings who were merely fortunate or powerful, made some efforts to quicken in his states the taste for the sciences; for Charles was doubtless enlightened enough, in the midst of the confusions that agitated his realm, to recognize that the pursuit of learning is one of the most infallible means of securing the tranquillity of monarchies, from a cause that, conversely, can prove harmful to free states if it is raised too high—namely, because the charm connected with the sciences, so to speak, isolates men from society and makes them cold and insensible to every other object.

This principle, whose truth I would wish neither wholly to combat nor wholly to defend, indisputably has a flavor of Machiavelli's Prince, and in d'Alembert's mouth could appear as half mockery, were it not more credible that with the same candor with which Machiavelli set forth the doctrines useful to princes according to his opinion, d'Alembert likewise uttered what we have just heard as something true according to experience
in his best judgment, without wishing to enter further into the question whether this principle for elevating the sciences—although, put somewhat differently, it holds validity for the rule of still little-cultivated peoples and their unbridled and unruly passions—is worthy of the fully developed state and its rulers, and need not shrink from a tribunal which, from a generally human and moral, and consequently truly political, standpoint, passes judgment on the motives from which the leaders of states have bestowed their favor on the arts and sciences.

If one applies that principle exactly as d'Alembert stated it to civilized peoples who are not first to be reclaimed from savagery, then the arts and sciences appear as a means of crippling the wings of the national spirit, in that they are supposed to make people indifferent to all important common affairs: from which there would necessarily have to follow an enervation of the noblest among the people: they are the women's garments, the maidens' adornment, the baths and ointments, of which that petty Italo-Greek tyrant compelled the youths to make use, instead of manly attire, manly bodily exercises, and a manly way of life, so that he might rule more easily; knowledge and science, the noblest thing that man can strive for, are administered as a sleeping draught, sung as a lullaby to soothe to sleep.

But if this purpose is thoroughly achieved, the consequences will not be long in coming: once the best men have first withdrawn from the common affairs out of love for scholarly leisure, or have been unmanned and lulled to sleep by learning, then the fatherland will fall into the hands of the ignorant and the wicked, whose leadership inevitably leads both the ruler and the ruled to ruin.
For who, then, might those men be who are to be set apart from society by science and learning and made indifferent to all other matters, so that the monarchy may stand more securely?

Naturally those who, were they not indifferent, could become dangerous to it: but the very same persons who bring danger as opponents are, as friends, the effective helpers; whoever therefore wished through the sciences to render the dangerous harmless, by thereby weakening their inclination
and their participation in the common weal, would necessarily estrange from public life those whose activity within it is most beneficial.

To be sure, human activity divides into these two principal directions, the theoretical and the practical, and an disproportionate increase of the one must do harm to the other; moreover, according to their disposition and capacity, some take up the one activity more and others the other, in which they believe they will find their calling or achieve the more significant success, and through the exercise of the one they have chosen they are also dulled for the other and become more or less unfit for it—apart from the few who can move with equal competence and ease in these opposite occupations, or who, like Frederick, recover and refresh themselves in the bosom of the sciences after the burdens of government. But the state, whose happiness, regardless of its constitution, rests in large part on the equilibrium of the forces united within it, will surely err if it should raise the scientific direction at the expense of participation in public life.
Moreover, insofar as d'Alembert's principle appears to be drawn from experience, it rests in part certainly on a confusion of effect with cause.

When the Roman state, exhausted by the most ruinous civil wars, was at last subjected to a single head, and interest in public life had diminished, the taste for the fine sciences spread ever further, not without the care of Augustus, to whom the poets were preeminently a useful instrument—not, to be sure, for the consolidation of his power, which rested on stronger supports, but yet for the glorification of his rule and thus indirectly for the increase of his prestige: the indifference toward public life to which many gave themselves over was, however, not the consequence of a heightened fondness for science and art; rather, the force of events had driven these men from the stage of the political world, and circumstances made them indifferent to the state.

Horace exchanged the sword for the lyre, because the former could no longer be wielded for the old fatherland, and with the latter he celebrated a prince in whose favor he could enjoy a carefree and comfortable life.

Disgust with the state,
in which they found no satisfaction any longer, at every period removed men of spirit and firm resolve from the administration of the state and led them to scholarly leisure, which offered them compensation for what they had lost and consolation in suffering; they buried their grief in the solitude of a contemplative and inquiring life, and soothed it with the noblest of remedies, study.

Plato advises the philosopher to abstain from all participation in the state: not as though philosophy made one indifferent to the commonwealth and the common good; rather, here too the recommendation of withdrawal from public life was only the consequence of weariness with existing conditions, or of the insistent conviction that an effective activity such as the philosopher must wish for was impossible under the given circumstances, while yet Plato himself, throughout the greater part of his life, even after the failure of the intended influence upon powerful princes, occupied himself with no subject of philosophy more zealously than with the state.

In these cases, which stand out significantly enough and to which many similar ones could be added, indifference toward the existing state was the cause of withdrawal into the sciences, not the effect of love for them.

Nowhere and at no time did the arts and sciences flourish more beautifully than in Athens under Pericles—the latter, to be sure, only in that form which the course of development of the human race brought with it at that stage—and the taste for them was certainly spread widely enough. But because the Athenian free state still enjoyed a vigorous life, the love of art and knowledge in the great majority of the educated at that time had not in the least weakened the public spirit; on the contrary, even the poets, who after all live mostly in a world of their own making, did not disdain—especially in tragedy and comedy—to let the life of the state and public affairs be reflected back as from a mirror, and even with seemingly wholly independent works of art to move the citizens toward particular political views, purposes, and plans.

Nearly a human lifetime ago, the opposite of d'Alembert's principle came to the fore; at that time people had
arrived at the conviction that the popular strength and power of the state rested in large part on knowledge and insight, and would in particular be strengthened by science, to which an arousing capacity was ascribed, not that calming one.

One and the same thing can, to be sure, produce opposite effects, depending on how the circumstances differ; and since the sciences themselves are manifold and are treated in very different ways, the results of scientific activity can also be varied, even without a particular direction first being given to science deliberately and from outside.
Knowledge calms the passions; why, then, should science not also play its part in the state in preserving tranquillity?

But knowledge at the same time awakens the slumbering powers and gives wings to the spirit: it is therefore indeed suited to refresh once more a life sunk in stagnation, to set what has grown rigid in motion, to heal the incipient decay, and to bring a people sunk in dull indifference to a consciousness of itself and of its conditions.

Even Richelieu, d'Alembert observes, felt—notwithstanding the despotic principles with which he was wholly filled and which he carried out everywhere as far as possible—that the democratic form is more suited than any other to the learned state, which lives only by its freedom; and he therefore introduced such a constitution into the French Academy. But if freedom is the vital spirit of the sciences in their own domain (and assuredly it is, not only because external restriction hampers thought, but because even the mere apprehension of it stifles thought in its birth), then the sciences, so long as they themselves are not somehow enfeebled and corrupted, must out of their inner essence promote, unintentionally, through imperceptible influence, the love of a lawful freedom in the life of all mankind, even beyond the domain of the sciences within its narrowest limits—all the more since the domain of knowledge in general is not a definitely bounded one, but is entirely unlimited with respect to the objects that fall under consideration.

Furthermore, no elaboration is needed to show that those sciences can have a more stirring effect which relate more directly
to the general affairs of the state and of humanity; the diversion from the latter through the promotion and increase of scientific activity would therefore be conceivable only insofar as one sought to restrict scholars to such sciences as are more remote from those affairs, and thus in the one and indivisible body of science to let the noblest and most important parts, indeed even the soul of this body itself, degenerate, in order also to condemn the rest to a sickly life.

Finally, a mechanical and pedantic pursuit of every science—one that consists in clinging to particulars and to what is given in experience, without enthusiasm and without the power to generate thoughts, and in the mere transmission of what has been handed down, for the memory—in a word, dead science, will awaken no life; it will therefore depress minds rather than stimulate them; and to the degree that a ruler, a government, a society, or an institution puts the learned trade, which is sometimes recommended under the name of thorough erudition, in the place of living knowledge, the spiritual vitality dies out in the people that yields to the influences of such an education.

Only where everything individual has been taken up into its universal, where matter has been transformed into thought, where thought is grasped with enthusiasm, does life dwell in science; and it then attains further progress through creative power and reflection.

Frederick, who besides the cultivation of taste desired intellectual progress, therefore censures in the brief survey of the advances of the human mind which he has woven into his history of his own time, in most German scholars, that they are craftsmen, and in the professors of the universities, apart from their coarse manners, that they are pedants; Wolf, whose writings he had eagerly studied as a youth, is repugnant to him because he merely chewed over Leibniz's system and verbosely repeated what the latter had written with fire; even a work relating to military affairs he begins with the indeed simple but unsurpassable sentences: "What avails it to live, if one leads only a plant's life; what avails it to see, if it happens only in order to heap up facts in one's memory; what, in a word, avails experience, if it is not guided by
reflection!" But reflection, sometimes even the bare narration of facts, when the former or even the latter deviates from a particular direction in which one wishes to see them steered, can produce a lamentable discord between free cognition and certain state purposes and principles whose unconditional recognition is commanded by the ruling power.

If the latter are correct, then that knowledge, if it does not agree with them, is false and sophistical; meanwhile it lies in the nature of progress that what is earlier, hitherto recognized as valid, resists it: in this struggle, which is no younger than science itself, the decision usually falls to the following ages, in which truth celebrates its triumph, often only after it has, amid the severe trials of its adherents, stood the fiery ordeal of opposition, in which the dross is separated from the gold.

But it is indisputably the duty of society not to hold back the victory of truth; and if on the one hand the scholar, to say no more, is to represent his insight on every field of knowledge with Socratic courage and without fear of men, because he cannot suffer a greater harm than that which he would suffer in his soul through a lie, so on the other hand the power of the state will ease the victory of truth if it does not employ science merely as a lever or even as a depressing weight, but values it for its own sake, and consequently grants it free course, in which error finds its settlement far more swiftly than when forces lying outside science exert a disturbing influence on the course of the latter.

Science is undoubtedly useful to the state; but it should by no means be pursued for the sake of so-called utility or of need, and equally little should it be promoted for that reason alone, because otherwise it truly would not be promoted at all.
It did not come into being until man had risen above mere need; and only after it had grown strong did it in turn become helpful to human neediness.

Thus, to use the clearest example, mathematics would never have come into being if need had been the determining factor; rather, in that case, as the Romans did according to Cicero's observation, people would
have contented themselves with the bare necessity of measuring and calculating. But once mathematics has freely climbed to the height of a knowledge independent of all need, from that height it bestows on society even more abundant benefit.

The influence of history and of philosophy and of all their branches—to which from time immemorial the science of the state has also belonged with the fullest right—upon the purification of concepts and views of life, upon the improvement of laws and principles of government, and consequently upon the general welfare, can never be rated too highly, especially where they have stood in alliance with pure and genuine principles of religion; and yet one would err if one wished to assert that those disciplines were intended primarily to serve the immediate needs of ordinary life.

I have taken the liberty of examining the observation that a learned man of great influence, closely bound to Frederick, set forth concerning the promotion of the sciences in the monarchy, in order thereby to indicate by comparison the relation of the great King to science—without any claim to an exact discussion, for which a deeper and more comprehensive engagement with the admirably rich literary activity of this much-occupied prince and general is required, and which must therefore be left to whoever shall one day publish Frederick's collected works in authentic form: an undertaking that would, to be sure, be most worthy of the Academy itself and would also be to be expected from the Academy, Frederick's most beloved creation, if our situation permitted us to set our hand to it with success.
On January 27 of the year 1772, Frederick had his treatise on the usefulness of the sciences and arts in a state presented at our academy.

Rousseau's opposing views gave occasion for it, and it is conditioned by its polemical direction against them; in noble anger over this the King says right at the outset that he is ashamed to say in this academy that people had had the audacity to call into question whether the sciences were useful or harmful to society, a matter about which no one should be able to be in doubt.

The King's observations have as little in common with d'Alembert's principle as this: that the latter, on the contrary, wishes precisely to draw those who have been educated through science
into the life of the state, whereas according to d'Alembert—if indeed one is to proceed consistently—one would have to keep them separated and removed from it as much as possible, since they are supposed to be indifferent to public life.
“The most comprehensive mind, stripped of knowledge,” says Frederick, “is only a rough diamond that first gains its value after it has been cut by the hands of a skilled artist.”
So how many lost spirits of society! and how many great men in every field, stifled in their first germs, whether through ignorance or through the low station in which they found themselves placed!

The true welfare of the state, its advantage, its splendor therefore require that the people whom it contains be as instructed and enlightened as possible, in order to supply the state in every sphere with a number of capable persons who are able to undertake with skill the various affairs that it must entrust to them. "False politicians," he says, "confined to their small ideas, had supposed that it was easier to govern an ignorant people than an enlightened one, whereas experience proves that the duller a people, the more obstinate and refractory it is, and that it has far greater difficulty in overcoming the stubbornness of such a people than in convincing of just things a people sufficiently educated to accept reason." The King next sets forth the usefulness of the natural sciences and especially of various branches of applied mathematics, the usefulness of history for military commanders, for officials, for the ruler himself; but the dialecticians are, in his view, the thunderbolts against the errors and the superstition that he ceaselessly combated.

He knows how to defend even the myths eloquently as meaningful fictions and allegories; and, he says, one would have to have a hard heart to wish to deprive the human race of the consolations and the succor that one can draw from the fine sciences against the bitterness with which life is filled: "free us from our misfortune, or allow us to alleviate it." He does not forget the fine words with which Cicero, "the philosophical consul, the father of his country and of eloquence," recommends literature.

Yet although Frederick also emphasizes strongly enough the common
utility of the sciences, it is nevertheless evident that he recognized a higher worth in them not only in his writings but also demonstrated it in his life.

With exertion he had striven after wisdom and truth from youth onward; the progress of the human race in civilization, in the purification, softening, and ennobling of principles, the true and the beautiful in themselves—whether these were brought forth through philosophy or natural science or poetry and eloquence in the broader sense, or by whatever means—the purely spiritual and human drew him above all else.

"The sciences," he says, "grant us the pleasures of the mind, which are more lasting than those of the body; they soften the crudest manners; they spread their charms over the whole course of life; they make our existence bearable and take from death its terrors." His sharp and penetrating understanding, though paired with a rich imagination, rejected everything unclear, all vain fantasticality, whose return he feared even in natural science; inspired by the Enlightenment, he nevertheless esteemed religious conviction more than is usually asserted, and wished to give offense to no one, though of course he did not for that reason weigh his words anxiously: moreover, like every great man who recognizes his age, he placed himself at the head of the intellectual movement, and guided and promoted it instead of combating it in vain.
If he nevertheless believed that he had been sent into the world too early, one will at least concede that, in spite of his advanced age, he departed from it too early for the course of the world.

Even his errors and prejudices, to which even the greatest of men is subject, were a consequence of the course of his education and of the conditions of that time; yet his taste for French now scarcely needs any excuse: he loved only what was fully formed and classical, which in his youth he did not find in the German tongue; toward the Italians and the English he was just, and he revered antiquity above all; indeed he would certainly have placed it above French culture, had he possessed a more complete knowledge of it.

If he preferred the Henriade to Homer, if he held the fair Gabrielle to be worth no less than the princess Nausikaa, then we ask how many in his youth—the time that was decisive for his taste—could
have said why Homer and Nausikaa are more poetic than Voltaire and Gabrielle.
His admiration for everything great and noble in antiquity abundantly compensates for such a judgment.

There he sought his ideals—Titus, Trajan, Marcus Aurelius; in the aforementioned memorandum he praises those remarkable times when Greece produced a Thucydides, to whom elsewhere he will not allow even a Frenchman to be set beside him, a Euripides, Xenophon, Plato, Aristotle, Pericles, Alexander; the times when the Stoic Cato went down with liberty, when Cicero thundered against Verres, wrote his books on duties, the Tusculan Disputations, his immortal work on the nature of the gods, and Varro his Origines and his poem on the civil wars (here Frederick, as often in such matters, has confused some things), when Caesar by his clemency eradicated whatever odiousness his usurpation had, when Virgil composed his Aeneid and Horace his Odes, and Livy handed down to posterity the history of all the great men who had glorified the free state.
The King's own literary activity likewise sprang purely from a genuine impulse toward knowledge and from his innermost disposition of soul, without any claims of vanity.

“The love of the sciences,” he writes when already sixty-two years old, “will be my last passion”; he composed his trifles, as he says, for his own entertainment, pondered subjects of philosophy in order to instruct himself, wrote poetry in order to give voice to his feelings, but he himself placed no such high value on his poetic attempts as to wish to be regarded as a poet: yet most of the qualities of a good writer—wit and humor, grace and fullness, power and loftiness of expression as of thought—stood abundantly at his command.

Above all, however, the genuinely human element gives his literary endeavors a worth that raises his cultivation above that of many learned rulers, and notably above Julius Caesar, Augustus, Hadrian, and similar figures, even though these were more perfectly cultivated in several respects.

But so deeply was scholarship a matter of the heart to him that even his dearest friendships were determined by it; and since the principal directions on which the progress of the age depended coincided with the King's own, there arose that enviable
relationship of unity between the government of a great prince and the convictions of the freest and most distinguished thinkers of the age, who paid him homage, while he, insofar as he came to know them, also gladly acknowledged them.
Seldom did a king live in such intimate connection with scholarly men as Frederick; seldom did a prince show such sympathy for a learned society as Frederick did for the Academy.

For if his surroundings presented, instead of a court, a circle of friends, a large part of whom were men of learning, then the Academy appears in turn as a wider, concentric circle drawn around that narrower one, into which he gladly steps forth with his more intimate associates, including the ministers and his comrades-in-arms; in the Academy he has some of his shorter writings, or parts of a larger work, read first, and made known in its history or in its proceedings; without hesitation he even appears as a fellow combatant, under the designation of a Berlin academician, in a scholarly dispute closely touching the Academy, with that vehemence which springs from moral indignation at a malicious personal attack.

To him the Academy, as indeed science itself, was a source of pleasure, a means of stimulation and satisfaction: if it achieved this purpose, it matters little how much it has besides accomplished for our fatherland, since what he himself accomplished for the dominion of the spirit surpasses everything that an academy may effect.
He had grasped the destiny and the calling of this empire: to grow and to endure through boldness of thought no less than of action, and, like Pallas, to be warlike with both.
May both, as under his leadership, pursue one goal in alliance, and may harmony never dissolve between the power that is founded on arms and the slowly but far-reaching power of a living knowledge!

div.head: XVIII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 4. Juli 1839.
Ueber Leibnizens Ansichten von der philologischen Kritik

p.s: In one of the countless letters in which Leibniz pours himself out on every subject of knowledge, and—since correspondence always relates to given circumstances—sets forth his views, free from the fetters of any particular theory, on the most diverse relations of science, he remarks with reference to Descartes that those deceive themselves who, indulging their indolence, sought the sum of wisdom in a writer however great, or rather boasted of it.
To be sure, this is the shortest path to wisdom, and in every age beginners have taken it, although they had to recognize that the master found his wisdom otherwise.

There are many blossoms in which humanity takes delight, and many fruits from which it nourishes itself; and the further the capacities of each individual reach, the greater the fullness of his own spirit, the further he extends his feelers, the more and the more varied things is he capable of drawing in and taking up into himself, without the danger of failing to work them properly within himself, of failing to transform them into his own blood and flesh.

If the individual sciences, because suddenly or gradually significant external or mechanical aids have increased activity, or because greater accessibility of the sources and a more general diffusion of trained and regular practice of the art have also enabled the great number of the less gifted to increase the scientific capital with some noteworthy contribution, receive through a disproportionately rapid accumulation of material so great an expansion that it becomes difficult to encompass several larger fields completely, as in our days has indisputably
happened in more than one domain of knowledge; then indeed the limitation—not, to be sure, to a particular system, but to a narrower circle of the science—is more directly occasioned and more cogently justified than by mere dilettantism or narrowness of mind.

But in such a state of the sciences, where they have all diverged into more or fewer parts, it stirs in the observer a feeling that comes to him as if from a foreign world, when he hears Leibniz speak, as it were in a single breath, of philosophical propositions, of mathematical discoveries, of laws of nature, of religious controversies, of subjects of law, of philological and historical researches and collections—not with the superficiality of the dilettante who goes as a guest to every table for his own and others' entertainment, but as a connoisseur.

If, then, it were advisable to draw exclusively from the writings of some great man the sum total of all wisdom, Leibniz was for the age immediately following him the most suitable, since he alone nourished and engaged many minds.

But even for the ages that follow later, his example remains an excellent antidote against the excessive isolation of scholarly endeavors; and whatever particular field a person may have devoted himself to, or whatever field he may always treat of, he will find some point of contact with Leibniz.

In accordance with the statutes of the Academy, on the Leibniz anniversary we announce the outcome of the prize competitions that we have instituted: two years ago the philosophical-historical class of the Academy chose for this purpose a subject which on the one hand concerns the history of philosophy and thus philosophy itself, and on the other hand is of a philological-critical nature.

The former point of view lies so obviously close to Leibniz's principal activity that we shall not dwell on it; rather, it is worth our while on this occasion to speak of Leibniz's views on philological criticism, which, even if as occasional remarks they are neither very original nor especially deeply drawn, and in a certain respect even appear somewhat antiquated, nonetheless always grant a not unimportant recognition to this principal part of the philological art and to philological endeavors and the study of antiquity in general.
Leibniz *) was pleased by the undertaking, carried out at higher instigation, of publishing the Latin writers for the use of the Dauphin, and thereby, as he says, of recalling the fleeing fine sciences, of reawakening the light of antiquity that was almost in its death throes, and of bestowing upon the most excellent writers now already a third life, since after the passage of scarcely a century contempt for them had returned and a new kind of barbarism had set in, and the great ancients were again beginning to close their eyes.

If the success of that undertaking for science has brought no considerable advantage, this does not deprive the judgment itself of its value; and equally well founded is the other point that he adds: that if a young prince, blessed with such hopes and destined for so great a fate, is initiated into the secrets of true culture, then provision will have been made for posterity for some centuries to come; for King Francis showed the world by his example how much the approval of a single prince can accomplish, and its fruit still lives on.

Leibniz recognized full well how much the study of antiquity contributes to the cultivation of a sound sense among the rulers and the ruled—of which kind of influence, to be sure, only very few traces still come to light—and how indispensable it is in the chain of human knowledge.

If one wished to say that this was not to be wondered at, because in his time the German language and literature were still uncultivated, but that he would speak differently nowadays, after we have brought it so gloriously far: then we should have to reply that the most cultivated European peoples, even after they had given their own language a high degree of perfection, did not cease to esteem antiquity highly; that the French, precisely in the celebrated age of Louis the Fourteenth and immediately thereafter, devoted themselves with great zeal to these studies; that the English, alongside their most excellent writers and great poets, never lost their veneration for classical antiquity; that in the fairest time of Italian liter- *) Letters to Huet, Sylloge nova epistolarum varii argumenti, vol. I, p. 637 ff.

Nuremberg, 1760.
Machiavelli, whom it suffices to name in place of all the others of his people, when he set about reading the ancients, put on his state robes expressly for this purpose.

In particular, with reference to philosophy and even to mathematics, Leibniz set himself against the voices of those who, as he says, cast off all reverence for antiquity and spoke of Plato and Aristotle as of wretched sophists: Plato's metaphysical and moral doctrine, he says, which few draw from the sources, is holy and correct, and what he says about the ideas and eternal truths is admirable; Aristotle's logical, rhetorical, and political writings are of the greatest usefulness for life when they fall into the hands of a good mind formed by experience; he also praises his physics, and whoever understands Archimedes and Apollonius, he continues, will admire the discoveries of the foremost men of modern times more sparingly.

Even in this respect he advanced far beyond his own age and the age immediately following; and in particular Plato and Aristotle, more than a century later than when he wrote those words, only then came again to the recognition that he had accorded them.

In particular, he regrets that some misused the recollections and complaints of great men—a Bacon, a Galileo, a Descartes—for the eradication of the old wisdom and for the cloaking of their own ignorance, so as to have the appearance of despising, as by right, things that did not deserve to be known, thereby deceiving themselves and, as far as in them lay, the world of all the aids and experiences of so many centuries.

Indeed, some utterances in this sense may well have escaped those eminent men, as though we stood in need of a correct recognition of a great transformation and renewal if we are to believe Bacon, or a blank tablet of the mind, if we are to believe Descartes; yet while these men themselves offered great discoveries out of their own resources, one must forgive them if they charged too immoderately against the perversity of their times and the stale idolatry of traditional doctrines: but the petty disciples, who had invented nothing and, no less than before, merely with a change of master, again clung to something handed down, would raise, on the strength of a mere faint rumor which they had received from the teaching, a
passionate clamor, and thereby contribute to the corruption of true culture, because youth, taken with such sweet and splendid ignorance, readily accepts the color offered to it, so many things being nobly unknown.

In a strange way he links to this the thought that, if all other studies were neglected and only experiments and the languages and affairs of our time were treated, religion would then be in danger, whose truth is to be confirmed either by the miracles of the present or by the oracles of antiquity.
In pursuing the same thought further elsewhere, he at the same time sets forth his views on scholarship and criticism.

But what he understands by learning (eruditio) is essentially for the most part nothing other than what is called philology, taking the expression in its original and true meaning; an assertion that could also easily be justified from the usage of that time. Yet he has, although not with clear development and without definite distinction, also included under the concept of learning more or less of empirical natural science, which no one counts as part of philology.

If we set aside whatever Leibniz, precisely because he did not distinguish carefully, seems to draw into his concept of learning from this domain, then by his own words he includes under it everything that we learn from human beings, in contrast to what is invented from the mind; it is distinguished by him from philosophy as that which is a matter of fact (quod est facti) is distinguished from that which is a matter of pure knowledge or of right (quod est rationis sive iuris).

Indeed, he says, theorems that have been discovered by purely intellectual means can just as well be handed down to posterity as histories and observations, and to that extent, we add, he will not have denied them a place in the domain of learning; but here, for science itself, without regard to learning, what matters is not the authority of the book, but the still convincing certainty of the proof vindicates the proposition.

Thus, for pure science, it is of no consequence whether Archimedes was the author of the little treatise De aequiponderantibus; but when the matter concerns history, the monument itself furnishes the proof of the truth.

In these words,
though they were somewhat disorderly and hastily thrown off, Leibniz aptly characterized the true essence of philology and recognized it better than other philosophers and than most professional philologists.

He does not speak of this, but on his standpoint he certainly could not fail to recognize that the two, philosophy and scholarship—or, to name in place of the latter, with reference to the history of all intellectual activity and the development of the human race, philology, and with regard to nature, empirical natural science—even when they are conceptually kept perfectly separate from one another and consistently carried through in this separation, do not form an absolute opposition, and in their result can as little contradict each other as ground and fact, unless the one or the other is to be false; but rather that true scholarship should proceed from the factual to thought, and philosophy from pure cognition and the inner ground to the real, which is identical with the factual; that therefore both, thought in their highest perfection—which, to be sure, for the present remains only an ideal—must meet in the middle from opposite starting points, and each of the two is the test of the other. From this, now—that in the historical domain, as Leibniz says, the monument itself must give confirmation to what has been handed down—criticism arose: this, he holds, was reawakened by divine providence and strengthened with the help of the invented art of printing, chiefly in order to bring the Christian religion into the light.

One could expect no greater benefit from history and learning than precisely this; indeed, the whole study of antiquity seems to him to confer almost this single benefit: that we free the ancient documents of our blessedness, and, so to speak, of our nobility, which, as those reborn, we would have to trace back to Christ, from doubt and corruptions.

It must be shown that the sacred books which we possess have come down to us authentic and, in the main, uncorrupted; this only he can do who knows the secrets of the critical art, the credibility of the manuscripts, the peculiarities of the language, the spirit of those centuries, and the sequence of the ages.

That the author of such great things had been sent from heaven, the prophecies
and miracles proved, together with the incomparable holiness of his teaching, the steadfastness of the martyrs, and the triumph of the cross; but that all this had happened as it did could be shown only if the whole of sacred and profane history were established with the utmost precision; for this purpose there was need of collections, manuscripts, coins, inscriptions, and the other tools of scholars, whereby history is given credence: for which reason he had often wished for collections such as he [had received] from Marq.
Gudius for the inscriptions, by Ezech.

He expects Spanheim for the coins; the history of the manuscripts he still misses insofar as the best ones that are still extant in Europe today would have to be enumerated, especially those from which the writers have been printed, and the unique or rare ones.

To be sure, anyone could also corroborate religion and providence in general with secure proofs who brings that ordering power of the mind into connection with the first attempt that comes to hand, which is the philosopher's business: since, namely, every cause can be inferred from each of its effects, God could be proved from every phenomenon; for proofs are nothing other than orderings of thoughts that make known the connection of things: but when the matter concerns, as it does for the truth of the Christian religion, the corruption and renewal of the human race, the differences among peoples, and the oldest writings, then one needs the scholar.

Great indeed is the usefulness of history: to set before us noble examples for the awakening of men, so that they too may undertake to accomplish things worthy of remembrance; to determine the boundaries of empires; to settle important controversies in the state; and finally, to delight us with the wonderful survey of events. Yet to this extent we could do without learning, and whole peoples would have to do without it, even though they led their lives in considerable comfort. But to establish the truth of religion, history and criticism are absolutely necessary.

If the critical art were lost, then the human aids of divine faith would at the same time perish with it, and nothing capable would remain by which we could prove our religion to a Chinese man or a Jew or a Muslim.

Suppose the legendary tales
of Dietrich von Bern, with which in Germany children are lulled to sleep by their nurses, could no longer be distinguished from the accounts of Cassiodorus, the contemporary historian who was Theodoric's chancellor; suppose the time should come when people were in doubt whether Alexander the Great was not, as the Turks believe, King Solomon's general; suppose that instead of Livy and Tacitus only a few elegant but farcical little books had survived to us, such as are written nowadays about the love affairs of great men; suppose finally that those times known only from mythologies should return, as they were among the Greeks before Herodotus, then all certainty about things will be lost, and far from its being possible to show that the books of Holy Scripture are divine, it will no longer even be established that they are authentic.
The greatest obstacle to the spread of the Christian religion in the East, he said, was those peoples' ignorance of universal history.

He therefore laments that critics were becoming ever fewer: at the beginning of the seventeenth century the critical tendency had flourished and had almost suffered from its own fertility, because no one was held to be learned who had not often said: "I strike out; I emend; I have an old manuscript; this passage the copyists have corrupted." As there is no evil that does not bring forth some fruit, so, if one is to speak the truth, this tendency was nourished by the disputes over religion; for since no one can judge of the sense of Scripture, of the agreement of the ancients, of genuine and supposititious books, who is not well versed in every kind of monument, nothing in the libraries remained untouched.
James, the King of Great Britain, and the foremost men in church and state had nearly worn themselves out over these disputes beyond all measure.

But after these had passed over into war and bloodshed, the more discerning saw that nothing would be achieved by this clamor, and once peace had been restored, disgust at these questions and at this kind of scholarship seized many.

Thus began a new period in the sciences: Galileo, Bacon, Descartes, Gassendi, and others—in Germany the only one who could be set alongside them, Joachim Jungius—aroused the hope
that nature would be knowable with the aid of mathematics.

Why the pupils of these men too, with so many resources, achieved so little, he would for now leave aside; but the study of antiquity and sound learning had from that time onward here and there fallen into decline, to such an extent that some were ashamed to cite writers, partly so that they might not appear not to have taken everything from their own heads, partly to indulge their indolence: so that this plague of neglect might not spread further, people must be reminded that it is important for the sake of religion to preserve thorough learning.

Even the greatest man, the most superior mind, is exposed—if not subject—to the influences of his surroundings, of the people among whom he was raised and educated, of the age in which he grew up; thus these utterances too bear strongly the stamp of their time.

But besides this, one must consider that Leibniz wrote this to Huet on the occasion of the latter's published work on the truth of the Christian religion; and without dishonestly feigning (for his soul was filled with reverence for the holy and consecrated by genuine religiosity, although the common people took him for an unchristian and no clergyman accompanied him to the grave), thus without hypocrisy he was nevertheless accustomed, with a peculiar gentleness and fairness, indeed with a fine, almost courtly worldly tone, to adapt himself to persons and each time to turn outward the side most fitting and most agreeable to them.

At the same time, however, he by no means failed to carry the discussion into the general, and he visibly works toward winning friends and patrons for learning in general, far beyond the limits of the immediate application he highlighted, on the side of zeal for religion.
In relation to certain views that are fairly widespread nowadays, I find our Leibniz in manifold contradiction with them.

One hears also in our own day—though not, to be sure, within the bosom of this Academy, which in the spirit of universal scientific inquiry and thus in Leibniz's spirit cultivates all branches of knowledge equally, and is pervaded by the conviction—not merely in accordance with its constitution but in the inner conviction of all its members—that the
flourishing of the sciences thrives through the harmonious development of all fields of knowledge and through mutual recognition of them all; here, then, not so, but elsewhere one hears from the one-sided and the less educated approximately the same thing that Leibniz already had to hear: that the study of the ancients no longer bears any fruit; and just as then, so now the new upsurge of the natural sciences, especially in connection with their powerful intervention in practical life, is supposed to serve as grounds for this narrow judgment.
At that time it did not justify itself, although it had been brought about by greater men; all the less, then, may we linger over it now.
But still more striking is another contrast between Leibniz's views and the talk of today.

Certain Eromme fear for religion on account of heathenism; Leibniz found in the ancient erudition and in the untroubled critical knowledge of the whole history of human development a support for that very same religion.

Yet who should not shake his head when Leibniz credits criticism with a positive contribution toward authenticating the Christian religion, after experience seems to have shown how the former denies and eradicates it more and more?
In general, people speak almost always only of criticism as an annulling and destructive activity.

In form, to be sure, it often presents itself in this way; but everything depends only on whether it is rightly practiced, and thus achieves what it intends—the true—and then it will not negate and destroy, but affirm and build up.
The true positive lies in truth, and error is the actual negation, however positively it may know how to posture.

In all ages, and not merely in heathen times, human error has declared to be divine what the maturer human spirit has recognized not merely as undivine, but even as no longer human; and the dazzling false semblance of divinity is all the more dangerous because, in conjunction with other prejudices, with weakness of the understanding and coarseness of mind, mingled with worldly and selfish purposes, and supported by the passions and desires of men, it even leads to crimes which for a long time were committed by authority of state and law, and which unfortunately even now still find defenders in disordered heads, wildly
and fanatically heated.
One may further object against the praises that Leibniz bestows on criticism, that this criticism is for the most part not exercised at all on the Holy Scriptures, but on entirely different subjects.

But this he did not overlook; rather, he repeatedly points to a much more widely spreading use of the same, and insists precisely that, given the close connection of all literature and history, only he is capable of judging even the sacred books who is well versed in every kind of monument, and thus demands not some so-called Critica sacra, which was wont to pay homage to principles peculiar and divergent from the rest of the art, but a critical, general scholarship.
We do not wish to deny that this too, by virtue of the established factual evidence, may be of use for the sacred books; but something else should perhaps be valued more highly.

Interpretation and criticism are learned and practiced with unmaimed freedom and impartiality on the non-sacred writings, whereas in relation to sacred writings they are often for a long time, on the one hand, spellbound to a predetermined point by preconceived opinions that have been entrenched in prescribed doctrinal propositions, and, on the other hand, easily led astray by so-called neology, which arbitrarily subordinates the sources once more to yet another equally preconceived view.
But if judgment has first grown strong in a freer domain, then the more developed method later transfers itself, with greater confidence and skill, to sacred writings as well.

If, finally, Leibniz in one passage expressed himself pretty much to the effect that scholarship and criticism had their sole use for religion, then it was only the address of these letters that led him to this—though in some contradiction with himself.

Lessing, who had been made aware of these letters to Huet and had extracted some of their content, considered advisable, besides other softenings brought about by incomplete communication, also the omission of that strongest passage; he undoubtedly saw that scholarship and criticism are devoted to the whole history of the human race, and he found the Leibnizian reminder—taken quite strictly in the connection in which its author gave it—noteworthy above all only because it seemed to him still far more necessary given the state of theology at that time,
since, as he adds, scarcely a shadow remained of the scholars who flourished in Leibniz's day, and especially the theologians, who ought most of all to have the preservation of thorough scholarship at heart, understood the very least of it: a string he gladly strikes, not out of hostility toward religion or Christianity, but out of aversion to every kind of mediocrity and shallowness, and to a superficial would-be enlightenment then beginning, which was very different from his own manner of enlightenment and toleration.

History, interpretation, and criticism are the only human aids for setting the sources of positive religion in their true light; by their hand the further development of doctrine and of constitution must at the same time be traced through all ages, and the disfigurements of the original, the involuntary errors or deliberate distortions and deceptions, and human presumptions must be exposed and repelled: but these can accomplish this only slowly in the course of centuries, in the struggle against great obstacles, and only successfully to the degree that they are not meant to serve predetermined ecclesiastical or political principles, but are entirely free.
In his commendation of learning, Leibniz, I think, also had this consideration in the background.

His direction was, in keeping with his versatility, everywhere mediating and reconciling: within himself he had resolved the oppositions of the scholar and the philosopher, of empiricism and speculation, more than anyone else; in philosophy itself he made use of the earlier systems, in contrast to Descartes, and sought to reconcile what was opposed in them, which likewise comes about through a particular kind of philosophical criticism, just as Plato already united the oppositions of the older philosophies into an inward interpenetration, pointing out their one-sidedness: Leibniz too found reason and revelation in harmony.
His whole soul, like his system, was harmony.

This conciliatory spirit Leibniz also extended to religion, and he set it to work for the union of the Christian religious parties; for that purpose, as has just been indicated, learning and criticism are necessary and beneficial aids, provided one is not disinclined to listen to reason; ignorance and rigid dogmatism, always
bound up with some kind of unfreedom, are on the other hand the most insurmountable obstacle.

Leibniz declares precisely in one of the letters of which we are speaking that he believes he now recognizes that happiness of the times, so that he almost hopes that ecclesiastical peace and concord will come about; he founded this hope chiefly on the wisdom and moderation of the princes of that day, namely of the one whom he served, of the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and of the then head of the Roman Church.

Meanwhile he also speaks of rejection; and if demands and conditions were made that it would not be in our power to grant, then this could not be held against us: at the same time he fears that if nothing were to happen now and the opportunity were lost, the public joy would be postponed by several centuries.

The intention was noble and sacred: for who would wish to destine, for all time, the religion of love to be the battleground of hatred, and the doctrine of spiritual freedom to be the enslavement of souls?
Every division within the general development serves only as a stage toward the restoration of unity on a higher standpoint.

But however little Leibniz was mistaken in his aim, just as little did he abandon himself to exaggerated and all-too-certain hopes of success; rather, with a foreseeing mind he recognized that, if the attempts of that time were to fail, humanity would for centuries to come not be able to partake fully of the blessings of ecclesiastical peace.

div.head: XIX. Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Neander als neu eingetretenen Mitgliedes der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 4. Juli 1839.
Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Neander in der Akademie

p.s: You, esteemed Sir, after briefly touching upon certain relations which you describe as personal, and in which you allow only that modesty to appear which is proper to the true scholar, have set forth the relation of theology as a positive science to the general sciences, and have pointed to the close connection in which, in particular, the field of theology that you have chiefly cultivated stands to the general history of humanity.

If the choice by which the Academy has given to your scientific merits, your learning, your acumen, your intellectual freedom as set against other endeavors of the age—in short, to your whole individuality as scholar and man—the recognition that it alone can give, if, I say, this choice required a justification before anyone, then your words would have furnished it completely.

No one can be more deeply convinced of this than I, who have the honor today publicly to greet you in the name of the Academy as one of our own: that the science of the divine and the history of the development of the religious spirit and life, kept free from the impediments of human ordinances and hierarchical dominion, is the noblest and most sublime occupation of the scholar and the flower of the general sciences, to which the Academy is devoted in accordance with its statutes; and the Academy can the less withdraw from this view, inasmuch as, as you have remarked, theology is through three elements—the philosophical, the philological, and the historical—as intimately connected with the general sciences
as is jurisprudence, whose masters it has never hesitated to count among its own.

No branch of human knowledge enters more powerfully and comprehensively, more beneficently or more disruptively, into the overall formation of peoples than does positive religious doctrine; its scholarly and historical study is therefore one of the most significant parts of philosophy and history, for the advancement of which this society is joined together.
