Indeed, on this occasion and on this day it must not be passed over in silence that that Royal Society of Sciences, which as the first form of this Academy was founded at Leibniz's instigation and initiative, was called into existence not without particular regard precisely to the field of church history cultivated by you with the greatest distinction; and it may be permitted to regard it as a favorable coincidence if there presented itself to me, who have today spoken about Leibniz as the organ of the whole Academy, a subject of reflection that lies as close to your studies, esteemed sir, as to my own, and can serve as a manifest example of how little your scholarly achievements and endeavors are foreign to an Academy which, among all philosophers and scholars, venerates the one and only Leibniz as its scholarly founding father.

If I myself, in my opening address, have to some degree captured the spirit and the disposition of this society—which was my endeavor and seems to me the duty of the presiding officer—and if I am not mistaken in flattering myself that the sense of my address is also in harmony with the words you have just delivered and with the whole direction of your noble soul: then you too are so fully in accord with the spirit of the Academy that nothing remains for us to wish for except that you may devote to our society as much of your interest as your other important professional duties allow, with the fidelity and selfless zeal that animate you as a highly esteemed teacher of youth, rewarded with deep affection and heartfelt attachment.

div.head: XX. Einleitungsrede gehalten zur Feier des Geburtsfestes Seiner Majestät des Königs Friedrich Wilhelms IV. in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften am 22. October 1840.
Ueber die Lage und Verhältnisse der Berliner Akademie unter der Regierung Königs Friedrich Wilhelm III.

p.s: As is well known, the author of The Spirit of the Laws—a man no less virtuous than spirited and learned, who was bound to Frederick the Great and also to our Academy, and whose name is still heard with great reluctance today, as it was a hundred years ago, by two closely allied kinds of people, the pietists and the servile, but whose principles are for the most part as harmless as they are well founded, through the study of law and of history, both of antiquity and of the Middle Ages and modern times, and, notwithstanding his distance from all school philosophy, are largely genuinely philosophical—stamped virtue as the principle of the free state and honor as the principle of monarchy, not so much out of mockery and irony toward the latter, although here and there in his treatment of details he does not fail to provide that too, but because, like Machiavelli, with natural impartiality and great objectivity he had immersed himself in what was given and had recognized the fundamental forces appearing within it.

He understands by virtue, however, the political virtue, that is, patriotism, or the love of equality, not the philosophical or moral virtue, nor yet the Christian or religious virtue; and so long as politics, philosophy, and the Christian life have not been fused into an undivided unity—which is likely still to lie in the far distance, since all three still contradict one another in manifold ways, and the attempts at reconciliation are very imperfect and fantastic—one will have to accept that distinction as a factual one.

But patriotism is not love of the soil, however beautiful and moving the memories that may
attach themselves to the land, to the fields and waters, the mountains and valleys, where our childhood played and our youth tried its first powers: otherwise the serf would have to possess the strongest patriotism, whereas in fact he has none at all. It is, indeed—I am not ashamed to repeat it, however ill a sound these words may have acquired through misuse—it is the love of equality, which in turn is one and the same as the love of freedom; and only in the fatherland, or the state to which he belongs, does each person enjoy his full rights and is politically free in the enjoyment of them.

By equality, furthermore, is not meant numerical equality, but proportional equality, according to the measure of worth or of merit, which age, talent, insight, education, ability, and property, and even nobility of lineage—that is, inherited standing—or, in the expression of Aristotle and of Emperor Frederick the Second, old virtue and old wealth confer: and the fairest consequence of true freedom is the concord of individuals bound together by language and custom into a common spirit, so that all, even amid otherwise opposed endeavors, feel themselves members of one whole, to whose welfare each at his post and according to his station, in accordance with his best conviction—although individuals may contradict one another in this—wishes to contribute, in that he holds his own welfare and the welfare of the whole to be inseparable, indeed subordinates and sacrifices the former to the latter, the individual and particular to the all-embracing; in whose honor and glory all feel themselves honored, whose disgrace and insult they feel as their own disgrace, to avenge which each will stake goods and blood far more than for his own name.

To be sure, none of this can take place in a perfected despotism, because in it no love of equality is conceivable; rather, just as the despot himself has only his own advantage in view, so all his subjects, equal only in servitude, striving to escape from this degraded equality, pursue their own advantage by every path and seek to indemnify themselves through it and through the sensual enjoyment arising from it; because equally little is any love of freedom permitted in it, and equally little can a public spirit arise where not even a single community is to be found.

To be sure, this assertion
seems to be contradicted by the fact that despotism too, through the cooperation of the entire forces of the people, accomplishes great things; but if one considers the resources that are set in motion in the process, one readily finds that it is not a political common spirit with which despotism brings about great things.

It may sound sacrilegious—and yet it is not—that in despotism religion, in its principal relations, takes the place of the political common spirit; indeed, that the most powerful lever by which peoples ruled despotically are driven to great deeds is religion—not the true and genuine religion, but, and precisely for that reason the assertion is not sacrilegious, the religious prejudices and errors by means of which such multitudes of peoples have at all times been fanaticized. And even if free men are fanaticized by the watchword of freedom, as common usage expresses it, this very fact shows it to be the less natural, since the name of fanaticism itself was transferred from the religious to the political sphere—roughly as one uses the name of hierarchy, clumsily enough, to designate a relation among secular states, when one speaks of a hierarchy of officials.

If a people ruled despotically has outgrown religious prejudices, then despotism has lost its strongest driving spring; hence it is of the highest importance to despotism to cherish and cultivate those errors.
If they have disappeared, then apart from the use of cunning and deception, only fear, ambition, and greed remain as the passions through whose arousal the despot can exert a powerful effect.
But how does it stand with the monarchy?

If there were no freedom in it, there could also be no love of country in it; but presupposing that freedom is in it—and only under this presupposition is it distinct from despotism, although in reality the forms are seldom perfectly and purely developed, just as in nature the elements seldom occur unmixed, but often and almost necessarily monarchical elements are found mixed into despotism and despotic elements into monarchy—presupposing, then, that freedom is in it, the monarchy offers in the person of the prince a center in which love of country gathers all the more brilliantly and is kindled all the more ardently.

For
in the prince the whole fatherland is presented to the mind not merely as a so-called moral person, but as one truly appearing; in him the ideal and universal idea of the fatherland is united with a personality to whom man turns his heart, recognizing, honoring, and loving the fatherland in him and him in the fatherland; and however powerful the dominion of the idea may be, yet love and trust toward a definite person, when the idea is borne by that person like a banner and is, as it were, embodied in him, still work greater wonders, just as an army, however inspired it may otherwise be, is more uplifted by the confidence it places in the person of a proven general and by its veneration for him than if it followed the orders of a senate or a court war council. 1 1 To be sure, this favorable relationship again takes place only when the spirit and direction of the prince and the spirit and direction of the people do not oppose each other, but either agree from the outset or balance each other and make themselves alike, in that the prince either grasps and follows the national spirit already developed and grown strong, or advancing with more or less strength, clarity, and consciousness toward a definite goal, while at the same time he guides it, or in that, with a superior spirit of his own, he outruns his people and his age and draws both after him and up to himself: the former with less danger, since it seldom happens, and usually only through the guilt or weakness of those in power, that the entire people pursues a pernicious direction, into which the prince is then also entangled; the latter only when the ruler already finds at least some receptivity in the people and the way is prepared, because even the most vigorous sovereign can educate and elevate his people only by gathering and strengthening the better elements from among them, and thereby beating down the lesser and worse ones.

If the harmony between rulers and ruled can thus proceed from either of the two sides, it can likewise, again with respect to time, arise in two different ways, suddenly or gradually: suddenly, when some great event, especially a great misfortune, sets the slumbering forces
in motion with inspiration, or when a great hope placed in the new prince is not only not disappointed but even surpassed, or when an anxious expectation and apprehension sees itself proved false; gradually, when in long peace prince and people, like the members of a family, as it were grow into one another, feel at ease in this community, and thus learn to trust one another reciprocally.

The first condition of political life, through which alone even free states can become great and flourishing, and did become so in antiquity, is obedience; but the obedience that in despotism springs only from fear is transfigured in monarchy, under that relationship of prince and people, into love, just as the fear of God or of an iron necessity of fate, which is suited to a servile people, has been beneficently and soothingly transformed by the mildness of Christianity, for the mind, into the love of God and submission to the counsels of divine Providence.

Although the political principle that the king does not die is undeniably correct and is the guarantee of the monarchy and of the peace and security of the monarchical state—a guarantee that would be endangered if the kingship, without a legally fixed succession, rested even for a single day—yet this principle loses its validity for feeling, and the king dies for every member of the state, however humble, as soon as this human sentiment of love has joined itself to the political relation; and unquestionably this sentiment is the nobler: for even if the state has not yet attained its purpose, the realization of the whole moral nature of man, through which realization the political would wholly merge in the human and the human in the political, in all its relations, yet in that love such a union of the human and the political is in part found.

Far from this attachment to the person of the ruler being servile and suited only to despotism, it can—setting aside perhaps the consummate cosmopolitan who has wholly detached himself, or believes he has detached himself, from the state—be a matter of indifference only to the consummate slave whom Majesty may clothe, and rather it is only in despotism that it is entirely all the same to the obedient subject
who bears Majesty, if indeed Majesty can be spoken of there at all; for in that system all bow without love beneath the same yoke, unconcerned as to who imposes it upon them, and seek and enjoy only their own advantage, so long as it pleases the holder of power to leave it to them.

In this, then—that in a monarchy love of country is fused with love for the person of the prince, and clings to him and holds fast to him with increased strength as the representative of the fatherland—lies the universally valid significance of the celebration with which the whole land commemorates the birthday of its king, a celebration that is rooted precisely in the consciousness that prince and people in a monarchy are bound together not merely by command and obedience, but by the bond of concord and love.

For since joy cannot be commanded and is consequently no object of obedience, such a celebration would be mere pretense and flattery, or at best only conventional form without thought or feeling, if it did not rest upon that foundation.

But lest it be believed that, precisely because in a monarchy the king dies for every subject, that joy cannot forthwith be transferred to the successor, it is enough to consider that the heir to the throne, even before he has shown or promised the people new benefits, is as heir to the rights and duties also heir to the love that was directed toward his predecessor; although this love will show itself more warmly when the people live beforehand in the firm conviction that the new prince will follow the example of his forebears, and from his goodness of heart, the loftiness of his sentiments, the noble cultivation and direction of his mind, and finally from his openness, prudence, and wisdom, sees a happy future foretold for itself.

How all this is confirmed in our illustrious princely house needs no detailed exposition for the listener who is accustomed to beholding the universal in the particular, and likewise to giving general reflections at once their own application to the particular.

Everyone recognizes how Frederick the Great, advancing ahead of his age, drew his people along after him and cultivated them, and by great deeds not alone but also by the continued blessings of a long reign filled the hearts of
his subjects with that love of fatherland devoted to his person; how Frederick William III, not merely under the favoring influence of extraordinary events and great misfortunes, but earlier already and again later, brought himself with his people into that enviable harmony in which the command became a fatherly summons and admonition, and obedience became love; and when at last, with deep sorrow, we saw that great and noble life succumb to the common lot of mortals, there shone at the same time into the night of our soul's grief a consoling star, and there mingled with our affliction a presentiment of the universal love for a ruler who knows how to win all hearts: and though at first, as was fitting and as feeling urged, grief predominated, yet the few months of the new reign have already kindled all noble spirits, and have gathered all the rays of that love of fatherland which was consecrated to the departed, ever more powerfully and more closely into a new point of light and focal point in the magnanimous prince, to whom the Prussian people has now for the first time celebrated that elevating festival whose after-celebration we commemorate today in our own particular and narrower circle; and advancing time, which proves all things, will give lasting confirmation to the enviable lot of our fatherland.
The best school of the community spirit, and thus of love of country, is the academic body.

To be sure, it is rightly regarded as a great evil when any society forms a state within the state; but here one has in mind two mutually contradictory and counteracting systems, of which the one—namely, that state within the state—seeks to dominate the actual state or, what amounts to the same thing, to abolish it.

The academic body, by contrast, of which I speak, is a microcosm within the macrocosm of the state, an organ within the total organism; the health of the state, as of the body, consists in the proper harmony of the particular and distinctive activities of these organs with the total life.

Within the narrower circle of the academic body, which indeed represents a small state, but one not separated from the whole but taken up into it, true freedom and the love of true equality are practiced and learned amid more
limited and more surveyable relations, and at the same time subordination and obedience—in a word, the common spirit; and insofar as this common spirit finds its center in the person of the prince, love for him comes most easily to consciousness in the academic bodies: they are therefore preeminently the ones that give expression to this love through their festivities.
The Royal Academy of Sciences, an academic body established by the King himself, has—not so much through deliberate intent as through a sure instinct—for the celebration of the...

On the birthday of the reigning King, besides giving expression to their veneration, attachment, and love for the hereditary ruler, [the celebration] is appointed for an overview of what [the academic body] has accomplished in the past year: for herein lies the acknowledgment that everything the individual academic body completes happens only by virtue of its being received into the great community, which has its life in the life of the King, and that it owes everything to the royal house.
From this statutory provision, however, I take the liberty today of departing, an exception which, however, should better satisfy the sense of the provision than strict observance of the letter.

If we ordinarily reckon the years from which the achievements to be reported are to be recounted from one royal birthday to the next, then by contrast we now stand at the dividing line between two reigns, which one may describe as great years of the nations.
Nothing, therefore, could be more fitting for this day than a presentation of what the Academy was under the long reign of Frederick William III and what was promoted by it.

Whoever, however, wished to set this forth with some completeness could not avoid enumerating a multitude of details, supplying registers of persons and lists of treatises and of subjects discussed, and thus, as it were, through these and similar compilations giving a statistics of the Academy.
But whether a picture would thereby be gained, and an insight into the inner nature of this scholarly institution, seems to me very doubtful.

Admittedly, one can say that even the names of the men who formed the Academy during this period showed the spirit of the latter; and certainly there are great names among them. But with equal right one could
reply that the names also of those who were not admitted into the Academy are indicative of this spirit, and all the more so since, unfortunately, great names are to be found among them as well.

Moreover, the entire activity of its members cannot be credited to their account; the academic activity of scholars is, in accordance with the nature of circumstances, always only a limited one, and most of them did not work for the advancement of knowledge because they were members of the Academy, but rather were joined to this association because they had already earlier proven themselves.

Indeed, the greatest expansions of knowledge have not proceeded from academies, and the writings of the latter, without their value being thereby diminished, can only be described as larger or smaller contributions to the mighty edifice of the sciences, and they are hardly, or only seldom, the foundation pillars of this edifice.

Let us therefore set aside the persons and writings, and content ourselves with a brief indication—one that does not overstep the bounds of an introductory address—of some general relations as they have especially emerged since the restoration of the state; for the earlier period, back to the accession of Frederick William III, lies partly outside the circle of my own experience, beyond which I would not wish to go, and partly, as far as I know, the character of the Academy at that time was little different from that which had been handed down from the preceding reign.

The Academy was, in full accordance with the concept of such an institution, and above all in contrast to universities and schools, from its very beginning a society of scholarly masters for the advancement and dissemination of knowledge, without regard to the education of the young and without any intended direct application to ordinary life.

In order to achieve this purely theoretical purpose, after the restoration of the society by Frederick the Great, in the course of his long reign, distinguished scholars in the field were assembled and were in part placed, through larger salaries, in a position to devote their full leisure to the sciences; to these were frequently attached—partly for other
reasons, partly because in earlier times the capital, for lack of comprehensive educational institutions, did not offer a significant number of actual specialists who would already have had a sufficient position independent of the Academy—apart from a few clergymen and public teachers, the literary elements that happened to be present among the statesmen or men of business: persons, to be sure, of no small importance in public life or in the most important relations of the general culture of that time and of the prevailing intellectual currents, but in part less distinguished in the cultivation of particular scientific fields.

The existing scientific collections and apparatus—namely the Royal Library, the botanical garden, the observatory, the chemical laboratory, and other institutions besides—were subordinate to the Academy as a governmental authority; it was the only more considerable literary body in the capital.
The substantial income required was chiefly provided to it by the possession of the calendar monopoly, and the Academy came to form a separate fortune of its own under its own administration.

Distinguished in particular by brilliant talents in mathematics, and not insignificant for the natural sciences, it was on the other hand of less importance for the philosophical, historical, and philological sciences, and stood notably in the last respect far below the French Academy of Inscriptions and of Belles-Lettres, which, despite many mediocre achievements, retains the merit of having introduced a more spirited and freer mode of treatment of the manifold subjects belonging to its sphere.

Meanwhile, in contrast to the pedantry censured by Frederick the Great and the crude tastelessness of the university teachers of that time, our Academy has certainly, imperceptibly, helped to spread a greater refinement and a more cultivated tone in scholarly presentation.

Its standing in the state rested not only on the king's personal favor but also on its own position; its scholarly reputation rested on the outstanding literary figures, mostly foreigners in earlier times, French scholars or scholars educated in the French manner.

The language of the Academy was French; this was not without influence even on appointment or admission to it: although German
elements were not excluded, the Academy nevertheless, taken as a whole, remained alien to the national spirit and a scholarly French colony in the capital.

To be sure, the disparity with respect to the mature German culture and with respect to the state of literature in Prussia steadily diminished over time, and had already almost entirely disappeared, when that fateful upheaval of the entire state and the effort to restore it brought about a new condition.

The expression of this condition lies, at least in form—though that form must first be filled out with activity—in the laws which, at the Academy's own instigation, have been newly drafted three times since that time; and if the Academy has thereby already made it known that it did not persist self-satisfied in inherited arrangements but strove to attain possible perfection, then both the manner in which these laws were given and their content likewise reveal the first and most important character conferred upon the Academy by the late lamented King—I mean the complete corporate freedom which it enjoyed under the ruler's protection and under the supervision of the highest authority to such a degree that the drafting of its laws was each time left to it, subject to royal confirmation, and that the last and most complete draft was approved without any alteration whatsoever.

It is already a great gain and the surest pledge of lasting well-being when a commonwealth is governed by well-considered, definite, and comprehensive laws that have issued from those versed in the matter; for these laws are nothing other than the simple expression of the nature of the thing and of the essence of the institution itself: whereas, when recourse must frequently be had to rescripts, manifold errors and contradictions cannot be avoided, because even the most discerning prince and the most discerning authority, in dealing with individual cases—which moreover may be incorrectly grasped and presented—very easily give one-sided decisions that take more account of persons than of things, and these are then just as easily applied incorrectly to other cases for which they were not intended.

Since, moreover, the content of our laws permits the Academy the freest movement;
since the appointment of its members proceeds from the Academy itself and no one can be forced upon it; since it disposes independently of the use of its income, subject indeed to the appropriate approval of a benevolent authority that liberally welcomes every promotion of science; since it is not subject to the predominant influence or even the unlimited decisions of an externally high-ranking president appointed by the state, but rather passes its resolutions freely by majority vote under the leadership of rotating officers whom it elects from its own midst; since finally, although no longer for the persons of its members as formerly, yet for itself as an academic body it is subject to no restriction by the censorship of the press: so under Frederick William III the Academy has asserted all that freedom which is appropriate and beneficial to a scientific community.

That only under this government did the Academy fully transform itself from a French into a German academy scarcely needs mention; but in this, that in an age when almost all European peoples have raised their own language to the rank of a learned one, it employs neither French, which still predominantly mediates social intercourse, nor Latin, which the universities rightly retain for certain purposes, the Academy has by no means withdrawn further from the general scholarly intercourse of nations; rather, it has entered into that intercourse more vividly.

The human race is undeniably moving in our time, more than ever before, toward the great goal of abolishing its one-sidedness and divisions: through the swiftest means of communication distances are so contracted that they are, as it were, annihilated, and the dissemination of thought, reaching far beyond the boundaries of nations, is so multiplied and accelerated by the greatest activity of the book trade and a multitude of periodicals that, instead of being able to complain of a lack of literary means, one is rather overwhelmed by the mass of what unceasingly streams in.

But notwithstanding these mighty aids to intercourse among peoples, it nevertheless seems to me to be the fairest purpose of academies and of all societies
resembling them to cooperate in the very progress in the life of humanity that has just been indicated—for the very reason that what matters is not solely the multiplicity and rapidity of communications, but also the inward befriending of those who communicate.

To be sure, the scholars of all nations, without prejudice to their patriotism, are closely bound together by one and the same purpose, the knowledge of truth; but this union gains greatly when, among the various nations, far-radiating centers of association are formed, each of which draws into itself the most distinguished bearers of knowledge abroad as members of its fellowship.

If these associations themselves again enter into friendly intercourse with one another, then not only is communication secured and facilitated to a high degree even without the intervention of the daily newspapers and the book trade, which are by no means generally adequate and often very unreliable, but also in the domain of scholarship the mutual recognition of nations is powerfully promoted.
To be sure, for the present only in this domain: but the power of knowledge is irresistible, and concord in knowledge must imperceptibly also influence concord of disposition.
A long peace has now moderated the mutual antipathies of nations; a just appreciation of what is foreign, without any mania for imitation, is no less conducive to the sciences than to industry.

It was precisely through the peace that the wisdom and prudence of Frederick William III knew how to preserve amid the most threatening circumstances that our association was enabled to fulfill completely that noble purpose of the academies and to establish significant connections in all the lands where scholarly cultivation prevails; at the same time, it has won abroad a recognition which, not to say more, does not fall behind the rest of the renown of German scholarship.

Indeed, not without pride may we recall the memorable words that we heard from the mouth of Frederick William IV—who with sure judgment appreciates the particular value of every endeavor—in reply to the expression of our veneration dedicated to the late king of blessed memory and his exalted successor; with pride, I say, may we let these words of his resound: that
the voice of the Academy carries great weight for Europe.

While, then, the academies are pre-eminently suited to maintain the position indicated for them abroad and in the scientific intercourse of the world, they seem, by contrast, at least in Germany never to be able to attain the influence that the institutions of the same name, now united into one great whole, after which the German societies of this kind are modeled, have attained for France; for even without taking the extent of their resources into account, no German academy will be in a position to dominate literary judgment to the same degree, even if a critical journal is at its disposal—which our association lacks—or if it wished to supply an annual survey of the state and progress of the sciences, which our academy under the past government set itself as a goal out of an overestimation of its powers, without being able to carry it out, or if, at the prompting of individuals or of the state, it gave its expert opinion on the most important scientific phenomena: for in Germany the universities intervene so effectively in scientific life that they make themselves felt pre-eminently and draw particular attention to themselves.

As long as the capital of the Prussian state lacked a university, the Academy did not feel this weight close at hand; when, through the founding of the university, it receded somewhat in outward standing, although its first rank officially remained with it, a certain compensation nevertheless arose from the intended union of the two institutions into a so-called organic whole, even though it remained unclear by what means the union—which indeed originally existed and still exists—was to become an organic one.

The Academy gave its support especially to the emerging university, in that several of its members taught at the latter, as indeed still happens; and the formal and legally declared connection of the Academy with the university here, and at the same time with all the other Prussian universities, and thus the Academy's possible influence upon our university, consists precisely in this: that the ordinary members of the former are entitled to teach at any Prussian university.

More significant, however, appears to be the reciprocal influence that the Academy has
experienced from the university.

Through the founding and the flourishing of the latter, a more varied and more extensive scholarly life has been generated in the capital, and in nearly all branches the number of scholarly men—and indeed of the true scholars by profession, who devote themselves to embracing the whole of their science or to the investigation of everything in detail, which in our time has risen to so high a degree through the division of labor—has been very considerably increased; thus the Academy became less restricted in its elections, and these fell for the most part on teachers of the university: yet we may congratulate the state and science that our city also contains, besides those, highly renowned representatives of science, who heighten the fame and splendor of the Academy and spread them far and wide.

The aforementioned predominance of the specialized and particular in the scientific development of the age made it appear temporarily more expedient to strengthen the activity of the individual classes of the Academy and to give the plenary sessions a subordinate importance; instead of this measure, which favored separation and isolation, the opposite was, however, rightly put into effect, namely the consolidation of the former four classes into two, in that the mathematical was merged with the physical, and the philosophical with the historical-philological.

The immediate occasion for this lay in the circumstance that at a certain point the mathematical and the philosophical classes had dwindled to very few members; if experience has since shown that we do not lack distinguished mathematicians, the Academy, by contrast, has not drawn so many philosophers into its association as to form a separate class from them.

If, as it seems to me, the neglect of famous philosophers cannot be excused by the fact that even Leibniz had not intended a philosophical section of the then Society of Sciences, nor yet by the fact that philosophers are not suited, like men in other learned fields, to pursue research together and to reach an understanding with one another, then the reproach that the Academy allowed the philosophical systems which developed one after another during the reign of the late king,
in Germany and first of all before our eyes, to pass by almost unnoticed can be removed only by the admission that, without any intended neglect of speculative philosophy, personal views and circumstances—the blame for which was shared between influential members of the Academy and the harshness of those distinguished men—formed for a long time a gulf which would nevertheless have been filled had death not torn those immortal ornaments of German philosophy from us too soon.

Moreover, the former philosophical class was by no means reckoned to include only speculative philosophy and its history, but also everything that abroad is understood under the name of the moral and political sciences; yet to all of this, insofar as it has flourished among us according to circumstances, the Academy has not closed itself off.

One may still — whether only in appearance or with justice, I scarcely dare to decide — especially in comparison with the French academies, find missing the aesthetic direction, fine literature, or whatever else was then called poetry and eloquence, to which Frederick the Great attached exceptional value: yet we may be justified in esteeming highly what exists, even if under more favorable circumstances and under other conditions of literature much could be conceived more completely and more perfectly, and one or another of these might be expected to have a more vital impact on the intellectual movement of the age.

Yet it cannot be passed over in silence that the Academy, at roughly the same time as the founding of the university, during the state's period of distress, suffered a reduction of its property and income which was not in proportion to the expenditures for the scientific institutions that were taken from it, and that it was thereby placed in no position to win for itself more scholars who could live preeminently for academic leisure: meanwhile this loss has at least in some respect been indirectly compensated by the fact that the circumstances already mentioned made it possible to attach to the Academy many from the increased number of scientific men who already had a sufficient external position apart from it.

Finally, at that very time and as a consequence of the founding of the university, the influence of the Academy was diminished in that the
supervision of the scholarly collections, which it had formerly exercised, was withdrawn from it; on the other hand, under higher direction these collections have been so enriched, and so suitably administered by men whom the Academy counts among its own, that they became far more useful for the use of the members of the Academy, and through these and similar arrangements the association was relieved of the burden of a manifold administration, which draws one more or less away from scholarship.

But however modest the Academy's means may be, it still sets aside enough of them to be able to devote a certain sum each year to scholarly undertakings, and thereby, for some twenty-five years, it has not only carried out larger works itself but has also given other scholars support or subsidies for costly works.

In this way it has more effectively remedied many a substantial need of science and scholarship than by the customary setting of prize questions, which serve approximately the same purpose: although we may assert that the latter too, since the restoration of the Academy, by intervening in a timely manner in the course of development of the sciences, have borne fruitful fruits and called forth works of lasting value.

The academic printing press, too, is to be regarded only as a scholarly enterprise, not a commercial one; it was established at no inconsiderable sacrifice, chiefly in order to obtain a stock of rare writings, especially Oriental ones, of which, to the disadvantage of the local scholars of the capital of the realm, there had until then been an almost total lack.

Much could still be added to show that the Academy, under the glorious reign of the late, deeply revered King, in its continual striving for heightened activity and for the greatest possible removal of the imperfections that cling to every human work, accomplished as much as was possible under the given circumstances; but I fear that these and similar reflections may be too dry and meaningless for this splendid time of universal enthusiasm with which the sublime spirit of the most gracious of kings—himself inspired by the noblest feelings—has given wings to his people, an example for princes and peoples such as the annals not merely of this country but of world history
may scarcely yet be able to point to.

We all have joined most deeply in those uplifting feelings and will always join in them; to give them a new and worthy expression today cannot even be attempted, because no words of any single individual are capable of coming even close to that mighty outburst of the living love of an entire people.

We have overcome fateful times in trust in the father of the fatherland who rests in God: to whom, should the wisdom of the King also succeed in dispersing the mists of present anxieties like the rays of the morning sun, to whom is the further future so evident that he would know whether those times are closed, since in our days renewed anxiety has so often sprung from the moments of hope, and every calm has given birth from its bosom to unexpected storms and upheavals?

But whatever times may follow—for this lies in God's hand—the newly and most deeply proven concord and love between prince and people, and their mutual trust, is Prussia's palladium, borne by its king; no storm will wrest it from his firm hand!

div.head: XXI. Zur Begrüfsung der Herrn v. d. Hagen, Wilhelm Grimm, Schott und Dirksen als neu eingetretener Mitglieder der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 8. Juli 1841.
Zur Begrüfsung der Herrn v. d. Hagen, Wilhelm Grimm, Schott und Dirksen in der Akademie

p.s: As I am about to welcome you, gentlemen, who have just spoken, in the name of the Academy as new fellows of our association and of our endeavors, the thought first presents itself to me unbidden: how different, after all, are the subjects and directions that are pursued not merely by the various sections of this society, but that lie even within the compass of the one class which I at this moment represent as speaker; and at the same time the awareness presses upon me how little an individual—unless he is comparable to the scientific hero of this day, but is, to speak in the Homeric manner, merely one of those such as mortals now are—can appear suited to measure the worth of each of our colleagues, and, to stay with the present occasion, first of each of you, not merely externally and according to the general reputation that you have acquired, but with scientific insight and precision.

The latter consideration would be depressing and humiliating if this limitation were not common to by far the greatest part of scholars, and if in the domain of science as well the division of labor were not recognized as beneficial; on the other hand, the former is unquestionably elevating, and opens to us a view into the infinity and all-embracing scope of the human mind, which—though only approximately, to be sure, and resolved into its elements—a society established by a
significant state, such as ours, is preeminently called to present.

Our native language, literature, and culture on the one hand, and on the other the character of the peoples of the Chinese, Tibetan, and Tatar stock—both treated by distinguished scholars whom we have just heard speak of their researches, partly already accomplished and partly still to come—present themselves to us as almost the extreme ends of our history of civilized peoples, since the former are what lies nearest to us, while the latter, if not the most remote in space and spirit, are yet so different from the shaping of our conditions and intellectual productions that one might say the common element in both is outweighed by the contrasting or divergent.

In this extension of our scientific knowledge over the entire globe, we perceive a twofold advantage of modern European education—one over the knowledge of the Orientals, the other over the knowledge of antiquity.

If the barbarian is confined to his immediate natural surroundings and is accustomed to regard the foreigner as an enemy, then nations that, moreover, can scarcely be denied a not insignificant degree of civil and even scientific development draw near to him in the measure that, confined or, self-satisfied, confining themselves to themselves, they recognize only their own culture and, so to speak, excluding themselves from the community of the human race, are incapable of perceiving and understanding the human outside themselves, or from deep-rooted prejudices arbitrarily limit their thirst for knowledge: at this stage the most cultivated nations of the Orient have fixed themselves fast, and they can therefore attain to no pure knowledge of the history of the human race, or—to use this word in a higher sense than the commonly current one—to no philology.

The classical peoples of antiquity, by contrast, were indeed able to comprehend what was foreign, and they did comprehend it, so far as their intercourse extended; but since this intercourse itself did not have the scope of that of today, they attained, to be sure, the depth of insight into the nearer and more immediate things available to them, but not the comprehensive survey of all nature and history, not the contemplation of all the forms in which the human spirit presents itself, and of all its paths and
wanderings in which our scholarship follows it.

By virtue of these advantages, European culture will be able to make the whole globe subject to itself, just as our religion is suited to become a world religion, and just as the Greeks and Romans carried their culture as far as their weapons reached.

But with this cosmopolitan circumspection, which makes man a friend to man and prompts us to know him not only in ourselves but also in others, Europeans unite a deeply rooted feeling of nationality; without its stamp they would soon blur into a flat universality. The finest and truest cultivation is attained precisely when a great breadth and universality of thought is enclosed within a particular individuality, drawn with firm outlines and sharply and deeply marked—the infinite bounded within the finite.

The Germans have very often been reproached by themselves for looking too much abroad, admiring what is foreign, and disdaining what is native; and certainly at times this has done no little harm not only to their literature and their customs of life, but even to their political condition.

Even this Academy, despite the fact that in earlier times our Leibniz had recommended the cultivation of the German language and had praised it in the period of its greatest disfigurement, out of tradition still paid homage to French even when we had long since learned to use our language worthily; may we now, without falling into the opposite fault of hollow self-satisfaction and arrogance, count ourselves all the more fortunate if our national character is so strengthened and secured that we no longer have to fear any pernicious influence of the foreign, and thus can surrender ourselves all the more freely to the general intercourse of nations, certain in the exchange of thoughts to impart at least as much, or—what is more desirable in this as in trade with external goods—even more, than we receive.

You have, esteemed Herr von der Hagen, eloquently set forth the value of language for a people—and above all, rightly, the value of our language for our people, and how in the times of oppression it had remained almost the only thing the Germans had in common. Through the restoration of external freedom it has lost nothing
of this importance for the common fatherland, and who could fail to recognize that its cultivation is a sacred duty for every educated German?

For it is not merely the philologists into whose hands it is entrusted; it is quite preeminently the public orators, who are to give it power, the philosophers, who are to give it definiteness and depth, the poets, who are to give it fullness and clarity for the imagination, and all the fine and delicate shadings for the expression of every mood and every feeling; but upon all of them together, in my opinion, there also rests the obligation to care for its purity, yet without tasteless pedantry.
Research falls first of all to our Society, and it is a happy fortune that today I am to turn first to such distinguished researchers in the field of the mother tongue and of patriotic literature.

The Academy, with sound judgment, has taken advantage of favorable circumstances to strengthen within its own body the representation of this branch of learning, so highly important to itself and to the fatherland; in doing so, it has, as far as lies in its power, given you, the first among the newly elected members, the thanks owed for laborious work that you have devoted from your youth onward—and already at a time when this field was still little cultivated—to the old national literature, and that you recently, after many years of preparation, crowned with a comprehensive work worthy of yourself and of the fatherland.

If I say that the Academy, in order to attain the stated purpose, availed itself of favorable circumstances, I mean by this chiefly the harsh adversity of fate that became favorable to us through the gracious and free spirit of Frederick William IV—adversity that had struck you, esteemed colleague Wilhelm Grimm, together with your excellent brother.

The noble and capable man, when a fatherland is lost to him, always finds a new one that receives and welcomes him with joy; and when the poet says of a citizen of two states that it is good, in a stormy night, to have cast two anchors from the swift sea-ship, so Germany's scholars rejoice in the advantage of having still more life-anchors, as long as its magnanimous princes value the inner worth of German sentiment and learning as our King and Lord does.

You, most esteemed Herr College, were already
previously not a stranger to our Society; and if your elder brother needed only to take the seat long since assigned to him among us, then for the Academy nothing more was required than a reminder furnished by circumstances in order to draw still closer than before the bond with you, who together with him, in brotherly concord, have promoted many a scholarly and congenial work, and in your own writings have demonstrated to general recognition the deep and comprehensive knowledge of German antiquity, of its language and poetry, of its simple and natural wisdom.

May the hospitable place that the King has prepared for you here grant both of you compensation for what has been lost and, where possible, even more; our esteem and friendship has striven, and will continue to strive, to show that all of us, even those who remain more distant from your particular studies, know your merits.
Yet I must not give free rein to my personal feelings; I hasten to another consideration.

The Academy has rightly attached considerable importance to the Oriental languages in its own work; in particular, ever since the study of Indian literature began to become better known among us, it has joined to its circle the most excellent connoisseurs and founders of this field of study in Germany.

Through the death of our dear colleague Wilken, not only the secretariat and the historical section of the philosophical-historical class, but also Oriental literature has lost a worthy representative. You, esteemed colleague Schott, move within a part of the field that he had cultivated; but beyond it you open up to us another field that the Academy has hitherto scarcely touched.

Leibniz had indeed directed his attention to China and Chinese science, and at the founding of the former Royal Society of Sciences he held out the prospect of nothing less than astronomical and geographical, natural-historical and ethnological observations from the Prussian frontiers all the way to China; the lively thirst for knowledge of his own age and of the age immediately after him also brought to light much instruction concerning that land and its peculiar wisdom and customs: even the proverbial constancy of its forms, however little it may be able to commend itself to European movement and longing for progress, even the image of a
perfected and consistent despotism—not, however, without many a grain of genuine statecraft—furnished serious thinkers of the previous century with abundant material for ingenious observations.

But only shortly before the last restoration of the Academy did our capital see two men, one native and one foreign, who devoted themselves to the cultivation of this field; and now, since this royal seat has become the scientific center of Germany more than ever before, a connoisseur of those particular formations of language, science, and art and of all the circumstances of life is an essential need for us.
In your person the Academy has found him.
Until then it possessed only Chinese characters; you are the first to use them, the first to bring them to life through application.
At the same time, even now you point toward a more fruitful treatment of the languages you have named, whereby the study of them is to be raised to the height of comparative linguistics.

The less Prussia is ever in a position to maintain a lasting commerce with the heavenly realm that Leibniz hoped to found upon amber, the more purely scientific, the more removed from common utility, and consequently the more purely academic is the cultivation of your field.
The purpose of the Academy lies in the promotion and expansion of the general sciences.
But even those sciences that stand in a closer relation to the purposes of the state would be ill advised if they withdrew themselves from the spirit of general scientific inquiry.

It was set forth earlier, on this Leibniz commemorative day in this assembly, that neither theology nor jurisprudence is foreign to the Academy, since both are intimately connected with the general sciences through three important elements: the philosophical, the philological, and the historical.

This connection, however, does not everywhere emerge with equal strength and equal purity in the treatment; where it appears in a striking degree in any one of these three relations, a academy of sciences would deprive itself of important branches of knowledge and of noble ornaments if it refused to count the masters of those learned disciplines among its own.

In particular, our Academy has enjoyed the membership of famous jurists, and for this
too Leibniz, the all-encompassing one, serves us as a model.

How then should we not have wished to win you, esteemed Herr College Dirksen, for our association—you, in whose learned and penetrating works of legal scholarship, carried through with vigor and self-sacrifice, precisely the historical and philosophical element stands out to such an excellent degree that the purposes of the academic class to which I have the honor to belong must be especially advanced through your cooperation?

You have just now given the Academy recognition: both through the election of its members and through the determination of the subjects of its prize questions, it has endorsed the view that knowledge of the legal constitution of antiquity exerts a beneficial influence upon the study of ancient history and of the other conditions of life of those peoples; you have set forth how nowadays one not seldom finds the historical researcher and the student of antiquity in the same field of inquiry, and how it is coming more and more to be recognized that a comprehensive understanding of classical antiquity can be attained only through the united efforts of those scholars.
Thus the views of the Academy and your own meet: your direction was long since an academic one; and it is a satisfaction to us—if not a merit—to have recognized it as such.

The first among the speakers to whom my reply is addressed has given his substantial words a conclusion that all those present will have heard with the liveliest satisfaction and the most heartfelt agreement.
What conclusion, as a similar one, ought to befit me as the one answering?

If Herr von der Hagen, as the scholarly representative of national literature in our Academy, has designated the King as the master of German speech and the most faithful cultivator of the beloved mother tongue, then it falls to me, as the official representative of manifold directions, moreover to emphasize that the King, paying homage to genuine culture—which I have placed above in the union of the most unrestricted universality with the most particular individuality—being devoted with love to his own national character, at the same time recognizes every other, namely that of his non-German subjects, so that, as far as lies with their
sovereign, their language may not die out, just as the tongue of the tribe from which this realm takes its name has fallen silent; that he esteems and loves the true and noble, wherever it may have grown, without regard to the appearance of origin, and finally that our exalted lord and protector too is animated by what is the soul of the Academy: universal scientific spirit.
God preserve the King!

div.head: XXII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Jahrestages Friedrichs des Grofsen am 27. Januar 1842.
Ueber Friedrich den Grofsen als Denker und Schriftsteller

p.s: Prudence, and in particular statecraft, which seeks to govern the peoples, consists in a calculation of circumstances and of the means through whose use certain ends are attained; prudence itself does not determine and choose the ends, but they are, in relation to it, indifferent presuppositions, which are given either by another's command, or by custom and usage, or by prejudices, self-interest, and passions, or finally by reason and, in relation to public life, by true state wisdom, which depends neither on habit nor on selfishness.

The former, even if they—custom, in particular—can hit upon what is right, contain no consciousness or knowledge of it; this, as far as the political is concerned, resides precisely only in statecraft: but the latter then requires prudence and calculation in order to carry out what wisdom has recognized.

Yet another difference between wisdom and prudence is this: prudence, calculating solely with the understanding, is capable of no enthusiasm or love, although by an outward activity, liveliness, and untiring exertion it can give itself the appearance of enthusiasm; wisdom, on the other hand, since it originally arises from inspired wonder, lives on continually in enthusiasm for the true, the good, and the beautiful; and if love is the beginning of wisdom, then love will not die out even in the further development of wisdom, but will rather purify and transfigure itself and, from an unconscious stirring of the mind, take shape as conscious virtue.

Again, there is a false and inauthentic enthusiasm that lacks wisdom; this rests on the dominion of dark and confused ideas in
passionately vehement characters, and appears now as religious, now as political, even indeed as scientific fanaticism: it is enthusiasm for error or for prejudice, into which not only youth falls because of its liveliness combined with still immature knowledge, but many carry it on into their old age; indeed, this inauthentic youthful enthusiasm, since it is after all directed only at error, at least permits a redirection toward the true through instruction and experience, whereas a vain and empty enthusiasm of old age for prejudices is seldom capable of improvement.

The highly gifted person—especially the highly gifted statesman—recognizes in wisdom the true and highest ends, is inspired for them and filled with love, and at the same time knows, insofar as human capacity suffices, how to invent the means to realize those ends; even if he is passionately seized by them, he nevertheless does not act in the service of the passions; rather, these are for him only powerful tools with which he fights through and puts into effect what he has recognized, the clear idea, in the struggle against what stands opposed to him in hostility, since in this world nothing significant can be realized without struggle: love and hatred are the elements of our activity.

Frederick the Great was one of those infinitely rare natures, endowed to the highest degree, in whom enthusiasm was wedded to the greatest circumspection and clarity of thought: through that enthusiasm even the cold calculation that is indispensable to the statesman was ennobled—a calculation he possessed, to be sure, in a high degree, yet without overestimating its worth; and his passion, since it was neither the ruling element in him nor the servant of base selfishness, stirred only toward the realization of the thought, was merely the expression of the inexhaustible power of the spirit, which overcomes all difficulties and, by great misfortunes, is only steeled, not broken.

Many talents have raised themselves, without any external means, in the struggle with want and hardship, from a lowly level to the heights of intellectual cultivation; but one will seldom find an example of this, that for a king's son, an heir to the throne, the lofty urge toward art and science was so stunted as it was for Frederick the Second by an honorable but strict father who was
averse to finer cultivation: but these difficulties heightened his love of the noble and the beautiful, of free intellectual creation and unprejudiced understanding.
It was from this enthusiastic love, not from petty calculation or a craving for display, that his restoration of this academy also arose.
Accustomed to giving words to his feelings in verse, he too greeted this new creation of his, and the new age that was to begin with it, in a poem.
What do I see!
What a spectacle!
O my beloved fatherland!
Behold at last the time when your fair days shall blossom!

Uncomprehending prejudice, error, and barbarism, driven from your palaces, are now banished forever; the fine arts triumph over senseless ignorance; I see the festive procession of their heroes advancing, in their hands laurel, lyre, and compass; truth and fame accompany their steps to the temple of memory.

Above the old monument of a ruined colonnade, torn down by the hands of brutality, there rises gracefully a glorious temple to the god of all the arts and of truth; here science, reason, and spirit, after with united strength they have overcome error, raise a trophy to the gods their protectors, just as on the Capitol the sign of victorious success rose on high.

Under the shameful rule of blind ignorance, the earth was a prey to stupidity; its tyrannical fetters held the limbs frozen under its power: man was timid, credulous, base, cowardly; then truth appeared and served him as a guide; he shook off the yoke of panic terrors, his hand shattered the idol whose worthless service nourished his errors." This enthusiasm for knowledge and, besides, especially for poetry never left the great king; it followed him even into the field camps, and it is not one of the least proofs of his mighty spirit that even amid the din of arms he did not forget the Muse, the companion of his youth.

In his case, if ever in anyone's, his own utterance proved true: "The soul is inexhaustible and can always bring forth." And yet he complains, while amid the most varied occupations, in reply to the Marquis d'Argens and in response to the sending of his Timaeus of Locri, he pours himself out in verses cheerfully enough but at the same time
not without passion, about the inadequacy of his mind to encompass many things at once.

Let us hear his own words, at least the essential part of them, without being frightened by the sharpness and bitterness mixed in; what under wholly different circumstances can appear excessive or even frivolous has its justification in the situation and time of the great man, and precisely this mixture of cheerfulness and seriousness, of mockery and anger, belongs to the peculiarity of his nature and especially of his poetic mood.

"In the bloom of my years," he says, "I occupied myself with Ovid, or followed Rinaldo into Armida's palace; and when the beard's hair shadowed my chin, I found a taste for Sophocles, Horace, and Cicero; when more mature I studied Caesar, Leibniz, and Gassendi, and above all Epicurus."

Now, when shameful old age, unnerving my strength, whitens my hair and announces to me that I shall shortly be united with my fathers, I have chosen the villainous priests as my favorite plaything, whose foolish ambition, arrogance, and gluttony revolt me and at the same time delight my ponderous old age.

I am indignant when I see the shameful weakness of slack princes who crawl beneath the tiara and basely kiss the feet of their tyrants, and I lament the blindness of mystical quarrels and the vain play with words.

Then I receive your tasteful work, upon which a wiser man than I would have immediately pounced and devoured it; but my mind, quite full of bulls, vigils, doctors, martyrs, interdicts, and councils, must first purify itself of this unworthy clutter before reading it.
And before I can devote myself to philosophy again, we must see the olive branch of peace sprout anew.

The chaste band of the Muses flees the din of arms; only in serene days, in the shadow of peace, does their temple open to the wishes of heroes; on bloody fields, beneath barbarism, Mars himself would court Urania in vain.
Our eyes are met only by inhuman objects, the accursed consequences of the confusion of the Germans, fruits of the ambition and hatred of the princes who, in order to conquer, lay waste their lands.

All of Europe wants to consume itself in fire; how can one think amid these
abominable upheavals?
In this movement of ebb and flood, I must first restore calm to my bewildered senses once again.

To be sure, Archimedes, when Metellus (he meant to say Marcellus) forced his way with the flower of the Romans over the fallen walls of Syracuse, remained calm and master of himself, and solved a geometrical problem in his garden; I, whose sluggish mind is long occupied by a single reproach, cannot, so that my understanding may work it through in detail, burden myself with more than one subject." If we knew nothing, or less, of the king's deeds as a commander and of his untiring occupation with administration, one would have to believe that his whole life had been absorbed in solitary thought.

He himself calls himself dreamy, uneven, restless, brooding, distracted, and gloomy as an algebraist combining numbers; nor is it merely a serious and profound thinking to which he gives himself over, but often, in his poetic attempts, a roving mood that takes pleasure in combining the most diverse things—maxims and philosophy of life, historical narratives as proof of his proposition, political reflections, subjective self-contemplation, the heartfelt expression of his friendship and love, of sorrow and longing, mockery of the vulgar and foolish, especially among the great, cutting satire against his enemies—blending all these together no less boldly than lightly and gracefully.

Many of these pieces can, without flattery, be set beside Horace's Satires and Epistles; and far from losing by the comparison, they have rather the advantage that for the most part they move in a higher circle of ideas, which his experience-rich life, his own great deeds and sufferings, his exalted station, and his involvement in the greatest affairs of the world offered to him.

Akin to that mood is irony—I do not mean the dissembling self-deprecation practiced in dealings with other people, but that grand and truly tragic recognition of the nullity of all earthly things, of the insignificance of all human strivings in the face of a higher power.

The general views—not so much speculatively profound as purely human—which he had formed on this matter are by no means the most consoling; but he was unwilling to surrender himself
to any self-deception, and the greatness of his mind allowed him to find composure within himself: these views, and the disposition of soul underlying them, deserve all the more to be brought into relief, the less princes and statesmen are wont to give themselves over to reflections of this kind.

“Life is a dream,” he writes to Maupertuis; “this flower that shines today will scarcely have opened before it withers tomorrow; everything is taken away by the harsh decree of the decisions of fate; your virtue, your great talents cannot obtain from time the postponement of a single day.
My good days have flowed away; like a fleeting wave my joys have fled, and no power can hold them captive: the present slips away without end, the future is uncertain, the past is less than a dream.
To be for a moment is what one calls life.
The lot of the day on which a person is born draws him toward the night of fate, in which all, thrown together into a heap, share one and the same fate.
You whom the deceptive splendor of a transient and worthless good deceives—why do you heap up riches and treasures?
For what purpose such immense designs for so limited a course of life?

You heroes who have forged chains for the unhappy world, peace ends your struggles, you will become victims of death; a word is said of your life, and soon the destroying centuries will wipe out your greatness: the man dies, the hero is forgotten.“ “The greatest enemies, the most ambitious men,” he says elsewhere, “they who thought to set themselves on the throne of the gods, who strove for dominion over the whole world, Pompey and Caesar, Lepidus and Antony and Augustus, Charles and the Czar—of all their fury, their struggles and their hatred, they have left behind scarcely a few vain shadowy images; their sorrows as their deeds have perished, and their ambition is confined to their graves.” “Why do we seek happiness, why do we fear the heavenly arm?”
The good is a flattering dream-image, the evil a gloomy one.

All these various events are matters of indifference to one who knows our duration; goods and treasures, titles and honors, fame and splendor are but smoke; a glance of truth makes the semblance of their transient beauty vanish.

Everything here below,
even the mightiest states, is a plaything of inconstancy.
The earth is a point; what, then, should man be?

Full of vanity, floating between the time that goes before us and the devouring eternity of the future, always occupied with vain things, true Tantaluses of false goods, ceaselessly moved by desire, we lose ourselves in nothingness.

"This is the lot of our life." As he himself says, he had made a particular study of Gassendi and Epicurean philosophy; but while the ethical side of it is alienated from public life and is least suited to forming princes and generals, he knew how to give it Stoicism as an antidote, which demands political activity, and he brought only his metaphysical views close to the Epicurean system, namely those concerning providence and chance; but these too display a heroic greatness, and, if one is willing to be fair, are by no means so frivolous as they have often been decried, although he takes pleasure in a harsh and hard presentation of them; rather, they proceed from the lawfulness of nature, which the highest ordering spirit has determined, and do not abolish the freedom of the individual; insofar as the divine determination is enclosed in veiled form within that lawfulness, which the destiny of each individual also follows, he unconsciously restores the guidance of the individual by providence, notwithstanding that he denies it—though, to be sure, not under the anthropomorphic conception of an arbitrary and temporal influence of the supersensible upon the sensible.
“God,” he says, “does not govern the individual, which is far beneath him; Heaven does not occupy its highest wisdom with our smallness, our fragile destiny.

The unknown mover, the first cause, in giving form to the old primordial matter, established immutable laws for beings: all that is heavy falls toward a common center; fire raises its fluttering flame into the air; water follows the course of its fall without flowing back; each kind is bounded by its own small compass; from an apple seed the tree is generated again, but this seed will never bring forth roses: effects are forever slaves of causes.

Thus man received with birth the passions, the tyrants of his heart and of his
actions.
We are all marked by a particular stamp that has its necessary consequences: a Heraclitus weeps, a Democritus laughs; the black-biled man is hard, the philanthropic man has tender sympathy.
God formed these passions; an unknown hand distributes them everywhere according to an unknown order.
As many are the diversities, as many the particular determinations that adorn the universe through their combinations, and ever renew the stage of the accustomed spectacle.
But the almighty Being does not trouble himself with concern over the role I play, nor over the lot that awaits me: my principle matures me onward, and I follow its current.

When the Most High casts his gaze down from the heavens, he looks with the same eye upon the rose and upon the hemlock; the great is his work, and in infinity he displays his full majesty. Deaf to our wishes and entreaties, while his altars smoke with our offerings, he subjects the universe to the original laws. He knows that nature fulfills his plan and preserves the powers he has implanted in it; certain of success, he lets things take their course; whatever seems to us good, whatever seems to us evil, all works together toward his world plan.

The laws that His wisdom gave to matter are confined to the preservation of the species; yet the vain individual, since he refers everything to himself, discontented with his lot, a blind mole, censures the Supreme Being: he vividly sees and feels the misfortune that touches him, but not the good that his evil brings to the whole.
In the universal order, a human being—even a state—counts for nothing.

Greece and Carthage were subjugated and destroyed by Rome, and Rome by the barbarian peoples; war and famine ravage the lands; the plague, which he describes with true poetry after the model of Lucretius, depopulated Prussia, but under a fortunate rule the losses were made good again.

If these misfortunes disturbed the order of things, the hand of the Almighty would halt their causes; but what appears to us as a great misfortune is nothing when it is considered from the general point of view.
This truth, though harsh and severe, must not turn us away from the necessary pleasure.

The wise man gains through everything: the school of
misfortune serves him as a means of feeling more keenly the true worth of happiness; he knows to what dangers his nature exposes him; a disciple of Epicurus in fortunate days, a disciple of Zeno in calamitous ones, he arms his reason against all foreseen cases.

If we silently honor these laws that Providence has given to the universe; if we shrink from the errors of our limited minds, if we fear to pass judgment on such great depths, and if we are assured, despite our misfortunes, that Heaven has more insight into them than all the philosophers — "But what, then," he says in a poem to his sister Amalie, "is the rich source of the various destinies that man has in the world, if God does not extend his power over them?"
Should man alone be the mighty master craftsman of successes and misfortunes?

Do you not see the multitude of fools, without grace, without talents or spirit or merit, raised to honors and sudden greatness, contemptuously, presumptuously, drunk with vanity, despising the homage of prostrate nations, while misfortune pursues the wise?
The world, then, is the realm of chance, or, in another word, of fortune; chance raises up, chance destroys: willfully it usurps the rights of our foresight.

Let no one understand by this that blind power, that deity of paganism, which, rivaling fate, determines all things without choice or plan: chance is the consequence of those secondary causes whose springs, wrapped in deep darkness, know how to elude us beneath their disguise and to deceive us by false appearance.
The philosopher knows that in all things the consequences spring from the fruitful womb of causes; with a sure but slow step he ascends through inferences, following the outcome, up to the principle.

The overweening politician, ambitious and somber, carries his light with a bold arm into these shadows; he presses into the future without having grasped it, regulates everything and confuses everything, and finds himself deceived.

The blind man, in groping, takes the deceptive semblance and unstable flux for certainty; and, eager to penetrate into this labyrinth but without a guiding thread, he loses his way and stumbles at every step on the edge of the abyss.

Who can reveal to him the willful moods of so many weak kings, who,
playthings of their passions, change in their favor?

A king dies, the son replaces him, and the political world takes on a different shape; he lets himself be governed by other passions, rules according to a different plan; new errors drive out the old and change the motives of favor or of hatred.
Indeed, even less suffices: one banishes a minister, a favored woman, and all plans change.

So many different interests, such terrible intrigues, the dreadful convulsions of political upheavals—that is the ocean given over to the angry north wind, which piles up the waves, rolls them furiously onward, breaks them, overturns them, and, lashing the roaring sea against its shores, casts up wreckage and corpses.
Our fragile vessel, without masts or compass, drifts rudderless at the pleasure of Aeolus; it sails along the cliffs, seeking shelter; one man finds his salvation where another had gone down.

Thus prudence is nothing but an art of conjecture." I pass over the examples which he draws, with truly Horatian humor and satirical talent, from court life and from warfare—especially Eugene's—and from the fortunes of the Stuarts, in confirmation of his views, in order to report a few more things that he adduces from the experience of his own life concerning the insufficiency of prudence. "When I entered the world in my young years," he says in the year 1760, "I owed everything to chance, nothing to reason."
Hot-headed and conceited, I burned to imitate the heroes whom I revered; from the center of pleasures and the arms of rest I flew on the trail of Mars to danger and hardships.

An old Sertorius from Eugene's school applied everything that experience and art can supply in order to banish chance; but fortune accompanied my steps in those days, and under its protection my mind became circumspect.
Afterward the unfaithful ones deserted my banners, and it now pursues my approaching old age; cliffs and dangers cover my paths, and pen and sword fall from my hands.
The banks of all our German rivers are flooded with peoples who have gathered from the ends of the earth.

If I cover one country, I merely expose the other; I fly against the boldest enemy, I reach him, and then a
voice calls me to another place.

Fighting on all sides against a Hydra of princes, my arm alone can no longer protect my provinces.” “Our resources are exhausted,” it says in another similar account; “skill and valor succumb beneath the power of the whole world, which has conspired against me.

Calculating my steps, I am nonetheless the fool of the whims of my lot and of events; in vain designs I lose the precious moments." "And while my soul is weighed down by so many evils, a demon confuses the minds of the soldiers; what is white to me appears black to them; their leaders too no longer have eyes to see; surrounded by intimidated souls, I set a remedy against the poison in vain; the number of the enemy, the growing danger, wholly new blows increase the terror.
I must fight the enemy or be defeated at this hour; the superior spirit of a hero must set an example for all, from the last to the first.
