Thus by the Euphrates an old palm tree lifts the branches of its proud head, offering defiance unbroken to the assault of the storm, while the north wind along the bank of its waters bends the slender rushes and shatters the reeds.
But these tubes decide our battles; what can a leader do when the hearts of the soldiers grow fearful?

Thus in the palaces and on the fields of Mars there is nothing but chance, and in spite of all calculations the proud intellect finds itself at last compelled to confess that man, wholly limited, follows the stream of fate by which he is swept away.

But if prudence is no panacea for healing the sufferings that weigh down our spirit, and does not extend to making us happy, it nonetheless alleviates our ills and moderates our desires; it preserves us from those ills that we recognize, and through the dangers of a step considered in advance it leads us between fear and recklessness along a narrow path that is little common to mortals.
Their patience often tires out fortune; it expects everything from time, but without anticipating it, and never did their pride govern the future.

Let us therefore leave it to Fate, in its dark dwellings, to conceal its obscure decrees from us; and bearing its blows without
being cast down by them, let us wrap ourselves in our virtue!" It is not, to be sure, a single poem in which the great King expresses himself thus; rather, these thoughts recur again and again, and consequently did not spring from the mood of the moment. His thinking—though not, indeed, without the influence of the spirit of the age and the philosophy of the age—had formed these principles in him, and he had proved them true through the experiences of his life; yet he by no means worked them up into a system, and so there are, to be sure, also utterances of his that are hard to reconcile with them.

In the hopefully well-founded assumption that it is especially fitting for the memorial celebration of the same man, in a society devoted to thought, to hear the honored man's own thoughts—since he himself did not disdain to have one or another of his small works read aloud in this academy—and being in any case convinced that his views deserve more attention than any reflections that I could undertake and present in my own person on this memorial day, I have taken the liberty of compiling from various poems of the King these his principles, mostly verbatim, rarely only according to their sense, or with the insertion of a thought or expression borrowed from another piece into the context of the one, as it were in mosaic work, tightly joined together, and I shall in similar fashion add a few more things hereafter.

If Athens at the Panathenaea heard the deeds of the ancestors from the mouth not of the heroes themselves but of the poet of the Iliad, the poet of the Perseis, then truly for us Prussians, on this day especially, there is no nobler thing to hear than the words of Frederick the Second.

To be sure, as I have just said, I have set down its content in compressed form, much as a historian of philosophy draws the scattered and copiously presented doctrines of Plato or Aristotle or Leibniz systematically into brief compass: for the king's overflowing eloquence develops all of this at far greater length, and thereby there do indeed arise prolixities and repetitions which I would by no means wish to censure unconditionally, since the character of the kind of poetry to which these little writings belong not only permits but even
demands that the author let himself go lightly and with apparent carelessness, but which have nevertheless been detrimental to the appreciation of his poems; whereas anyone who looks to the core must admit that, apart from the incomparably cheerful humor and the ease of presentation, many parts of them are distinguished by noble inspiration and poetic fire: and should this person or that, with the haughtiness of today, turn up his nose at the commonplaces interspersed here and there, we would suggest considering whether these do not have a more lasting value for the cultivation of mind and heart than most of the contrived new thoughts and clevernesses now in fashion.

Undoubtedly these works, whose worthy renewal we shall soon owe to the sublime spirit of our royal lord, offer, along with manifold instruction, elevation, and even edification, manifold offense as well; but this too must be given, if the great King is to appear in his full peculiarity, and even in this small presentation I would have been unfaithful had I shrunk from setting forth, at least with some softening, whatever offensive matter I encountered along its path.
But let no one demand nothing but sweet harmony; dissonance too must retain its right.
Anyone who has asserted himself as Frederick did may appear before posterity as before his contemporaries exactly as he was, without embellishment.

As the last Superior General of the Jesuits formerly declared, on the eve of the order's impending dissolution, regarding a proposal for changes within it: "They must be as they are, or not be at all!" — just as, following the model of a Greek turn of phrase, one may exhort the worthy man with the brief call: "Be who you are!" — so our hero was who he was, and he shall remain so as long as his memory endures.

But his passion and his sharp tongue also belong to his nature; if their outpourings are expunged from his writings and consigned to oblivion, then a part of his nature—and not even an entirely ignoble one—is, as far as it lies in our power, destroyed. "When my iron grows blunt," he says, "my pen must surely avenge me for the insults whose vexation wears me down"; "I cut arrows from every wood." The rhetorical form of the thought, too, and not the thought alone, is the impress and outflow of
the man's peculiar individuality; and so this likewise must be left equally untouched.
But the laws of language, including usage, are a universal to which everyone ought to submit, and in the French language, which the author has mostly employed, everyone is also accustomed to submit.

The Academy, into whose hands our exalted King has entrusted the works of his great ancestor, has therefore laid down for the new edition the principle of bringing the grammatical or linguistic element into agreement with the universally valid laws and with usage in the easiest possible way, while in the rhetorical element, by contrast, permitting no alteration.

This principle is to be regarded, as in diplomatic negotiations, as a general determination of boundaries; if one then proceeds to the execution, to the actual regulation and marking out of the boundaries, doubts may indeed arise in some cases as to whether something is to be assigned to this side or to that; but the general determination that has been adopted is certainly the correct one, and it corresponds to the author's own views, who had also thought much about style and presentation.

In his instruction for the direction of the Nobles' Academy the King draws exactly the same distinction between the fields, without assuming a third between them; with reference to the compositions of a certain class he says: "The grammarian, who is a supplement for this class, will correct the errors of language, and Herr Toussaint the errors against rhetoric." And to correct what concerns language is certainly entirely in the spirit of the royal author; for although in this respect he was not exact according to the original manuscripts, he nevertheless laid weight upon it.

Enumerating the troubles that the sorry business of being a scribe to a gentleman who is a writer and, so to speak, a fine spirit entails, he writes to Darget: "Daily you bring his verses into fair copy by the quire, and when you give them back to him, he makes heaven knows what a clamor; the captious doubt of strict examination extends over every period and every comma; here are silent e's that ought to be open, or there is one word too few, which makes the verse limp." But I return from this digression.

We have seen how the King thinks about prudence, and about what
it is capable of; at the beginning of our reflections we designated this as something subordinate: what matters above all are the ends that it serves.

Meanwhile, I do not regard it as my task to demonstrate the particular and, as it were, external aims that Frederick pursued in his political and military undertakings, in foreign relations, and in internal administration; rather, I have in mind the intellectual and moral goal and the motives for action related to it: in the present respect the two are one and the same, for the goal he strove for was also what moved him.

Here we must first of all separate out every relation to a beyond; his religious consciousness is limited to the knowledge and inward veneration of a supreme being, a supreme reason, which has determined the laws of all that has come into being, and to subordination and submission to fate.

The remark in a letter to the Marquis d'Argens that our spirit is merely a brilliant effect of the laws of matter seems to be fairly close to his true conviction: "The last breath," he says in another letter to the very same man, "makes man once again what he was before his coming into being," and he expresses similar things more often.
In the poem "The Stoic," he offers reassurance in the ancient manner for both cases.

"If a single blow kills body and soul, death makes you inaccessible to pain; if not, then God, the only perfect being, is kind and gentle, but man, here below trembling and frightened by dangers, is in the divine eyes an object of compassion, and through his death becomes for them an object of grace: place your trust in this kind God, and, sure of his help on the day of your death, cast yourself full of sweet hope into his arms." "We, who renounce all retribution," he says in a masterly imitation of Lucretius, "we, who do not believe in your eternal torments—self-interest has never stained our sentiments; the welfare of the human race, the virtue that inspires us, the love of duty alone made us flee from crime; yes, let us end without disquiet and die without complaints, leaving the world behind filled with our benefactions!"

Thus the star of day, at the end of its
course, spreads a mild light over the horizon, and the last rays that it casts into the air are the last sighs that it gives up to the universe." So, without linking earthly life to the beyond, he practiced human virtue.

The first driving force behind his great designs was, to be sure, a passion, but the noblest and most fitting for a prince: the desire for glory. "The virtues," he says, "lead to glory, and glory to the virtues." Perhaps, he remarks later, enchanted by history, he sacrificed too much to the love of glory, since the example of so many famous men filled him with the wish to rise as they had; yet soon corrected by philosophy, he learned through its counsel to reshape his life.

After he had acquired for the state a larger extent, in order to make it to some degree independent, his own honor and the honor of the empire and love of the fatherland compelled him to defend himself.
“The throne,” he says, “is a thing that has never tempted me; the splendor that surrounds it is vain pomp: but honor and duty compel me to defend it.”

If it is greatness to be able to descend from it, then it is shameful disgrace to let oneself be driven from it; whatever misfortunes may be, which I defy, I will neither rule as a tyrant nor die as a slave." Although the striving for greater power of his state has the appearance of selfishness against it, he was yet in truth far from this, lived despite his veneration of Epicurus not for pleasures, or only for the noblest of the soul and of friendship, for the happiness and glory of his people, finally for the general interests of the spirit and of humanity: "You are composed of spirit and matter," he speaks as a Stoic to men; "the former thinks and guides you, the other is nothing but dust."
Of the gifts which man has received from heaven, the soul is the most exalted, and it must take the first rank among you.
That one, then, sacrifices this flesh, this blood.
Seek to understand, and consider for what ultimate purpose Heaven has given you your existence.

Man is not cast into the universe for himself alone; our common misfortune, our shared misery prove sufficiently that we are brothers, that through our help, softening our ills, we must stand by one
another to bear the burdens.
Keep alive the flame of this noble striving; place the happiness of your soul in virtue.

The most selfless disposition is the most virtuous; it sacrifices to the common weal, without regret, its labors, its advantage, its life; watchful and strict toward all its faults, it curbs at their birth the tumult of its passions. "Virtue is worth more than intellect and knowledge." Steadfast in misfortune, without arrogance in good fortune, a strict king and, as he himself calls himself, a philanthropic citizen, he sought and found in the depth of his mind and heart the peace of soul of the sage, and surrendered himself to posterity—unconcerned, as he says, about an irritated, peevish, perverse, and too severe judge of his weak virtue—so that it might judge him with all freedom.

He has been much judged—by friends and enemies, by admirers and censurers, by kindred spirits who with this royal eagle looked toward the sun, toward the shining, warming, and enlightening luminary that in that ode To the Prussians he sets before his people as a model, and again by natures wholly opposite, who applied the one-sided and narrow measure of their own cast of mind and temper of soul to the hero.

A man of such surpassing greatness can be viewed from countless sides, of which I have today brought out only a few, and these too more by way of suggestion than exhaustively, so as not to weary you through greater fullness of detail, or to overstep the limits and the customary manner of our unassuming and lightly fading introductory speeches: but the more Frederick is grasped in the whole of his rich intellectual being, the more must he, even without our sharing all his convictions, views, and sentiments, be not merely admired but also loved.

div.head: XXIII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 6. Juli 1843.
Leibniz in seinem Verhältnifs zur positiven Theologie

p.s: The academies of sciences in Germany, especially in contrast to the universities, have often been regarded as an appendage of the court; and much could be adduced in support of this: the seat of the academies in the residences, from which the universities were deliberately kept at a distance; the close connection of many princes with them, as of Frederick the Great with our academy, while he favored the universities less; the admission of high-ranking persons into the academies, in order on the one hand to enhance the splendor of the academic body and on the other to link it precisely with the more distinguished circles; and finally even a disparity between the academies and popular education, by virtue of which notably our academy could be regarded as an extension of the court circle, since, like the former German courts, it was entirely French.

For our time all this has lost its validity; but today's celebration is devoted not to the present but to the past, and precisely the great man with whose name this celebration is linked, the immortal Leibniz, whom we today honor in our capital as the true originator of the first association of this kind, might seem to furnish a strong proof of that assertion for the past.
Who has not heard that Leibniz was a courtier, a court philosopher?
The influence of this his direction of life, his position, his circumstances is especially brought to bear on theodicy.

It is well known that the spirited and highly cultivated Queen Sophie Charlotte gladly engaged, in company with Leibniz, in the most difficult theological and philosophical investigations,
conversed with him both in writing and orally on such subjects, and indeed even complained that he treated everything so superficially with her because he did not credit her mind with enough, and seldom answered her with precision on the points she was examining.
She wanted, as Leibniz said, to know the why of the why.

Beyond dispute, these conversations—especially those about the doubts and misgivings of Bayle, whom the Queen read with particular fondness—gave occasion for the Theodicy, as Leibniz himself often explained.

Thus he writes on March 1, 1708, to Bignon*): "As the Queen of Prussia, most distinguished in her lifetime, who read Bayle very gladly, had often commanded me to set forth in words and writings my view concerning the objections which he had advanced and which do not seem to me irrefutable, so some urgently exhort me that I should collect all these writings and combine them into one work." Likewise to Thomas Burnet**): "The greater part of this work was composed piecemeal while I was with the blessed Queen of Prussia, where these matters were discussed on the occasion of Bayle's Dictionary and his other works, which were much read there."
In our conversations I used to reply to the objections raised by Bayle and to show that they were not as strong as certain people little favorable to religion would like to make them believe.

Her Majesty quite often commanded me to set down my answers in writing, so that they could be considered with greater attention, and indeed in the French language, so that they might be read by her, as well as abroad by those who were unacquainted with Latin.

After the death of this great princess, at the reminder of my friends at the Berlin court, who were informed of this matter, I collected these pieces, augmented them, and formed this work from them, so as to fulfill the Queen's command completely.

Since I have reflected on this subject from my youth, I believe I have discussed it thoroughly, down to its very foundation." He expresses himself no differently in the preface to the Theodicy***): "He had had the honor, this *) Dutens, Praef. gen. to Leibnit.
Opp.omn.
Vol. I, p. X. After Guhrauer's translation, Biogr. of Leibniz.
Vol. II, p. 250. ***) Berlin short [form].
Edition of 1840.

Vol. I, p. 23.
To tell the Princess his opinion on several passages of Bayle's wonderful dictionary, where religion and reason appear as contending against each other, and where Bayle wishes to reduce reason to silence after having previously allowed it to speak too much: what he calls the triumph of faith.

The author, he said, had made it known that he was of a different opinion, but was very satisfied that so excellent a mind had given the opportunity to fathom these subjects, as significant as they are difficult: he had admitted that he had long investigated them and had at times resolved to publish thoughts on them, whose chief purpose should be the knowledge of God, such as it must be in order to awaken piety and nourish virtue; the princess, like some of his friends, had urged him to carry out his old plan. Notwithstanding these statements, I venture to free him from the reproach that his position as a so-called court philosopher had any substantial influence on his Theodicy.

As he says in the passages just cited, he had for a long time, indeed from his youth onward, occupied himself with these subjects, and I shall further show that he had already embraced as a young man the position toward positive religion that he adopted in the Theodicy—that very position which might seem calculated precisely for the Royal Court—and the fundamental idea of the Theodicy.

If, furthermore, the Queen read Bayle so gladly, then Leibniz, supposing that he had wished to arrange his philosophizing according to her views, could almost rather have taken Bayle's side, or one akin to Bayle's views, than the opposite one; and if she wished for a refutation of Bayle, she could do so only on the presupposition that Leibniz had decisive counterarguments, and only his conviction that he had such could determine him to speak against Bayle, since the Queen had after all sufficiently demonstrated, through her diligent reading of Bayle's writings, her inclination toward this thinker.

Consideration for the Queen is conceivable only for the undertaking and the beginning of the work, not for its continuation and publication: for the Queen died on February 1, 1705; through her death and external obstacles the composition of the Theodicy was interrupted; it was not nearly finished until 1707,
and did not appear until the year 1710.
But perhaps Leibniz was moved by that circumstance to write the Theodicy in a popular style.
I doubt it: for the Queen was so accustomed to thinking that she had no need of this common intelligibility.

One can find fault with much in the presentation that is nevertheless only apparently blameworthy; I count under this head the anthropomorphism in the manner in which God is represented as deliberating: this, as with Plato, is merely ordinary usage of expression, and Leibniz himself declares himself more than once against such anthropomorphism—not only against Bayle, but precisely with regard to the point touched upon. *)

But if, besides this, the work has no great metaphysical depth and contains much that is so superficial that the passages of Bayle woven into it, which are refuted, often stand out to their own advantage by contrast through their genuinely dialectical acuteness and ingenious formulation, then the reason lies for the most part in the fact that the author here did not so much wish to give philosophical principles as to apply them to a specific purpose; that he further, as he himself says,**), sought to relate everything to edification, and that he also believed he must enliven the subject, whose seriousness might deter, by mixing in some things for the sake of curiosity and entertainment, such as the episode of astronomical theology to be touched upon below, the examples of the influence of circumstances on conversion or perversion***), which are more jest than earnest, or the little conversation of the two kitchen maids about purgatory, or Trajan's deliverance through the intercession of Gregory the Great and the prohibition given to the latter by God to entreat anything of that sort a second time.
A philosopher can do all this without being a court philosopher, without ever having stood in connection with a court.

Only then could one apply that name to someone if he deliberately arranged his philosophy so that it pleased the courts in general or a particular court, in such a way that he gave the views of a prince—and indeed in opposition to the people or the scholarly state—a seemingly philosophical character, arbitrarily chosen and contradicting his own conviction. *) Ed.

Vol. II, p. 201. **) Vol. I, p. 37. ***) Vol. I, p. 216 ff.
...physical foundation, or if he trimmed a deeper doctrine to serve as the subject of a mere court entertainment and flattened it for that purpose.

But however much Leibniz lived at courts and among the high-born, however much he accommodated himself to them, however much he calculated upon them, one would still be very unjust if one were to impute such endeavors to him.

An independent consideration is this: whether Leibniz everywhere expressed his full opinion; whether, especially in theological and religious matters, he did not, as the saying goes, keep his cards close to his chest; whether he may not even have allowed himself to be determined by some more general considerations to speak otherwise than he thought.
Here I come to the doubt, discussed in many quarters, about his sincerity as the author of the Theodicy.

The Tübingen chancellor Pfaff had, in the third of his Dissertationes Anti-Baylianae**), which appeared in the year 1720, given to understand that Leibniz had confessed in a letter to him that what he had said against Bayle in the Theodicy had not been his serious opinion; in proof of this he had the following printed in the Acta Eruditorum of the year 1728***), which I give translated as well as possible from the clumsy Latin.
"The highly renowned man," he says, "had asked me what I thought of the Theodicy and of that method by which he had refuted Bayle."

I wrote to him that I believed he had devised that system of philosophy at least for jesting amusement (animi saltem causa), and that, just as Clericus, in order to refute Bayle, played the Origenist, so he had, for Bayle's refutation, struck out upon this new path of philosophizing, which on the one hand, although it throws dust in the eyes of those who at any rate do not look very high, is all the more ingenious in that, once properly seen through, it rather confirms Bayle's more massive view in a subtler manner under the appearance of refutation, yet in such a way that the secret cannot be discovered at once; and which on the other hand is again applicable to the purpose of clothing and whitewashing with a coat of plaster the various *) systems and opinions of the religious parties
that contradict one another, which otherwise could scarcely be defended, and even of capturing the favor of the theologians of almost all parties, but especially of our own countrymen: I wished, however, that Bayle's so dangerous view might be refuted seriously, soundly, and weightily (serio, solide et graviter).

What, then, did Leibniz answer to this—he of whom I had believed that, on account of my candid reply, he would be annoyed with me? He then gives Leibniz's own words from a letter of May 2, 1716, the year in which Leibniz died: "It is exactly as you write, Reverend Sir, concerning my Theodicy."
You have hit the nail on the head, and I am surprised that until now no one has noticed this game of mine.
For it is not the business of philosophers to treat their subject always with seriousness; in forming hypotheses, as you will recall, they test the powers of their minds.
You, a theologian, will proceed as a theologian in refuting errors." (So it is entirely, most reverend sir, as you write, concerning my Theodicy.
You have hit the nail on the head; and I am surprised that there has been no one until now who has noticed this joke of mine.
For it is not the way of philosophers always to treat a matter in earnest; in framing hypotheses, as you rightly remind me, they test the powers of their own intellect.
You, who are a theologian, in refuting errors will play the theologian.) Clericus, Des Maizeaux, and Ludovici*) were also of Pfaff's opinion.
But most of the older generation, and likewise the more recent writers, have declared themselves in favor of the view that Leibniz had made a fool of the theologian.

To be sure, Des Maizeaux maintains that no reason could be conceived why Leibniz should have wished to conceal his true opinion from the friendly man; and if he deemed this man worthy to be asked what he thought of the Theodicy, how could he at the same time deem him worthy of such a base irony?
And why should Leibniz, contrary to all truth, attach to himself something that brought him little honor?

Nevertheless, the tone of his confession is not without an ironic coloring; and if the chancellor's language really was as coarse as he reports, then Leibniz may indeed have felt inclined to give the arrogant theologian a mocking rebuff. *) Cf.
Dutens, op. cit., p. IX f.
Tennemann, History of Philosophy.

Nevertheless,
Leibniz would still be unjust to himself if he found in his soul not the slightest ground for conceding to Pfaff's discourse any truth at all, even a remote or partial one.

Not that the philosophical element of the Theodicy is not truly his most earnest conviction: for, without laying weight on the fact that in his letters he more than once acknowledges the Theodicy as a work containing his teaching, its philosophical content stands in thorough connection with his other philosophemes, the polemic against Bayle bears the stamp of the highest earnestness, and it is altogether inconceivable that so comprehensive a work, evidently executed with great love, should be nothing but an ironic play of the mind.

But theodicy has one side, and a strongly prominent one, which is not philosophical but is rooted in positive religion, or rather in dogmatic theology; and one easily arrives at the thought that in this respect he did not wish to contradict the Chancellor's judgment.
Pfaff's remark in the Acta Eruditorum also points in this direction, against Bilfinger's opinion that Leibniz had been joking in that letter to him.

"I am, on the contrary," he says, "most fully convinced and entirely assured that Leibniz in the Theodicy defended various doctrines of our religion at which he otherwise laughed and turned up his nose, for example the dogma of the real presence."

Those to whom it has fallen to know the man fully know the mind of the courtier and philosopher and his opinions in regard to religion." (Ego e contrario persuasissimus, sum certissimusque etiam, varia religionis nostrae placita in Theodicaea Leibnitium defendisse, quae risit alias et naso adunco suspendit: e. g. dogma de praesentia reali.

(The courtiers and the philosopher know his mind and his views concerning religion, since it has fallen to them to know the man more intimately.) Yet in order to be able to judge of this, it is necessary to determine the relation which Leibniz in the Theodicy assigns to philosophy and to positive religion, or positive theology, with respect to one another, and how he, as a philosopher, positions himself toward the latter.

The guiding thoughts on this matter are contained in the preceding Discours de la conformité de la foi avec la raison; chiefly from this, though with the addition of some passages from the remaining parts of the work, I will gather
together a few points on the subject. "I presuppose (je suppose)," he says, "that two truths cannot contradict each other; that the object of faith is the truth which God has revealed in an extraordinary manner; and that reason is the interconnection of truths, but especially, when it is compared with faith, of those truths to which the human mind can attain without the aid of the light of faith." *) Reason, he continues, in the sense in which he takes it, is sometimes opposed to experience; since it is the interconnection of truths, it falls to it also to connect those truths which experience offers to it, in order to form mixed conclusions from them; but pure and bare reason is distinct from experience, and has to do only with those truths which are independent of the senses.

Faith could [—] *) The truths of faith and of reason are kept distinctly apart in the Theodicy; a somewhat divergent view is given by the Nouveaux essais, vol. II, p. 402 ff. of the Opp. philos., ed. by Erdmann, to which Erdmann's Gesch. der neuern Philos. [refers].
Vol. II, 2.
Section.
p. 137 fufst.

But this cannot come into consideration for the Theodicy, and in the latter the more precise determinations on this point are contained; moreover, in the Nouveaux essais that divergent view is attributed to the speakers only in the course of the dialogical investigation, and further on (p. 404, especially § 7) one will again find the doctrine of the Theodicy.

And what is the main point: the grounding of faith in reason described in the Nouveaux essais refers only to the motives of credibility; for this is what that assertion is initially connected with there. Nevertheless, Leibniz expressed himself differently in that place than in the Theodicy, and grasped the concept of reason in comparison with faith less precisely.

To be sure, in the Theodicy he compares faith with experience, and he also has the truths of experience taken up by reason; but since the content of what is revealed is different from the content of experience of what is not revealed, and since everything depends solely on the content, the distinction that has been drawn between revelation and reason nevertheless remains valid: and that the revealed mysteries are not comprehended in the interconnection of the truths of reason is taught by the entire context of Leibniz's exposition; he says so clearly, among other places, in the Theod.
Vol. I, p. 100.

To have excluded revelation from reason by virtue of its admitted supra-rationality, and then to smuggle it back into reason by means of the motives of credibility resting on experience, is sleight of hand, and amounts to the same as showing a man out of the house by the front door and letting him in again by the back door.

Moreover, the highest ground of credibility, namely the conviction of the inerrancy of holy scriptures, always already presupposes faith. [It
may] be compared because, with respect to the grounds that authenticate it, it depends on the experience of those who saw the miracles on which revelation is founded, and on the credible tradition that has brought the reports of those miracles down to our time: without prejudice to the fact that one also speaks of the inner movement of the Holy Spirit, which takes possession of souls and persuades them and impels them to the good, that is, to faith and to love, without their always needing the grounds.

The truths of reason are partly eternal, which are absolutely necessary, in such a way that their opposite contains a contradiction—namely, those whose necessity is logical, metaphysical, or geometrical; others may be called positive, because they are laws that it has pleased God to give to nature, or because they depend on these laws.

These positive truths are known partly through experience and partly through reason; but their necessity is not a geometrical necessity but a physical one, by which the order of nature is determined—an order that rests on God's free choice, and by virtue of this free choice on moral necessity, that is, on the choice of the wise being, which is worthy of his wisdom.

But the general grounds of goodness and order that determined him in this choice can in certain cases be overcome by stronger grounds of a higher order; God can therefore release creatures from the laws that he has prescribed to them, and bring about in them what their nature does not of itself produce, by working miracles.

Perhaps, however, God also works miracles through the ministry of angels without the laws of nature being violated; there are many miracles that appear to be performed through the ministry of such invisible substances, as Malebranche likewise holds; since these act according to the ordinary laws of their nature, these are miracles only by comparison and in relation to us *).
Of this kind, perhaps, was the transformation of water into wine.
Other miracles, by contrast—namely creation, the Incarnation, and certain other acts of God—exceed all the power of creatures and are true miracles or even my- *) Cf.

Theodicy vol. II, pp. 7 and 260. 20
*steria.

Incidentally, he said above that revelation is founded on miracles; but miracles, insofar as they are real miracles, belong to revelation as well, since they depart from the ordinary laws of nature; yet revelation cannot be founded on apparent miracles, which are natural, any more than on anything else natural: consequently, according to Leibniz, it could be founded neither on the one nor on the other, and if he nevertheless says that it is founded on them, he probably meant that it itself consists in them, since he evidently takes the concept of miracle very broadly.
Furthermore, he now teaches that the eternal truths, like the geometrical ones, exclude all exceptions, and that faith cannot contradict them.
With regard to the latter, one must, as he says, distinguish between explaining, comprehending, proving, and defending (soutenir).

The mysteries can be explained, so far as is necessary in order to believe them; but one cannot comprehend them nor make them intelligible, how they come about: just as also in physics we can explain many sensible qualities up to a certain point, but in an imperfect manner; for we do not comprehend them.
Just as little can the mysteries be proved by reason; for everything that can be proved a priori can also be comprehended.

Celsus says against the Christians: if they withdraw to their usual "Do not investigate, only believe," they must at least tell me what the things are that I am to believe; and in this he is right: but one must not always demand adequate concepts, and ones that include nothing that is not explained; an analogical insight into such mysteries as the Trinity or the Incarnation is sufficient, so that we do not, in receiving them, utter wholly meaningless words; the explanation need not go as far as would be desirable, that is, to comprehension and to the how.

It is enough for us to have the what-is (τί ἐστι); the how (πῶς) exceeds our grasp, and of the explanations of the mysteries that are offered for sale here and there, one can say what Queen Christina had placed on a medal when she laid down the crown: "I have no need of it, and it is not enough for me" (Non mi bisogna, e non mi basta).

Just as little do we need an a priori proof of the mysteries; it is enough for us to know that
the matter is so, τὸ ὅτι, without the why, τὸ διότι, which God has reserved for himself, as Jos.
Scaliger says: To wish not to know what the best Master does not wish to teach is learned ignorance*).

All that remains to us is this: after we have accepted the mysteries, supported by the proofs of the truth of religion, by what are called motives of credibility (motifs de crédibilité), we can defend them against objections. If this is not possible, then we are not entitled to believe them; for whatever can be refuted with full force of proof is necessarily false, and against the proofs of the truth of religion, which can give only a moral certainty, absolutely certain objections would not merely be held in the balance but would outweigh them.
How, then, does the relation of philosophy to positive theology stand?

To pass over earlier times: he speaks of the Reformers, and especially of Luther, who often spoke as though they rejected philosophy—of Luther's anger against Aristotle, of Melanchthon's moderation; in Holland, he says, people had finally begun to speak of rational and non-rational theologians, against the former of whom Bayle declares himself; in the churches of the Augsburg Confession, and specifically at the University of Leipzig, he says, through a few magistri artium who taught the so-called sacred philology, under the influence of the study of the Holy Scriptures, the sect of the Pietists was formed—a name by which, willy-nilly, people in Germany designated those of whom they suspected, or pretended to suspect, that under the appearance of a reform they were fanatics or hypocrites; some hearers of those masters had distinguished themselves, among other things, by their contempt for philosophy and, as is said, had burned their notebooks from philosophical lectures; the masters themselves had very well defended themselves against the charge that they rejected philosophy.

Others declared philosophy to be the handmaid, not the mistress, in the domain of theology, following the book of Robert Baronius: "Philosophia theologiae ancillans"; it was a Hagar beside Sara; one must drive it out of the house with its Ishmael if it made itself the rebel — Vol. I, pp.
91, 93.

There is indeed something true in this; but since these principles can be misused and the natural truths and the revealed truths can improperly be set in contradiction to one another, the scholars have endeavored to distinguish what in the natural or philosophical truths is necessary and indispensable and what is not.
At least here he does not apply this distinction to revealed [truths/teachings].
Finally, he borrows from the earlier theologians the distinction, which Bayle had contested, between what is contrary to reason and what is above reason.

Bayle had said: if by reason one understands reason in general, the highest reason, which is in God, then it is equally true that the mysteries are not above reason and that they are not contrary to reason; but if one understands the one and the other of human reason, then the distinction is unfounded; for even the most orthodox confess that we do not know the agreement of our mysteries with the principles of philosophy; it therefore seems to us that those do not agree with our reason; but what does not seem to agree with our reason appears to us as opposed to our reason, just as what does not seem to us to agree with truth seems to us opposed to truth: why then should one not likewise say that the mysteries are contrary to and above our weak reason?

Leibniz, by contrast, upholds that distinction by virtue of his peculiar definition of reason, which we gave above; for him a truth lies above reason when our mind, or indeed any created mind, cannot comprehend it, and of this kind, in his view, are the Trinity, the miracles reserved to God alone, such as, for example, creation, and further the choice of the order of the world, which depends on the universal harmony and on the determinate cognition of an infinity of things at once.

Since, according to him—and indeed according to his rational knowledge—everything in the world is determined and regulated, one could say that God cannot perform miracles**); the prayers, the vows, the good and evil acti- Vol. I, p. 99.

Vol. I, p. 173.gen
served no purpose, since nothing could be changed.

But the miracles that occur in this world were possible in this very world—this world considered in the state of mere possibility—enfolded and represented, and God, who afterward performed these miracles, had resolved to perform them when he chose this world; and matters stand similarly with the other things.
But a truth can never be contrary to reason; and far from a dogma refuted by reason being incomprehensible, nothing is more comprehensible and more evident than its absurdity.

Tertullian's famous passage "Mortuus est Dei Filius, credibile est, quia ineptum est; et sepultus revixit, certum est, quia impossibile" is said to be a witty conceit that relates only to the appearance of incongruity.

To refute the objections against the truth of the faith, when these are drawn solely from reason, there is needed only a mediocre mind, capable of sufficient attention, that knows how to make good use of the rules of ordinary Aristotelian logic.
It is otherwise, he maintains, when only probabilities are at issue, in whose theory our logic is still very deficient.
But when it is a matter of setting reason against one of our articles of faith, we do not dwell on objections that amount only to probabilities.

For everyone knows that the mysteries run counter to appearances and have nothing probable about them when they are considered from the side of reason alone; but it is enough that there be nothing absurd in them: to refute them requires demonstrative proofs.

With reference to such an appearance it has been said that the wisdom of God is foolishness before men; for fundamentally no contradiction of truth against truth is possible, and the light of reason is just as much a gift of God as the light of revelation.

Thus it is also, he says, a settled matter among the theologians who understand their field (métier), that the grounds of credibility justify the authority of Holy Scripture before the tribunal of reason once and for all, so that reason yields to it at once as to a new light, and sacrifices all its probabilities to it: roughly as a new commander sent by the prince presents his commission to the assembly over
which he is in future to preside.

We have no need to renounce reason in order to give a hearing to faith, nor to put out our eyes in order to see more clearly, as Queen Christina said; it is enough to reject the ordinary probabilities when they are contrary to the mysteries: and this is not even contrary to reason, since even in natural things we are undeceived about what appears to be so by experience or by higher grounds.
From these utterances Leibniz's view of the matter in question can be recognized clearly enough, with all its strengths and weaknesses.
He separates philosophy and revelation entirely from each other in their essential nature.
Thus, in the first place, no proposition of his philosophy is taken from revelation or positive theology, nor can it be, because for him philosophy is the science grounded in reasons of reason.

He does not borrow the invisible substances from revelation, but only the name of the angels, and even this only in relation to what has been revealed, namely in the case of the miracles and among the creatures, from which, in order to defend the dogma of the very small number of the blessed, he forms his overwhelming majority of the non-damned as against the damned*).

He also weaves Christ, the God-man, into the doctrine of the choice of the best world, and he expresses himself especially strongly on this point in the Causa Dei asserta per iustitiam eius cum ceteris eius perfectionibus cunctisque actionibus conciliatam**); but this work contains not his philosophical system, but rather an outline of the rest of the Theodicy, which indeed is only partly philosophical.

An intrusion of revelation into Leibnizian philosophy would have turned out roughly as did the mingling of revelation with astronomy, of which we have an example in the Theodicy***) in the astronomical theology of the unnamed author.

Accordingly, the earth was originally a sun; the angel who was the governor of the earth sinned together with some lesser angels of his province, perhaps through rebellion against the angel of a larger sun, and in this way the present disorder *) Causa Dei asserta §. 57, and even earlier in the Theodicy itself. **) §. 49. ***) Vol. I, p. 141.
came into the lower world.
At the same time, by virtue of the pre-established harmony of the kingdom of nature and of grace, our earthly globe was darkened, displaced from its place, and made into a planet.
In this consisted the case of Lucifer.

The head of the evil angels, that prince and god of this world according to Scripture, now sought, together with his retinue, to make human beings participants in their crimes and their misfortune; whereupon Jesus, for their redemption, has perhaps come from our great sun.

What further will then happen, how the earth perhaps will become a comet and finally a sun again, I suppress all the more since even Leibniz found it necessary to excuse the inclusion of this foolish fantasy in the Theodicy.

Secondly, Leibniz by no means proves the agreement of reason and revelation, but only that they do not contradict each other; yet they frequently say different things; where, then, revelation teaches something that reason does not teach, he wishes to free dogma from the charge of being contrary to reason or of unreasonableness.
Thus, thirdly, his endeavor is purely apologetic; to this end he brings to bear all the arts and subtleties of logic, and especially of syllogistic.

We have the finest proof of this in his refutation of Wissowatius, composed as early as around the year 1669, which is entitled "Defensio Trinitatis per nova Reperta logica"*); in this connection Lessing too must not be forgotten, for he remarks that Leibniz had not the slightest intention of supporting the doctrine of the Trinity with new philosophical arguments of his own, and that for this purpose of defense no great dialectical acuteness and agility is required, so long as one keeps within the bounds of a mystery.
Fourth, it follows from this that he wished to show only the possibility, not the reality or truth, of the revealed doctrines, and this was his endeavor from youth on.

In a letter to Johann Heinrich, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, dated March 26, 1673**), in which, in order to recommend himself, he enumerates his achievements and inventions, and where already his "ratio ultima re- *) Best in Lessing in the Lachmann edition, vol. IX, p. 263 ff.
Cf.
Guhrauer, Biography.

Vol. I, p. 69. **) Guhrauer, Leibniz's German Writings, Vol. I, p. 282.
... seu harmonia universalis, id est Deus"*), and the fundamental idea of the Theodicy occurs—that God is not the cause of sins, although these are in accordance with the universal harmony—he expresses himself on that point as follows: "In theologia revelata I undertake to demonstrate, not indeed veritatem, for that flows a revelatione, but the possibilitatem mysteriorum, contra insultationes infidelium et atheorum, whereby they are vindicated from all contradictionibus, namely the possibilitatem trinitatis, incarnationis, eucharistiae." He speaks especially fully of the last; its reality had been held to be an impossible thing, and he first "had at last, through deep investigation, come to the point that he ventured to demonstrate the possibilitatem eucharistiae, as it has been explained in the Concilio Tridentino, salva philosophia emendata, which will seem incredible to many."**) For there is, he says, "in omni corpore a principium ultimum incorporeum, substantiale, a mole distinctum, which can at the same time be in several places, indeed at the same time among widely separated, different speciebus: thereby the possibility not only of the praesentiae realis but also of transubstantiation itself is made clear."

In how many things, indeed, are conscientious people, and especially high potentates, to whom the welfare of many people is to be answered for, supremely concerned." In this respect, therefore, philosophy or reason serves faith, instead of being opposed to it, as it [faith] itself at the beginning *) Note the "harmonia universalis, id est Deus"; cf. Erdmann, History of Modern Philosophy.
Vol. II, 2.
Section.

p. 55, to whom this passage has escaped notice. **) In the first letter to Arnaud (in Grotefend, Correspondence between Leibniz, Arnaud and Landgrave Ernst of Hesse-Rheinfels, Hanover 1846), which became known only three years after the delivery of this lecture, the same assertion is already found at p. 145, and indeed with the remark that it was four years since he had occupied himself with proving possibilitatem mysteriorum eucharistiae.
This passage was formerly known only as a fragment from the letter, through the French translation of Emery cited by Grotefend.
The date of this letter can be approximately determined, according to Grotefend's remark (p. 137), from a letter from Du Fresne to von Boyneburg dated the 27th, mentioned at the beginning.
November 1671 determine.

I do not cite the passages from the letters to Des Bosses that bear on the same subject, since these passages were written in Leibniz's later years, as far as I can see from the
year 1709 onward in the first part of the Theodicy; but philosophy does not presume to want to derive or prove dogma from reason.

Depending on the nature of the theology, the apology also takes a different shape—different in relation to Roman Catholic doctrines, different for the Protestant ones; not as though at other times he had held a different religious conviction, but according to circumstances and occasions, and yet without any actual hypocrisy; rather, this is connected with his certainly not unpraiseworthy intention to bring the various religious parties closer to one another or even to unite them.

And he was indeed convinced, as he says at the close of his treatise de vera methodo philosophiae et theologiae*), that his theorems had a great influence on the establishment of a sound foundation of piety, on the peace of the soul, and on the peace of the Church.
Fifth, in keeping with his standpoint, he frequently had to fall back on his own ignorance.

If one asks why God does not give the grace of conversion to all, then he does not know the grounds of God**), but wishes only to show that such grounds could surely not have been lacking to God, and that there are no valid grounds against that doctrine; and concerning damnation***) God has revealed to us what is necessary for us to fear this greatest evil, not what is necessary in order to recognize and understand it.

This appeal to ignorance with respect to faith is, after all, very little different from Bayle's Pyrrhonian ἐπέχειν†) with respect to reason, insofar as faith is set aside, to which he too sincerely confesses to submit himself.
Sixth: Every positive dogma, whether revealed or ecclesiastical, appears in Leibniz as a presupposition; he does not play the theologian—he lets the theologians hand him everything.
An example of this, and of other things already said, is furnished by his consideration of Bayle's seven theological propositions++).
He first separates out from the same [body of material] everything that is not merely revealed; only the third, fourth, and fifth *) Opp. philos., ed. Erdmann, vol. I, p. 111. **) Theod.
Vol. 1.
Theod.

Vol. I, p. 266, ++) Vol. I, p. 223
fg. stood in need of revelation; he accepts the third and fourth, concerning the creation of Adam and Eve and the Fall, just as they are narrated, defends them on the presupposition of his philosophical determinations, and finally retreats to ignorance: "We know neither the nature of the forbidden fruit sufficiently, nor that of the action, nor its consequences, to judge concerning the particulars of this matter; yet one must do God the justice of believing that it contained something other than what the painters represent to us." Bayle's fifth proposition concerns the election of grace granted to very few; to be sure, he remarks in this connection, some of the ancients had asserted that the number of the damned is not as great as one imagines, and he himself repeatedly endeavors to reduce it in proportion to the rational inhabitants of the rest of the world outside the earth, who possibly supplied only few of the damned *); those ancients also seemed to have believed that there is an intermediate state between eternal damnation and perfect blessedness; but we have no need of those opinions, he says, and it is sufficient for us to hold to the views accepted in the Church.

Thus, setting aside serious examination and without carefully entering into the so-called motives of credibility, he presupposes the ecclesiastical ordinances; yet to be sure he frequently prefers the milder opinion, for example that children who have died without baptism are not damned, nor yet all the heathen, and that not all the virtues of the latter are shining vices and not all their actions are sins.

In exegesis, on the other hand, he engages extremely little; to be sure, he speaks of the various principles of interpretation, of literal and metaphorical understanding, and that the interpreters are agreed on this point: when our Lord calls Herod a fox, the latter was not, as some fanatics supposed, actually transformed into a fox for the duration of these words; but it is otherwise in the fundamental texts of the mysteries, where the theologians of the Augsburg Confession judged that one must adhere to the literal sense; and since these investigations into the art of interpretation and *) Theod.
Vol. I, pp. 143 ff. and p. 258.

Vol. II, p.
21. did not properly belong to logic, he would not enter into it, all the less since they had no connection with the recent disputes over the harmony of faith and reason.
Still less is anything to be found of criticism of the sources of faith or of historical investigation concerning them, however significant his historical knowledge otherwise is.
He speaks as a philosopher, not as a philologist, and so all the tasks possible in the latter respect are either presupposed to be solved, or rather are not even posed at all.
Thus there is no justification whatsoever for the motives of credibility, which, apart from the direct influence of the Holy Spirit, can in his view be only of a historical kind.
He had set himself a firm boundary: this far and no farther!

From his youth Leibniz had a lively zeal for religion and theology; even before his university years Luther's book De servo arbitrio, along with other theological writings, had come into his hands; eagerly he had read many polemical writings of the Lutherans and the Reformed, later the books of the Jesuits and Arminians, the Thomists and Jansenists, and on his travels he had sought the counsel of many esteemed theologians, especially Arnaud.
The fruits of these studies, and of the great erudition of Bayle that he drew upon, lie before us in the Theodicy.
These studies supplied him with the rich abundance of those presuppositions to which much of his own teaching attaches itself.
Such a connection could be made in two ways: either he accommodated his system to the prevailing doctrines of the various parties, or the prevailing doctrines to his system.

Lessing**), in the treatise on eternal punishments according to Leibniz, regards the former as impossible; how could it have occurred to him, he says, to use an old proverb, to want to make a coat for the moon?
And he is certainly right; as noted above, Leibniz allowed the opinions he adopted no influence on his philosophical doctrine.
Thus he did *) letter to Jablonski in Guhrauer's Leibn.
German Writings, vol. 1.

p. 141, **) Works vol. IX, p. 159,
Lachmann, and others: "in the firm conviction," says Lessing, "that no opinion can be accepted which is not true from a certain side, in a certain sense, he surely had the kindness to turn and twist this opinion so long until he succeeded in making this certain side visible and this certain sense intelligible"; that is, he fitted these opinions to his system.
If by this means he had wrested a tolerable meaning from the premises, then, as the very same man judges, he also assented to them, namely according to this tolerable meaning.

But still distinct from this is the question whether Leibniz acknowledged all the presuppositions—including those that could not be accommodated to his system as a philosophical one, because in his own view they do not fall within the domain of rational cognition—not merely as objectively given for the purpose of his exposition, but believed them subjectively.
Lessing*) in the other treatise, concerning the objections of Andr.

Wissowatius, against the Trinity, remarks on this with justice that Leibniz believed no revealed doctrine, if to believe means to hold something true on natural grounds; that he, as the noble man ironically expresses himself, unfortunately had to hold it true from the prejudices of his youth that the Christian religion, merely by virtue of one or several or even all explicable grounds, to believe, properly speaking, does not mean to believe it, and that the only book which, in the proper sense, has ever been or could ever be written for the truth of the Bible is none other than the Bible itself**).

He speaks thus about Leibniz with an orthodoxy that sounds paradoxical in his mouth, against the shallow enlighteners so repugnant to him, just as his favorite Bayle spoke against the so-called rational theologians of his time; what he said is also entirely in accordance with Leibniz's principles, and Lessing thereby proved precisely what he had asserted shortly before***), namely that the light of Leibniz's understanding had been equally diffused everywhere, but that in him, as in the class of *) Works vol. IX, p. 293. **) Nouveaux Essais p. 402 seems indeed to contradict this; but little weight is to be placed on this passage, and just as little on similar ones from which I have drawn elsewhere. ***) Ibid., p. 287. ordinary philosophers,
sense and nonsense had not dwelt side by side in neighborly and peaceful coexistence.
But here Lessing does seem to overlook something.

For, as already said, Leibniz avoids almost all biblical research, cautiously refraining from discussions that might offend against the accepted dogmas and cast doubt on the presupposed positive content; for he held that one must be very restrained with theological meditations*).

His endeavor is to defend the accepted ecclesiastical dogma, without great concern about its authentication; he sought, to speak with Lessing, to lead each person to the truth along the very path on which he found him.

But that he had not made every dogma that he objectively accepted and logically defended into his own subjective conviction, men like Pfaff believed they knew; and what the latter says about this can scarcely rest on nothing. Indeed, he himself, when he wrote that letter to Pfaff, may well have recalled that he had spoken in favor of many a dogma without taking into consideration the grounds of its credibility, that he had kept something in reserve in doing so, and had perhaps even felt some irony in the process.
Nor is it evident that Leibniz regarded that tolerable sense indicated above as the historically correct one every time.
A large part of what Pfaff said refers to such matters.

But the investigations bearing on this lay in another field for him; they were theological, not philosophical; he therefore did not regard them as his own, and did not wish to become involved in theological disputes.

Thus he could answer Pfaff—though not without irony regarding theological pride and regarding the fact that the latter regarded his entire philosophical system in the Theodicy as a fiction—quite truthfully: "You, a theologian, will proceed as a theologian in refuting errors." But what if he says: "It is not the business of philosophers always to treat the subject seriously; in forming hypotheses they try, as you well recall, the powers of their mind"?

He certainly did not mean thereby to encroach upon the philosophical content of the Theodicy; in view of its connection with what follows, it is [a reference] to *) the letter to Thomas Burnet of June 21, 1695, in Guhrauer, Biogr.

Vol. II, p. 257,
to relate the theological [matter], and here he did indeed try the powers of his mind in defense of the dogmas through propositions which, for the theologian from whose words the name of these propositions is taken, were in fact only hypotheses.
But was this defense not in earnest?

To be sure, he was in earnest once the dogma had been accepted, and for those who had accepted it; for he had chosen this standpoint with great objectivity and maintained it consistently; but not entirely in earnest, because he leaves the serious business of the theologian aside and proceeds only as a philosopher.
Nor is it any irony that philosophers do not always speak seriously.

He says of Descartes*) that he cannot imagine that the latter ever seriously advanced the proposition that God is the free cause of truths (namely, of necessary truths) and of essences: "this was presumably one of his artificial turns, one of his philosophical tricks (un de ses tours, une de ses ruses philosophiques); he was preparing a way of escape for himself, as when he found an artificial turn in order to deny the motion of the earth, while he was a Copernican to the utmost." Yet however churchly Leibniz conducted himself in his writings, he could not in his time escape the condemnation of some clergymen, chiefly because he did not attend church; although Lessing**) rightly remarks that even if he had been a diligent churchgoer, he would not have fared any better than his academic eulogist Fontenelle, of whom, since he had fulfilled all the outward duties of a Catholic Christian, it was said after his death that he had done this precisely only out of contempt for Christianity!

Yet people doubted Leibniz's religion precisely for this reason***, because after Bayle's passing he had expressed the hope that Bayle would now be surrounded by the light that is lacking to us here below, since it may be presumed that he did not lack good will!
Whatever Leibniz may or may not have believed, he possessed true religiosity; the purpose of his Theodicy was+) to bring people back *) Theod., vol. I, p. 326. **) Ibid., p. 294. ***) Opp. omn.
Leibniz, in Dutens, vol. I, p. 115.
Note. +) Theod.

Vol. I, p. 131.
From the false ideas that represent God to them as an absolute prince who exercises a despotic power, little suited and little worthy to be loved; animated by a zeal that must be pleasing to God, he hoped from God enlightenment and assistance in carrying out an undertaking that he had begun for the honor of God and for the welfare of mankind.
Truly in him, if in anyone, was confirmed what Bacon had said: "Philosophy, tasted in moderation, removes us from God; but those who fathom it, it leads back to him."

div.head: XXIV. Einleitungsrede gehalten zur Feier des Geburtsfestes Seiner Majestät des Königs Friedrich Wilhelm IV. in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften am 17. October 1844.
Das Verhältnifs des theoretischen Lebens zum praktischen

p.s: Of the countless celebrations which are devoted to joy over the return of the happy day on which Frederick William the Fourth was born as successor to the Prussian throne, every one has its justification in every year, but most especially in this one, in which he has, as it were, been given to us a second time by divine Providence, because he is the common lord, protector, and benefactor of all who beneath the wings of the Royal Eagle lead a secure existence—secure, and, so far as the limitations of human circumstances and the difficulty of the times permit, and so far as it depends on the ruler, not an uncheerful one.
But not all these festivals possess a justification peculiar to themselves, as ours does.

For most academic bodies, municipalities, institutions, societies—even the higher and lower schools—by which the birthday celebration of the dearest and noblest King is commemorated, are indispensable parts of the state; they arise with a certain necessity in every country advancing to any degree toward human cultivation, are everywhere present, in this or that form, more or less perfect, and are more or less fostered: our Society of Sciences, by contrast, although the first in the state, has so little claim to indispensability, and is—to speak somewhat bluntly from a standpoint that persons of very high and very low station share with one another—so superfluous that in our German fatherland not merely smaller states lack such a society, but even the first German state in outward rank, if not in intellectual movement,
which for many centuries was in possession of the German imperial crown.

It is not some pressing need of the past, nor of the present, nor of the future, to which our Academy owes its existence; it is a wholly free and disinterested foundation of our princes—one might almost say, were this not an inner contradiction, a foundation placed outside the state—certainly less closely bound up with the purposes of the state than the church, which yet by preference and not seldom lays claim to leading a life independent of the state; it is, like the pious foundations of earlier times, a work of love, and—not to go further back—of the love of Frederick the Great for the sciences, that love which, inherited by his successors, radiates in the purest and most brilliant light from the thoughtful spirit of the King to whom our homage is paid today.

Herein lies, besides our general duty, yet another particular obligation, to acknowledge with heartfelt gratitude what we owe to the exalted princely house; and if this is not done as worthily and adequately as we could wish, there remains to us only the regret that the seclusion of a purely scholarly institution—so beneficial in many important respects, yet on the other hand assailed in manifold ways—cannot surround itself with the pomp that is at the disposal of other academic bodies, indeed that from this table, in fitting manner, not even that loftier tone of ceremonial eloquence can be struck up which is appropriate to the orator's chair.
I say that the Academy is a disinterested foundation of our princes, arisen out of love for the sciences: for every true love is free of self-interest.

But if in the circumstances of ordinary life every educated person admits that he is not truly loving who, instead of finding a spiritual ideal in the beloved object, seeks its possession merely for the sake of external goods and advantages; if even the better among those whose life's purpose is science or learning are convinced that it is to be pursued from inner impulse and from enthusiasm for knowledge, not as a means of gain: will this not always be recognized when there is talk of that love of the sciences which their protectors are to have or do have? And precisely this is the relation
into which our exalted King, following the example of his glorious ancestors, has placed himself toward our Academy, in that he does not disdain to be called its protector.

A prince's inclination toward the sciences is often directed only toward pastime and pleasant entertainment; often it springs from vanity and a craving to shine. Others, to be sure, seem to love science itself, but they do so only because they expect benefit from it, if not precisely for themselves, then at least for those they rule. They therefore also make the demand upon the sciences that they should make themselves useful, and thus they will be supportive, solely or preferentially, of those parts or directions of knowledge from which they expect such advantages. How could one still call this calculation and hope of gain love, even if the gain should not be their own?

An old division distinguishes three kinds of goods: those that are desirable for their own sake; others that we seek because of their consequences; finally, others that are worth possessing both for their own sake and because of their consequences.

Beyond dispute, science belongs to this third class: but whoever seeks or honors it merely for the sake of its consequences casts it among that class of goods which is plainly the least, and for him it has no higher significance than, say, money, which no sensible person loves for its own sake.

Since the greatest part of activity in the state relates to practical matters, and the prince, as the highest statesman, the more he enters into affairs the more he will also take a practical direction, one can scarcely blame a prince, even one of no ordinary endowments, if, precisely from this standpoint of his, he directs his attention, even with respect to science, to the utility that appears in practical life: only an eminently excellent intellectual nature, an original idealism, freedom and liberality of mind in his intellectual direction, an innate love for the true, the good, and the beautiful in themselves, can raise him above these considerations.

As this direction once revealed itself openly in Frederick the Great, so I declare it—removed from all flattery, which would be equally unworthy of the king of whom I speak and of the society in whose name I speak—out
of full conviction, experience, and direct perception: that only this pure love of science and art, the enthusiasm for all that is noble, under which above all knowledge is comprehended, in the most intimate union with a deeply feeling and delicately sensitive heart and mind, animates and inspires our exalted protector.

Insofar as reflection on human life in its various directions reaches back, the distinction between the theoretical and the practical life has come to light: by the latter we understand the whole activity of man insofar as it relates to the family and the household and acquisition of every kind, and to the state, the great family of the people; by the former, not merely science or knowledge, but also art, which embodies ideas, and religious consciousness.
The two directions are not absolutely separate.

In almost all things, practice is older than contemplation, and so, taken as a whole, practice is older than theory; for the most part, practice first supplies theory with its material, so that by separating and combining it, theory may clarify and order it.

And however much practice may also resist theory and stubbornly insist that it has its own laws within itself and follows rules of its own making, it cannot keep theory away from itself—theory, in which it first comes to consciousness of itself. Indeed, it has been found countless times that the practice of centuries has been false and reprehensible, that it has had to let itself be directed by strengthened theory onto a different path than that of custom, to which practice clings so gladly; and the progress of humanity rests precisely on this, that practice is ever more thoroughly penetrated and transformed by theory or knowledge—as one can recognize, to choose only the most evident examples, in the gradual realization of better principles of law and of political economy.

Despite this undeniable commonality of both activities, the two—the theoretical and the practical life—have from the most ancient times been relatively separated; the isolation of the former presents itself in the oldest history of peoples, at the most primitive stage of culture, in the Oriental priestly
castes, as they existed especially among the Indians, Babylonians, and Egyptians: and yet even here the dominion of the theoretical over the practical already appears, in that the whole knowledge of the national spirit was gathered and concentrated in the priesthood, and from here the entire life of the people was regulated.

If ever and anywhere practice and theory have been powerfully and vitally formed into one another and have come to a mutual interpenetration, it was in Hellenic life; but even among the Hellenes they again separated from one another and entered into opposition, and so that old struggle between statesmen and philosophers was kindled, which we see driven to its extreme in Socrates and his opponents, to the death.

This gulf between the two activities was established by Plato; and Aristotle too, when he designates the life of enjoyment, the political life, and the theoretical life as the three most conspicuous kinds of life, is far from seeking any mediation between them, but decidedly gives the preference to the theoretical life.

Just as in the structures of nature, the higher the natural product, the more distinctly, the more articulatedly, the more significantly do the individual organs, systems, and vital activities stand apart, whereas on the lower levels, less differentiated and less developed, they flow together as it were into a chaotic mass, in which only the microscope of our indefatigable researchers still finds a microcosmic order; so too, the more cultivated the age, the livelier the movement of minds, the more perfect the development, the more must the opposition of directions assert itself and the endeavor arise that the one overcome the other—that presumption of theory to dominate practice, this presumption of practice to restrict theory, to set it a limit which it should not overstep, or to demand of it that it submit and conform to tradition or support it: thus arises what one is accustomed to call the conflict of science with life, when the former does not rather withdraw and separate itself from life, until a higher power, Providence, which has traced out the world plan with quite other lines than those with which men often believe they draw it, brings about that reconciliation
which it has already brought about more than once.

Many considerations press themselves upon us here, and I do not wish to turn them all away from me: many demands, and quite opposite ones, are made upon science from many sides, and I will not maintain that any one of them is entirely without foundation.

That science should not enter into the machinery of so-called life is demanded now by the power of the state, now by science itself; if the latter is right, then the former is right too, only perhaps not for a correct reason, insofar namely as the former frequently banishes science from life only because it does not agree with the prevailing practice: but in itself this demand seems to me, although not universally and absolutely valid, by no means so reprehensible as it may seem to some.

Science, namely, is the universal, the common possession of all peoples and states, and to that extent something abstract: an expression by which, in the old manner, I designate something genuine and sound, without troubling myself that the whole world rails at abstractions and seeks the much-praised concrete: whatever differences science, and especially philosophy, has assumed and may yet assume in its various courses of development, the same threads, the same eternal fundamental truths run through all ages, and no science, be it philosophy or history or natural science, can let itself be determined by what lies outside it, whatever name that may bear.

To be sure, I know very well—and I have also applied this in the field in which my scholarly activity moves—that according to ages and peoples certain differences have emerged and asserted themselves in all science and especially in philosophy: people speak of Eastern and Western philosophy, of Indian and Chinese, of Greek and Roman, of German, of English, of French, of pagan and Christian, indeed recently even of Catholic philosophy; but whatever in these differences has a justification lies partly in the necessary and involuntary course of development, partly in the predominant emphasis and cultivation of one or the other side appropriate to a particular
national spirit, partly in an unessential coloring that scarcely touches the inner core; whatever else appears in those differences has its seat in what, in a given so-called philosophy, is precisely not philosophy: for just as there can be no special monarchical and no special aristocratic or democratic philosophy, so too no other differences whatsoever can have validity in it that are not grounded within it itself, and whoever introduces such a one stands on the same level as the sophist, whose essence it is to think as the prevailing opinion thinks and to give this a semblance of grounding, but not to seek the truth.

Now, insofar as cognition is to be untroubled by all that is external, it is evidently advantageous for it to separate itself from everything by which it is diverted from the straight path, from everything accidental; but what people are commonly accustomed to call life is, for cognition, something accidental, and is subject to far greater change than is thought, which, like the ideas of the Attic sage, persists equal to itself and unchanging.

If, further, science is to enter into life, then the scholarly man is moved to involve himself in practical affairs; although, to be sure, outstanding talents such as Leibniz was are capable of uniting both the practical and the scholarly direction, yet a manifold activity in affairs nevertheless deprives the scholarly man of that collectedness of mind which he needs above all; even in the case of a Leibniz that distraction certainly did not have a beneficial effect on his scholarly investigations, and all the more will scholars of lesser endowment, who were nevertheless capable, given freer leisure, of accomplishing things deserving of gratitude, when they plunge—whether involuntarily or even out of their own inclination—into the whirlpool of busy activity, scatter their best powers in it and are lost to science.

If any learned institution is called to promote science in and for itself, without any regard to life, it is the academies of sciences; and so, as some among us will still recall, Schleiermacher once set forth in one of these public assemblies the thought that in the establishment and maintenance of the
