academies the state gives expression to the validity and recognition of knowledge and science for their own sake, without any secondary purpose.
Also, in turbulent times it is no small prize, as Cicero, after the toils and sufferings of a perilous activity in the state, refreshed himself with philosophy, to have a noble retreat from life.

Granted that this praise, this good fortune of the academies may seem to many a very ambiguous thing, still it will be admitted that through this their position they are equally removed from unreasonable and unjust demands as from reasonable and just ones; one may hold up against me, the student of antiquity, that Solonian law which visited with banishment the man who in civil strife had taken no party: we accept this objection, because it does not touch the science that stands above the parties.

We do not wish to assert that science should have no influence on life; indeed, I assert the contrary, that the highest perfection of human life is attained precisely in the unity of theory and practice, of knowing and acting, of thought and deed; but before this ideal, or rather this ideal-real condition, the divine within the human, shall have been fully won, let us at least allow every one-sidedness, provided only it be sound, to have its way; let us not demand everything of everyone, but of each what he is suited for, and let us not confuse all standpoints and spheres of life.

One cannot demand of mathematics that it come to the aid of church dogma, nor of the church that it increase mathematical knowledge; and just as little as one will expect the daily press to make the investigation of the strict sciences its task, just so little can one impose upon an academy the duty of translating science directly into life.
These two institutions form, so to speak, opposite poles of intellectual activity, and between them there is need of manifold and skillful mediators and reporters.
The influence of science on life concerns partly the material and partly the ideal.

It has a material benefit insofar as it improves and increases the means for satisfying the needs and comforts of life, promotes the acquisition
of physical goods, brings about physical well-being, and removes the natural and bodily ills: the natural sciences and the applied parts of mathematics are especially suited to this; but even those branches of knowledge which lie more on the side of the historical and are akin to political science have great importance for material welfare, which depends very much on whether correct or false measures of legislation and administration favor or hinder production and manufacture, agriculture, the trades, and commerce and traffic; and that theory has a great influence here will scarcely be able to be disputed.

Now, to be sure, spiritual [goods] do not necessarily arise from material well-being; on the contrary, the latter is even endangered by luxury. But without prosperity no spiritual progress of the people is possible, because poverty and want, with the countless evils that accompany them, oppress the mind, and when they have reached a high degree, they also corrupt the morals of the people.
The promotion of material prosperity therefore paves the way for spiritual well-being.
Nevertheless, the ideal benefit of science is to be rated higher—the benefit that lies in bringing about a more moral disposition and a more moral life through better knowledge.

It is indeed a great good fortune when a people possesses old inherited customs and usages and institutions, deeply rooted, by virtue of which it walks almost unconsciously in the right track and does what is right: but humanity does not always remain in this state of paradisiacal innocence, and many false habits, defects, and disturbing prejudices are often mingled with the old customary morality, however good and idyllic it may be.
If it is true, and I hold it to be true, that virtue is knowledge, then it must be raised to consciousness.
The state is to be the realization of human virtue; thus the highest morality is to be demanded first of it and of its action, if private morals are to improve.
In this respect, however, the ideal side of scholarship generally has no sudden influence, but rather a gradual and slowly acting one.

To be sure, some hold that the present morals of civilized peoples are worse than formerly, and since the sciences have
indisputably advanced, it would follow from this that with the progress, indeed even a very wide diffusion, of knowledge a decline in morals had set in.

But even if I grant that the course of the human race does not consist of nothing but progress, since rather, as in nature so in history, overwhelming upheavals occur which, destroying good and bad alike, cast society back for the moment, until out of the ruins of the old civilization it builds itself a new edifice and out of decay a new life arises: yet the great periods of world history show, alongside the undeniable decline of noble phenomena, a forward movement in the highest and most important relations of humanity, one that is nowhere more clearly evident than in public and private morals.

Whoever asserts that in our age morals are in decline should at least prove that in the celebrated Middle Ages, in which immorality appears on a mass scale, or in the sixteenth or seventeenth or eighteenth century, more morality and fewer vices and crimes were present: it is not in the least doubtful to me that a thorough investigation will bring out precisely the opposite.

But this inquiry is scarcely needed: the true measure of the morality of a people or an age is the morality of the state itself, that is, of the laws and of the manner of their execution; and it would be to slander the state of our time if one were unwilling to recognize that it has become more moral: in the name of the law and in good faith, to act piously and in a manner pleasing to God, the state once committed deeds which the better insight of a later age had to recognize as manifest crimes; deliberation and wisdom have, taken on average, stepped into the place of passion; reason rules as a rule instead of force, even under absolute governments, openness instead of deceit and cunning, human feeling instead of harshness, coarseness, and cruelty: one seeks to govern more through instruction and conviction than through fear and terror.

Those who hold such gloomy views of the present and see in it only ruin deceive themselves about the significance of individual phenomena, and, however isolated these may stand, they attach to them, as so-called signs of the times, an
exaggerated importance through improper generalization, without knowing or considering that the very same things were formerly much worse and more frequent; and even if they do know it, their knowledge recedes into the background for them, because, as is well known, history teaches no one whose passionate ill humor deprives him of his composure.

Why should it be surprising that the judgment of laymen is subject to the strong impressions made by individual significant events, when even heroes of historiography allow themselves to be so confused by them that they view the age and the consequences of these occurrences from the most distorted side?

Undeterred by those who claim unconditional reverence for their friends and ours and for great scholars, and who brand the mere mention of a human weakness—even when it is made for the sake of the matter, not to disparage the persons—as at once a violation of piety, it will be permissible to cite how two former members of this Academy, distinguished as historians, who were moreover statesmen as well, erred concerning their own age.

Johannes von Müller, after he had long fought Napoleon's rule with the weapons of speech, prophesied to the world, in its invincible fortification after the defeat of Prussia, a new golden age; Niebuhr found in the July Revolution the downfall of humane culture and the irruption of barbarism.

Both have already been refuted by the years that followed—the hopes of the one as well as the fears of the other; they had followed only the impression of the moment, as so easily happens to the most feeling of souls, that they let themselves be carried away by temperament, inclination, and mood—in short, by their own subjectivity—whereas in order to set the horoscope rightly for the present and the future, there is required the unshakable composure of the most disciplined thought and that objectivity of spirit which we admire in Thucydides, with whom those two men, in other respects highly excellent, have been very ineptly compared.

A similar prejudice is that which believes it finds a deterioration of morals alongside an undeniable advance of knowledge and science; not to speak of those who seek the source of the imagined evil in
knowledge itself.
Only through the spirit can the human race move forward, but the activity of the spirit is knowledge.

To be sure, this spirit must be a holy one; but sanctification does not lie in rigid dogma—rather, the religious consciousness too must continually purify and transfigure itself: otherwise all progress would be denied until a new revelation appeared.

If now, as has been said, the ideal side of science exercises a particular influence on this ideal progress, one would nevertheless sin against the natural sciences if one were not also willing to acknowledge in them a significant share in this.

If the mind takes nature up into itself, if it recognizes laws in nature, even if it merely reduces nature to measure and number, then nature has itself become something spiritual for the mind, and the science of nature therefore also has all the effects of the spirit.

Frederick the Great in particular had grasped this, in an age whose strivings, even if they are not free from fault, are nowadays very often judged very unjustly and not without arrogance, whereas it is precisely our own age that supplies the proof that they were not superfluous.

Poetic and mystical natures may find it very trivial, and zealous champions of fanaticism not offensive, that I regard it as a major advance in human cultivation that the natural sciences in particular have contributed to the destruction of the most manifold forms of superstition, in which a great part of human ills and crimes had its most effective foundation.
If in former times peoples and armies trembled before an eclipse of the sun or moon, it is no insignificant influence on life that astronomy has dispelled this fear.

To be sure, by virtue of that error, as history teaches, peoples and armies could sometimes be better kept in check; but apart from the fact that the opposite also occurred, will people want to reverse astronomical enlightenment for the sake of that incidental advantage?

One may well smile with pity at this example, but only because it is too obvious, lies too far off, and is therefore so entirely innocuous: if one wished to cite others to which one can apply it from this one, the features might well settle into more serious folds.

The general sciences stand in the closest connection with the ideal formation of
humanity; they are partly philosophical, partly historical, or—what in my view is equivalent—philological.

In our own day people have often disparaged philosophy, and have to an equal degree exalted the historical, with the exception of classical philology, which has been much contested: I shall set aside the grounds for this judgment; if one looks to the essence of the matter, not to the aberrations and excesses of philosophers, on the one hand into the fantastic, on the other into the unbridled, then one must, with the same right, apply to philosophy what Aristotle says of poetry—that it is worth more than history, because it contains the universal and consequently the universally valid.

That these branches of knowledge—although not with every one of their manifold members—exert a significant, though for the most part indeed only indirect, influence upon life: of this, among other things, the very circumstance already bears witness, that those who wish with force and consistency to hold life bound in narrower fetters deem it fitting to hinder and ward off the free development and cultivation of these branches.

But, as already remarked, the entire ideal influence of science upon life requires time; in quiet labor, for the most part withdrawn from the world, it brings better insights and principles to maturity, the enjoyment of which often benefits only posterity; unsought and unintended, a benefit arises from it which it would scarcely be able to produce if from the very beginning it had aimed only at utility.

The latter, and therefore practice in general, can consequently not be authoritative for science; rather, science consists in free theoretical exercise. Thus Archimedes, with a genuinely scientific spirit, placed the chief emphasis not on his mechanical inventions, the useful ones, but on his theorems; and while those inventions, which certainly seemed far more significant to the great mass of his contemporaries, have for the most part been lost, these theorems have nonetheless borne far richer fruit.

Even if the golden tree of life is green, all theory is not for that reason gray; and those who so often have that saying on their lips forget that it is spoken by the spirit that ever denies, and they would be ashamed to apply it if they had to cite it in its full, rather frivolous context.
In the consciousness from which I have proceeded—that our entire academic activity is but an outflow of Royal favor—it is ordained in the statutes of the Academy that every year on this day, in connection with this introductory address, a report be given on the academic achievements.

Since we already set down in our monthly reports everything relating to this, insofar as it is suitable for publication, the briefest indications—scarcely even a bare nomenclature—will suffice for today's purpose; yet even these will show that the Academy finds its calling in theory, and that only a few of its achievements approach the practical: and never has this been less impaired for it than under this spirit-filled King!*) *) To this was attached the enumeration of the Academy's achievements in the past year.

div.head: XXV. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Jahrestages Friedrichs des Grofsen am 29. Januar 1846.
Ueber Friedrichs des Grofsen klassische Studien

p.s: The individual person, like an entire people, is formed partly out of his own nature, and partly he is determined by the circumstances in which he stands and by what is given, that is, by the influences of the contemporary world and of the world of the past, and in particular by the world of thought, whose foremost bearers are the writers.

The more vigorous a people, the greater the individual, the more will the former and the latter determine themselves from their own peculiar nature and give it strong expression; but just as the noblest and most gifted people, if it keeps every foreign influence away from itself and willfully seeks to form everything only out of itself, will deprive itself of all the instruction that a more advanced development of other peoples holds before it—indeed, just as such a people might in the end even present the repugnant spectacle of a Chinese rigidity and isolation—so too would the individual endowed with the greatest capacities, were he to draw only from himself, remain poor in insights and to a high degree one-sided; rather, the great man, without prejudice to his peculiarity, will from his whole surroundings, from the wealth of thought of past and present, bring all the more abundant nourishment to his spirit the more capable he is of comprehending much and taking it into himself.

Yet much will he also reject and cast aside from himself: just as, according to an old principle, like is recognized only by like, so too our spirit takes pleasure only in what is akin to it, and among the intellectual products given to it seeks out that which is suited to it, which is congenial to it.

Frederick the Great, whose imperishable memory we commemorate today, was not only a hero
in deeds and a hero in principles; he not only acted much and thought much, but had also read much. Yet one would misjudge the greatness of his mind if one were to attribute it to the writings he read, if one were to attribute it, say, to Voltaire, that he thought as he thought; rather, he was drawn to those to whose spirit he felt himself akin, and he took their spirit and feeling into his own capacious mind and his own capacious heart.
But these were not merely Voltaire and the other French scholars of his own or of an earlier time, although he could come to know most of what he read only through the medium of the French language.

If an apology is needed, my discipline will apologize for me if today I commemorate the love that Frederick the Great cherished for classical antiquity; truly not in order thereby to glorify and recommend it: at least the success of such an undertaking would have to be very doubtful, because by most of those who fail to recognize the value of the studies of antiquity Frederick is condemned or pitied as a despiser of German culture and as a freethinker: but only in order to show one not unremarkable side of the many sides of this sublime man, and indeed precisely one such side for whose comprehension and presentation I might seem both authorized and qualified.

Yet I promise—although the citations of the most learned connoisseur of his writings and his life have come to the aid of my own knowledge of the works of the great King—by no means an exhaustion of my subject, for which greater preparations would be required than one will reasonably expect of the speaker of words that swiftly die away.

If we may apply to an earlier age concepts that at that time were not yet developed at all, or only imperfectly, then we say: Frederick's taste and direction in literature was almost exclusively turned toward the classical, and turned away from everything romantic, especially the medieval.

Even in French he loved only the age that strove after classical antiquity with equal zeal, whatever its success; and this inclination was so free from prejudice that *) expression of the Chevalier de Neufville (Oeuvres posth. de Fréd.

II. Berlin edition, vol. XII, p. 198). [Oeuvres de Frédéric le Grand, Berlin academic edition, vol. XVII, p. 241.]
He himself revered works whose fundamental ideas might appeal to him but little, in a purely aesthetic respect: he was so taken with Racine's Athalie, which he read again and again, that he even once said to d'Alembert that he would rather have written Athalie than have conducted the Seven Years' War*).

If he esteemed English literature, though without finding any pleasure in the language, to which he denies euphony and whose wretched wit he retells—that of a scholar who, when asked in what language the serpent had tempted our first mother, replied, "in English, for the serpent hisses"**); if he honored Dante, Petrarch, Ariosto, and Tasso, and declared the great poems of the latter two, together with Homer, Virgil, and Voltaire, to be those works of the imagination to which one must hold fast***): then, by contrast, the contempt is well known with which he speaks of the greatest of the romantic dramatists, of Shakespeare, and that level of literary culture—of the French as of the Italians and the English—which suited him he derives precisely from the fact that these, having drawn from the rich sources of antiquity, had imitated these great models as much as possible, had appropriated their manner of thinking, and had admired their great beauties without failing to recognize their defects, since one must esteem with discrimination and never give oneself over to blind flattery†).
The points of view under which he read and used the ancients we may reduce to these three: the rhetorical-aesthetic, the philosophical-moral, and the historical-political, including the military.

Although in his time no stage was open to true eloquence, such as the ancients practiced, except in England, he nevertheless, in a genuinely antique spirit, laid great weight on rhetoric, and his frequent use of rhetorical technical terms proves that he *) Letter of June 25, 1763, Œuvres posth. de d'Alembert, vol. I, p. 197 (Paris, 1799). [Oeuvres de Frédéric le Grand, academic edition, vol. XXV, p. 273.] **) De la litt.
To all.
p. 84 f. in the Œuvres publ. du vivant de l'Auteur, vol. III. [vol. VII, p. 103 of the new edition.] ***) Ibid.
p. 81 [101 f.] and in a letter to Voltaire of the 17th
Dec. 1777, Oeuvres posth.
Vol. X, p. 82 [Vol. XXIII, p. 417]. +) De la litt. 'Allem.

p. 74 [98].
he had studied it; in a letter from the first period of his reign *) he calls himself a pupil of Cicero in rhetoric, and he thought especially highly of Quintilian, praising the clarity of his presentation and the completeness of his precepts and of his rules of the art; whoever did not attain eloquence by studying him would never attain it**).

He likewise holds firmly to Aristotle's Poetics; its rules—by which he means chiefly the three unities of drama, which were not altogether correctly inferred from it—are, in his view, not arbitrary, but the only means of making tragedy attractive; he finds Shakespeare's plays abominable for the very reason that they sinned against all these rules of the theater ***).

As his taste, which admittedly also passed many a judgment that now sounds not a little strange, inclined toward the antique also in the outward form of poetry, his opinion on German hexameters, which he had come to see in later years†), shows above all; these rhymeless verses, he says, had a cadence and a harmony that arise from the mixture of dactyls and spondees; full of meaning, they had pleasantly taken possession of his ear through full-toned sounds, of which he would never have held our language capable; perhaps this kind of verse were the most suitable for German, and probably progress would be made if one took the trouble to perfect them.

Whatever of the ancient poets was accessible to him in tolerable translations, he read, or had read aloud to him, for entertainment, for the cheering and elevation of the mind, or for the cultivation of poetic taste, and reminiscences from them occur here and there in his work; among the Greeks he knew especially Homer and the Anacreontic songs; from the tragedians too he seems to have read some things: the Roman poets were more familiar to him—Lucretius, Virgil, Lucan, Horace, Catullus, Ovid, Tibullus, Propertius++).
In the philosophy of the ancients, especially insofar as it is of a practical kind, he was quite *) Oeuvres posth.
Vol. VIII, p. 184 [Vol. XVII, p. 213 of the new edition]. **) De la litt.
To all.

p. 67 [94]. ++) See, among others, loc. cit. p. 66
[93]. ... thoroughly versed; he knew the systems that could be seen through without deeper metaphysical investigations or philological research, namely the Epicurean and the Stoic, and he made manifold use of both, especially also in his poetic attempts: however opposed the two are to each other, he drew strength from both, because both grant the soul tranquility, and from their teachings and from the example of their adherents he drew consolation in severe suffering.

During the Seven Years' War he refreshed himself with the splendid maxims of Epictetus and with Marcus Aurelius, whose work at that time gave him occasion and inspiration for the long poem "Le Stoïcien"*).

Besides these, he had Lucretius almost always at hand, especially the third book, with which he fortified his contempt for life and death: "When I am troubled," he writes to d'Alembert,**) "I read the third book of Lucretius, and it consoles me; it is a palliative, but for the diseases of the soul we have no other remedies." Cicero, whom he calls his friend***), he indeed also revered as an orator and as the defender of freedom, but most of all in a philosophical and moral respect; the Tusculan Disputations especially appealed to him; the books On Duties he calls the best work on moral doctrine that has been written and can be written; the books On the Nature of the Gods are to him an immortal work+): in his own writings there is no lack of passages where he has made use of Cicero.
He was likewise a lover of the ethical writings of Seneca.
Of the older philosophers, even of Plato and Aristotle, he had evidently only a superficial *) Cf. on all this Oeuvres posth.
Vol. XII, p. 9 [Vol. XXV, p. 225 f. of the new edition], de la litt..
To all.

Oct. 1777, Oeuvres posth.
Vol. XI, p. 271 [Vol. XXV, p. 56]. ***) Ibid.
p. 273 [57]. +) Letter to Voltaire of April 19, 1738 [vol. XXI, p. 193], Epitre à Myl.

p. 100 [112], Oeuvres publ. du viv. de l'Auteur vol. II, p. 402 [vol. IX, p. 178].
superficial knowledge; of still older thinkers, naturally only the most commonplace is found in him: with particular fondness, however, he seems to have looked upon the free-thinking Anaxagoras, the friend of the great Pericles, whom he knew from Bayle, and in letters to the latter he gives his own friend d'Alembert the name "his Anaxagoras"*.

Here, where the utmost precision of designation is not at issue, we may also count Lucian among the philosophers, whose free manner of thought and satirical tone were very much to his liking, and likewise the Emperor Julian, whose veneration, however one may judge of his position toward Christianity, is not unworthy even of the noblest prince.
Of the historians of antiquity the King made the most extensive use, both in reading and in writing.

Herodotus, Thucydides, and Xenophon are not unknown to him; Polybius was of particular importance to him in tactical and strategic respects—indeed, he helped him win a major battle. He had, to note this in passing, also read Vegetius; he uses Diodorus, Plutarch frequently, Sallust, Caesar, Nepos, Livy, Velleius, Tacitus, Suetonius, Curtius, and Ammianus Marcellinus.

Among these, Thucydides, the master of historiography, is indisputably the one whose spirit and artistry of language can least of all be recognized from a translation, especially a French one; hence one will forgive the King if, in a courteous letter,**) he designates the author of the Roman History, Rollin, as the Thucydides of his century—and all the more readily forgive him, since even scholars who could have been better informed later bestowed this honorary title just as lavishly.

Without doubt Frederick penetrated more deeply into the mind and representation of Tacitus, whose worth he knew how to appreciate fully***), forming a significant contrast to Napoleon, who hated Tacitus as a bilious slanderer of princes: for it surpasses all calculation what difference of spirit and mind, as of principles of government, there must be between rulers whom Tacitus disgusts and *) Oeuvres posth.
Vol. XI [XXIV]. **) From the 4th
Sept. 1748 [vol. XVI, p. 237]. ***) Cf.
Posthumous Works.
Suppl.

Vol. III, p. 63 ff. [Vol. XXIV, p. 341 ff.], Stein, Charakteristik Fr. d. II. Th. I.
p. 83. — rulers who love and praise him, and how Frederick took pleasure in the free and bold characters of a Thrasea Paetus and Helvidius Priscus*), knowledge of whom he ...
...owes sketches of this magnificent historian.

To pass from here to the orators, since their importance is preeminently a political one, the King did not, for instance, content himself with Cicero, whom, together with Hortensius, he ranks as the most cultivated of the Roman orators; he had made himself acquainted with Isocrates, Aeschines, and Demosthenes.

From Demosthenes and Cicero, he says,** one receives the great taste of eloquence; if he adds, in order to mark the difference in their merits, the observation that nothing could be added to the former and nothing taken away from the latter, then here, through an oversight of the kind that are frequent in his writings, the judgment of his Quintilian*** has been turned by him into its opposite.

By translating Demosthenes, he holds, one should cultivate our language, and take care to reproduce his power; with equally correct judgment he gave exceptional approval to the crown of Demosthenic eloquence, the speech On the Crown, which stands out as much through the greatness of its sentiment as through the perfection of its expression.

He had already woven a key passage from Demosthenes into the Betrachtungen über den politischen Körper Europa's [Reflections on the Political Body of Europe]++), from the year 1738, and the same passage recurs, among several others, in the Briefe über die Vaterlandsliebe [Letters on Patriotism]+++), from the year 1779; its application in that earlier work may serve as an example of how he was accustomed to make use of such material.

For in that place he compares the policy and the conduct of Philip of Macedon and of the Romans with French policy and public conduct, and he weighs the frivolity with which the Greeks regarded Philip's advances, foolishly imagining that his death would free them from their most dangerous enemy. "That is precisely the language," he says, "which people now *) Oeuvres publ. du viv. de l'Auteur vol. III, p. 10 [vol. IX, p. 217]. **) De la litt.
To all.
XII, 1, 20. +) A. a. O. p. 86 [104]. ++) Oeuvres posth.

Vol. VI, pp. 40 f. [Vol. VIII, pp. 21 f.] 1 +++) Oeuvres publ. du viv. de l'Auteur, Vol. III, p. 32 [Vol.
IX, p. 228]. ... in Europe; people flatter themselves that the death of a French statesman will put an end to French policy, that another minister who succeeds him will not have the same points of view, the same plans: people entertain themselves with small hopes, which are usually the consolations of weak souls and small minds.
"Allow me," he continues, "to bring to mind here the censure that Demosthenes pronounced against the Athenians in the First Philippic."
These are his words: Philip is dead, one will say; no, another will reply, but he is ill ....
Well, whether he lives or dies, what does it matter to you?

If you no longer have him, Athenians, you will soon have made yourselves another Philip, unless you change your conduct; for he has become what he is not so much through his own powers as through your negligence." Thus there run through Frederick's writings allusions and references drawn from the mythology, history, and literature of antiquity—ornamental fruits of reading that are seldom to be found nowadays in similar works, because such studies are seldom undertaken.
And these studies not only nourished his youth, but he returned to them again and again.

Since in his youth he had already divided his books into two classes—those he wished to know more closely and others with which he merely wished to entertain himself—the former continually came up again in turn for reading or reading aloud, and among them was the greater part of the ancients whom we have already named; because the existing translations did not satisfy him, he also made a list of those he wished to have newly translated.
When his personal library had been lost in the Battle of Soor, he asked his friend Duhan de Jandun to procure new books promptly, among them Cicero, Horace, and Lucian.

Still, from the year 1784 until July 30, 1786, his last reader, Dantal, read to him the Greek orators, Polybius, Livy, Tacitus, Suetonius, Lucretius, Lucian, Lucan, the Iliad and the Odyssey, Ovid, Nepos, Velleius, Diodorus, and Curtius. *) Preuss, Frederick the Great.

Vol. I, p. 413. **) 2 Oct. 1745 [Vol. XVII, p.
289]. The study of the ancients has been handed down to us by our forefathers as a means of school instruction; of it one may say what Plato*) said of music and gymnastics, that it is hard to find a better education than that found by the long ages of antiquity: but some of those who wish to see the existing order preserved merely because it exists, at once fall away to the opponents of the existing order when this does not seem to them to suit their other views or intentions, or when they do not believe they can give it a direction suited to their plans.
Frederick the Great found that educational means, though by no means the manner in which it was handled in instruction, to be in agreement with his views.

Just as he believed that our literature could be improved by translating the best writers of antiquity, and moreover wished for translations also for the reason that even those ignorant of foreign languages might better instruct themselves, so in the year 1779**) he issued the well-known cabinet order to Minister von Zedlitz, in which he expresses himself on the value of the ancient languages for the instruction of youth and on the neglect of rhetoric and logic and other subjects of instruction in the small schools; these sciences should be the first in the education of youth, because whoever reasons best always gets further than whoever draws false conclusions: he at the same time recommends history, geometry, and philosophy; the teacher must go through all systems with the young people, but by no means make any new ones, and philosophy must be taught by laymen, not by clergymen: otherwise it would be just as if a jurist were to teach an officer the art of war.
For rhetoric, he recommends Quintilian here as well, who ought to be translated into German, perhaps also made into an abridgment.

But above all he insists on the learning of Latin and Greek as the most essential subjects of instruction, from which he absolutely would not depart; even those who intended to devote themselves to the merchant's calling or similar pursuits should learn Latin.
In essentials, the passage at Staat II, p. 376 E. **) 6 agrees with this as well.

September, in Stein, op. cit., p. 140 [vol. XXVII, part III, pp. 251
ff.]; it agrees with the remarks thrown off in the essay on German literature; here too he insists on the reading of the ancients in the original language.

“If one wishes,” he says, “to train the ear on the harmony of Homer’s verses, then one must be able to read him fluently without the help of a dictionary”; “the same,” he continues, “I say with regard to Demosthenes, Aristotle, Thucydides, and Plato.”* Aristotle has, to be sure, here slipped into a passage that does not suit him, at least insofar as he has been preserved to us.
The classical ancient world breathes the spirit of lawful freedom; the great king honored this as well.

In the poetic letter "On Freedom," addressed to Lord Baltimore**), the subject is indeed for the most part intellectual and religious freedom of thought, but in it he at the same time certainly praises the political freedom of the Greeks and the Romans.

He loves the great republican characters, most especially the younger Cato, who perished together with freedom; in desperate situations, when he wished to make himself familiar, in poetic outpourings of the heart, with the Stoic resolve of a voluntary death, he calls upon those heroes, sacrificed on the field of Pharsalus, and sings of the magnanimous shades of the last Romans***); as M. Brutus and Cremutius Cordus, to whom this expression brought death, called Cassius the last of the Romans +).

In Frederick's place, the absolute rule of a wise man was evidently the best; and precisely because it was the rule of a wise man, a man of the noblest spirit and the most comprehensive insights, whom we proudly call our own++, was permitted to apply to him what Tacitus+++ says of Nerva: that he had earlier united things previously incompatible, the sole rule *) A. a. O. p. 74 [98]. **) Oeuvres posth.
Suppl.
Vol. I, pp. 263 ff. [Vol. XIV, pp. 71 ff.] ***) On Cato, see the letter to Lord Baltimore, p. 264 [Vol. XIV, p. 72], and other passages, such as Oeuvres posth.
Vol. XII, p. 9 [Vol. XXV, p. 226], Oeuvres publ. du viv. de l'Auteur, Vol. II, p. 402 [Vol. IX, p. 178], Oeuvres posth.
Vol. VII, p. 179 [Vol. XII, p. 53], Vol. VIII, p. 33 [Vol. XII, pp. 211 ff.].
Yet he also praises Otho's death, in the same volume p. 26 ff. [vol. XII, p. 207 ff.] +) Tac.
Ann.

Plutarch, Brutus 44. ++) A. von Humboldt (flysheet of June 1, 1840). +++) Agricola
3. and freedom.
But his true field was that intellectual freedom which he also highly praised in classical antiquity.*)

Rising above everything that presented itself to him as prejudice, he followed his own understanding, and as far as his power reached, he gave to all the same freedom that he had taken for himself, convinced that in the element in which he lived securely and at peace, others too could live securely and at peace, and for that reason he was without worries about the consequences of independent thought and of its free expression.

Frederick the Great is the true founder of scientific freedom; not merely because he is the founder or restorer of our Society, but because he raised this primal ground of scientific life, and thus of our own life, to the principle and law of the state, his memory must be sacred to us.

I do not mean that this direction first sprang up in him or in his time; he merely grasped it more powerfully and stirred it more vitally. Moreover, it is as old as science itself, and even in the times when it met with the most violent counter-pressure, it emerged all the more admirably.

It is to this recurrence of memorable phenomena—which has given rise to the maxim that nothing new happens under the sun, while it is equally true that no one steps twice into the same river—that historical parallels owe their origin; and these have also tried their hand a great deal on Frederick the Great, although the epithet of "the Only" bestowed on him again excludes every comparison with another. Now even if these comparisons are of no great value, but are for the most part mere games of wit, which, unduly emphasizing inessential similarities while neglecting the more important differences, shifts the point of view, or takes very trifling matters into consideration—for what, for example, is more trifling than that Hadrian and Frederick were fond of dogs?—yet a more deeply lying similarity of great natures, especially when they have developed under very unequal circumstances, may deserve an intimation; and so it may be permissible to set our hero alongside one of antiquity, to whom even the similarity of name should have led lovers of parallels *) Letter to Baltimore, loc. cit., pp. 263 f. [Vol. XIV, pp.
71 f.]—namely King Frederick the Second of the House of Hohenzollern with Emperor Frederick the Second of the House of Hohenstaufen, although the former, disregarding the Middle Ages*), paid no attention to the latter **).

The emperor's rich life lies vividly before us in the excellent work of my nearest academic colleague, and I shall not recount it again; much of it need only be cited in order to make the king's resemblance to the emperor recognizable, without my drawing the comparison.

Let us pass over the external power and the splendor that surrounded the great Emperor, his struggles on a wider stage than that of the King's glorious deeds, his legislation and his external and internal statecraft, whose foundations and directions were very different from those of more recent times, although in his Neapolitan-Sicilian kingdom he had considerably developed the administration, and not without regard for the welfare of his subjects***), while on the other hand, by entering even into the smallest details of his own household, he had regulated it+), and finally had moderated it++), by means of a truly representative body of the people, standing at that time entirely alone, composed of barons, prelates, and elected deputies.
More important for our purpose are his intellectual disposition and cultivation, and the convictions and endeavors that were connected with them.

He was distinguished by the noblest gifts of mind and heart and by substantial learning; he understood German, Latin, Greek, Italian, French, and Arabic; he was a poet of such individuality and skill that he himself invented artificial verse measures and melodies+++); in an age in which the observation of nature lay almost entirely dormant, he was an excellent and learned naturalist*+), and knew how to [combine] his researches at the same time *) Cf. e.g. de la litt.
To all.
p. 105 [114]. **) In the excerpts from Fleury he speaks of him rather indifferently. ***) By Raumer, HSt.
Vol. III, p. 537. 497. +) The same.
Vol. III, p. 554 f.) ++) The same.
Vol. III, p. 515. +++) The same.
Vol. III, p. 577. *+) The same.
Vol. VI, p. 483.

Vol. III, p. 570 f.,
to set forth clearly.

In his own states and in the East he collected books of every kind, and had the works of the Greeks translated from the Greek and from the Arabic, namely the Almagest and several writings of Aristotle, not merely for his own use, but he also shared them with others; he wished, as he himself says, to give his subjects the opportunity to instruct themselves, so that, trusting in the glorious support of knowledge, they might better protect themselves and their own and the fatherland.

He also sought to raise learning and knowledge by founding and maintaining educational institutions, and rightly, therefore, a learned and acute ceremonial orator of the university*) recently renewed his memory on the memorial day of the late King Frederick William III.
Thus he combated the barbarism of his century, its superstition, its stubborn priestly spirit—worthy of a better age.
He loved knowledge for its own sake and because of its consequences; the soul, he says, is enlightened and strengthened by science, without which the life of man lacks rule and freedom**).

His eager study of nature seems to have led him to the view that the pope reproaches him with, that man may believe only what can be proved by the force and reason of nature (vi ac ratione naturae)***); if in his early youth, following the spirit of the age, he had issued strict laws against heretics, yet later his thinking, his experience, and his intercourse and friendship with noble men of a different confession made him tolerant, and where he expressed himself without reserve, his utterances attain precisely the degree of disregard by which King Frederick gave offense.

With the great Emperor's struggle against the ecclesiastical authority that stood hostilely opposed to him, the King's purely spiritual struggle against that same authority can, to be sure, scarcely be compared; but in relation to the triviality of the provocations and hostilities which the King, under entirely different and scarcely difficult circumstances any longer, received from Hecker in the speech of the 3rd—
Aug. 1845. **) Ranmer, vol. III, p. 557 f. ***) The same.

Vol. IV, p. 35 f.
— once he learned of that power, long since broken, his vehemence, bitterness, and satirical mood toward it appear very significant.

If the historian of Emperor Frederick*) finds in him "an almost unprecedented union of the highest seriousness, the greatest rigor and consistency with the most natural cheerfulness and a mind everywhere spirited and capable of every kind of pleasure and jest," which also did not disdain the enjoyments of a good table**); who here does not recognize the very image of the great King?

Both have been loved and hated, praised and reviled in equal measure; of both it has been judged that, had they loved their own soul, few on earth would have been their equals: both also had, like all mortals, their flaws and infirmities.

But let us leave the censure of the King, which does not become us, to those who find themselves privileged to it by profession or station or by their own heart; but that the princes I have compared have been rightly compared, of that even the one assured reflection is already a guarantee: that the very same persons who praise or censure the one will likewise praise or censure the other.
The relationship in which an outstanding mind can stand to its age is twofold.
If he finds the age prepared, then the movement of the national spirit will correspond to his own movement; he will seize upon the latter, place himself at its head, and be certain of success.
If his age is still incapable of following him, then unfortunately he has come too soon.

Emperor Frederick had visibly outrun his age, and King Frederick too said of himself that he had been born too soon; indeed, most great men are great precisely because they rise above and leap beyond their age: they break through, as it were, the bounds of finitude, compressing past, present, and future within themselves; they are the seed ripened out of the blossom of the old plant that returns to dust, for future growths—if indeed they find a soil in which the seed can germinate and the germ can develop.
But are they [equal to] their age? *) Raumer, vol. III, p. 568. **) The same.

Vol. III, p. 573.
Having advanced thus far, they necessarily come into conflict with it; indeed, it cannot fail that they fall into some conflict even with themselves, because they must act in accordance with the given circumstances and yield to these more or less against their conviction.

King Frederick more or less achieved his aim, because he had only powerless intellectual opponents, because he wisely limited himself and knew how to keep a prudent measure and a beneficent middle course; for his own mind and his studies had taught him what was possible and impossible.

He knew that the ruler must limit himself in his plans for human happiness, because all perfection cannot be realized on earth *); he was deeply convinced of the impossibility of securing general acceptance for his principles **).

The eternal conflict between the ideal and reality—that cliff on which all founder who fail to consider that the ideal of the state may indeed be set up but cannot be attained in appearance—moves only in the course of millennia, even where the king is a sage and the sage a king, very gradually and slowly somewhat nearer to its solution, and indeed sometimes in a strange and paradoxical course of human affairs, which Kant***), the great contemporary of the great king, not without reference to the foundation which had been laid by the latter, indicated in foresight. *) Oeuvres posth.
Vol. VI, p. 87 [Vol. IX, p. 210]. : **) Especially in religious respect, Oeuvres publ. du viv. de l'Auteur, Vol. II, p. 304 [Vol. IX, pp. 135 f.], Oeuvres posth.
Vol. X, p. 18 [Vol. XXIII, p. 115], Vol. XII, p. 19 [Vol. XXV, p. 243]. ***) At the close of the essay: What Is Enlightenment?

div.head: XXVI. Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Trendelenburg als neu eingetretenen Mitgliedes der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Gedächtnifsfeier des Geburtstages Leibnizens am 1. Juli 1846.
Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Trendelenburg in der Akademie

p.s: Esteemed Sir!

Both the Academy as a whole and, in the first instance, the philosophical-historical class had long recognized the need to strengthen themselves through more than one representative of philosophy, because precisely for this science—although it is the science of the sciences and the aforementioned class bears half its name from it—only a single, though indeed very illustrious, member was associated with our society.

That this highly renowned man was chosen by us even before he had taken up residence in Berlin serves as proof that academic elections for some considerable time have no longer left speculative minds such as Fichte, Solger, and Hegel out of account; and you could therefore, without fear of giving offense, recall that exclusion of three Berlin philosophers from the Academy, whereas such a recollection—which I nevertheless permitted myself long ago—could easily have wounded earlier.

You have just now named those names in connection with the observation that a successor might easily regard the achievements he has to offer the Academy as slight; for that which you offer us, you have pointed above all to the history of philosophy, which is not concluded with Christianity but develops on and on.

Clearly it would be a misunderstanding if I took this to mean that you wished to exclude speculative philosophy from the Academy in opposition to its history; and such an interpretation would presuppose a contradiction in your words, since in that case you would have justified the unapproved slighting
of great German philosophers. By the history of philosophy, which has not ceased with Christianity, you understand—your words say so plainly—the life of philosophy itself, not the account of its past life.

If the individual sciences are branches of academic activity, and all the individual sciences are rooted in experience and speculation at once, then the latter too—a conceptual cognition that seeks ideas—must not be excluded from the academies; rather, it is a necessary counterweight to the historical and empirical mode of consideration, provided that speculation is not—to adopt your expression—a national, or even merely a personal, fantasy, which unfortunately may well apply to many a German philosopher.

You, esteemed colleague, do not fantasize instead of philosophizing; you will therefore also not let yourself be deterred by a traditional notion from philosophizing in the Academy and for it, and all the less will you separate the history of philosophy—I mean the presentation of its course of development—from the treatment of philosophy itself, since that history too itself becomes philosophy, if it succeeds in comprehending that course of development, in agreement with the results of historical-critical research (which will be no less welcome to us from you), as the necessary course of the philosophical spirit.

And, it seems to me, the Academy offers convenient ground for philosophy, because philosophy requires the complete freedom of cognition, yet nowhere is it less demanded than in this place that philosophizing should accommodate itself to predetermined notions: for the Academy is, according to its laws—the palladium of its existence—devoted to the general sciences without any particular teaching purpose, and least of all can philosophy here be regarded as an auxiliary science of theology, which more than any other practical branch of instruction has long been foreign to the Academy; least of all can there be any question here of philosophizing according to the standard of positive dogmas.

If in this respect our views surely agree, then your remark as well—that it is an honor to belong to a scholarly academic body that is still wholly so—gives me a welcome opportunity to state
that, sharing your feeling, I find honor, satisfaction, and joy in the academic position.

Yes, the Academy is a scholarly academic body, and it remains wholly so—wholly an academic body, wholly scholarly: for under the protection of exalted princes it possesses the full freedom and independence due to an academic body, and, unconcerned with favor or disfavor, while at the same time averse to rigid guild spirit and narrow-minded exclusiveness, it pays homage to knowledge itself in free and liberal-minded movement, without which knowledge can never thrive.

div.head: XXVII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 8. Juli 1847.
Das Verhältnifs der Berliner Akademie zur Philosophie und zum Christenthum nach Leibnizens Ansicht

p.s: Although human beings, in order to designate their original ideas—which in further development were determined into concepts—invented arbitrary and contractual sounds no more than the original political association rested on a social contract, yet nothing is more arbitrary and accidental than proper names or the designations closely related to them; and if from the original words, provided they were understood down to their ultimate ground, one would have to recognize, if not the essence of the thing, yet certainly the view from which the thing was regarded by the language-makers, then one would be very much mistaken if one wished to draw any inference from that other kind of designation as to the essence of what is thereby designated.

In this domain, at least very often, chance prevails to such an extent that one might almost come to disdain the magnificent instrument by means of which we not merely designate our thoughts but handle them, were one not to recall that naming, as Plato observes, is an art, and that there is a true and a false art, and hence also a good and true naming and likewise a bad and clumsy one.

Nowhere, perhaps, is this arbitrariness of names more striking than in science, and above all in philosophy, of which one might yet expect that it could take its names from its own definitions of concepts: nevertheless, the old philosophy contented itself for the most part with such names for its principal schools and sects as were borrowed from the most utterly accidental circumstances, as, for instance, Academic, Peripatetic, Cynic, Stoic philosophy.

They also undergo, in the transformation
of things and conditions, further changes of meaning, whereby they are quite diverted from their original sense; this is especially true of designations that have become very current, particularly of the names of public institutions, which, when transferred from one domain to another, signify something quite different.

Who would find it credible, were it not certain, that the noblest fruit of the poetic spirit, the most sublime work of verbal art, which reveals the highest tensions of our powers of will and the whole pain of life, the innermost depths of the human heart and the dark course of the world's destinies, bears a name that originally means nothing but a goat-song?

What, then, is a liturgy in the sense of the ancient Greek state—one that in peace unfolded the flower of the arts, and in the destructive sea battle the horse-like swiftness of the war galleys—but something altogether different from the ecclesiastical liturgy, which in the end nevertheless has in that former one the root of its name?

And how different is the political Ekklesia, self-determining and wholly free, from the one so named later, whose existence, although as a community of the spirit it presupposes a shared inner conviction, in fact rested for many centuries only on submission to the opinion and will—not merely to the surpassing reason—of a single spiritual head!

By a university we now understand the highest pinnacle of learned educational institutions, and the French, by "university" pure and simple, the aggregate of nearly all public schools, because only in the scholarly domain, in which the Latin language had made itself felt, did this word find entry and continued use, whereas according to its basic meaning any other commercial guild or legally constituted association of artists or craftsmen has an equal claim to this seemingly distinguished designation.

Wax can be kneaded into any shape; just as pliantly, the word—the form of our thoughts—endowed with wondrous elasticity and capable of the greatest expansion and compression, patiently submits to any content, even the opposite content that one wishes to put into it, so long as the slightest common element, the smallest trace of the original meaning, the remotest point of connection with what came before,
is still present; indeed, whoever—as some nowadays well understand how to do—knows how to put a vigorous catchword into circulation at the right moment, a catchword that, under the appearance of a definite meaning, is so indefinite that the most diverse things can be comprehended under it, that person, since most mortals are idolaters of words without weighing the things themselves, can rule and deceive, delight or terrify merely with the word.

This, as it were, philological introduction to the opening of today's celebration, which it falls to me to perform, would be stranger than it really is if it did not—apart from the last incidental remark—have a very illuminating application to the name of this highly esteemed society over which I have the honor here to preside; nevertheless, since names are only shadows of things, I would not have permitted myself to speak of mere words if some substance did not also attach to them.

That famous place near Athens is said to have been named after a hero, Hecademus, where Plato maintained a free philosophical intercourse with his pupils and, as may be supposed, also delivered before them connected lectures on speculative subjects; at his death a regulated school formed there under a fixed elected head, which, although its doctrine underwent manifold changes in the course of time and of development, in all its forms—as the Old, Middle, and New Academy, indeed even as a fourth and fifth Academy—was nevertheless regarded as the continuation of the original direction and was rooted in Plato's speculative and ethical philosophy.
This school was restored by Inlian at Athens as a school of Platonism, and it continued until Justinian's blind zeal forced the Hellenic philosophers to seek refuge with the king of Persia.

The Platonic Academy at Florence, founded in the fifteenth century under the protection and patronage of the Medici as a free scholarly association, was dedicated to the spread and defense of Platonic philosophy, especially in the form it had received from the Neoplatonists, and above all to the dissemination of its sources.

Until then the name of the Academy had remained true to its origin; for until then it designated an
association of philosophers, and indeed of those whose orientation was speculative, and specifically Platonic speculative, or who at least Platonized.

I pass over less famous societies; only in passing do I mention the foundation of Bernardino Telesio, the Academy of Cosenza, which indeed gave natural philosophy an empirical direction, yet was nonetheless a philosophical one, and, although not Platonic, was the declared opponent of the Peripatetics.

But all the significant scholarly associations that have been founded under this name since the French Academy established under Louis XIV, the model for all that followed, have little or nothing in common merely with Platonic philosophy, but almost uniformly with speculative philosophy in general; the latter has rather remained, from Scholasticism onward, as an inalienable inheritance to the institutions of higher learning that stem from the Middle Ages, the universities, which have likewise, by misuse, called themselves academies.

The academies have preferentially become those learned academic bodies in which the mathematical, physical, historical, and philological—taken as a whole, the not speculative but learned and empirical—branches of knowledge are cultivated: these, with the exception of mathematics, which was especially highly esteemed and promoted by Plato, are precisely those that lay furthest from the original Academy and instead fell to the Peripatetics.
And ever more and more has the name of the Academy spread around it.

If one of those old owners of the Athenian Academy were to awaken, how he would have to marvel if he found the academies of all the sciences and arts—musical and philharmonic and singing and painting academies, indeed even agricultural and forestry and commercial academies, and how many other institutions and establishments—adorned with this much-beloved name of his garden!

Truly the hero—or, as a poet calls him, the god Hekademos—to whom, when the immortals divided the earth among themselves, there fell only that modest outlying estate before the Double Gate of Athens, rich in olives and shade, where the plane tree whispered to the elm and musical cicadas chirped down from the branches, has in the most recent times made significant acquisitions, and has won from Hermes and his betrothed Philologia, from Apollo and
the Muses, indeed even from the gods of the woods and fields, very noble and very considerable properties.

Our Academy of Sciences has exchanged the hero Hecademus for a greater and more substantial one, for Leibniz: to him it renders—though not with offerings of flesh and banquets, yet with a solemn and public commemoration of his memorial day—truly heroic honors.

And rightly so: for he embraced everything that a university, by present-day notions, ought to embrace, and indeed somewhat more besides; he was, in general, a thoroughly academic nature; although, for reasons of religious confession, because he did not wish to convert to the Catholic Church, he declined as a young man the position offered to him in the still new Paris Academy, he sought everywhere to found academies wherever he trusted himself to have influence enough for it or believed he could find suitable ground for it.

His versatility, indeed his universality, therefore presents the observer with countless facets; and if we, the presiding officers of the Academy, are not inclined to count ourselves fortunate that one and the same man, after a few years, must again and again speak about the same great men on the same recurring occasion, in an official capacity and indeed by virtue of a secondary office to which one can devote only a lesser share of one's activity, as orator of the academic body—whereby one almost inevitably falls into repeating earlier thoughts, and perhaps also, because the enthusiasm for the honoree has lost its freshness, gradually lets the tone sink or even once falls into a wearisome one—then with this many-sided subject one seems least exposed to this danger.

But it only seems so: for Leibniz, to be sure, has many sides; but the man who is often to speak about him does not have them, and cannot have them, even if he possessed very great intellectual powers, given the present state of the sciences: he will therefore easily relapse again into turning out the same sides, especially at the same place and before roughly the same assembly, where only general reflections are expected, and not, for instance, the exposition of individual parts of Leibniz's doctrines or inventions.

Nothing lies closer at hand here than to speak of Leibniz's academic spirit, and above all of his relations to the Academy here, of the
intentions he had in founding it, of the scope he gave it, of the perspectives it was to pursue according to his plans; but since I have already spoken of this at greater length earlier, I confine myself today to discussing two individual points belonging to this subject, points that are not remote from the movements of our own time either: the relation of the Academy, on the one hand, to philosophy and, on the other, to Christianity according to the view of this, its founder.

Twenty-nine years ago now—that is, almost a generation ago, toward the end of which something from the internal history of the Academy may be related without offense—the dissolution of the Academy's then philosophical class was proposed, after that class had long been ailing, chiefly at the instigation of Schleiermacher and its other few members, because the conviction had been reached that a separate philosophical division was not really appropriate to an Academy, since metaphysical subjects were suited neither to joint treatment nor to fruitful discussion, and consequently philosophical speculation, as a distinct scholarly activity, was of all things least receptive to and in need of support through an academic association; moreover, philosophy must dwell equally in all classes, and with the exception of the metaphysical, all the other branches of philosophy could be dealt with partly in the physical and partly in the philological-historical class.

The cause of philosophy, which the men of the profession seemed to have abandoned, was taken under the protection of a high-minded statesman, and to those men he replied on this point: precisely philosophical knowledge, genuine philosophical speculation, must find its place in the Academy; it was not suited to the universities; it flourished only when men could devote themselves to it wholly and exclusively, solely for the sake of the subject itself: such a position only the Academy could grant; within it could be brought up for discussion and debated what otherwise, out of fear of misunderstanding, from an ordinary and narrow standpoint, could nowhere be brought up for discussion: one would not wish to give one's voice to
abolishing the philosophical class of an Academy whose first president was Leibniz, and it could not be justified to refuse to recognize the scientific value of philosophy in itself, without an inclination toward another branch of science.

Germany in particular, he said, ought not in this matter to follow the example of other countries, which at that time were probably inferior to that one in the correct estimation and treatment of philosophy; the more harshly philosophy was threatened in recent times, and the more incorrect the views about it were, the more important it remained to secure for it a place of its own in the Academy of Sciences." Truly remarkable words, and noble and magnanimous reasons for the protection of philosophy!

Yet the most striking reason for retaining the philosophical class, the most penetrating arrow shot, aimed so truly at the heart—the reference to Leibniz's relation to our Academy—could be turned aside without difficulty by the observation that in the old Leibnizian constitution of the Royal Society of Sciences, for which, as anything but a philosophical association, the name of Academy had been skillfully avoided, no class of philosophy existed at all, but only one for the natural sciences including medicine, a second for pure and applied mathematics, a third for German—especially Prussian—secular and ecclesiastical history and the German language, a fourth for literature, chiefly Oriental, for the propagation of the Gospel among the unbelievers: a philosophical class, however, was first established under Maupertuis in the year 1744, and the last two of the former classes were then merged together, without any further mention of Oriental literature and its connection with religion: from which it was then concluded, not without justice, that "speculative philosophy seemed to have quite properly taken the place, as a contrast, of the earlier-mentioned relation to Christianity."
How did it come about, then, that Leibniz, the philosopher, excluded philosophy from a Royal Society of Sciences?

Did he too already believe that philosophical activity permits no community and that discussion of metaphysical subjects yields no gain for knowledge, even though
he exchanged letters on philosophical subjects with so many persons, and even though philosophizing together is almost as old as philosophizing itself, and was practiced very extensively, especially in the Platonic Academy, albeit under an outstanding leader?
Was it enough for him too that the philosophical spirit should make itself felt in the particular sciences?
Or did he believe that he would find too little sympathy among his patrons for speculative philosophy, or too few philosophical men to form a philosophical society?

These questions, some of which I raised earlier without being able to answer them, I now settle by declaring them superfluous, because the exclusion of philosophy from the Leibniz Society of Sciences seems to be intelligible from a peculiar point of view, in which a keen and ingenious historian of modern philosophy finds grounds for Leibniz's zeal for the founding of academies, or with which this zeal is at least closely connected.

Our hero had, namely, conceived the idea of a universal science, or, as Erdmann finds himself justified in calling it, a universal doctrine of science, of which he entertained the greatest expectations.

His task was a twofold one: to examine and judge what had already been recognized, and to find new knowledge, and indeed from what is given; but what is given is for him partly facts or contingent truths, partly eternal and necessary truths knowable a priori; and to say nothing of the latter, in the case of the former he assumes a graduated scale of significance, and posits as the most important of them certain fundamental facts, from which others could be derived with the help of the correct method: these fundamental or principal facts would have to be collected and encyclopedias and repertories formed, in which the quintessence of all discoveries would be contained, and which would afford entirely the benefit of logarithmic tables, which made calculation easier.
Such factual data should bring together scholars connected with one another, in order to make possible that work continue without loss of time.

If in this connection the academies were chiefly in his mind,
without our wishing, to be sure, to maintain that he did not also expect the ascertaining of individual new facts from their members, then such societies certainly had no need of professional philosophers—unless he also meant to accomplish the bringing together of eternal truths or pure rational cognitions in a similar manner, which he certainly, with great justice, did not mean to do.
It seems rather that in the manner indicated the necessary empirical material was merely to be supplied through learned societies to the philosopher standing outside them.

But whether this project (for a touch of project-mongering, to which that age had a certain inclination, comes to light in Leibniz rather often and was sometimes necessary to him in order to win over the great), whether this project, I say, could have had a scientific result of significance—that I would doubt.

Since Leibniz, enough encyclopedias and repertories have appeared; but they have hardly become such logarithmic tables as would shorten the course of scholarship: even granting that the encyclopedias had the greatest possible perfection, the researcher in important matters can nevertheless never easily take up precisely where those leave off, but must as a rule traverse once more the whole path that the investigation has taken, and generate within himself once again, independently, what has been found; he cannot, however, without having transformed the earlier into his flesh and blood, and in particular without recognizing it in the context of the whole of science—which is won only through lengthy and comprehensive studies—proceed from given premises: the speculations of the philosophers themselves, insofar as they relate to matters of fact, frequently suffer precisely from this, that the latter have not acquired the empirical by the indicated manner through penetrating research, but have merely received it as a lemma from the researchers and consequently have come to know it imperfectly.

Even if Leibniz, to whom this certainly was not unknown, was in a position to use results that had been deposited in such repertories in order, as he puts it, to calculate further with them, most people would presumably not be capable of this, or would set up very false calculations in this way.

Time, too, the surest tester of all things, has not justified such a purpose for
scholarly associations: far from these having worked out encyclopedias and repertories, they have rather thrown themselves precisely upon the opposite, upon the monographic, have set individual points in a clear light, have advanced the progress of the sciences through individual investigations, and thereby certainly had more effect than could have been possible through the production of repertories; indeed, nowadays people may be fairly agreed that encyclopedias, with few exceptions, do not themselves extend science or even form a foundation for its extension, but rather chiefly disseminate science only among wider circles, and thereby also very easily become shallow.

Individual academicians could, to be sure, be living encyclopedias, just as Leibniz himself was an entire academy and an encyclopedia of encyclopedias; but for that they would need even greater leisure and freedom from business than he had, and the academies an endowment such as is not to be expected, indeed for many reasons is not even to be demanded at all.

Leibniz had, as was said, intended a part of the Academy to be devoted to the treatment of church history and in particular to the propagation of the Gospel among the unbelievers: it seems that a theological-philosophical man of the first rank covertly reproached Frederick the Great, or Herr von Maupertuis, with having put philosophy in the place of Christianity, although the same acute and profound thinker was otherwise for the most part not especially well disposed toward Leibniz.

Leibniz's lively participation in everything pertaining to the Church, and thus also in the history of the Church and of dogma, is well known; but as regards the other point that I have just emphasized, he undoubtedly wished for the spread of Christianity for its own sake, and at the same time because from the missions and conversion institutions—so frequently attacked in recent times and indeed not always attaining their purpose—he expected the establishment of a more humane and more moral condition among the heathen and an enrichment of the sciences.

Nowadays the linking of academic activity to missions and conversions appears so strange that we must admit that this Leibnizian view has not been
borne out by time; and some share in the fact that he gave the Royal Society of Sciences this secondary purpose may well have been due to his extraordinary skill in accommodating himself to other inclinations and ideas.

So far as I know, no empirical science is forgiven accommodation to ideas that lie outside science; philosophers have not seldom allowed themselves such accommodation: indeed, the name "Christian philosophy"—a designation which, moreover, if I am not mistaken, was not yet familiar to our Leibniz, and which, although he occupied himself with confessional questions more than any other modern philosopher, lay outside his horizon—this name points to some extent to a fairly frequent accommodation of philosophizing.

I hold the opinion of him, as of Descartes, and not to his discredit, that he was not entirely in earnest about everything; but even where he is in earnest, mediation very often presents the greatest difficulties, and where he touches on theology, he may not always have succeeded.

Leibniz stood at the height of ideal speculation, in order from there to penetrate the universe in all its phenomena and to see through it in its concordance: the highest summit of all speculation is philosophical theology, in which the unconditional harmony must also be recognized; the mediating beings between God and the phenomena are, for Plato, the Ideas, for Leibniz the monads, to which, as Lacroze maintained against Leibniz himself, he seems to have been guided by Giordano Bruno.

To save himself from Spinozism, he posits independent monads; but when he arrives at the concept of God in his ontological investigations, the monads lose their independence and become fulgurations or emanations of God, and he falls right back into the notorious Spinozism.
Thus, then, in speculative theology the most important mediation did not succeed for him.
It must have been still more difficult, for one who has dared to call the universal harmony God, to reconcile philosophy with ecclesiastical theology, if he thought consistently.

Skillfully he took the way out of merely placing the two side by side, of saying that dogma does not contradict philosophy, that philosophy can
prove the possibility of dogma, but not its truth.
But precisely in order to prove this possibility, he sacrificed the consistency of his system.

Already early, in the year 1673*), he had believed that he could demonstrate the possibility of the real presence of the body of Christ in the Lord's Supper, indeed even of transubstantiation; but since space was nothing real to him and bodies were only appearances, he was brought into difficulties precisely with regard to this real presence, because, under his presuppositions, as was objected to him, Christ's body too would be only an appearance; and so he came, evidently driven or prompted by others, being as if made for uniting and mediating and likewise always inclined to it, gradually persuading himself in the best or even the worst case, later on to invent the so-called substantial bond, incompatible with his idealism, by virtue of which the body was to become a unity through itself and more than an appearance.
In this, it seems to me, he nevertheless did what I earlier wanted to acquit him of along with Lessing: he accommodated his teaching to the dogma.

Finally, I can surely leave it to anyone's judgment whether the connection just mentioned—a connection, perhaps timely in its day, between a purpose in itself certainly serious and well meant, and in many cases beneficial, and the Society of Sciences—is suited to the essential nature of an academy; for by our conceptions such an academy does not, as under Louis XIV, insist on an exclusive confession of faith; rather our Academy is—what even under Frederick the Great was still without example, although already earlier, in an age more inclined to religious struggles, a Protestant Elector had offered a professorship at a university to the noble, or in the words of Fr. H. Jacobi and Schleiermacher, the holy Spinoza—our Academy is, I say, now in fact accessible to scholars of every confession; already five years ago it counted it an honor to elect a distinguished man of the Mosaic religion as its full member: a proof that it has also advanced somewhat further in the views that move the age than some would have one believe.
I can [place it] even earlier; see above, p. 314.

Note
also to leave it to each person's own decision whether that connection favored by Leibniz is to be counted among his fortunate attempts at mediation, or whether it is a potentially dangerous conflation of heterogeneous domains and standpoints, and whether Frederick the Great and President Maupertuis, or Leibniz, hit upon the truer view of the matter itself and without regard to particular circumstances.

But should anyone find it inappropriate if I have once turned up a side of this wonderful subject that speaks to us less, then I have not only had in this very place a predecessor worthy of imitation, but I also consider it more decent to think for myself than always merely to proclaim the unconditional praise of the great master.

I cannot and will not conceal the fact that my views on this point agree only with those of the great King; and I have already declared myself on another occasion to the effect that, as it seems to me, the Academy offers a convenient ground for philosophy, because philosophy requires the full freedom of cognition, yet nowhere is it less demanded than at this place that philosophizing should accommodate itself to predetermined notions; for the Academy is, according to its laws—the palladium of its existence—devoted to the general sciences without any particular teaching purpose, and least of all can philosophy here be regarded as an auxiliary science of theology, which more than any other practical branch of instruction has long been foreign to the Academy; least of all can there be any question here of philosophizing according to the standard of positive dogmas." This freedom, and the whole of scientific freedom, the Academy claims for itself, and, so far as I can judge of it from my own experience, it has never been disputed, nor has it ever been surrendered by the Academy.
