div.head: XXVIII. Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Dieterici als neu eingetretenen Mitgliedes der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 8. Juli 1847.
Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Dieterici in der Akademie

p.s: In my capacity as secretary of the philosophical-historical class of the Academy, and for the present as its sole secretary, I have today to welcome you, most honored Herr Colleague, as our new member.

Such a greeting is brief and not burdensome; it is a gratifying task. Yet I am not the worthiest person for it: more fittingly called to it was my friend of many years and harmonious colleague in the secretariat, whose studies lie closer to your own.

You have set forth that great and far-reaching, stimulating achievements in the field of statistics have emerged from the bosom of the Academy; however, this is mostly accidental, because what members of the Academy accomplish is not yet accomplished precisely in and by the Academy; the names of a Leibniz and an Alex. von Humboldt adorn the Academy, but they belong to the whole world.

Only recently has it ceased to be regarded as merely a matter of chance when statistics is promoted by the Academy; of late it has recognized it as an essential need of its scholarly association to have a representative of statistics in its midst; it has designated a separate position for such a one, and since our worthy Hoffmann, weakened by age and illness, can no longer fill it, you are here, as elsewhere, his natural and in the first instance rightful successor.

The Academy encompasses all those sciences that are not merely practical or positive—that is, in truth, all science: for the practical is merely the application of knowledge in action, not a knowledge itself; and where the power of the positive begins, there the force of cognition
ends.

Knowledge is directed partly toward nature, partly toward the spirit and its development in the history of the human race; in both principal domains it strives to recognize the laws, the immortal harmony of reason.

The laws of nature are immutable and bound in eternal fetters; the spirit unfolds itself freely, but its highest freedom is equal to the highest necessity, and however much the forms of the state, within which—as the all-embracing organism of society—the intellectual development moves, may change and be reshaped, all state relations too possess a more than positive lawfulness, which has been recognized for thousands of years, ever since it was recognized—what later the practical men forgot or obscured—that politics is a part of ethics.

But between nature in itself and the pure works of the spirit there lies yet a third thing, which, seemingly accidental and without rule, appeared most of all to mock reduction to laws and thus to scientific knowledge, and therefore was for the most part left to unconscious and instinctive practice—I mean, to designate it by a general and current word, the so-called material interests, which for that reason form a transition from the natural to the spiritual and a mediation between the two, because in them nature appears employed for human and state purposes and, as it were, raised to the ethical.
These are the subject of the theory of public finance and of a large part of statistics, which supplies the former with its surest foundations.

Man, weak and insignificant before the eternal God, yet the mightiest of all mortal beings, has subjected nature to himself since time immemorial; her strongest and wildest powers are steered and guided by him, as a boy steers the bold horse with a small rein: but how all these natural elements are to be ordered and interwoven into the full harmony of civil life, and what laws they follow in the household of the people and of the state, has only later than the more spiritual laws of politics been attempted to be fathomed scientifically and artistically.

And yet, how can a people raise itself politically and intellectually, and maintain itself at its height, if it loses its prosperity
through neglect or perverted use of the means thereto?

So that this may not happen, the sciences are needed for that purpose—the sciences to which your leisure is devoted; and once science has taken hold of these subjects, there is again no need to fear that state and people will sink and perish in the material, or will neglect the cultivation of the spiritual and of that which gives the spirit its highest uplift—the free development of reason—without which all earthly goods are not only worthless but would also soon themselves be lost, and which, precisely for that reason, in a higher sense is the most material gain for a people.
In this sense, I am certain of it, you grasp the task of your life; and therefore you are welcome to me, and therefore welcome to us all, at this place!

div.head: XXIX. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Jahrestages Friedrichs des Grofsen am 25. Januar 1849.
Ueber Friedrichs des Grofsen Ausübung der unumschränkten Macht

p.s: Today's celebration honors a man of world-historical stature, a hero and commander who may without flattery be compared to an Alexander and a Caesar, and to whom among later men only the one Napoleon approaches in vigor of action; a man who in peace was as great as in war, who as a true statesman-artist won for his country, despite all the exhaustion brought on by protracted struggles, prosperity and flourishing and a European significance; a man who, alongside military and political activity, nonetheless devoted so much leisure to art and science that we need not shrink from calling him rather a sage and scholar than a lover of wisdom and learning: his day of honor, which deserved to be commemorated by the whole land, is here commemorated by a society whose second and more effective founder he was, and which, established by him as the first scholarly community of this realm, was fostered and honored by him with particular affection.

If a world-historical fame can be enhanced by such a festival of honor as little, or even less, than by any vivid monument, then the significance of the festival lies only in grateful remembrance of the merits of the one honored, in joyful acknowledgment of those merits, and in the strengthening and invigoration that the present wishes to draw from the past, and the grandchildren from the memory of their forebears: later generations dedicate festivals and monuments to their great ancestors for their own sake; they honor themselves in the honor they pay to the sublime spirits of the ancient world; they bear witness that they know how to value greatness, that
in grateful hearts they feel that, just as children owe thanks to their parents, so in state and people the descendants are obligated to those who earlier raised up state and people; they thereby make a vow of fidelity, to follow the example of their forebears and, according to their powers and each according to his own station, to work for the welfare and honor of the fatherland.

This noble feeling has never entirely died out among noble peoples; other things besides statues and festivities are rooted in it: people have even honored the merits of ancestors in their descendants, even when those descendants were no longer personally distinguished; just as the Athenians once granted high privileges to the undeserving son of Aristides, and the world-ruling Romans forgave the Athenians for the sake of their forefathers.

Only recently this feeling has also shown itself vividly among the Germans, in the newly awakened zeal for the erection of monuments—extending all the way up to Hermann the Cheruscan—and for honorary foundations of every kind.
And woe to the people that, in the urge of progress, would deny its earlier history!

We have now reached the point where no one can any longer think of living merely in the memory of the ancient world, of forever looking backward and wishing to preserve the earlier condition like a mummy: we know that we ourselves must act and bring forth, must shape what is our own and new, as the course of world history requires, and that in the life of men and of the state nothing comes to be if one does nothing but forever wait until something makes itself of its own accord: for human conditions do not grow involuntarily like the formations of nature, but are meant to be created through actions: yet if we strive forward, we must not go so far as to break entirely with the past, as someone has said.

A Roman would have called such a demand parricidal; whoever makes it forgets that the present is a child of the past, that we are begotten by our parents and did not spring from the oak and the stone: he must with sacrilegious hand destroy the graves of his forefathers, so that he may appear as one originally born of the earth.
Ingratitude is a sure mark of an ignoble nature.

Not without reason may it seem striking that I, as it were,
excuse or at least first justify the commemorative celebration of the greatest man of his century, the most brilliant star in the history of Prussia, with this introduction, and indeed in an assembly that owes its existence to him, and especially since, as far as is known, no one has yet found this often-repeated celebration unjustified.
I therefore freely confess that it is perhaps a gloomy and false view that has disposed me to this.

The kindled sense of freedom, the swift wingbeat of a new development of the state, seems to make us dull and unreceptive to the admiration of a greatness that rose under entirely different conditions and by entirely different means than those that might suit the present mood of minds and the present circumstances, and that created something entirely different from what we now want.
The moment does not seem favorable for praising an absolute ruler.

Frankly speaking, I imagine that there are now not a few from whom one might hear something like the following: "The man whom you are celebrating was indeed a great man, like Alexander and Caesar and Napoleon; but like these he too was after all only a tyrant, and moreover a non-German ruling over Germans; and whether the Academy commemorates his honorary day or not is a matter of great indifference; for academies too are only foundations of princes and appendages of courts, they do not stand at the height of the culture of the age and do not suit the spirit of the age, which rejects all preferential treatment and assigns equal rights to all: but you wish to be especially select, and are not even chosen through a larger electoral assembly, but fill up your own ranks: we do not recognize you at all." Incapable as I am of presenting the deeds and merits of the great King, of which the world is full, compressed within the narrow compass of an academic introductory address and yet not altogether unworthily, and also not minded to remove myself from the subject of the celebration and, say, out of fear of the reality of life to take refuge in the ideal realm of scholarship, it seemed to me—much as I would gladly avoid the political here—most appropriate to the present moment to address precisely that which I have just put into the mouths of others.

Just as every great man has opponents and enemies
among his contemporaries and in posterity, so against Frederick three things in particular have been asserted: his conduct toward religion, his conduct toward what is national and popular, and his exercise of unlimited power.
The first two points have been discussed so extensively that I touch on them only in passing.

Frederick was not a dogmatic Christian like his forebears, but neither was he the despiser of God that he had been decried as: he held the religion of man and of the philosopher, and amid the turmoil of the most restless and most cunning political life he preserved more heart and feeling and sympathy than most in similar circumstances, and that too is a religion; toward all positive religion he was, as private man and as ruler, as indifferent as the state itself now is, and yet not wholly unreceptive to the elevation into which the devout mind is transported by churchly worship of God.

To be sure, his turning away from the religious has not reached the level of those who now, with gigantic rebellion, banish all reverence for a higher moral being from their own hearts and those of their disciples, and would fain eradicate the very name of God, in order to found humanity upon its own strength and, as they suppose, to establish freedom.
This reproach, which struck him most deeply, may therefore be considered to have fallen silent, or to be raised against him only by a small party.
I shall likewise be brief in addressing the second charge.

Frederick did not love French in such a way that he would have sacrificed the advantage of the Germans to a foreign advantage; not in such a way that out of a mania for imitation he would have wished to inject French attitudes, customs, and institutions into his country: he sought cultivation, and found it first of all in French literature; he made this language his own, which at that time was the language of the greater part of the educated, and, when during his reign the German language had received its development, he could no longer reshape himself and take part in the more recent advances of the national tongue, which he only sensed in advance when much of it was already fulfilled.
How, after all, could one wish that instead of French he had made use of the uneducated German tongue, of which he was so masterful?

Even if he loved French society and drew French scholars to the capital, he
did not aim to make his country French, but rather to enjoy and spread culture and learning. If in doing so he neglected German scholars, I will not excuse this; yet I doubt that those German scholars who, by virtue of their intellect, would have been suited to a closer relationship with him would have brought themselves to the dependence into which a Marquis d'Argens entered.
But I come now to his absolute rule.

If I have allowed the designation "tyrant" to be used in reference to him, it goes without saying that in my sense it contains no moral censure of his conduct, but is taken in its original political meaning and is meant to denote only rule according to arbitrary will, as opposed to rule according to law; thus it concerns not at all the content of the actions, but only the form.

There is so little that is offensive in this expression that Pindar, in an ode addressed to Hieron, the prince of Syracuse, calls him himself without hesitation a tyrant, when he says: "The lot of happiness follows you; for upon the people-ruling tyrant, if upon any man, shines the great fortune." As long as the political consciousness in a people is not yet developed, that distinction between arbitrary and lawful rule does not yet exist, and therefore even the name of a tyrant was at that time unknown; the kingship was a patriarchal one with the will of the ruled, and the king ruled as the living law after the likeness of paternal authority, with which a very natural belief connected a divine right, indeed originally even divine descent and the highest priesthood belonging to the god-descended one and to the patriarch: not as if the kingship had necessarily been propagated from the paternal authority passed down from the household father through primogeniture by means of the expansion of the family into a tribal people, but because the peoples have found it necessary to transfer that paternal authority to one man, in order, as Frederick himself teaches*), for their peace and preservation, to have judges for the decision of their disputes, defenders against the enemy, a supreme ruler for the *) Antimach.

Vol. VIII, p. 65 of the new edition,
to have the unification of their various advantages in one common advantage.

But as soon as political consciousness has awakened, a distinction arises between the ruler according to arbitrary will and the ruler or king according to law, as Aristotle already names him; indeed, only then can there be any talk of a lawful or an unlawful ruler, because in the condition of patriarchal rule the state is only a larger family, and in the family only custom and tradition prevail, not the measuring out of rights according to a law.

That, now, with political consciousness, unlimited or arbitrary power over everything in the state—with the exception of a temporary dictatorship, extended at most, under the utmost pressure of circumstances, to the lifetime of a single person—should have been legally transferred is unthinkable; "one would have to be," says Frederick the Great,*) "caught up in madness to imagine that men had said to one of their own kind: We raise you above us because we love to be slaves, and we give you the power to direct our thoughts according to your will; they said to him," he continues, "on the contrary: We need you in order to uphold the laws which we wish to obey, in order to govern us wisely, in order to defend us; finally we demand of you that you respect our freedom." Perpetual arbitrary power has therefore usually been acquired without law, under the indolent and uncomprehending gaze of the people, and in many cases by cunning or force, suddenly or gradually—not seldom, to be sure, to the greatest advantage of the people—and, in consequence of its usefulness for certain periods, or from weariness with the rule of the nobility or with ochlocracy, through the length of time, as it were through prescription, further through habit, the trust and affection of the people, and by means of inheritance in distinguished ruling houses, it has attained a recognized legitimacy, confirmed in fact by formal homage; but in a higher sense we shall call constitutional rule lawful, according to the truth of the concept, because in it the ruler governs in accordance with the law*) both with respect to the acquisition and to the exercise of rule. *) Essai sur
les formes de gouvernement et sur les devoirs des souverains, vol. IX, p. 208.

The happiness and security of the state in which this rule is founded are increased to a high degree when that rule is one that has been hereditary for centuries and is thus bound up with the people through mutual love and common advantage; and if previously the rule had rested only on the basis of patriarchal tradition or on the legality of inheritance, it is now secured—especially in times of great turmoil—against every contradiction, however apparent, by being transformed into a constitutional one.

If Frederick *), after speaking of tyrannical usurpation, sets forth three lawful ways of becoming master of a country—hereditary succession, the election by the peoples who have the power to do so, and the conquest of a province from an enemy through a justly undertaken war—then one must grant him entirely right in this: for even the third, though a dubious kind, rests on a contract of submission. Yet one will find it missing that, although he spoke of usurpation beforehand, he does not note that dominion obtained through hereditary succession or election can also become usurpatory through exceeding the lawful powers.

He does not prefer the legitimacy conferred by hereditary succession to that conferred by election; on the contrary, he says in this connection**: "For more than one reason I must love the blood of the heroes; but I love merit still more." Frederick the Second had, in order to follow his own determinations, the legitimacy of the first and the third kind, through hereditary succession and conquest; but the inherited power was an arbitrary one—we must admit it even against our will—and its arbitrariness had come strongly to the fore in his father; moreover, this power had, before the time of the monarchy, not been attained without the removal of existing rights and restrictions, although here too it was attained for the true benefit of the country and with its consent and satisfaction.
This lawfulness and factual legitimacy do not yet correspond to the full concept, Antimachus.
Antimachus.

not the
doctrines of the state that have now come into currency, which could even be derived from Frederick's own propositions; rather, since his rule, like that of a Pittacus and Periander, who were counted among the Seven Sages, or that of a Trajan, Antoninus Pius, and Marcus Antoninus, was limited only by the limitation that the wise and temperate man imposes upon his own resolutions, his sovereign power, as he had received it, remained an arbitrary one: yet by this designation—I repeat it so as to leave room for no misinterpretation—only the form of the acts of government is touched, not their content and essence.
Was the great king, then, lacking in awareness of the excellence of a constitutionally limited monarchy?

By no means: even before Montesquieu's praise of the English constitution, Frederick* says: "It seems to me that if there is a government whose wisdom one could set up as a model in our days, it is that of England; here the Parliament is the arbiter between the people and the king, and the king has all power to do good, but he has none to do evil." Why, then, has he done nothing during his long reign to moderate the absolute power in his kingdom?

On this point there is more than one answer; but all of them, if I am not mistaken, agree in this: that no just reproach attaches to him, and that he hit upon the right course for his time and position.

The true statesman knows the unconditionally good, or the best, in the state; but at the same time he recognizes how much of it is possible according to circumstances. Yet what is possible in the state is not to be called that which no external power stands invincibly against, but rather what is useful to it; and what is useful to it, that the statesman is necessarily obliged to do.
Whoever wants to realize the impossible certainly does harm, even if it is in itself better than the possible; and whoever does not recognize the useful as the necessary falls short of his duty.
As for unlimited power, then, history teaches—especially the history of republics—that it is at times necessary; it therefore appears among the peoples most accustomed to freedom, under *) Antimach.

p. 125.
the name of aesymnetia or dictatorship, not only for protection against external foes, but also in order, when the state is inwardly shaken in its foundations, to lead it back again into the path of order and to set it aright: it is a necessary remedy against dissensions and civil wars, a poison that acts as a medicine.

Moderation of the people can avert its application; but when the wild torrent of passions and of lawlessness threatens to burst through all dikes and to bring about the general overthrow not merely of a particular form of state but of the entire social order, civilization, and culture, and to sweep away at once what centuries have sown and planted, then timely dictatorship is the only anchor of salvation, and, so to speak, a necessity of nature, whose justification may indeed, as with the Romans, lie in the constitution itself, but where this is not provided for, lies, like that of every political upheaval, outside the law and only in success.

Frederick says: “The floods that lay waste the lands, the lightning that reduces cities to ashes, the plague-poison that depopulates provinces, are not so pernicious to the world as the dangerous morality and the unbridled passions of kings; the scourges of heaven last only for a time, destroy only certain regions, and these losses, however keenly they are felt, are made good again: but the crimes of kings bring suffering upon whole peoples for long periods of time.” What he here does not scruple to declare before his own peers, equity requires us to apply also to their opponents, who are manifestly capable of causing as much or even greater calamity, and have caused it, and whose morality is no less pernicious than the Machiavellian morality against which Frederick here speaks.
Where the weapons of reason no longer suffice against such minds, one must resort to the last means, to dictatorship.

Furthermore, in the regular development of states and of history there are stages or periods in which absolute rule is borne by the entire system of states and is necessary for the strengthening of the individual countries.

Of the latter France gives a great example, which would never have reached the summit of its power had not Richelieu's despotism and Mazarin's cunning so increased the royal
authority against the great men of the realm and against the parliaments that Louis the Fourteenth could even declare himself to be the state.

The former, however, proves itself throughout Frederick's entire age by the predominant pursuit of dynastic aims: Frederick the Great at least did not separate these from the purpose of the state; rather, his house served more the formation of an independent empire than the state served the family purpose. He created a power that entered the ranks of the European powers with a distinctive character and calling, a state of world-historical future, which, amid severe struggles and changing fortunes, moved toward the, as we hope, not yet completed solution of great tasks.

The founding of such an empire was not possible without unlimited power—not possible without first creating a military state and, through wars and victories, acquiring a glory that became the most precious inheritance of the people and a mighty support of the empire.

A small state, attackable from every side, not protected in the long run by the jealousy of other powers or by particular treaties and alliances, perishes all the more certainly in a struggle with more powerful neighbors if all authority is not lodged in one firm hand.

Even Demosthenes, when he weighs the advantages that the absolute ruler Philip had over him, excellently emphasizes that Philip commanded those who followed him with unlimited power in what is the first of all things in war; that these men then always had their weapons in their hands; that, rich in money, he did whatever pleased him each time, without announcing it beforehand in decrees of the people, without being able to be called to account by others—alone lord, leader, and potentate over all things.

Only by uniting this full power in himself was Frederick able to emerge victorious from the struggles that secured the land's independence and won for the future a position commanding respect: it is a blessing when Providence sends a great man to a people precisely at the moment when it needs an absolute rule, a man on whom, as Frederick says somewhere,*), the weight of his government rests as the world rests on the back of Atlas. *) Antimach.

who
regulates internal as well as external affairs and at the same time fills the offices of chief magistrate, commander-in-chief, and lord high treasurer.

For in his time there was also much to set in order and to arrange in domestic affairs; and it is very doubtful whether what he accomplished as sole ruler would have come about under a freer form of government, and whether the errors into which he fell would then have been avoided, since the principles from which they arose were shared by his age along with him.

Moreover, everything has its time, and "too early" is just as dangerous as "too late"; but constitutional endeavors—not to speak of political maturity—did not yet lie in the spirit of that age, and a need for freer political development was little felt.

Finally, like his lofty models in antiquity, he regulated the arbitrariness of absolute power according to a higher moral principle, according to what he recognized as duty, and thus transfigured this form of rule.

Prudence, justice, and goodness were in him the predominant qualities of the ruler; apart from foreign policy, in which few at that time kept their hands clean, a passion seldom led him astray—rather, a witty notion did so.
He honestly willed the good of his people, to be sure according to the maxim "Everything for the people, nothing through the people"; but truly, had he not done it, the people would not have done it.
"The prince and his peoples," he says*), "form but one body, which can be happy only to the degree that concord unites them.

The prince is to the society he governs what the head is to the body; he must see, think, and act for the whole community, in order to procure for it all the advantages of which it is capable. Even for the lower class he had, notwithstanding all his predilection for the nobility, which has often been reproached in him, a lively sympathy; "the prince," he teaches**), "must often remind himself of the condition of the poor people; he must put himself in the place of the peasant and of the manufacturing worker, and then say to himself: If I had been born in the class of these citizens, *) Essai sur les formes de gouvernement et sur les devoirs des souverains, vol. IX, p. 200. **) Ibid.

Page
205. whose arms are their capital, what would I demand of the prince?" Serfdom is, in his eyes, the unhappiest of all conditions, and the one that most outrages human feeling: "surely no man is born," he says, "to be the slave of his equal"; he abhors this barbarous and hideous abuse, and regrets that it is impossible to abolish it at a single stroke, because one would have to overturn the entire agricultural economy and in part compensate the nobility for the losses to their incomes.
Undoubtedly, even under unlimited rule, his principles—through the general intellectual freedom that he fostered—prepared the way for political freedom as well.

His views on the difference between tyrannical and truly royal government are consistent with this, although one thing always remains outside the scope of his reflections: that a constitutional form of state first provides some guarantee for the duration of a government calculated for the welfare of the people.

"The peoples," he declares, "have given themselves supreme rulers (souverains) so that they might be protected by them, and have submitted only on this condition, whereas if they obey the usurper they sacrifice themselves and their goods to him in order to satisfy the greed and every whim of a tyrant." Or: "They called tyrants those who seized dominion by force, and who, following only their passions and whims as their guides, overturned the laws and the principles which society had established for its preservation." And we have no need of his frequently recurring words of this kind, which some have suspected of not being truthful, since the whole of his government speaks for exactly that.
Yet I will not pass over a saying that he uttered not only in his youth but also repeated often in later years, although it is on everyone's lips and rather worn by use.

While he censures Frederick the First's love of splendor and extravagance, he says**): "A prince is the first servant and the first official of the state (le premier serviteur et le premier magistrat de l'État); he is accountable to it *) Antim.
Cf.
Essai sur les formes de gouvernement, p. 197 f. **) Works, vol. I, p. 123. Cf.

Vol. IX, p. 197 and p.
208 — he is indebted for the use he makes of the taxes; he levies them in order to be able to defend the state by means of the troops he maintains, to uphold the dignity with which he is invested, to reward services and merit, to establish to some degree a balance between the rich and the indebted, to relieve the unfortunate of every kind and every class, and to display splendor in all that concerns the body politic in general.

If the ruler has an enlightened mind and an honest heart, he will direct all his expenditures toward the public good and toward the greatest advantage of his peoples." And elsewhere: "The prince is only the first servant of the state, bound to act with honesty, with wisdom, and with a perfect unselfishness, as though he had to give his citizens an account of his administration at every moment." Less well known are expressions from his youth that are stronger and exceed the measure so significantly that even the most extreme democrat would sign them with pleasure: the sovereign, far from being the absolute lord of the peoples who stand under his rule, is only their first household servant (le premier domestique); and the princes must regard the peoples not as their slaves, but as their equals and in a certain respect as their masters (leurs maîtres).

His alienation from constitutional concepts did not allow it to become clear to him that, in the most liberal shaping of kingship, the king is not the first servant of the state or official, but a power of the state; for every official is, by the nature of the matter, responsible, but a responsible king is no longer a king.

The clearest historical proof of this distinction is expressed in the fact that some civilized peoples allow the kingship to pass even to women, while it has never occurred to any of these peoples to appoint women as officials.

That estrangement goes so far that in the distinguished essay on forms of government**) of the year 1777, among the various kinds of monarchy, he does not mention at all such a one as the English, which was not unknown to him, except in a also *) Réfutation du Prince de Mach.
Vol. VIII, p. 168 (Antimach.

p. 65) and p. 298. **) p. 197
ff., an incidental remark worth our heeding, occasioned by the Roman Republic.

"The Roman democracy," he observes, "was overthrown by the people themselves; the blind mass of these plebeians allowed itself to be bribed by ambitious citizens, who subsequently enslaved them and robbed them of their freedom."

This is the fate that England has to expect if the House of Commons does not prefer the true interests of the people to the dishonorable corruption that degrades it." As Frederick's splendor has remained untarnished despite all the attacks of theologians and politicians, so will it remain hereafter through all the change of times and principles, even after the state that he raised has been transformed in all its branches, in the entire administration and constitution, in legislation and the administration of justice, in army and military affairs, in customs and taxes and the remaining finances, in all the relations of property, money, trade, and commerce, in religious and private life, in art and science.

Indeed, on conscientious consideration the accusations against him appear so weak that, at the close of this defense, I am overcome by the feeling that it was not necessary at all; meanwhile I am consoled by the thought that it is no painful reproach to a defense if it leaves the impression that it was not necessary.
Yet I do not wish to put my advocacy to this test twice in the same hour; if, then, I have mentioned voices or sentiments which [belong to] this Academy—
If they are unfavorable to Frederick, then I will let these matters rest almost entirely on their own.

Academies, to be sure, did not spring from the German spirit and have never found in Germany the approval they found in France and Italy; and it is therefore very natural, even without contributing secondary reasons, that among us they should be exposed to this or that attack.
Whether someone stands at the height of the age or not can be judged only once the barometer has been constructed with which the height of the age is to be measured.

That the academies are necessarily an appendage of the courts would seem highly doubtful for the very reason that, in the first French Republic, the National Institute was the recognized leading scholarly body.

In that republic of the most perfect equality, the whole people upheld the members of that institute, although they had not
emerged from the choice of the people or of a larger assembly of scholars: as proof that it did not wish to transfer this outflow of political equality onto the territory of the republic of letters, where it stands open to everyone, apart from the bond of a corporate community, to make himself felt as far as the reach of his spirit extends.

That learned societies, finally, apart from appointment by the state authority—of which there is no longer any question among us—should ever have replenished themselves through any election other than their own, is not known to me; and we do not claim to be anything more than a learned society, except that whatever has remained to us from Frederick the Great's endowment of this Academy we gladly share with others whose scholarly purposes stand in need of support.

The statutes of the Academy prescribe for today's celebration that, after the introductory address, a connected report be given of the events of the past year that concern the Academy, reckoned from the previous session of the same name.

The achievements of such a society consist chiefly in its scholarly accomplishments, and indeed both in the lectures delivered and in its own scholarly undertakings or those supported by it; but another day is appointed for the report on these matters.

Thus, under those events, other things are meant, and these can only be such as have either changed the position of the Academy as a whole or individual circumstances and institutions of it, or are changes that have occurred in the persons of its members.

In the first respect there is nothing essential to report; the Academy, ordered eleven years ago by well-considered statutes drawn from the experience of earlier times, has been neither extended nor restricted in its rights or in its duties, neither in its financial resources nor in its effectiveness.

If everything is being reorganized, then we do not wish to deny that the Academy too may undergo a reorganization; yet however many proposals for innovations in the field of scientific institutions have also been brought forward this year, so little of them has to date been carried
out, and the Academy could therefore at most incur the reproach that it has not itself made such proposals or accepted them from others who perceive the defects of what exists.

In this connection I do not take into account the fact that, in response to a wish communicated to it, it has given its plenary sessions a greater degree of publicity; for anyone who was really concerned with the matter could already have gained access to these sessions beforehand, and the slight use that is made of the expanded publicity proves that no significant need was to be satisfied here. But publicity for the academic class sessions is no more to be demanded than, say, publicity for the deliberations of the committees of the estates, and it would be even more purposeless than that of the plenary sessions.

But if there is to be talk of a more far-reaching so-called reform, then I would wish for such a reform, if it were possible on a grand scale and measure; but for that, above all, great means are needed, which in the present distress are presumably less to be hoped for than ever.

Anyone who knows our building more closely will find it moderately well equipped for moderate demands, and we would not wish to tear it down before a more perfect one had been founded; yet we are glad to improve it when something better has been demonstrated and what has been demonstrated proves practicable.

The other kind of events touched upon earlier consists in the change of persons; and if, with regard to the first kind of these, we had neither disadvantages nor advantages to cite, here only losses remain for us to mention.
Since the last session of the same name, the Academy has lost three foreign members through death: Berzelius in Stockholm, Letronne in Paris, Gottfr.
Hermann in Leipzig; an honorary member, Wheaton in New York; four corresponding members, de Chambray in Paris, Delbrück in Bonn, von Hormayr in Munich, Orelli in Zurich.

The very names show the magnitude, and in some respects the irreplaceability, of the losses such as scarcely any earlier year has brought: but to celebrate the departed heroes of science, for that too another academic day is appointed; and yet if, as would surely be permissible, I were to devote a few words to each of these names—partly acknowledged as great, partly highly honorable—my speech would have to fall far short of
the fame of those men.

May the seed they have so abundantly scattered also bear noble fruit in the soil of a new age, plowed through and through, an age into which only some of them have still looked, and may it not be suppressed by weeds; and may their example and memory as well bring forth upon a grateful posterity those uplifting influences which I designated at the beginning of my present address!

div.head: XXX. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 4. Juli 1850.
Vom verschiedenartigen Fortschritt in den menschlichen Dingen, über Leibniz, besonders als Philosoph und Mathematiker, und über Alexander von Humboldt

p.s: Fontenelle, in his eulogy of Leibniz, which he delivered in 1716 at the Paris Academy, after he has dealt with the invention of the differential calculus, also speaks of the experiments that Leibniz made in mechanical engineering, descending from the lofty theory.

He first cites the well-known fact that Leibniz had thought of making wagons and coaches lighter and more comfortable; a doctor, he says, who reproached Leibniz for not having received an annual salary from the Duke of Hanover, seized the opportunity to attribute to him in a public writing that he had wanted to build a vehicle that would travel from Hanover to Amsterdam in twenty-four hours—an ill-placed joke, the orator adds, because it could only redound to the glory of the man attacked, provided that the thing were not simply impossible.

Despite Fontenelle's sensible observation, it seemed absurd at the time: nowadays one may indeed ask by what means Leibniz could have intended to produce such an effect, but one must laugh at the Doctor if he believed he could make the philosopher ridiculous by nothing more effectively than by reproaching him with such an undertaking.
The attempt did not succeed.

The present advances in the application of artificially developed natural forces, which is founded on the advances of knowledge, put all previous ages to shame through the conquest—scarcely or not at all dreamed of before—of the conditions of space and time that confine mortals, and through the incalculable consequences of these inventions; if ever and by whatever means, then here and now has been vindicated what Sophocles said thousands of years ago:
"Many are the mighty things, and nothing is mightier than man." But so that we do not exalt ourselves, it is useful to observe wherein and in what domain the rapid and immeasurable advances are possible and are achieved, and wherein humanity advances so slowly, imperceptibly, and uncertainly that some may despair of whether any progress at all takes place therein.

Man is the lord of earthly creation and subjects all of sensible nature to his needs and purposes; since time immemorial he has made land and sea serviceable to himself through agriculture and mining and navigation, and at the same time the whole animal world capable of any taming, and he also catches untamable creatures for his consumption: after he has subjugated open nature to himself, he also gradually draws from hidden nature more and more of its secrets, not only observing, as originally, with unarmed senses, but through the ingeniously and inventively devised means or apparatus and instruments of experiment, combined with measurement and calculation, he sets the forces thus discovered in activity according to his will by machinery and compels them into the direction that corresponds to his intentions.
Everything sensory and individual is finite and limited, and yet with this finite material he knows how to almost overleap the bounds of finitude, or nearly to expand them into the unbounded.

In this respect one age surpasses another extraordinarily, and, unless great upheavals so destroy or throw back the entire state of civilization of mankind, or of a great part thereof, that it must begin again as from the egg, the later age surpasses the earlier ones.
On the largest scale, the comparison of classical antiquity with the most recent centuries supplies the proof of this.

In the age of Louis XIV especially, which seemed to surpass all earlier ages, the dispute flared up over whether the ancients or the moderns had achieved greater things; Charles Perrault, in his poem "The Age of Louis the Great," exalted this golden age above all else, and in his Parallel between the Ancients and the Moderns he showed how gloriously far the latter had brought it.

Others entered the lists on behalf of the ancients; out of a misunderstood zeal for the honor of antiquity, almost all the inventions of modern times were soon claimed for it
as well—printing, the microscope, burning glasses, burning mirrors, telescopes, clocks, the Copernican world system, magnetism and electricity, and more of the like.

It is true that in the ancients there lie beginnings or presentiments, prior knowledge or hints of all this, and that the discoverers in part proceeded from these; it is further true that the keenness of the senses, and the attention and exactness of observation connected with it, enabled them to recognize many things that were rediscovered by the moderns only late, or even after long denial: I cite by way of example the sting in the lion's tail, at which people smiled before Blumenbach, the live-bearing of sharks, which our Joh.

Müller has restored to honor, the family of plants, the judging of empyemas by ear, for which the ancients had no need of a stethoscope: but although they also possessed a natural aptitude in mechanical matters, as especially their buildings show, although in this they even achieved such great things that it appears incomprehensible to the men of the profession and therefore, despite the most conclusive testimonies, fabulous, as [for instance] their great ships; yet it cannot be denied that they were not capable of more precisely determining and grounding their fairest presentiments, because they developed the instrumental [sciences] but little, partly because the age was not yet ripe for it, partly out of too aristocratic a contempt for the empirical and mechanical, to which the great minds far preferred theorems and philosophical speculation: hence also many practical matters which we have brought into scientific form were by them left almost exclusively to practice and were not reduced to general scientific principles.
Whoever wants to attribute everything to classical antiquity misjudges its spirit and worth, because he seeks it in something other than that in which it was truly great.
Empiricism—or, in German, experience—has made us great, and our mighty and most convincing advances lie in this empirical investigation of nature.
But there is yet another side of experience besides that of nature: it is the experience of human things, the investigation of all that is historical.
Who would want to deny that in this too a great advance is taking place?

The knowledge
of peoples and states has in recent times been broadened across the entire globe through extensive travels and discoveries of lands; the knowledge of past times in all directions of human activity—in the civic or political, in the religious, scientific, and artistic—has become more correct and more complete, partly through the opening of new sources, partly through the collection of the known ones, but most of all through the working-up of these sources and through more comprehensive and more penetrating research; the views of antiquity and of the Middle Ages are now almost entirely transformed; the science of languages has attained an extent against which the narrowness of antiquity forms a mighty contrast, and its mode of treatment has been changed and substantially improved by comparative linguistic research.
Here too, the most evident and most important progress lies in the empirical field and rests on an empirical foundation.
What, by contrast, is that in which humanity, and in particular its knowledge, advances most slowly?

I believe I am not mistaken when I assert that the more immaterial, inward, and spiritual things are, the more imperceptible, slight, and disputed is the progress within them; and when I have said that man, through his finite and sensory powers, almost overcomes finitude itself, then the unrestricted, unfettered—indeed, we may say infinite—spirit, by means of the resources lying within itself, advances but a little way and only very slowly beyond the boundaries to which, by virtue of its primal creative—in the etymological sense of the word, poetic—power, it has long since drawn near.

Neither observations nor experiments disclose the ultimate grounds, nor do they build a bridge from the sensible to the supersensible, from body to soul, from matter to spirit—a bridge that Leibniz had hoped to throw by means of the pre-established harmony, which sheds so little light.
Here applies what the profound poet says: "You instruments mock me, with wheel and combs, roller and hoop": no lever bursts the gate to the innermost spirit, no tool rolls up the veil of Isis.

But the highly gifted natures of all ages, even of the most ancient, are animated by the whole fullness of the freely creating supersensible power: the depth
of spiritual intuition by no means grows with the ages; spiritual content does not increase like the sum of experiences, but rather repeats itself in the most distinguished individuals, lives in each of them whole and undivided, although in its exposition it is variously conditioned and modified, and it is chiefly only in these modifications—among which I count, to be sure, many a not insignificant difference of apprehension and form, the entire technique of development and combination, and the more limited or more many-sided course of contemplation—that progress seems here to lie. Thus through all ages there runs a revelation of the most sublime speculative thoughts, not, as it were, instilled from without but springing from the spirit itself, which are at first veiled and chrysalis-like in myth, then unfold in the more ingenious philosophemes.

These great ideas of the creative spirit, which are not of yesterday, cannot so easily be multiplied by deliberate or accidental discoveries or inventions, but can only be brought out more clearly; although even this does not happen in steady progress, but they are likewise at times for a while weakened and obscured or skeptically denied, and again newly created and strengthened, and again unraveled like Penelope's web.

Precisely because they are ancient and are a Promethean gift to humanity on its thorny path of life, antiquity retains an imperishable value for the whole of posterity: for in the youthful freshness of inspiration it produced and shaped, nourished and tended those ideas, and later generations, especially amid the ever-growing dominion of cold rationalizing and corrosive criticism, can always warm and nourish spirit and mind anew at that sacred flame.

If philosophy continues to be pursued for thousands of years yet to come, Plato and Aristotle will always maintain the high rank that they held for thousands of years among philosophers and still hold among the great thinkers who are an ornament to our fatherland: these names alone suffice to show that in the domain of philosophy, with respect to ultimate grounds, progress is not of the same kind as in empirical knowledge.

Furthermore, from the original source of the creative spirit there also flows poetry,
with which it stands in much the same case.

Almost the oldest poetry among the peoples with whom our culture stands in the closest connection is the Homeric: this is so unsurpassable and in its genre so immediately anticipated the best that none of those who followed could rival Homer, and all could only learn from him: indeed the whole history of this genre in antiquity (I deliberately go no further down) shows almost only a gradual weakening of it, and rightly, already in the times of the Peloponnesian War, the sensible Choerilus of Samos began his Perseis with those remarkable words: "Ah! blessed is he who once, well skilled in song, was a servant of the Muses at the time when the meadow was still unplucked!"

Now that everything has been distributed and the arts have reached their limits, we remain the last in the race; and never does it succeed, peering everywhere with a new team, to draw near the racetrack." Surely a weighty judgment for epic poetry, and one borne out by the times that followed; although the broadly framed proposition that the arts had reached their limits*), uttered even then, provokes in us a smile similar to that of Fontenelle's or Leibniz's doctor.

Roughly the same thing that holds of the epic holds of dramatic poetry, especially when its spiritual content—which is what chiefly concerns us here—is taken into view; for no poet, not even Shakespeare himself excepted, has grasped the secrets of the spirit and the dark course of world-ruling destinies more greatly and deeply, and revealed them more clearly, than Aeschylus and Sophocles.

Even the entire form of the arts of speech—by which I mean verbal expression, which is closely bound up with the inner life—apart from whatever new element individuality may introduce into it, received in antiquity so complete a development that we must learn from it.

And, not to speak of the other arts, whose inclusion in these considerations might perhaps, and yet not with full right, seem inappropriate—what should we say of religion, which is enthroned in the innermost sanctuary of man? *) Aristotle makes a similar remark in his Politics.
II, 5, p. 1264 a 3 ff. (academic).

If with
this [adherence] the most stubborn clinging to what has been handed down is almost necessarily bound up; if Zeus and the daughter sprung from his head and the whole host of the gods of polytheism reigned for thousands of years; if centuries had to pass before the cross of the new salvation prevailed; if in fifteen hundred years Christianity, with the widest diffusion, has not only not become purer and more spiritual, but rather has been so disfigured that a far-reaching transformation of religious life was needed, and if this religious improvement had to be sought in the fullest possible return to the original, while only dreamers or fools could imagine that the empirical sciences would gain by being led back to some earlier standpoint; if finally that improvement brought forth by the Reformers has until now not been able to prosper any further to a significant degree: then we shall have to admit that in the innermost realm, the religious, progress is the most difficult and slowest of all.

But here too the moral circumstances of life and moral principles stand in a very close connection; and even if the former may in many respects have become purer and better, and the latter may perhaps have gained in systematic arrangement and interconnection, yet many an age brings unexpected relapses into a barbarism that seemed long since cast off or driven away; and the deep and sublime teachings of ethics, which were developed by the philosophers at an early date, can scarcely be surpassed.

The principles of law have undoubtedly grown milder, but they still lag far behind the demands of ethics and religion, and they advance even more slowly than moral principles do, because they are more or less a merely subsequent expression of an already established national custom and national sentiment, and can therefore change only after a significant change in these; and because the formula of law, the statute, like ecclesiastical dogma, precisely as something established not only for the present but also for the future, resists its own transformation, and even when it has outlived its time it is clung to as old law with the utmost tenacity: a tendency carried to such an extreme in the earlier antiquity that Chilon the
Spartan is said to have renounced his friendship with Solon because the latter had said that the laws are mutable.

Even political law, the constitutions of states, and political science advance very slowly: how long did it take for slavery, which Aristotle still sought to justify on thoroughly scientific grounds, to disappear from the more educated states—and yet even today it has still not entirely disappeared, even among Christians; how long did serfdom, only a more moderate form of slavery, outlast full slavery!

However much the forms of the state may have changed in theory and in practice, the categories established early on by the Greeks still assert their deplorable validity: the most significant advance is the development of constitutional monarchy, of which the ancients had only a distant inkling, in their form of state mixed from the three basic constitutions, which was almost nowhere realized; but even this is only slowly gaining a healthy life.

Nevertheless, I do indeed hold the firm conviction that the human race is engaged in progress; I merely wished to point out that the more inward and spiritual the circumstances are (and the moral belong among the spiritual), the more difficult and gradual is the advance.

The great Leibniz, to whose memory our celebration is dedicated, tested the power of his mind in both realms—that of the empirical sciences and that of the supersensible—and finally in a third, not yet mentioned, which according to Plato lies midway between the sensible and the supersensible: in mathematics.

As a philosopher he will always retain a place among the ranks of the stages of development as one of the coryphaei, because he had placed himself at the center of all the great problems of the pure spirit, and gave to those eternal ideas—the core of the higher speculation of all ages, which has been offered now in this vessel and now in that—a distinctive form and shape for his own time and the time immediately following, even if only scattered in individual expositions, not in the coherence of a system, in which his thoughts, stretched apart, would have gained neither in depth nor in clarity, since his spirit
dissolved under the hands of the analyzers.

Among those thoughts I count above all that he recognized in God, as the Monas monadum, the absolute unity of all that exists, in which the All has its universal harmony; in him all other essences or monads are and from him they radiate—the mirrors in which the whole All is reflected, according as they are exposed to it; those monads which are human souls are at the same time mirrors or images of God himself and microcosms, and therefore capable of knowing the macrocosm of the All; in which at the same time lies the doctrine of innate concepts: these same enter, by virtue of reason and the eternal truths, into a community with God as members of the divine state (civitas Dei).

Herein is contained the ground of a deep philosophy of nature, which is rooted in the idea of the unity of life of the universe, and the ground of an ethical and religious philosophy whose center is the moral world order; and just as in Leibniz everything takes harmonious shape, so too these two principal directions of philosophy are joined in him in a higher unity: yet as a philosopher he followed more the side of nature, while in the moral and practical he threw himself chiefly upon the religious-theological, and again in this field dealt so much with positive theology that he might seem to have stripped off the philosopher, if one could not read between the lines what was not hidden from the keenly spying watchmen of Zion of his time, that in spite of this he had formed his natural theology, alongside which he let the positive theology—which he, to be sure, knew better than most—go its own way, at the same time very consistently, where the understanding and union he vainly strove for was not possible, recommending quite especially religious toleration.

Although Leibniz presented everything in his own distinctive way and not without new and inventive argumentation, he nevertheless readily acquiesced and conceded that those fundamental ideas—which Plato in particular had proclaimed with Hellenic clarity and plastic power—were, apart from their form, not entirely new.

He does not belong among those philosophers who wish to withdraw from the natural and rational interconnection of minds and to walk entirely from the outset along a path of speculation never before trodden: on the contrary, he sharply censures
the Cartesian disciples who, in genteel and comfortable indolence and ignorance, despised the treasures of knowledge inherited from antiquity.
From his earliest youth he had read a great deal, had picked out the good from everything and drawn instruction from it, and in the history of philosophy he was especially well versed.
He held Plato in very high esteem.
We have, he says, learned not long ago that Plato has more in reserve than commonly appears.

No philosophy of the ancients, he says, comes closer to the Christian than the Platonic — though by "the Christian" I take him not to mean precisely what is nowadays called Christian philosophy in the division of the history of philosophy into great periods, a usage which I earlier said was unfamiliar to him. Yet, he continues, one must censure those who believed that Plato is everywhere reconcilable with Christ; but the ancients are to be forgiven if they did not know "what one can know only through revelation" — which, according to Leibniz's view, discussed by me elsewhere, means nothing other than "what is not philosophy at all."

He praises the Platonic doctrines: that there is one cause of all things; that in the divine spirit there is an intelligible world, which he himself also calls the region of the ideas; that the object of wisdom is the truly existent (τὰ ὄντως ὄντα), namely the simple essences, which he calls monads—God and the souls, and the most excellent among these the rational spirits, images of divinity brought forth by God; but that the sensible, and in general the composite or, so to speak, substantiated, is in flux and becomes more than it is.
Plotinus also says with good reason that every spirit contains an intelligible world.

Leibniz continues: In us are the seeds of what we learn, namely the ideas and the eternal truths springing from them; Plato's innate concepts are far to be preferred to the tabula rasa of Aristotle and Locke, who philosophized exoterically; and more of the same.

Yet one must, in order to philosophize correctly, join Aristotle and Democritus with Plato: and in fact his monads are Democritean atoms impregnated with the Platonic idea, and he also applies the Aristotelian entelechies to them; although some also sought to prove against
him that he had borrowed them from Giordano Bruno.
He had delved deeply into the Scholastics, and he was not afraid to say that the older among them were to be preferred to his contemporaries in acuteness, thoroughness, and modesty of research.

He also did not leave unheeded the later figures of every hue before and in his own time, especially the alchemists, mystics, and enthusiasts; he knew his Paracelsus, van Helmont, and the like as well as anyone, but he did not place the weight on them that some of the present-day do, because the deeper element of their views was not new, while everything is embellished with fantastic trappings, which Leibniz always left lying aside.

Moreover, he had an uncommon gift for adapting what was foreign to his own purposes in the service of scholarship, and for drawing his own views closer to those of others in a mediating way; yet he did not appropriate the thoughts of others out of personal vanity, but rather took pleasure in acknowledging the merits of others.
Thus Leibniz stands in the highest spiritual relations, as in his other achievements, intimately linked with the whole preceding world and with the world of his own time.

In those respects he did not surpass the men of earlier ages to the degree that his followers believed; but neither has he been surpassed by posterity to such a degree that similarly disposed speculative thinkers, who still allow a Plato and an Aristotle to count, would not also acknowledge the depth of his mind and gladly number him among their own.
The form of his philosophical ideas has been broken, as every mortal form breaks; their content is eternal and imperishable.

After the Leibnizian philosophy had become a dead letter within Wolffian philosophy, the critical philosophy arose among the Germans, and from it new systems emerged which deepened by stages and at last also acknowledged their kinship with those of the older time.

When one speaks of German philosophy, one understands by it—unless in earnest or in jest one means that of Jacob Böhme—the philosophy after the Leibnizian; and in fact it would be mere irony to want to call the Leibnizian one German, since, apart from the epigones, it had appeared only in Latin or French dress, and has its roots in world-historical philosophemes.

At all events, one may speak of German philosophy,
since in more recent times the speculative thinking that was formerly more generally widespread has become almost exclusively peculiar to the Germans, given their intellectual bent and in consequence of their other circumstances; but only in the beginnings of philosophy does the national-popular element have a significance for it, as the oldest schools of the Hellenic philosophers prove: for in these beginnings philosophy appears almost only as the heightened collective consciousness of the people-tribe to which the philosopher gives expression; in its further development, by contrast, this increasingly disappears, and among the Hellenes it had already disappeared by the time of Aristotle.

Moreover, philosophy, like every science, is a universally human good of a cosmopolitan kind, except that some peoples have none, or no longer have it; and if something of the national and individual clings to it—it, which is supposed to raise itself to the unconditional—as indeed it will always tend to cling to it, then precisely by that fact it is deficient.

Hence the philosophical language, or terminology, also rests on the common root of the culture of all European peoples; and Leibniz, who belonged to the whole world, was so far from granting a role to national peculiarity in this domain that he had set himself the project of inventing a universal philosophical language, in which all peoples could make themselves understood by means similar to algebraic signs: not, it seems to me, his happiest thought, since, if language already gives only copies or shadows of intellectual intuitions, signs are altogether only shadows of shadows, and through their use the presentation of philosophy would be deprived of all life.

Nevertheless, Leibniz's heart beat warmly and vividly for the German fatherland; of this his great studies in the history of his country bear witness, as do his German writings, both in praising and extolling the German nation and in censuring its defects.

He saw the badly ordered conditions of trade and manufacture, the utterly corrupt coinage, the uncertainty of rights, the dilatoriness of lawsuits, the worthless education of youth, the morals infected as with a foreign plague, the indifference in faith, in morals, and in politics, the consequently rampant atheism, and again the embittered religious disputes;
he brings out the dangers that an internal or external major war could bring, against which we, wholly blind, sleepy, bare, open, divided, unarmed, would necessarily be either the prey of the enemy or, because we are not equal to him, the prey of the protector.

He wrote, among other things on a similar subject, around the year 1697 his "Unprejudiced Thoughts concerning the Practice and Improvement of the German Language," and sent them, still unprinted, at the time of the founding of the local Society of Sciences also to Berlin, unquestionably so that they might receive consideration, which was granted them only when it was no longer necessary, under Frederick William II, by the minister Herzberg: for something greater than a private institution seemed to the author to be required, a union of forces arising from the impulse of a most enlightened head seemed to him necessary in order to put the proposed work into effect, whereby he thought to promote "the flourishing of the beloved fatherland of the German nation," the German nation, which has the preeminence among all Christian nations because of the Holy Roman Empire, whose dignity and rights it has brought upon itself and its head.

If Leibniz's name will never perish in the history of philosophy, even though we no longer find the true bearers of his system with all its peculiarities, he nonetheless made a more widely acknowledged advance in mathematics, precisely because here, unlike there, what is at issue is not something purely intellectual, but something hovering between the sensible and the supersensible idea.

Here too he acknowledged the great predecessors, such as Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga; but with Newton he invented a doctrine through which the science of magnitude advanced from the finite to the infinite.

His mathematical studies, however, do not merely run alongside his philosophical ones; just as mathematics was in its origins one with philosophy and only gradually emerged from it and became independent, so Leibniz thought the two together in their connection, and quite in the Platonic spirit he says: "The mathematical sciences, which deal with the eternal truths rooted in the divine spirit, prepare us for the knowledge of substances."

I wish to place less weight on the fact that he wanted philosophy to be treated in the form of exposition
as mathematics is, without himself carrying this out on a larger scale; and his successors have gained little by it: on the other hand, he prepared the way for that successful application of mathematics to the natural sciences.

I could now attach to this the manifold merits that he has acquired in almost all empirical branches of knowledge, and his general comprehensiveness; but I fear that I would weary you, and I hesitate, even in so ephemeral a performance, one soon consigned to oblivion, once again to set forth at length what has often been said elsewhere and also in this place.
May only a few brief remarks be permitted.
Fontenelle avails himself of the happy expression: "antiquity made only one Hercules out of many; out of the one Leibniz we shall make many scholars."

But, I add, ten scholars, each of whom for himself pursues a single science according to the principle of the division of labor, do not yet make one man who alone unites the ten sciences within himself in equal breadth, depth, and power: for in this "meeting," as one of my predecessors in this place said, "the analogies of the individual sciences come together, they illuminate one another, and also cast their light or their reflection into the general philosophical view."

Leibniz did not set aside the philosopher in the individual sciences; his wide learning is not atomistically fragmented; everywhere he seeks general thoughts and principles, and, undistracted even by the simultaneous pursuit of the most diverse subjects, he was able to resolve everything into the ultimate unity as a philosopher and to grasp each particular in its particularity.
When one speaks of Leibniz in this academy, one feels irresistibly compelled to consider him in his academic aspect as well.
But here I feel the truth of Choerilus' words: "Everything has been allotted, and art has its limits."

That Leibniz sought to found academies in Germany wherever he could, in order to establish many centers for the common promotion of the sciences, independent of teaching activity and of particular state purposes, and, as it were, living encyclopedias; that in his many-sided comprehensiveness, in his extraordinarily extensive literary intercourse through correspondence,
in his endeavor to stimulate others to scholarly work, especially also to necessary collections, and to support them therein, he alone was already an entire academy: this has often been shown to the full.
To be sure, he seldom sat in the academic chair and never read papers aloud; yet for all that, he is the ideal of an academic man in what he did and also in what he did not do.

Today there would indeed be a more immediate occasion than usual to sketch the picture of an academic man; but this sketch would have to be founded on an exposition of the essential nature of an academy, which today, for more than one reason, I must decline to give. Let me therefore be permitted simply to say this: whoever does not wish to see the concept of an academic man developed, but wishes to see it realized in a single person, let him look to the great Leibniz.
I mean him himself, his spirit, not the bodily likeness that has been set up here out of gratitude toward him.
Equally involuntarily, in this connection I come to the fulfillment of a commission which, since like can be recognized only by like, another more worthy person would have fulfilled.
On August 4, 1800, Mr. Alex. v. Humboldt was appointed an extraordinary member of this Academy; only one month is still lacking before he will have belonged to it for half a century.
The Academy has rightly deemed it consonant with piety to link the mention of this gratifying fiftieth return of his academic birthday with the Leibniz celebration.

Solely in consideration of the measure by which he himself is pleased to measure himself, not by the measure by which we and the other contemporaries measure him and posterity will measure him, this celebration has not been postponed by a further month; rather, the present day has been appointed to commemorate Humboldt's academic jubilee, together at the same time with the resolution to set up his marble bust in this hall, when—may that still lie in the far distant future—the common lot of humanity shall have removed him from our eyes.

By the former arrangement we have been deprived of the advantage that Humboldt's scientific greatness would be set forth at this place by an initiate, and the uninitiated speaker is almost wholly reduced to a bare epilogic mention of the conclusions
referred to.
In complying with this, it is very natural for one who gladly dwells in the unity of contemplation to draw comparisons.
But the memorable moral maxim of the popular wisdom of Old England — "Make no comparisons!" — must restrain us from it as far as possible.

Only a very general one will nevertheless be permitted: Alexander von Humboldt is, like Leibniz, the true academic man, and as the latter was for his age, so is he for ours the ideal of the academic man.
I do not elaborate on this; I merely state it, and offer it for silent reflection.
But he belongs not to one [academy] alone, nor even merely to all academies, but to the entire educated world.

To point to his versatility in only three words: what did he not stimulate and accomplish in all the fields of natural science—in zoology, physiology, and comparative anatomy; in botany, through monographic treatments and the great works on the equinoctial plants and on the new genera and species of plants, through plant geography and investigations into the distribution of plants over the earth according to temperature and elevation; in mineralogy, geology, and geognosy, together with mining and metallurgy; in chemistry, meteorology, and climatology, on galvanic and electrical conditions, terrestrial magnetism, heat, and sound. Alongside astronomical observations, he investigated the atmosphere, the earth in the most varied zones, at the highest elevations and in subterranean depths; he opened America and Asia anew to our gaze and founded physical geography in its widest scope.

But he also encompassed the history of humanity—everything pertaining to cultural history, the political history of distant lands, the conditions of the population, and whatever else one is accustomed to include under statistics; with noble and grateful love he traced every presentiment and seed of later knowledge of the cosmic and the telluric through classical and Oriental antiquity and into the Middle Ages, and followed the worldview of all peoples and ages with fine sense and feeling.

By his own account, driven by an irresistible urge toward varied knowledge, he devoted himself to the minutest particulars and yet never lost sight of his principal task, "to comprehend nature
as a whole moved and animated by inner forces," and everywhere formed general, far-reaching views upon the foundation of the particular—not aggregated encyclopedically or polyhistorically, but created artistically, and every side mutually illuminated by the others.

Not deterred by others' youthful misuse of their powers, he also does not deny the spiritual element its place in the contemplation of nature; he does not wish that, through the opposition of the physical and the intellectual, "the physics of the world should sink to a mere accumulation of empirically collected particulars."

Nature and spirit had interpenetrated in him; with the poetic power of imagination and all the charm of language, he spreads over the real the magic of the ideal, which wafts over the older among us like a zephyrous breath from the days of youth, when Alex. von Humboldt lived with the immortal brother in the fellowship of the most gifted men of the German tongue, to whom the Horae and Charites were still gracious.

Enthusiastic for all that is purely human, he is elevated above the prejudices of the age and of station, takes part in every noble endeavor, and acknowledges every achievement; to this are added free and open judgment, independent conviction, mildness and forbearance, and a universal, actively promoting benevolence.

And so I may without hesitation end with the words with which an ancient poet closes a hymn for a man who was indeed more powerful, but certainly not nobler: "How many joys he prepared for others, who could recount them?"

div.head: XXXI. Einleitungsrede gehalten zur Feier des Geburtsfestes Seiner Majestät des Königs Friedrich Wilhelm IV. in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften am 21. October 1852.
Ueber den Einfluss der Fürsten auf gelehrte Körperschaften

p.s: The existing statutes of our Academy contain, for today's celebration, the provision that at it "an annual report should be rendered on the achievements of the Academy in general, especially with regard to its own treatises and to the scholarly undertakings both its own and those supported by it."

These laws are well considered and therefore also lasting: a great good fortune for any community whose stability can have no guarantee if its laws are continually changed and thereby a hovering and wavering condition arises.

But only those laws will be lasting which are the expression of the essence of a community, and not those that arose through accidental circumstances, that are founded on a momentary and transient need, or that were called forth by party spirit and passions.
If, then, our laws express the essence of the matter, the rule just mentioned cannot be accidental either.
But how, then, may it lie in the nature of the thing that, for the celebration or post-celebration of the birth of the reigning king, the achievements of the...
