are to be stated for the Academy during the past year?

Yet only insofar as the personality of that individual, his principles and views, and his particular activity are preeminently authoritative and determinative for the collective life and thus also for the principal activity of such a society established by the state.

Against this it may be objected that this far-reaching influence of the prince is possible only in an absolute monarchy, and
indeed in one that rules all circumstances without regard for them, which does not even leave the established legal corporations untouched, as, after all, in some absolute autocracies communities of various kinds have readily been granted the self-government of their internal affairs: if the autocracy is a limited one, then the whole life of an academic body can no longer be determined by the personality of the ruler; rather, something can be forced upon him against his inclination—not merely a favoring of science or of scientific associations, when he is not favorably disposed toward the one or the other, but also defamation, oppression, curtailment, or whatever else one may call it—while by him himself the sciences and their cultivators would be held in high esteem.

This can all the less be entirely denied, inasmuch as the striking fate that has recently befallen a respected academic society leads us to mention it, which we may do without hesitation, since it has become a matter of full and official publicity.

The Royal Netherlands Institute for Sciences, Literature, and Fine Arts was founded in turbulent and perilous times by a prince imposed upon the country, recognized by Napoleon after Holland's union with the French Empire, and subsequently maintained for a long time by three kings of the old House of Orange: meanwhile, with its consent, its revenues were reduced from 15,000 florins to 11,000 florins, but from the year 1850 onward were cut altogether to 6,000 florins.

When the Institute was now on the point of adopting measures for its dissolution, because under this reduction it no longer considered itself able to continue an honorable existence, it was once again supported to such an extent by a personal gift from its Royal Patron that it could regularly continue its work; since further negotiations did not lead to the goal, and the Institute in the year 1851 was again about to demand its dissolution in an address to the King, it received once more 4000 florins from an anonymous donor, who had signed himself as a person who honors the sciences, literature, and the arts, so that the publication of its scholarly works and the continuation of the latter might be possible
for the Institute, until at last the learned academic body, which until then had consisted of four classes, was dissolved, in order to put in place of the first class alone, with the abolition of three—namely the second, for Dutch literature and history, the third, for the remaining history and philology, and the fourth, for the arts—and without its consent, a society devoted to the mathematical and physical sciences; a measure that is all the more remarkable because it was taken in a country which, after fine beginnings, still has only yet to establish an independent national literature, which for several centuries had been the glorious cultivator of philological studies and had achieved in the arts what is recognized and distinctive.

As may be inferred from the circumstances cited and as one seems able to read between the lines, there is here indeed a case that can count as proof of that for whose sake I have touched upon this matter. But let people judge of this as they will, I cherish the firm confidence that in our state, to which I wish the best prosperity under its constitution, a condition will never arise by virtue of which the King's personal weight would be without significance for the collective life of the academic bodies.

But with even greater plausibility one could maintain that far more than the personal influence of the prince, the age or the so-called spirit of the age would exert an influence both on the whole state and on the societies established by him, and would be determinative for their activity.

To be sure, it would be a matter for regret if such an influence were absent, provided that a progress lies in the spirit of each age, and perhaps even then, if it had not granted any essential progress, since for the most part even in this case it will have to be assumed that it prepares a future progress.

Meanwhile, there are examples enough from which one may recognize that the influence of the prince upon learned academic bodies can be very effective even against the spirit of the age: I cite two that lie close at hand, one that remained only a project, but even as such does not lose its probative force, and one that has vigorously entered into life.

Frederick William, the Great Elector, equally distinguished by the arts of
peace as by those of war—in the words of Frederick the Great, no less admirable at the head of the armies with which he became the liberator of his subjects than at the head of his council, where he administered justice to his peoples and raised up again from destruction a fallen land—had, as is well known, the intention of founding a university of all peoples, sciences, and arts. If the idea was first offered to him by others, we may nevertheless call it his own, since he had made it his own.

"If," it says in the charter of foundation signed by him, "there are any servants of the gracious Muses there, if any investigators in the most excellent sciences, persons experienced in the nobler arts, if any have been brought into straits by their worship of God and their religious usages, if any, weary of a harsh dominion, lovers of freedom, driven by ostracism from their fatherland or exiled from their country for any other cause that is not dishonorable, if any find the charm of the world in the society of scholars and in scholarly conversation; then let the aforementioned and all good and honorable men, of whatever people and respectable occupation and faith they may be, know hereby that they will find in this university a Parnassus, a Maecenas, the honor of the arts and sciences, the proper freedom of consciences and of all things, comfort for the suffering, refuge and sanctuary for the exiled, the fellowship of excellent souls, the association of noble spirits, the delight of the more cultivated and, beyond the great multitude, discerning part of mankind." He wishes, it continues, to give and consecrate to this university "a place as the seat of the Muses, as the temple of the sciences, as the workshop of the arts, as the dwelling-place of virtue, as a royal castle of the best and most sublime ruler of the world, Sophia." He promises to all dissidents in the Christian faith freedom of conscience and of the exercise of religion, namely to the Reformed, the Arminians, the Lutherans, the Roman Catholics, the Greeks, and all who confess the triune God and find in the merit and blood of Christ the hope of the soul and the ground of salvation; even if distinguished Hebrews, Arabs, and others of the unbelievers wish to establish their seat in this university,
this shall be permitted them upon seeking special permission, yet with the promise that they will keep their errors to themselves and not seek to spread them, and will lead a respectable life without giving offense.
Free access without conditions is permitted to all, and likewise free and unimpeded departure at any time.

In the administration the greatest freedoms are granted, and it is promised to secure neutrality for the university in cases of war, while to the electoral troops entry into the place, whether for passage through or for staying, is unconditionally forbidden.

At all events, one may declare this plan—whose remaining details I do not wish to enter into—to be adventurous and impracticable, as indeed it never came to be carried out, presumably at first only because of the inadequacy of the means, which better times and a larger state would have required: yet it will be conceded that the idea was a grand one and one that surpassed its age, and that a prince who could conceive or approve such designs was able, in the patronage of the sciences and in the establishment of scientific institutions, to run far ahead of what is customarily called the spirit of the age.

Frederick the Great shows another contradiction with the spirit of the age in the formation and preservation of a scholarly academic body, with reference to our Academy itself; and if it was precisely from him that a leading of the way could have been expected, the contradiction here consists rather in the fact that he did not yield to the spirit of the age, but in its place let his own prevail.

We are unwilling to reproach him on grounds that have often been discussed for making this Academy, at its restoration, a thoroughly French one; but we cannot deny that in regard to literature he resisted the German national spirit of his time to the very end, in that he was, as good as not at all, touched by its vigorous stirrings, through which during his reign the formation of a literature of its own, independent of the French, had been more than prepared, and in particular in the Academy he granted the German element the least possible scope: it remained a French one until his death—a striking proof of how the spirit of a prince, even in contradiction with people and
time, can be decisive for such a society.

Since, then, the principal objections to the view from which I set out have been removed, we may be permitted to hold fast to the position that the personality of the ruler is pre-eminently influential for the collective life of academic bodies established by the state.

It does not, of course, follow from this that the history of these institutions must have a turning point simultaneously with every change of government; on the contrary, the previous state of affairs can long continue under the succeeding government, and a change may come about only gradually, or not at all, if the institution has attained a certain stability or the prince behaves indifferently toward it. But one will scarcely be able to disapprove if the historian of an academy, in acknowledgment of the influence of personality, which for the most part predominates...
directions of the princes, marks out its epochs according to their reigns, as Christian Bartholmèss did in his philosophical history of our Academy, composed with much love, knowledge, and spirit.
This Academy in particular has felt to a high degree the dependence of its fortunes on the intellectual bent of princes.

The Society of Sciences founded at Leibniz's initiative rightly counts as our Academy, and it was only for this reason that he did not give it the latter name, so that it would not be confused with a university: its foundation had been resolved upon ten months before the King's coronation, on March 18, 1700, as part of the glorification of his reign; the founding charter was executed in the following month of July, on the Prince's birthday, and later the inauguration was scheduled for the day after the coronation festivities—all of it truly as proof of the King's personal favor. Its founding, however, proceeded even more from the Queen than from the King, and Leibniz, the soul of the new creation, after the Queen's death president in name only, was from this time on increasingly neglected and forgotten, which could only have a detrimental effect on the Society: indeed, he was not even invited to the Society's inauguration and installation in its building, when this finally took place on January 19, 1711—again precisely because personal inclination alone prevailed.

But what should one say of the personal
influence of King Frederick William I?

With good reason the aforementioned historian of the Academy's philosophical achievements says that few epochs have shown better than the reign of this king how great an influence the personal character of the ruler has upon the intellectual development of a country.

The other virtues of this sovereign, who ruled with a wholly peculiar kind of fatherly authority, and his very considerable services to the realm, which his great son duly acknowledged despite all the injustice he had suffered, lie far from my present consideration; and the temper of mind and cast of spirit, averse to the arts and sciences, indeed to all finer culture, of this man who was capable in his own fashion, and the wretched condition of the Academy under his rule, are too well known for me to wish to dwell on them long: I say only that the sword always hung over its head, that every academician feared to see him in person, that he stood with the Society in almost no relations except the comical ones known from the widely circulated anecdotes, that he was somewhat reconciled to it by the establishment, imposed upon it, of a medical-surgical college out of its modest revenues, chiefly for his military surgeons, that he gave it, as the representative of the sciences, fifty thalers in gratitude for the help which one of them, medicine, had rendered him in a severe illness, and that, in compensation for the humiliations which its president, his merry councillor, allowed himself to endure for the King's entertainment, he confirmed and even extended the Society's privileges, on which its revenues rested.
Still fewer words are needed to recall that under Frederick II the Academy was everything it was through him.

He established its institutions; in place of a practical-religious purpose formerly assigned to it, he introduced philosophy into it, both speculative and practical, and thereby gave it a distinctive direction.

For a time it even held its meetings in the Royal Palace. At first only the patron of the Academy, he soon drew all parts of its administration to himself; he gave it a special splendor by having several of his literary productions presented in
it, and by the fact that through him, as Formey says, the academic seats became honorary patents "which ranked together with those of marshals and ministers, which were sought by princes and heroes"; and for foreign countries it gained, although through outstanding scholars, especially mathematicians, it was already significant enough in itself, through his own fame and through the prestige to which he had raised the state, so many names that it served as a model in the founding or renewal of other academies.

For a scholarly institution at the center of a state sustained and celebrated by public opinion will, since some rays from that state and its ruler fall upon it as well, certainly draw more attention to itself than one equally entitled by its own worth in a country held in low esteem.

I admit that under the immediate successor of Frederick the Great the effectiveness of the reigning head's direct influence on the Academy cannot be demonstrated to the same degree as earlier; even Wöllner's admission to it, which followed barely three months after the change of throne, produced no essential change, and the strengthening of the German element in the Academy had long been demanded by the times, and one can only say that Frederick William II had no motive to offer any further resistance to that in this respect.

And I will not descend further in order to carry through my proposition; I say only this: what the Academy owes to Frederick William III — its full scholarly freedom, which remained with it even during the reign of the censorship, its proper independence, and the removal of all vain semblance, from which no one was more removed than he — will always be preserved in faithful remembrance; and that the noble King, to whom today's celebration is dedicated, inspired for art and science, and, if ever a prince was born and destined for the promotion of these, showed himself gracious from the beginning of his reign, in his original receptivity to all that is good and beautiful, to the Academy as to the other educational institutions, but especially turned his whole goodwill and confidence toward our Society, and not only favored it in manifold
ways but even preferred it — this is impressed upon our consciousness too deeply and indelibly for me to be moved to show in the present what I have preferred to demonstrate in the past; that to which I now proceed according to prescription has been assigned to this very day not by arbitrary decree but by the nature of the matter itself *). 1 *) To this was attached the enumeration of the Academy's achievements in the past year.

div.head: XXXII. Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Ernst Curtius als neu eingetretenen Mitgliedes der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 7. Juli 1853.
Zur Begrüfsung des Herrn Ernst Curtius in der Akademie

p.s: The not very comfortable form of public introduction into our Academy imposes upon the newly admitted member the almost unavoidable necessity of speaking about himself: of indicating the course his studies have taken up to that point, the scholarly standpoint on which he finds himself, the place he assigns himself within the developmental history of knowledge in general and in particular of that attained in the present, of what has been done and left undone in his field by earlier scholars and by his contemporaries, and of where he is moved, gifted, prepared, and inclined to intervene and to advance the work further—at least to suggest this in general outlines.

The noble and sensitive man is not equal to this task—not, to be sure, because he lacked self-knowledge, which is precisely what dwells in him most of all, but because his words will fall short of him.

The one who replies finds himself in a position not much more favorable, since he too must be careful not to wound delicate feeling. They have touched upon the difficult position of classical studies in this age, and in doing so did not even mention the enemies, but only the friends, since to these the most and the best in this field seemed already to have been done.

I too have heard, within my own circle, from excellent men of other sciences who are not averse to antiquity, the misgiving whether the study of antiquity, without the uncovering of new sources, can long hold out, since after all everything must soon be worked through.

I do not by any means wish to disparage the new sources, in whose discovery our age is not poor: if, however, the further progress
of the science of antiquity were to be founded on these alone, then, to be sure, no long progressive life could any longer be promised to it, since precisely these could be worked through so much the more quickly if the earlier material were already disposed of: for this disposal must already have yielded so many and such great results that what newly came to be added could be brought to understanding and exhausted in the shortest time.

But it is not the mass of the phenomena before us, which by new sources is each time increased only by a relatively small amount, that is what matters: the countless historical phenomena are not to be merely collected; they are to be analyzed, brought into relation with one another, and combined, and this combination, which multiplies itself into the infinite, always makes new things and ever new things spring forth as if through electric contact, always reveals new relations of attraction and repulsion among the mass-like elementary substances: this analysis and synthesis of philology, no less than the mathematical or the philosophical, will never find an end, so long as the human mind deems it worth the effort to contemplate itself and its creations.

But it is not the factual alone, taken by itself, that must be penetrated; the spirit of antiquity, too, must be penetrated in all the directions and formations of human activity, and the infinite manifold must be contemplated and comprehended in the unity of a historical organism. For this, as you rightly remark of the science of antiquity, only the first paths have just barely been opened up; and whatever the earlier centuries since the restoration of the sciences and the invention of printing may have accomplished in part with heroic greatness, our science in this respect is still rather young.

To the view on which this latter judgment rests, I have held fast, almost without wavering, for nearly half a century, amid every distraction and every kind of sifting of particulars—which is the necessary foundation for further research—and today, in this place, I meet you in that view.

You have made ancient geography, from the most general down to the topographical, a principal part of your investigations, partly stimulated by the views you had absorbed in the land where the old culture grew up;
in these local conditions nature appears in its influence upon the mind, and the mind as lord of nature: they are the foundations of all further construction and at the same time the enclosing frames of the picture.
I need not first say with what distinction you have solved the task that you set yourselves in an important part of the Hellenic land, at the same time with historical observations.

But it is not merely this significant work that gives us a glimpse into your intellectual direction and activity: I cannot refrain from recalling the beneficent and graceful impression which, alongside the manifold instruction, your smaller and occasional lectures in the fields of geography, art history, and mythology made upon me and others through their ideal sensibility, noble form, and dignified expression.

If, toward the close of your lecture today, you mention the continuation of the Greek Inscriptions work that you have taken upon yourself, then I wish you—to whom for the present the later portion of the material falls, which is unedifying in the degree that Byzantine culture stands below Hellenic—the perseverance and patience that its treatment requires, until the time shall have come when the Academy can think of a completion of the entire work, with which your connoisseurship, proven also in this field, and your philological artistry can return once more to the richer and more fruitful soil of ancient Greek life.
And so I bid you a heartfelt welcome in our midst, esteemed colleague, in the name of the Academy and in my own.

div.head: XXXIII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Jahrestages Friedrichs des Grofsen am 26. Januar 1854.
Der Philosoph von Sanssouci

p.s: Plutarch, to whom one cannot deny skill and subtlety in setting things side by side and comparing them, attempted in a work that has come down to us incomplete to settle the question whether the Athenians won greater glory through their deeds in war or through wisdom.
With him, wisdom comes off worse.

To give just one sample of his comparison, he asks what benefit the beautiful tragedies brought the state, how Themistocles' energy of action walled the city, Pericles' care adorned the citadel, Miltiades won freedom for the state, Cimon the leadership of the allies: if thus the wisdom of Euripides or the noble speech of Sophocles or the magnificent expression of Aeschylus removed something bad from the fatherland or acquired something splendid, then it would be fitting to set the spectacles over against the trophies and the stage over against the general's tent, and the theatrical performances over against the heroic deeds.

For battles won that brought the state glory and power, people celebrate festivals and offer sacrifice to the gods, not for the theatrical victories of Aeschylus and Sophocles; Marathon, Plataea, Salamis, Mycale, where the Athenians established the freedom of Hellas with steel-like firmness and handed it over to the rest of mankind—these are the reason why Pindar called Athens the pillar of Hellas, not because of the tragedies of Phrynichus and Thespis.

One could call this reflection extraordinarily narrow-minded, were it not to contain at least one far-seeing view—the view that the struggles of the Greeks against the barbarism and servitude threatening from the East had raised up a bulwark and had handed freedom over to the rest of mankind as well: these battles were
world battles, of decisive influence on the course of civilization of all mankind, just as Creasy, in a book much read in England, among the fifteen world battles that he lists, assigns the first place to the battle of Marathon and, and rightly so with greater justification than to that of Waterloo, the last place.

Nevertheless, we may be angry with Plutarch for preferring the violence of arms to the power of the mind: not as though military glory rested merely on crude physical strength and on the effectiveness of the instruments of combat, since war too is guided by the intellectual talent of its leaders, but because the fruits of purely intellectual activity are, to say the least, just as beneficial to nations, because furthermore the consequences of victories won in the intellectual sphere far outlast the consequences of those won in war, and finally because these military victories are worthless unless through them goods are protected that have imperishable value for their own sake.

Without fear of erring, we may judge the beneficial character of activities according to the measure in which virtue develops in them—virtue which, though in itself only one, is nevertheless different in its various directions.

The Christian virtues are customarily said to be faith, love, and hope: war has no relation to any of these; rather, it would have to cease if Christianity were to become truth in its full depth and fullness, or one would have to concede that this [Christianity] has no mission at all to regulate the affairs of the state exclusively and without the admission or allowance of other elements, but belongs to an entirely different domain, one to which the state does not reach—the domain of the mind and heart on this side, and the heavenly domain on the other side—and if Christians nevertheless wage war, this arises precisely from the fact that they are at the same time human beings and citizens, and that in this human and civic capacity of theirs, which lies outside Christianity, the state of war also finds its justification—a justification that cannot be found if one chooses to proceed from the idea of a Christian state, with which so much abuse is practiced; for one will surely not want to justify it by [claiming] that faith is to be defended with weapons, love compelled
with weapons, hope realized through struggle, or that faith, love, and hope can at all be supported and spread by force and war—propositions that all prove to be self-contradictory.

If, then, one measures by the standard of the Christian virtues in order to find out whether the military or the purely spiritual activity is the more fruitful, the former withdraws from comparison altogether, because, lying outside these virtues, it disappears.

If we return to the universally human cardinal virtues, which the Greeks established as valid for all time, then war develops from among these the one that is not without reason placed last, namely courage; the first is wisdom, and the middle virtues, prudence and justice, are more closely related to it than to the last: how, then, could one maintain that military activity is more fruitful than purely intellectual activity, in which the virtue of wisdom develops?

That a mind so versed in the treasures of wisdom of his forefathers as Plutarch could have overlooked this must justly surprise us; but he, least of all, should have left out of account that the fruits of this intellectual life outlast those of the martial life — he who reaches with predilection for these fruits, which lay spread out before him in their fullness, and winds garlands of ears of grain and of flowers from the sayings of ancient wisdom; he who saw that Hellenic art and science far outlived Hellenic prowess in action, and that the Hellenes, although conquered by Roman arms, made the stern Romans subservient to themselves in the realm of the spirit, just as, what he of course could not yet surmise, later the conquerors of Rome had to adopt the intellectual culture of the conquered, and the Hellenes became, partly indirectly and partly directly, the teachers of the world.

What, in the end, do all great deeds of war avail, if they are not done for valuable goods that receive protection through them? What standing would the world battles of Marathon and Salamis and Plataea have, if through them the inestimable good of freedom and a nobler education had not been preserved, if by them only a barbarism had been entrenched?

This is the immortal merit of warlike heroic courage, which I am not minded to belittle: that with a mighty arm it protects the noblest goods, pre-eminently the very works of intellectual activity.
If we do not already presuppose the acquisition of what it protects, then the splendor of arms is a vain one.

The one whose day of honor we commemorate today—a feeble testimony, given by feeble powers on behalf of a strong spirit that is itself a fully valid witness—nourished himself with predilection from antiquity, whose heroes he was kindred in spirit to: that he gladly starts out from it or returns to it, gladly lets his eyes rest upon it—this gave me the justification to make the view of a brilliant Greek, to whom he too had turned his attention, the starting point of a similar reflection, which presents itself unsought in connection with the person of our hero.

Frederick united in his long life many sides of human activity and virtue; he promoted science and art and himself practiced them; he guided every kind of internal administration, the cultivation of prosperity in general and in particular of agriculture, the trades, and commerce, the finances, legislation and the administration of justice, foreign relations, the military system, and war according to his own insights. The extreme opposites of this comprehensive activity, the opposing poles, are the philosophical and the martial, which Plato already described as difficult to reconcile and yet wished to see united in his guardians of the state.

He is not the first distinguished ruler who has united in himself statesmanship and science, the art of war and philosophy: to pass over lesser or even repugnant examples, I recall only the founders of the Roman monarchy, C. Julius Caesar and Octavianus Augustus; Hadrian, who took scarcely as much credit for his imperial virtues as for his rhetorical and philosophical accomplishments; M. Antoninus, the philosopher on the throne; and the great Hohenstaufen Frederick the Second. On a smaller scale, but perhaps all the more purely, the union of these opposites appears in a far more distant age in the person of Melissus of Samos, who led a fleet into battle against Pericles and at the same time holds a place in the history of speculative philosophy—admiral and dialectician at once.

If a place such as that of Melissus cannot be assigned to Frederick the Great, still an influence on the direction of thought in his time cannot be
denied him; and he himself, as he says, instead of all the titles which, in the general opinion, the German princes cannot have enough of, was content with the name of the Philosopher of Sanssouci, which he himself had bestowed upon himself*).

If, then, the hero of so many fierce battles placed such great weight on his philosophizing, it is fitting to consider wherein his philosophy consists, the philosophy that, together with poetry and historiography, filled the circle of his literary activity; and this consideration is especially in place here, since he was the first to introduce philosophy into this academy and even designated two of the classes he established as philosophical—the one of speculative philosophy, the other of physics or experimental philosophy.

Closely connected with this, too, is the question—especially when one comes to it from Plutarch's Parallel Lives—whether his purely intellectual influence holds its own against his military influence, or whether from now on we are to concern ourselves only with Frederick the master of war and the victor, and the philosopher of Sanssouci is to be abandoned.

If, at the beginning of this lecture, I placed Athens' intellectual activity higher than her military activity, it is not my intention here as well to give the decisive weight to that same side; yet I was surprised when I found that the great man himself is said to have preferred his philosophizing to his military activity.

Our corresponding member, Mr. Bartholmèss, in the excellent philosophical history of this Academy,**), after he had dealt with Frederick's philosophy with little favor toward it, drew the concluding judgment that in every period of his life it lacked distinctiveness and often also truth; as a rule, Frederick—who, to be sure, elsewhere calls himself merely a lover of philosophy—overestimates his philosophical worth (sa valeur philosophique) as a pupil or imitator of Voltaire and d'Alembert, when in his "Mémoires sur la civilisation des différentes nations de l'Europe" he says of the whole of his career: "I believe that, if one weighs the voices, the works of the philosopher will be held in higher esteem than those of the warrior." *) Preufs, Avertiss. to Vol. X of the Works of Fr. d. Gr.

p. XIII. **) Vol. I, p. 322.
(Je crois qu'en pesant les voix, les travaux du philosophe seront jugés supérieurs à ceux du militaire).

Since I could find neither such a writing by the King nor this passage in his known works, I took refuge in Mr. Preufs, whose knowledge of everything concerning Frederick the Great is admirable: he has, with good reason, declared that what was meant was the "Mémoires historiques et critiques sur la civilisation de l'Europe aux XVIIe et XVIIIe siècles," which by J. Alex.

Borrelly, a member of this academy under Frederick, published in Paris in the year 1807, and listed in Quérard's France littéraire under the article and name of the royal writer, with the remark that, by reason of the time of their appearance, they could not be contained in any edition of his works.
Under no circumstances may we trust this book. *)

The purpose and the limits of an academic introductory address justify my confining myself, in order to characterize Frederick's philosophizing, to a few indications, without entering into the manifold details of his positions and without taking his various stages of intellectual development into account throughout, since I have become especially convinced that his fundamental views have changed far less in the course of them than is asserted.

I do not believe I could begin better than with the conclusion of his preface to the extract from Bayle**), which he had made around the year 1764 amid many occupations: "If man is a rational animal, as the school assures us, then philosophers must be more human than others; so too have they always been regarded as the teachers of the human race, and their works, 'which are the catechism of reason,' cannot be spread widely enough for the benefit of mankind." From youth into old age he set great store by the formal element of philosophy, by logic and a logical education; just as he had studied Wolffian logic as a young man, so this logic still seemed to him, in old age, when he wrote the treatise on German literature, the best and clearest***).

Does he not praise rhetoric no less, which methodically trains the students' minds, *) on this see Oration XXXVII. **) Works vol. VII p. 129. ***) Works vol. VII p.
106. which teaches the invention of arguments, the arrangement and connection of thoughts, the choice of the style appropriate to each subject, the art of moving spirits and hearts, of arousing the passions and through the mere.
to rule by means of the word; so he in turn knows how to appreciate admirably its difference from the philosophical method.

The use, he says*), that orators and philosophers make of logic is entirely different; "the orator is satisfied with probability, the philosopher rejects everything except truth"; what he says in developing this contrast between the course of the philosopher and that of the forensic and ecclesiastical orator is on the whole masterfully set forth.
This attention to the organon and to method is something genuinely philosophical.

As for what is speculative or metaphysical, then, one will not expect a new system from the royal philosopher, and will be satisfied if he has looked around the history of philosophy in a thoughtful way, even if he frequently drew only from very derivative sources.
In fact, he places great weight on the history of philosophy, and he does not want one to be satisfied with the knowledge of a single system.

Plato and Aristotle, to be sure, lay further from him; but with the doctrines of the younger Academics, of the Stoa, and of Epicurus he was fairly well acquainted; he was especially a great admirer of Lucretius, and he esteemed the Epicurean philosopher Gassendi.

His gaze was turned away from medieval Scholasticism; but Descartes, Malebranche, and Spinoza did not lie outside his field of vision: his esteem for Leibniz was, so to speak, an heirloom of the royal family, and even if he distanced himself from his doctrines, he nonetheless holds him in high honor, and recognizes the great mind even in the aberrations, in the systematic visions into which his imagination had drawn him **).

He was devoted in his youth to Wolffian philosophy, and not merely to the Wolffian logic just mentioned, and he never laid aside all respect for Christian Wolff, not even after he had been turned away from it chiefly through Voltaire's influence by the great *) Vol. VII, p. 128. **) Ibid.

p. 118, and similarly elsewhere,
had returned to a reverent esteem for him, and the burdensome prolixity and clumsiness of Wolff's presentation, as compared with the spirited presentation of Leibniz, had become repugnant to him.*)

In the course of time he inclined more toward empiricism: Locke became for him "the only one of the metaphysicians who sacrificed the imagination to sound sense, who follows experience as far as it can lead him, and wisely stops when this guide begins to leave him"**).
Bacon, Galileo, and Newton are now especially praised by him.

Above all, however, he was drawn to Bayle's dialectical-skeptical method, which had also greatly engaged the attention of the witty Queen Sophie Charlotte alongside Leibniz; he calls him the first dialectician of Europe***).

“If we,” he says†), “compare Mr. Bayle with his contemporaries, with Descartes and Leibniz, though they were creative minds, or with Malebranche, we shall find him, we venture to say, superior to these famous men—not because he discovered new truths, but because he never departed from correctness and precision of thought, and because he developed the consequences of principles (les conséquences des principes) better than anyone.” Thus he took up, in a manner suited to the age in which deeper speculation had died out, the turn toward a critique of the dogmatic systems, with which he deals very easily++).

If the Stoics say that human souls are parts of the divine, then, however sublime the thought may be, a contradiction lies therein: man would then have to possess infinite knowledge, which he does not have; and if God were in man, it would follow that the English God does battle with the French and Spanish God, that the various parts or aspects of the Godhead would mutually destroy one another, and that all vices and crimes would become divine works.
The Epicurean indifference and calm of the gods would contradict the divine nature.
The system of the afore- *) Works vol. I, p. 231.
II, p. 38 f. Cf. another kind of mockery of Wolf, vol. IX, p. 119. **) Works, vol. VII, p. 112.

IX. p. 119. ***) Vol. VII. p. 107. +) Vol. VII. p. 125. ++) Especially Vol. VII. p. 110 ff.
— a novel by a great genius, [namely] that harmony which is supposedly attuned; Spinoza is easy to refute in the same way as the Stoics; Malebranche's doctrine leads back to the untenable doctrine of the Stoics concerning a world-soul, of which all living beings are parts, confuses creatures with the Creator, and turns man into an automaton that is moved by the highest will*).
The most questionable thing that could be found in Frederick's views is a leaning toward materialism.
His commemorative address on La Mettrie, read before the Academy in the year 1752, vigorously defends this most frivolous, shameless, immoral materialist and atheist.

"Mr. La Mettrie," it says among other things, "was seized by a violent fever: an illness is for a philosopher a school of physics; he believed he recognized that the capacity to think is only a consequence of the arrangement of the machine, and that the disturbance of the gears has a considerable influence on this part of us which the metaphysicians call the soul:**) thus he boldly carried the torch of experience into the darkness of metaphysics and found only mechanics where others had presupposed a being exalted above matter." And further on: "Mr. La Mettrie, after he had lost sight of the hospitals and the sick, gave himself over entirely to speculative philosophy; he wrote his 'Homme machine,' or rather he threw some powerful thoughts on materialism onto paper, which he had doubtless intended to bring into order." This work, it says, displeased people who by their station were declared enemies of human reason; since he had therefore been persecuted, as earlier in France, so then in Holland, the quality of a philosopher and of an unfortunate man sufficed to procure for him a refuge and a royal salary in Prussia.
The king's whim to praise this his reader and jester, whom d'Alembert, d'Argens, Diderot, and even

That he abandoned [them] to Voltaire is not enough to accuse the king of a materialism bordering on the excesses of La Mettrie; it seems rather to arise from a not uncommon mixture *) Vol. VII, p. 126. **) Cf.

Frederick's remark in a letter to d'Argens, Works vol. XIX, p. 262, is said
to have sprung from good-naturedness and tolerance combined with embittered malice—the latter being given free rein in this commemorative address against the theologians and the clergy.
In a letter to Voltaire*) Frederick writes in the year 1775: “I am quite certain that I am not double: therefore I regard myself as a single being.

I know that I am a material, living, organized being, and one that thinks; from this I conclude that matter can think, just as it has the property of being electric." "I attribute thought to the five senses that nature has given us." That is certainly rather strong, and I hardly believe that he said this with full deliberation.

"If the blood circulates in the brain with too great a violence, as in the drunk or in burning fevers, it confuses and inverts the ideas; if a slight obstruction forms in the nerves of the brain, it gives rise to madness; if a drop of water spreads within the skull, loss of memory follows; if a drop of blood that has escaped from the vessels presses upon the brain and the nerves of the understanding, then we have the cause of apoplexy." This influence of the body upon the mental, the dependence of the latter upon the sensory organism, no one can deny: but from the admission of this experience the road to complete materialism is still very far, and in the first place it is clear to me from the King's words only that he did not assume a dualism of spirit and matter, not yet that he ascribed priority to matter.

Yet in his works there are, to be sure, some very questionable passages, if indeed one is to regard every remark tossed off in a letter or poem as decisive; I have dealt with these earlier already**) and leave the final verdict to others.
It is the grossest untruth when he is accused of atheism for any period or point in his life.

"Everything," he says***), "down to the growth of a blade of grass, proves the Godhead; and if man enjoys a degree of intelligence that he has not given himself, then all the more must the Being to whom he *) Frederick's Works, vol. XXIII, p. 357. **) Cf. my speech on Frederick of 1842, p. 16 [above, p. 296]. ***) Works, vol. VII, p. 111.
owes everything be an infinitely deeper and more immeasurable spirit." His refutation of the notorious system of nature brings this conviction of his fully into the clear; if he found this occasion to set it forth only in the year 1770, one is not entitled to regard this as a reversal.
If he often says that chance governs events, then by this, as I have shown elsewhere, he means only our ignorance of the causes.
The question has been asked: was he a deist, a theist, or a pantheist?

He can scarcely have distinguished the first two determinations: for him God is the final cause presiding over the universe, the highest intelligence, and the absolutely good; and the slight pantheistic tinge of his thinking was so little deeply rooted that at various times he declared himself very decidedly not only against Spinoza but even against the Stoics and Malebranche.

He did not hope for personal immortality: but this is not necessarily connected with vulgar materialism; in him it is bound up with sublime greatness of soul, with the resignation of self-sacrifice, and it has no influence on his practical conduct.

If, finally, one looks at his moral doctrine, it is no systematically derived system, nor one free of contradictions; but in spite of the fact that he has set up self-love as its principle, it is free of selfishness and contains pure and elevating principles that are diffused throughout the entire series of his philosophical writings.

Instead of all elaboration, let the one sentence suffice *): "Philosophy teaches us to do our duty, to serve our fatherland faithfully at the price of our blood, of our peace, to sacrifice to it our whole being." And so he not only thought, so he acted.

This spirit of heroic self-renunciation, recalling Codrus and Regulus and similar heroes, breathes upon us especially from the memorable secret instruction to Count Finck von Finckenstein of January 10, 1757, written in his own hand, which in recent days has been published by the Royal Administration of the State Archives in a faithful reproduction and has already passed into the public newspapers.

Here he says, word for word: “If I should have the misfortune *) Letter to Voltaire in the King's works, vol.
XXIII, p. 53. to be taken prisoner by the enemy, then I forbid that the least consideration be shown to my person, and that the least account be taken of what I might write from my captivity.

If such a misfortune should befall me, I will sacrifice myself for the state, and my brother shall be obeyed, he as well as all my ministers and generals, who will be answerable to me with their heads that no province nor ransom be offered for me, and that the war be continued, pursuing all its advantages exactly as if I had never been in the world." A king who thus understood self-love might well set it up as a principle of moral teaching.

Besides, however zealous a part he may also have taken in speculations, he withdraws more and more into the practical, because from the metaphysicians one learns only the incomprehensibility of many things, which nature has placed beyond the reach of our mind; that man is destined more for action than for knowledge; that learning to know is often only learning to doubt; that it is a wise precept which Aristotle gave his students: "doubt is the beginning of wisdom"*).
But for that reason he does not renounce thinking.

If someone says, "But why should one waste one's time on the investigation of truth, if this truth lies beyond the reach of our circle?" he replies "that it is worthy of a thinking being to make at least efforts to draw nearer to it, and that, if one devotes oneself faithfully to this study, one infallibly derives from it the gain of freeing oneself from an infinity of errors."
If your field does not bear many fruits, it will at least bear no thornbushes and will become more suitable for good cultivation **).

Common usage distinguishes the wise man from the philosopher: the former is at once more and less than the latter—more, in that, according to the literal sense of the word, wisdom has been attained by him, whereas the latter strives after it; less, in that wisdom is a simple disposition or virtue of the mind, while philosophy *) Works, vol. VII, p. 126.
Vol. X, p. 97.
Cf.
Bartholmèss's Philos.
History of Berlin.
Acad.

Vol. I, p. 309. **) Works, Vol. VII, p.
127, but it requires a highly articulated technique of reason and, at least in an age that no longer stands in its beginnings, a many-sided turn of scientific thinking and its broad extent, as well as the most varied kinds of knowledge.

However highly one may esteem the wisdom of a Solon and of others from the youthfully fresh age of the so-called Seven Wise Men, one would place Frederick the Great too low if one wished to ascribe to him merely, like those men, a noble wisdom of life, and in addition the autocratic ruling power of a Pittacus or Periander, who was not undisputedly regarded as one of the Seven.

As this very incomplete report already shows, Frederick reflected on the greatest questions of philosophy—not without knowledge of the most important views set forth by the masters—with a thirst for knowledge that was never satisfied and an ever-active, unprejudiced drive for inquiry that extended in every direction: no prince before him, so far as my knowledge reaches, developed such power of thought.

Anyone who has thought as much about so many branches of knowledge as he did might well call himself a philosopher—the philosopher of Sanssouci—even without possessing a distinctive, internally consistent system in scholastic form; and I do not believe that he ever regretted his earlier choice of this title when he later exchanged it for the other one, that of the hermit of Sanssouci.
Frederick was a thinker through and through; his tranquility, his life free from care, consisted in the activity of thinking, to which I also count poetry.
If winter quarters were for others a time of sensual pleasure, he studied and wrote poetry during them; the most strenuous affairs of state and war did not draw him away from literature.

During the siege of Schweidnitz in the year 1762 he studied from the ground up Fleury's great work on church history; in the summer of the year 1761, which was so disastrous to his arms, he read in the field camp the eight volumes of Bernier on Gassendi's philosophy with such interest and zeal that in a letter of July 2 to the Marquis d'Argens he is able to report on the impression that the individual parts—physics, astronomy, moral philosophy, and especially the article on freedom—made upon him, and that at a
moment when he must add: "I hastened to finish, for fear that this Laudon, who is certainly no philosopher, might rudely interrupt my studies."*) This admirable union of study with the most turbulent life, like his intrepidity on the battlefield and his composure in misfortune, shows us the truly philosophical sublimity of the man above events; the former also lets us understand how he could form the principle that the sciences and arts do not, as is commonly believed, make men unfit for business. "The capable mind," he says **), "makes the same progress in all subjects which it encompasses."
The sciences, far from weakening him, lend a new luster, in every office, to those who cultivate them.

The great men of antiquity formed themselves, under the guardianship of literature—if I may use that expression—before they concerned themselves with the dignities of the state; and whatever serves to enlighten the mind and to widen the circle of knowledge surely forms people who are suited to every kind of calling." He loved and cultivated the sciences not merely as a ruler but as a scholar; if the counsels that he gives to the specialized scholars on method are not exactly of great significance, he nevertheless correctly recognized many defects of the German scholarly system, even in his ignorance of the advances of German literature, while refraining from any interference with academic freedom.

Yet I would find no end if I wished even only to touch upon the King's stance toward philosophy and toward science in general in all its relations: only his conduct toward religion and positive theology may I not pass over in silence.

Since, however, this has often been discussed and quite recently, in an essay on "Prussia and the Protestant Principle,"*** his views on priestly rule and Christianity, the papacy and the Reformation, Catholicism, Jesuitism, and the relation between church and state have been set forth together, I shall say only this much on the matter here.

Frederick, wholly a thinker, did not find in his thinking the specifically dogmatic concept of revelation;
he distrusted the metaphysics of reason, and did not put in its place a metaphysics of the historically transmitted faith.
He professes the moral teaching of the Gospel, declares Christian morality to be the rule of his life, and esteems Christian piety.

With reverence he says of his teacher Duhan*): "He died with the courage of a philosopher and with the piety of a Christian"; certainly these words are his own, even if the passages of this commemorative address which in his mouth would be an excess of self-praise may have been inserted by an academic hand.

He is not an adversary of religion, nor of what appeared to him as genuine Christianity**); he defends the Christian religion with warmth against the system of nature; but he combats superstition and the misuse of religion, the false dialectic, presumption, lust for power, and persecuting zeal of the priesthood.

If even his father, a simple, devoutly churchgoing man, had called the intolerant dispute over the differences between the Lutheran and Reformed confessions clerical bickering, then Frederick declared himself all the more comprehensively against all intolerance.
That in the struggle against the previously dominant tendency he at times, through sharpness and

That it has gone beyond measure in bitterness with royal frankness, and in particular has not treated the historical element of Christianity with the respect that is its due, I concede; and especially in this regard the preface to the extract from Fleury gives offense.

Yet it cannot have appeared so to him: for this writing was made known in Berlin in May 1766, and as early as the next August 13 he writes***) to Voltaire that toleration must not extend so far as to give a license to the insolence and licentiousness of young hotheads who boldly assail what the people revere.

May we recognize in that arrogance his share in the infirmity of the age, to which even the greatest mind pays its tribute — yet let no one believe *) Werke Bd. VII. S. 12. **) This has rightly been emphasized also by Mr. Ch. de la Harpe in the treatise "Étude sur les oeuvres philosophiques de Frédéric le Grand" (Berlin 1848, in the Programm des Collége français) p. 41. ***) Werke Bd. XXIII. S.
104. — only not that a later age advances, when it puts another infirmity in the place of the one and perhaps falls from the hypersthenia of the mind into an asthenia.
The health of the soul, as of the body, consists in the harmonious mean. *Frederick was a man cast in a single mold.
“I am quite sure that I am not double,” he says, to be sure, in a wholly different connection; but the same holds of him in a much higher sense.

His strategic insight and his heroism, his statesmanlike prudence and wisdom, his firmness of character and ruling power, his philosophical thought—all are rooted inseparably in the one undivided greatness of mind, in his own most personal virtue.
Let us not tear apart what was so intimately linked, so intimately linked that even the field camp was at the same time his museum.
Let us therefore not cast aside the philosopher of Sanssouci merely in order to keep the hero and king.

I am, as I have already indicated, far from preferring his philosophy to his deeds; but if it is once to be considered how the worth of the two stands in relation to each other, then I ask: what have his deeds, what has his philosophical thinking brought about?

Had his political and military activity only protected, enlarged, and strengthened a Prussia that was insignificant beyond its borders, it would not be world-historical: but he raised Prussia to the height at which, as a great power, it independently takes part in the steering of European destinies, without doubt with a distinctive political vocation, to define which is not the task of this place.
And what is the innermost core of his philosophical thinking?

Truly not this or that conviction or assertion, in which we may or may not agree with him: for he has required no one to adopt his opinions; it is the spiritual freedom, which also includes religious freedom within itself, the freedom of thought and of faith, of research and inquiry, the realization of humanity, justice, and morality in the state, the spirit of religious peace and of toleration within the limits of what is proper to a good citizen.

This spirit he proclaimed from the throne more truly and more powerfully than anyone before him—likewise a world-historical principle that reaches far beyond his state and
his time.

Thus, having become world-historical in both spheres of activity placed here for comparison, he gave the Empire the same twofold world-historical significance; and both sides of it are, in my judgment, so closely intertwined and grown together in this state as in his own spirit that the existence of both is conditioned and grounded in their mutual interaction.

In this unified comprehension of his nature, we shall worthily honor the great prince for whose celebration we are assembled here today, and at the same time, in him, acknowledge and hold in honor the noble king, our lord, who has understood the spirit and strength of his greatest ancestor.

div.head: XXXIV. Zur Begrüfsung der Herrn Haupt und Kiepert als neu eingetretener Mitglieder der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 6. Juli 1854.
Zur Begrüfsung der Herrn Haupt und Kiepert in der Akademie

p.s: Whoever wishes to achieve anything fruitful at the present stage of development of scientific education is almost necessarily directed to immerse himself in the investigation of some particular subject, because science has gradually acquired an immeasurable extent, in which anyone who wished from the outset to encompass even only a significant part of the whole would, as it were, wander astray or lose himself in an endless space.

A special field, though one not measured too narrowly, gives each person's study, by contrast, a freely chosen and distinctive center from which, by virtue of the interconnection of all parts and branches of knowledge, he may expand in every direction as far as his powers reach and his mind's eye can carry him.

This general interconnection of the sciences, of which people often speak, may appear to the beginner as a conventional commonplace and a presupposition still to be proved; but the further we advance, the clearer it becomes to us, and the more one recognizes precisely for that reason that, if our knowledge in general must remain a patchwork because of the limitedness of the human mind, it is also a patchwork for the reason that every particular first attains its full meaning in the light of the whole and of universality.

It is this thought, above all, that moves me to address not one reply to each of you individually, highly esteemed members of the Academy who have just spoken as recent
entrants, but a single response to both of you; for seen from the standpoint of the interconnection of scholarly endeavors, your studies, which at first glance appear to lie far apart, seem to me very closely linked.

Even if one of you were devoted to natural science and the other to the investigation of what the human mind has produced, I would still consider this combination unobjectionable; all the more so, since I regard you both as bound together by the common bond of philology.
Even in this we find the necessary separation of different domains, and indeed according to more than one principle of division; what has just been indicated by the first of our new colleagues.

Times and countries, or peoples, form one ground of division: that a single person should encompass the consideration of all of these with equal inclination and equal success is not merely difficult but impossible.

The flourishing of the sciences requires that many share in the work: in its extent the whole of science does not consist in one mind, but in all minds, just as nature does not consist in one organism, nor even in one world-body alone, but in the universe.

But, following the same comparison, we are indeed entitled to the demand that every scholarly endeavor should reflect in microcosm the image of science as a single and undivided whole, and that in every particular the whole and the universal should be intensively contained; and the division of labor must not reach the degree of a complete separation of the fields.

Time is an uninterrupted stream that is checked and dammed by no sharply cutting epochs; the ancient, the medieval, the modern follow one another in steady connection: who could so fix himself in the contemplation of one that he would obstinately and stubbornly close his eyes to all the others?

And the nations—apart from the case in which one of them surrounds itself with a Chinese wall, which in the end is itself also overleaped—exercise upon one another a greater or lesser effect; and neither he who devotes himself to the investigation of the Oriental world, nor he who subjects Western culture, especially the Hellenic, to his contemplation, can with impunity confine himself to his own narrower field.

I therefore greet you with joy, the first speaker,
since you have joined the study of antiquity, especially of the Roman world—which now stands almost more in need of cultivation than the Greek—with that of the medieval period, and the Germanic studies with the Greek and Roman; and our Academy, as a German one and moreover, following the example of the man to whom today's celebration is devoted, inwardly bound to them, is to open a further field to these studies.

With joy I welcome you as well, whose extensive geographical works spread out before us the stage of ancient humanity, separated from and yet joined with that of our present-day history, embrace with equal force the Eastern and the Western, indeed the entire globe, and, founded on a comprehensive scholarship and on the aids newly grown in your field—perhaps more than in any other in this century—stand incomparably higher than the achievements of this kind that earlier issued from this Academy and that you have nonetheless not forgotten.

You too, esteemed colleague Haupt, have already drawn attention to the second ground of division, which I wish to single out here as well, passing over the less significant ones—I mean the ground that lies not in the subject matter but in the activity of contemplation and treatment.

You have emphasized the distinction between philological criticism on the one hand, which is inseparable from the investigation of the individual, from the penetration and sympathetic entering into the personality of the ancient writers, and on the other hand the striving after knowledge of the general, and you have not failed at the same time to suggest how this distinction too is sublated through the relation of the individual and particular to the whole and general.
Both sides are subject to manifold deficiencies and faults which, if not exclusively, yet for the most part have their roots in the fact that each of the two is pursued one-sidedly.

It is a strange and yet undeniable contradiction that in philological research the particular cannot be grasped without the general, and again the general can be seized only through the intuition and inner interconnection of as many details as possible; in the solution of this circle I find the proper task of philological art, which for that very reason
stands all the more in need of rule and method, to which you rightly attach great weight.

Like every empirical science, we require much mechanical and, in a certain sense, technical work, and the neglect of it—to which the more intellectually gifted are easily inclined—often takes a painful revenge; we stand in need of the collecting and sifting of endless details, in the midst of which one easily neglects, to speak with you, to fix the grounds of phenomena in one's eye.

We go astray—often reliant on divination, whose successful outcomes are the triumph of our art—easily into the subjective opinion and conjecture that you have censured, from which present-day philological criticism is once again suffering severely.

It is the rule and method that keep us from these aberrations—the rule and method that are a work of deliberateness and lead to deliberate activity; but the foundation of all methodical procedure is secure intuition, which, freed from subjective representation, immerses itself objectively in the particular object at hand, and this intuition, insofar as it is not merely a natural gift, presupposes a knowledge of the spirit of the ages and of peoples, and of the most cultivated among and within them, gained from many elements taken up into us—thus, in the contemplation of the particular, already the universal.
That second direction, which you have just designated as the one directed toward this universal, is, at its highest level, the direction of philosophical thought.

Nowadays many take pleasure in the fact that, as they believe, philosophizing is ever more on the decline, and they exult that philosophy will soon be carried to its grave: to my mind that means nothing other than rejoicing that the light of humanity will soon be extinguished.

If philosophy is the bearer of the universal and the ideal, and the particular and the real have no value unless the universal and the ideal dwell within them, then we must not depart from the old demand that the philosophical thought should dwell within all science: those opposites should live in one another in the unity of a higher harmony, as soul and body do.

Only, this interpenetration is not attained by stretching and straining the actual details upon the bed of a system, or by seeking to dissolve them into the Idea through arbitrary and fantastic constructions: to destroy these
illusions is the business of criticism, which is by no means negative, as it is often reproached for being, but affirms the true through the negation of the false.

By your own estimate, you have placed yourselves on the side of criticism, which you exercise with measure and prudence, on a foundation that you call re-feeling, I intuition—different names for the same thing or nearly the same: but, setting aside your unpretentiousness, and without wounding your modesty or mine, I take the liberty of remarking that one can possess the universal and philosophical without saying much about it, and that not seldom those who have it much on their lips possess not the true universal filled with the true particular, but only empty compartments and schematisms, hollow formulas and formless or emaciated abstractions, vain dreams and chimeras.

And you, our new d'Anville, you will permit me to count you likewise among the philologists in my sense of the word, and indeed among those who understand how to resolve those oppositions into harmony.

Your course of study is still more closely bound up with an arduous and time-consuming technique, which you have pursued with distinction from your earliest youth; but you have practiced it with a scholarly spirit from the very beginning.

Even in your next field, conjecture has wide scope, although the mathematical foundation of geography somewhat restricts it—an advantage that the other philologists can acquire only by giving themselves some training in mathematics, without, however, weakening the capacity for freer combination, which, to be sure, easily happens.

The gift of divination—what in your field, if I am not mistaken, is called geographical sense, the very quality that distinguished that d'Anville—and sober criticism are thus what you, like every philologist, must rely upon, and these you have admirably proven.

Again—and here I gladly make use of your own words—you place geographical science in a relation of mutual interaction with the history of peoples and the development of states, and bring it into connection with linguistic studies; in this way you lift it out of its isolation, give it that generalization of which it is capable as a link
in the chain of all knowledge, and unite it with the history of the human race, in which the development of the spirit, and thus of thought, is actually stamped with its impress.

Thus both of you, highly esteemed gentlemen, each from his own particular standpoint, strive toward the goal of the whole of scholarship, whose representatives are to be gathered together in our Academy.
Allow me once again to greet you most kindly.

div.head: XXXV. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 5. Juli 1855.
Ueber Schellings Verhältnifs zu Leibniz und dessen Philosophemen

p.s: The modest celebration that our Academy dedicates to the memory of our great Leibniz may be considered from various points of view.

Leibniz is regarded as the founder of this society, and rightly so; Leibniz accomplished significant things in many fields of science and scholarship, and made an epoch in philosophy and mathematics; he also sought to exert an influence on the practical spheres, on state and church: thus we too today can consider him in his direct relation to the Academy, or as the man of the highest scientific significance in general or for this or that field, or in his activity directed more toward the outside.

The universality of his mind also makes it possible for one and the same person, at short intervals, as must happen in our case, to speak repeatedly about him without being exposed to the danger or necessity of falling back upon the same material.

Nevertheless, a more frequent change of those who have to speak about him here should not be unwelcome, and one would most gladly hear such men speak about him as, without first making the makeshift studies required for a lecture, are fully equal to the subject through frequent intercourse with the great man's most characteristic and principal achievements.

Who would not have preferred—to take this example that lies so close at hand—to hear the profound philosopher whom death recently snatched from us speak about Leibniz on this commemorative day, rather than me?
How then, if it should be possible or should succeed in bringing about a mediation, so that this one spoke through my mouth?

Philosophers, with the exception of the few
who know, or wish to know, almost only their immediate predecessor, readily attach themselves to one or more of their earlier predecessors, and one can count with certainty on this: that whoever acknowledges this particular one will also feel drawn to other particular ones.

Whoever is disposed in favor of Plato also holds Bruno and Spinoza in high esteem, however different Plato and Spinoza may be; and most of those who acknowledge these three are also devoted to our Leibniz: indeed, I would state this even more generally, were there not still a significant exception that I recall.
Schelling stands in that line, and he loved to take account of kindred spirits.

On this present day, which is at the same time meant to be a day of remembrance for colleagues recently departed, it therefore seems to me not inappropriate to offer a few remarks—even if only cursorily taken up and, if one will, dilettantish—on Schelling's relation to Leibniz and his view of the latter and of his philosophemes.

Gathered together from many of his writings, they can nevertheless lay no claim to completeness, and I even deliberately omit lesser material: I am still further removed from the presumption of delivering, in this guise, a memorial address for Schelling, which for today a man of the profession himself has supplied.
To be sure, one thought could also deter me from this more limited undertaking.

If Socrates says of the great Parmenides—that venerable, mighty, profound thinker—that he fears he does not understand his words, and still more that he falls far short of what Parmenides had in mind in saying them, then a similar misgiving on my part in the present case may the less be held against me, the more often that profound philosopher whose views on Leibniz I am attempting to assemble has complained that he is not understood or is misunderstood, and the more easily a misunderstanding can slip in when isolated judgments are retold.

Even the fact that the noble and well-disposed older colleague of mine occasionally gave expression to a somewhat ambiguous piece of courtesy toward me—[saying] that he was convinced I could understand him if I wished—cannot [remove] this misgiving, in the case of the *) Plato Theaet.

p. 183, E.
cannot relieve me of my best will.
In addition, his remarks on Leibniz are contained only in earlier writings, from which I too mostly know them from youthful memories, and people accuse him of a significant change in his views.
But in the case of what subject of contemplation would doubts not arise?
Whoever wished to consider every scruple would have to condemn himself to utter silence, of which I cannot say whether it is the least or the most scrupulous.
When Schelling complained that he was not understood, he said of himself only what he also said of Leibniz.

It is indisputably a true word when he declares in the Ideas toward a Philosophy of Nature*) that "from time immemorial the most ordinary people have refuted the greatest philosophers with things that are comprehensible even to children and minors."

One hears, reads, and marvels that such common things were unknown to such great men, and that people so admittedly small could master them.“ “Many,” he says, “are convinced that Plato, if only he could read Locke, would go away ashamed; some believe that even Leibniz, if he rose from the dead to sit at his feet for an hour, would be converted, and how many minors have not struck up songs of triumph over Spinoza's grave?" There is an almost insurmountable gulf between people of common sense and speculative minds.

"What was it, then," he has those people ask, "that drove all these men to abandon the common ways of thinking of their age and to invent systems that are contrary to everything the great multitude has from time immemorial believed and imagined?"

It was a free, soaring impulse that raised her into a domain where she no longer even understands her own tasks, just as, conversely, much became incomprehensible to them which seems to you utterly simple and intelligible." Such is surely the case with Leibniz, and not only ordinary minds—no, even distinguished spirits, whose greatness, however, lies in another field—bear witness to this: I need only recall Frederick's *) Part I, vol. 2.

Edition (1802) p. 13 [Complete Works, Division I, vol. II (1857), p.
19].
to recall the great judgments concerning some of Leibniz's most important doctrines.

That Schelling should have directed his attention precisely to these ideas, which had appeared to the common sense only as figments of the imagination—namely, to the Monadology and the pre-established harmony—is to be expected from the outset: but he ascribes to himself a new and peculiar understanding of them, and never tires of repeating that Leibniz has not yet been understood.

It seems to me that he was not already in possession of this understanding right at the beginning of his philosophizing, namely in the treatise "On the I as Principle of Philosophy"*), when he says that the transcendent realism which he ascribed to our Leibniz regards objects in general as things in themselves, and can therefore regard the changeable and conditioned in them only as a product of the empirical I, and can consider them as things in themselves only insofar as they have the form of identity and immutability: thus, in order to save the identity and immutability of things in themselves, Leibniz had to take refuge in pre-established harmony; the Leibnizian monads were supposed to have the primal form of the I—unity and reality, identical substantiality and pure being—as representing essences, whereas all those forms which pass over from the not-I to the object—negation, plurality, accidentality, conditionedness—had to be explained empirically-idealistically as present merely in the sensible representation of the object; Leibniz regards all appearances as so many limitations of the reality of the not-I, and everything that is, is for him not-I, even God, in whom all reality, but outside all negation, is united.
Here we are not yet speaking of a misunderstanding of Leibniz's doctrines.

But not long afterward, in the Essays toward an Explanation of the Idealism of the Wissenschaftslehre**), he is enraged at the half-wits who have heard from Kant what Leibniz asserts, but have become too enlightened to read him for themselves: "Immortal spirit, what has become among us of your teaching— *) p. 72 ff. (1795), philos.
Writings, vol. I. [Complete Works, Division

I do not take his very first writing into consideration, although even this already concerns itself with Leibniz; it has probably been deliberately omitted from those collected philosophical writings. **) Ibid.
p. 212 (1796–97) [Works, Division

What has become of the oldest, holiest traditions; — doctrina per tot manus tradita tandem in vappam desiit! Just as in the history of philosophy there are in general examples of systems that have remained enigmatic through several ages, so only now has the time come to understand Leibniz; for as he has hitherto been understood, he cannot be understood, if, as someone said at the time, he is after all to be right at bottom*).

Even among those who professed allegiance to him or wished to lead philosophy back to him, the doctrine remained wholly misunderstood in its main points—the pre-established harmony, the relation of the monads to God, and others**).

Since, as a congenial spirit—because like can be recognized only by like—he penetrated more deeply into Leibniz, he soon*** goes so far as to say: “the time has come when one can restore his philosophy.”
His spirit, he continues, "disdained the fetters of the school; no wonder that among us he has lived on only in a few kindred spirits and has long since become a stranger among the rest."
He was one of the few who also treated scholarship as free work.

He possessed within himself the universal spirit of the world, which reveals itself in the most manifold forms and spreads life wherever it comes. Yet he does not absolve him of the charge of not having been understood through his own fault+), and he also does not disparage Leibniz's rival without moderation.
