If it has been justly objected against him and the school most closely related to him that they displayed toward Newton a contempt carried to the point of the unintelligible and the indecorous, then what he says about the relation between the two deserves not to be forgotten.
"Rarely," he says, "have great minds lived at the same time without working toward the same goal from wholly different directions."
While Leibniz founded the system of the spirit world on pre-established harmony, Newton found in the equilibrium of the world's forces the system of a *) Ibid.

p. 328 [443]. **) Bruno, p. 229 (1802). ***) Ideas toward a Philosophy of Nature, p. 14 [20]. +) Bruno, in the place cited. ++) Ideas toward a Philosophy of
Nature, pp. 20 f. [24 f.], material world." The resolution of both systems into one, or the resolution of the spiritual and the natural, of the ideal and the real, into one, is for him the final goal of our knowledge: "If indeed there is unity in the system of our knowledge, and if it ever succeeds in uniting even the last extremes of that system, then we must hope that precisely here, where Leibniz and Newton parted ways, a comprehensive spirit will one day find the center around which the universe of our knowledge will move the two worlds between which our knowledge is still divided, and that Leibniz's pre-established harmony and Newton's system of gravitation will appear as one and the same, or merely as different views of one and the same thing." The first and principal misunderstanding of the Leibnizian doctrine, then, Schelling*) finds in the fact that a world of things in themselves is attributed to Leibniz—things that are intuited and known by no spirit, yet act upon us and produce all representations in us. "Leibniz knew of no existence except one that knows itself, or is known by a spirit."
The latter was for him mere appearance.
But what should have been more than mere appearance, he did not make into a dead, selfless object.

Therefore he endowed his monads with powers of representation and made them into mirrors of the universe, into cognizant, representing beings, and only insofar as they are not cognizant, not representable beings." His first thought, from which he proceeded, was: that the representations of external things arise in the soul by virtue of its own laws, as in a world of its own, as if nothing but God (the Infinite) and the soul (the intuition of the Infinite) were present: no external cause could act upon the inner being of a spirit.
When Leibniz said this, he was speaking to philosophers: nowadays people have forced their way into philosophizing who have a sense for everything else, but not for philosophy.
Therefore, when it is said among us that no representation can arise in us through external influence, there is no end to our astonishment.
Now it is incumbent upon philosophy to believe that the monads have windows. *) Ibid.
p. 14 ff. [20 ff.] compare.
By way of explanation of the idealism of the theory of science.

p. 212 [357 f.]:
"through which things rise up into it and out of it." The entire systems of Spinoza and Leibniz, he says, are nothing other than the attempt, made by these two alone, to derive from the nature of the finite mind the necessity of a succession of its representations, and, so that this succession might be truly objective, to let the things themselves at the same time come to be and arise in it along with this succession: Spinoza had recognized that in our nature the ideal and the real, thought and object, are intimately united, that between the actual things and our representations of them no separation takes place; but, soaring beyond himself, he had at once lost himself in the idea of an infinite being outside us, and his system offers no transition from the infinite to the finite: according to Leibniz, by contrast, that necessary union of the ideal and the real, of the absolutely active and the absolutely passive, which Spinoza placed in an infinite substance outside me, is present in me originally, without any doing of mine, and precisely in this consists my nature.

Without having taken up this point—where Leibniz separates from Spinoza and is connected with him—one could not understand the former, whose entire system proceeds from the concept of individuality and returns to it: he passes neither from the infinite to the finite nor from the latter to the former; rather, both are, as it were, made real at once for him through one and the same development of our nature, through one and the same mode of action of the spirit.

Leibniz holds only representing beings to be originally real and truly real in themselves, because only in them is that union originally present from which everything else that is called real develops and proceeds.

According to the view of the misunderstood pre-established harmony, "to be sure, each individual monad produces the world out of itself, but nevertheless this world exists at the same time independently of the representations; yet according to Leibniz himself, the world, insofar as it is real, itself in turn consists only of monads, and consequently all reality in the end rests only on powers of representation." *) The spirit is said to be the absolute self-ground of its being and knowing.
The ordinary conception of *) System of the transc.
Idealismus, p. 65 (1800) [Works, division

Vol. III (1858), p. 378].
Leibniz's pre-established harmony, then, does not hit on the right thing; it lies in the Leibnizian system itself that the agreement of which we are speaking follows from the essence of finite natures in general, and not that a higher hand first arranged us in such a way that we [have] such a one.
world, and are compelled to represent to themselves such an order of appearances *).

"I cannot think otherwise," he said in another passage, than that Leibniz, under the substantial form, thought of a governing spirit dwelling within organized beings.**) Nor does he hesitate to declare in his own person the necessity of a pre-established harmony of the two worlds, the ideal and the real***); the system of nature is at the same time the system of our mind, and there is no longer any separation between experience and speculation.

The Leibnizian idealism, which he had earlier designated empirical idealism, on a par with transcendent realism, becomes for him, because it rests on the proposition that all the forces of the universe ultimately come back to representing forces, not different from transcendental idealism; and when Leibniz calls matter the sleep-state of the monads, or when Hemsterhuis calls it congealed spirit, there lies in these expressions a meaning that can be seen very easily from the principles he himself set forth, and he recognizes therein precisely the abolition of all dualism and of all real opposition between spirit and matter+): in that Leibniz, rightly understood, derives matter, which as is well known does not count for him as real, solely from the representations of the monads, which, when they are adequate, have God as their object, but when they are confused, have the world and sensible things as their object++).

Likewise, the claim that one attributes to Leibniz the doctrine of innate concepts is supposed to be a misunderstanding: Locke, it is said, contends against this figment of the brain; from *) Ideen zu einer Philos. d. Natur p. 40 [38], cf.
System of the transc.
Idealism, p. 344 [545], and on the misunderstanding of the pre-established harmony, ibid.
p. 268 [500]. **) Ideas toward a Philosophy of Nature, p. 51 [46]. ***) System of the transe.
Idealismus, p. 16 [348]. +) Ibid.

p. 190 [452 f.]. ++) Philosophie und Religion, p. 48 (1804).
— innate concepts, which he presupposes in Leibniz, who was far from holding this: "There are concepts a priori without there being any innate concepts."
Not concepts, but our own nature and its entire mechanism, is what is innate in us."*) We do, however, also find some concordant judgments concerning the first principles of Leibnizian philosophy.

If in the Bruno he has set forth intellectualism in contrast to materialism essentially along Leibnizian lines, he himself finds in the starting point of the concept of the monad a limitation of his exposition **).

That dead matter is a sleep of the representing powers, animal life a dream of the monads, and the life of reason a state of universal awakening—this, however, is for him only "a meaningful dream"***).

Even Leibniz, he says elsewhere, did not entirely escape the mistake of turning determinations that are unreal by their very nature and do not touch the positive at all, which only false thinking produces, into defects of things+).

He does not, to be sure, accuse Leibniz of dualism, but he does censure him for having expressed his doctrine in a form that dualism could once again appropriate, even if his followers bore more of the blame than he did ++).

Finally, later on, he nevertheless declares the Leibnizian system, in strong words, to be one-sided: "Idealism, if it does not receive a living realism as its basis, will become a system just as empty and abstract as the Leibnizian, the Spinozistic, or any other dogmatic one."
The whole of modern European philosophy since its beginning (through Descartes) has this common deficiency: that nature is not present for it, and that it lacks a living foundation.
Spinoza's realism is thereby just as abstract as the idealism of Leibniz.
Idealism is the soul of philoso- *) System of transc.

Locke, however, writes not against Leibniz but against Descartes' philosophic doctrine of innate ideas. **) Bruno, p. 229. ***) First Draft of a System of the Philosophy of Nature, p. 200 (1799) [vol. III, p. 182]. +) Exposition of the True Relation of the Philosophy of Nature to the Improved Fichtean Doctrine, p. 63. ++) Lectures on the Method of Academic Study, p. 136 (1803).
...phy, realism is its body; only both together make up a living whole"*).
Schelling's critique of Leibniz's doctrines everywhere bears the stamp of a forbearing benevolence; nowhere in it does arrogance or dismissal appear, nowhere irony; one finds only gentle.
Censure.
Thus we find the treatment of the subjects of theodicy in the essay on freedom to be of this same character, even though he also finds much to criticize in it.

For according to Schelling, until the discovery of idealism (the most recent), the proper concept of freedom is lacking in all systems of the modern era, in the Leibnizian as much as in the Spinozist**), and he rejects all the improvements that were sought to be applied to determinism as insufficient, including the Leibnizian one, that motive causes only incline the will, not determine it.

Schelling finds the general possibility of evil in this: that man, instead of making his selfhood the basis and the organ, can strive rather to raise it to what rules and to the all-will, and on the other hand to make the spiritual in himself a means***).

For the most part, people have sought the source of evil in matter; Leibniz departed from this, but because he could not explain the confused representations of the monads and the privations of evil and of moral evil necessarily connected with them, he had to submit to the justification and, as it were, the defense of God on account of the infliction or permission of the same†).

The source of evil (du mal) lies, for him, in the ideal nature of the created being, insofar as that nature is comprehended among the eternal truths that are in the understanding of God, independently of His will.

For there is an original imperfection in the created being prior to sin, because what is created is essentially limited; hence it cannot know everything, and hence it can deceive itself and commit other faults++).
God could not impart all perfections to man without thereby making man himself a god. *) On Freedom, philos.
Writings, vol. I, p. 427 (1809). **) Ibid.
p. 474. +) Philosophy and Religion p. 48. ++) Theod.

I, 20.
To make [this possible], there had to be various degrees of perfection and limitations of every kind.

Leibniz distinguishes two principles in God, the understanding and the will: the understanding, whose object is the nature of things, contains within itself the ground for the permission of evil; but the will is directed solely toward the good, and the possibility of evil is independent of the divine will.

Schelling finds this distinction consonant with the ingenious manner of this man; he even adds that the representation of the understanding or of the divine wisdom as something in which God himself behaves rather as passive than as active points to something deeper; only he no longer acknowledges Leibniz's doctrine of evil and of the bad as mere privation, as he formerly did when he found it more closely accordant with his own view and had appended to it only the corrective remark that the penetrating mind of Leibniz could not have missed the inference from it—suppressed, as is hinted, out of prudence—that the substance in all things is only one, and indeed God, "whereby his pronouncement: If there were no monads, Spinoza would be right, is reduced to its proper value"**: a remark that is without doubt very well founded: now, however, he censures the fact that in Leibniz's explanation the evil, which can spring only from that ideal ground, amounts to something merely passive, to defect, limitation, deprivation, which entirely conflicts with the proper nature of evil, and he invalidates the attempts by which Leibniz seeks to make the origin of evil from a natural defect comprehensible: and since Leibniz can after all derive evil only from God, and the deprivation itself, in order to become noticeable, requires something positive, the same is compelled to make God the cause of the material element of sin and to ascribe only the formal element of it to the original limitation of the creature.

Schelling***) declares two passages to be the core of the whole theodicy: the one, that God wills in the first instance all good in Himself, and subsequently the *) On Freedom, p. 443 ff. **) Aphorisms toward the Introduction to the Philosophy of Nature, Yearbooks of Medicine as Science, vol. I, p. 84 ff. (1806).
In this treatise, reference is also otherwise made to Leibniz with particular fondness, as on pp. 29, 50, 61. ***) On Freedom, p. 491.

Böckh, Reden II,
regards the best as an end, the indifferent and physical evil sometimes as a means, but the moral evil he admits only under the title of a conditio sine qua non or of the hypothetical necessity that links it with the best; hence the subsequent will of God, which has sin as its object, is only permissive; the other view holds that vice is not the object of the divine decree as a means, but as a conditio sine qua non, and therefore it is only permitted.

Schelling declares himself against all of this: "The will to creation," he says, "was immediately only a will to the birth of light and thereby of the good; but evil came into consideration in this will neither as a means, nor even, as Leibniz says, as a conditio sine qua non of the greatest possible perfection of the world."
It was neither the object of a divine decree, nor, and much less, of a permission.

Why God, since He had necessarily foreseen that evil would, at least as an accompaniment, follow from self-revelation, did not prefer not to reveal Himself at all—this question seems to Him to deserve no reply: nevertheless He does also give such a reply, which I may pass over, and afterward even the Leibnizian concept of evil as a conditio sine qua non is granted a limited application, namely to what Schelling calls the ground or nature in God*), a being inseparable from Him, yet distinct from Him, which excites the creaturely will, the possible principle of evil, as the condition under which alone the will of love can be realized.

Schelling rejects Leibniz's deliberation of God with himself concerning self-revelation or the creation of the world, or the choice among several possible worlds**): as soon as the more precise determination of a moral necessity is added, the proposition is undeniable that from the divine nature everything follows with absolute necessity, that everything which by virtue of it is possible must also actually exist, and that what is not actual must also be morally impossible: Spinoza by no means errs through the assertion of such an inviolable *) On Freedom p. 429. **) Ibid.

p. 484.
necessity in God, but rather in that he takes it in an unliving and impersonal way; the grounds against the unity of possibility and actuality in God are taken from the wholly formal concept of possibility, which Leibniz evidently adopts only in order to bring out a choice in God and thereby to distance himself as far as possible from Spinoza.

"In the divine understanding itself, as in primordial wisdom, in which God realizes himself ideally or archetypally, there is, just as there is only one God, so too only one possible world." But let all nature tell us that it exists by no means by virtue of a merely geometrical necessity: that there is not pure reason alone in it, but personality and spirit; otherwise the geometrical understanding would long since have penetrated it and would have had to prove its idol of universal and eternal natural laws more fully than has hitherto happened: that there are no outcomes from universal laws, but the person of God is the universal law, and everything that happens happens by virtue of the personality of God, not according to an abstract necessity that we would not endure in action, let alone God.

He regards it as one of the most gratifying aspects of Leibnizian philosophy—which otherwise is only too much governed by the spirit of abstraction—that it acknowledges the laws of nature to be morally, and not geometrically, necessary: for Leibniz found that the laws demonstrable in nature are not absolutely demonstrable; being neither wholly necessary nor wholly arbitrary, they stand in the middle as laws that derive from a wisdom perfect beyond all things, and they furnish a proof of a supreme intelligent and free being against the system of absolute necessity *).
I am merely recounting, and I suppress the misgivings about the consistency and cogency of these speculations.
Leibniz himself knew how to find grains of gold in the midst of the jumble.
In this respect too, Schelling acknowledged him.

Already in the treatise On the I as Principle of Philosophy**) one finds a predilection for the enthusiasts: their expressions, he says, very often contain a treasure of surmised and felt truth; "they are, in Leibniz's comparison,
the golden vessels of the Egyptians, which the philosopher must take away for a holier use." When Schelling defends himself against Fichte on account of his inclination toward the enthusiasts,* he does not forget the precedent of Kepler and Leibniz and "the many soulful and heartfelt utterances" of these and of various others, which, according to Fichte, must all be held to be nonsense.

"I am not ashamed of the name of many so-called enthusiasts, but will still openly profess it and glory in having learned from them, as Leibniz too has gloried, as soon as I can glory in it." In a connection with this that is indeed not accidental but nonetheless unexpected, Schelling has touched on a point very important for the correct understanding of many of Leibniz's utterances.

Among the scholars of the last centuries, he remarks, there seems to have existed a kind of secret and tacit agreement not to go beyond a certain boundary in science, and the so highly praised freedom of spirit and of thought had at all times truly prevailed only within this boundary, while no step beyond it might be ventured without punishment or vengeance; he need not describe this boundary more closely to the true connoisseur, and need only say that even the most brilliant men who actually crossed it, such as Leibniz, nevertheless avoided the appearance of doing so.

Aptly do these words describe Leibnizian caution and accommodation, which were all the more necessary to the great man the more distinguished and elevated his connections were, and the farther-reaching his plans for science, state, and church, which he sought to achieve through them.

This, in my full conviction, appears especially in his relation to positive theology; and Schelling too cannot have meant anything else when, in the question concerning the origin of evil and of the bad, he credits him with a fairly clear consciousness of the only answer possible to it, "which he also in individual utterances for the most part really expressed," but immediately adds: "that he did not show it carried through with consistent clarity" — *) Exposition of the true relation of the philosophy of nature to the improved Fichtean doctrine, p. 154 ff.
— "the wise man may have found reasons enough in his age" *).
Schelling had long since frankly set aside such considerations, but in the relation described above he occupies a somewhat different standpoint from Leibniz.

This man never went further than the assertion that two truths cannot contradict each other: the truth extraordinarily revealed by God, for which the sufficiency of the motives of credibility is presupposed, and the truth of reason could not contradict each other. Moreover, he left the two unmixed, and the outermost limit to which he went was this: to prove the possibility, but not the actuality, of the truth of the revealed doctrines.

To our colleague, who had been closer to us, the natural world is a self-revelation of God, but history as a whole is likewise a continuing, gradually unfolding revelation of the Absolute**), "an epic poem composed in the spirit of God"***): from which there then grew up in him the first rudiments of a philosophy of history+).

These doctrines are not incompatible with the Leibnizian system: if the monads, despite their asserted self-sufficiency, are fulgurations or emanations of God, and if in man too everything is foreordained, determined by God, then what Schelling set forth also follows from the Leibnizian system.
But despite much similarity, the two men's gait is nevertheless very different.

Among the similarities I count the gift both men had for a rich imagination, which also led them away from dry schematizing toward freer presentations, although Leibniz did not disdain to enter even into the finest scholastic subtleties and afterward to convert what had been presented more freely into syllogistic form, and Schelling too practiced dialectical philosophizing and treated dialectical philosophy as something in itself be- *) Aphorisms toward an Introduction to the Philosophy of Nature, in the same place. **) System of the transc.
Idealismus, p. 438 [603]. ***) Philosophie und Religion, p. 64. +) Cf.
System of the trance.
Idealismus, op. cit., and the partial reshaping in the lectures on the method of academic [study]

...recognizes a
[principle] standing at page 175 of the study and separated from religion and poetry*).

Perhaps it seems petty if I too find it strange that, just as Leibniz wrote a Latin poem on phosphorus in the style of Lucretius, so Schelling presented to the philosophical-historical class a quite similar little Latin work, of the genuine color of the very model just mentioned, on the views concerning the origin of language—to be sure, delivered as though it were a foreign work, yet without strongly contradicting it when it was said to his face that he himself had composed it in his youth.
But Schelling placed far greater weight on the poetic and artistic imagination.

For him the aesthetic intuition is the transcendental intuition become objective, and art is at once the only true and eternal organon and document of philosophy: it opens, as it were, the holy of holies to the philosopher, where in eternal and original union, as in one flame, burns what in nature and history is separate, and what in life and action as in thought must ever flee itself; therein, as in a magic and symbolic mirror, he beholds the inner essence of his science **).
"The true objectivity of philosophy in its totality is only art" ***), and "beauty and truth, poetry and philosophy form a unity"+).

Thus he arrived early at the thought that philosophy, just as in the childhood of science it was born and nourished by poetry, would, together with those sciences which are brought by it toward perfection, flow back after their completion into the universal ocean of poetry from which they had set out; the intermediate link in the return of science to poetry lay in mythology, although he is unable to specify how the new — *) On Freedom, p. 509.
I scarcely venture to connect with this the passage on actual dialectic in the lectures on the philosophy of revelation published by Paulus, p. 463. **) System of transc.
Idealismus, p. 475 [627 f.].
Lectures on the Method of Academic [Study]
of Study, p. 321. ***) Ibid.

p. 161. +) Bruno p. 23. would
have to be constituted for the mythology still to be formed*).

One cannot blame anyone if, in this connection, he thinks of a reversal in the sciences; but one does him an injustice if one lays to his charge a significant change of mind, since his earlier writings contain very vigorous seeds of later developments**).

With what has been said, the enthusiasm for the old myth is now essentially connected; and this was heightened by the conception—perhaps later abandoned—that the human race, as it now appears, could not of itself raise itself from instinct and animality to reason and freedom, but enjoyed the education and instruction of higher natures, who, after they had scattered on the earth the divine seed of ideas, arts, and sciences—being immediately partakers of reason—had vanished from it, like the great animals of the primeval world; and in this instruction lies the first origin of religion, whose symbols the myth contains, as well as of every other knowledge and culture†).

According to this conception, as fantastic as it is rich in imagination, the myth would thus be the tradition of a race of spirits that had descended into earthly bodies ++) and hence in fact a kind of revelation in the narrower sense; elsewhere it is said, less conspicuously, only that when the human spirit invented the mythologies and poetic fictions concerning the origin of the world, it was still youthful and vigorous and fresh from the gods, and that religion had earlier, set apart from popular belief, been preserved like a sacred fire in the mysteries, [and] with philosophy *) system of the transc.
Idealismus, p. 477 [629].
Cf. also p. IV of the preface to the first edition of the work On the World Soul (3.
Edition 1809) [Works, Division

Vol. I, Vol. II, p. 347], where the return to the oldest poetic philosophy is spoken of still more definitely. **) See the author's own hint in the Lectures on the Philosophy of Revelation, p. 394 in Paulus: which presumably is not in contradiction with the promise of the final alteration of philosophy in the main point (Preface to Becker's translation of the foreword of the 2nd
Edition of Cousin's Fragmens philosophiques). ***) At least I cannot reconcile this with what was said in the lectures just mentioned, p. 554 (Paulus). †) Bruno, p. 197.
Philosophy and Religion, p. 64 ff.
Lectures on the Method of Academic [Study]

Studies p. 167. ††) Philosophy and Religion
p. 66. had a common sanctuary*).

Thus the construction of myth became for him a subject of philosophy, and—not without the dangerous play of etymologies, yet always with intellectual brilliance—he fulfilled the task of "spreading the light of truth even in that boundless realm which mythology and religion have filled with poetic fictions for the imagination."

As far as Christian revelation is concerned, it might seem that he formerly placed it no higher than myth, when he says that the biblical books, in respect of genuine religious content, cannot bear comparison even at a distance with so many others of earlier and later times, especially the Indian ones**); but the harshness of this judgment is offset by another statement standing alongside it, to be sure no less harsh, namely that the first books of the history and teaching of Christianity are themselves nothing but one particular, and moreover imperfect, manifestation of it***), and other utterances contained in the same writing, which point to a symbolic meaning and a requisite speculative reinterpretation of the doctrines, are amply outweighed by the definite declaration that God first became truly objective in Christ+): indeed, one cannot express oneself more strongly in this direction than has been done in the treatise on freedom++): "The light of the higher spirit appears, in order to confront the personal and spiritual evil, likewise in personal, human form, and as a mediator, in order to restore the rapport of creation with God at the highest level."

For only what is personal can heal what is personal, and God must become man so that man may come to God again." Later he defined the difference between mythology and revelation to the effect that the former is rather a consequence, not the revelation, of a divine will; that the latter becomes revealed only afterward, beyond the former; that from mythology one may infer that divine will, but that revelation may not [be so inferred]. — *) Ideen zu einer Philosophie der Natur, p. 14 [19 f.].
Philosophy and Religion, p. 1. **) Lectures on the Method of Academic
of study, p. 199. ***) Ibid.

p. 193. ++) p. 460.
The effect of this will is*).

He has, then, already earlier declared the transformation of revealed truths into truths of reason to be absolutely necessary if the human race is thereby to be helped, by which, however, I can understand only the "deduction of Christian dogmas."

However, if one may trust the lectures not made public by him himself, the truths of revealed religion are not to be traced back to those which reason produces from itself, but must be something transcending reason—truths which without revelation were not only not known, but could not possibly have been known.

But revelation should not be left standing as something incomprehensible: man must expand the narrowness of his concepts to the magnitude of the divine; God's action surpasses all human concepts, but not in such a way that it would be incomprehensible; rather, we must have for it a standard that surpasses all ordinary standards. It is the task of the philosophy of revelation "first to place ourselves on this standpoint, elevated above all necessary knowledge, and then not to establish a priori that resolve which is the proper object of revelation, but, after it has been revealed, to make it comprehensible, both in general and in its execution"+).

This is precisely the point where Leibniz and Schelling diverge significantly: the mysteries, Leibniz teaches, can only be explained up to a certain degree, but cannot be comprehended or made intelligible as to how they come about.

With this principle of his, which even his least scientific work, the Theodicy, acknowledges, it does indeed seem to stand in contradiction that, although not the truth, yet the possibility of the mysteries—namely the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the Lord's Supper—he early on boasted of being able to prove, and attempted these proofs, in that he indeed asserts the supra-rationality of the mysteries but denies that they are contrary to reason: if one wishes this *) Lectures on the Philosophy of Revelation
p. 610 (Paulus). **) On Freedom, p. 507. ***) First Lecture in Berlin, p. 13 (1841). +) Lectures on the Philosophy of Revelation.

p. 215, 612 f., 618.
But even if one cannot count on his striving for accommodation, which he carried very far—and to which well-informed contemporaries attributed certain utterances of his touching on the theological-dogmatic domain—he nevertheless remained far behind Schelling in this respect, if one may trust what has been ascribed to the latter.

I believe I have shown elsewhere—not without the due regard owed to Leibniz's just-mentioned attempts concerning the mysteries, which are purely apologetic—that he kept revelation and philosophy entirely apart*), so that in his case there can be as little question of a philosophy of revelation as of a philosophy of mythology.
But enough of this: let a few more words be permitted concerning the myth, which attracted Leibniz but little.

The myth, which we are to regard as the dogmatic expression of the ancient religions, is a product of primeval and original enthusiasm: in its natural, chrysalis-like form it contains deep presentiments of the supersensible, as also of the natural and the human, in all their relations.

Like all poetry, it is a remedy against the aridity and dryness of thought; it awakens the religious feeling, the eternal foundation of a nobler intellectual disposition and thus also of philosophical speculation; it is suited to elevate and warm the imagination, the mind, and the heart; it spurs one on to cast off one's own sensory husk and to press through to the clarity of thought.

At the same time, it is a graceful form for rendering perceptible in an image what may seem difficult or premature to present without an image, just as Plato fashioned myths so that in the image the supersensible reality depicted might be beheld.
But the mythical view is not the philosophical one.

Philosophy, strictly speaking a product of the Hellenic spirit as mathematics is, began only where myth comes to an end—myth that merely encloses its seeds—and philosophy into myth *) Leibniz in his relation to positive theology, academic address of the year 1843, in Friedrich v. Raumer's historical pocketbook, new series, 5.
Year.
Did I later (address of July 8, 1847, Monthly Report of the Academy
Granted (p. 255 [above, p. 365]) that Leibniz in a certain case accommodated his doctrine to dogma, this does no damage to my assertion above.

One cannot ascribe full consistency to him. To
want to trace it back seems to be nothing other than to want to return the educated human being to the womb and to the condition of the embryo, or, to speak comparatively in Leibnizian terms, to the condition of sleeping monads.

The spread of the mythical view is therefore a serviceable means of counteracting clear thinking and knowledge, and of lulling the minds—if I may put it so—into a symbolic slumber and dream, in which alike the clear shaping of philosophical ideas and the correct knowledge of historical truth vanish.

Whoever wishes to save himself from dialectical philosophy into myth is, so to speak, on the same path as the Sophists, who in despair over knowledge threw themselves into rhetoric, which strives to produce persuasion or conviction, or opinion and belief, in the place of knowledge.

But the mighty man whose utterances about Leibniz I have assembled certainly did not mean it so; and if we understood him thus, we would without doubt fall into the misunderstanding whose avoidance I declared difficult right at the outset.

For although he earlier wanted to let all philosophy flow back into a mythology still to be created, he nevertheless allowed his preceding philosophy to stand alongside the philosophy of mythology and of revelation.

And after he has repeated what has often been said—though not in exact relation to the myth, yet in a closely related sense—namely, that it is assuredly not his opinion that man first gradually raised himself from the dullness of animal instinct to reason, he expressly adds:* "Nevertheless we believe that the truth lies nearer to us, and that for the problems which have become active in our time we should seek the solution first in ourselves and on our own soil, before we walk to sources so remote."
The age of merely historical faith is over once the possibility of immediate knowledge is given.
We have an older revelation than any written one—nature." Thus he spoke in the times into which his judgments on Leibniz fall. *) On Freedom, p. 510.

div.head: XXXVI. Einleitungsrede zur Feier des Geburtsfestes Seiner Majestät des Königs Friedrich Wilhelm IV. in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften gehalten am 16. October 1856.
Ueber die Herausgabe der Werke Friedrichs des Grofsen durch die Berliner Akademie

p.s: The history of Prussia, which only since the previous century, or at most shortly before it, has gained a significance more than provincial or dynastic, is for that very reason, to be sure, only a small part of world history; but through the strength of its princes and its people it has nevertheless quickly become a part of that history, and this land or realm has intervened in the movement of the spirit which we—because it produces deeds and through deeds we regard what happens as the true core and root of history—look upon in turn; but the same has also been determined by this movement.

Every memorable era of a considerable state has a world-historical significance for the progressive development of the human race—only not the eras of stagnation, in which the spirit lives on only as in sleep and dream; and the era of Frederick William IV is certainly a memorable one of this state.
We now stand in the seventeenth year of his reign.

Half a human lifetime seems sufficient for a definite character of the national spirit and of the state to take shape within it, and in this the prince indisputably has a prominent influence; yet one must not forget that this influence is conditioned in many ways.

However great and mighty the personal qualities of the ruler may be, he cannot decisively determine his age, even in relation to his own state; in the last analysis it is determined by the course of the spirit in world history, in which the state is interwoven, and which the outstanding spirits serve as executors of a higher plan, in
a wondrous harmony of necessity and free resolve.

The prince's activity stands in an indissoluble relation to the age into which Providence has placed him, and to the conditions that he finds in it, and every age is dependent on the one that preceded it.

Thus, under the long and eventful reign of the late blessed King, the first foundations were laid for manifold formations that were reserved for the future: for in the realm of the spirit the scattered seed seldom perishes entirely, nor does it spoil like the seed of a plant through heat or cold, drought or moisture; rather, even if its germination may be checked, it nevertheless remains—provided it was originally fertile—in its power until the moment when more favorable circumstances promote the sprouting of the seed.

Frederick William IV found before him a lively and excited national spirit, not only in his own land but in many countries of Europe, each of which exerts an influence on almost every other; new means of communication, too, had already begun to bring widely separated lands closer to one another, as it were, by leaping over space: a new lever of thought, of a power and reach comparable only to that which the spreading printing of books possessed for a similarly excited age.

A spirit of the age had formed itself, the result of the interaction, the interlocking and confluence of many elements of the past and the present, of many events and experiences, of many inner and outer impulses, of many strivings, hopes, and fears: such a spirit is a mark of a particular world-historical stage; it can be fought against, but its effects cannot be annihilated.
The King came to meet the course of development, though in riper age, yet with youthful strength and enthusiasm, which was suited to call forth the enthusiasm of the people as well.

Agriculture, industry, commerce, and shipping were promoted by him, and the beginnings of a naval power were also formed; legislation, the judicial system, and the tax constitution were significantly changed; the army fought glorious, though relatively only smaller, battles in the extreme north and south of Germany; participation in the great world conflict was avoided, and
thereby external peace was preserved for the country.
We have not had the good fortune to enjoy inner peace in equal measure, neither in the state sphere nor in the church sphere.

We have lived through a time of unrest, of action and reaction, of building up and tearing down, full of party factions, vacillations, and reversals, entirely in keeping with the rapid turning of the wheels of these times.

But I turn away from this: what lies nearest to us is art and science, in which the spirit of each age and the rise and decline of nations in respect of culture are also most clearly presented and mirrored.

Frederick William III had raised the arts and sciences in this land, with great expenditure and under the counsel of the most discerning statesmen, more than even the most glorious of his forebears, who himself practiced them with love and in them alone found his recreation from the labors of state business and from the exertions of a warrior's life; Frederick William IV, taking up the progress of the arts and sciences that he found before him as a paternal inheritance, promoted them further with a generous spirit.
What he has done for art and continues to do is in part, and in individual examples, to be seen in the works that serve this city as new ornaments.

As for the sciences, suspicions had earlier arisen through circumstances that I shall not discuss more closely, suspicions that had chiefly affected the universities; the petty restrictions that had been a consequence of those suspicions soon fell away, and new forces were brought in to enhance the efficacy and the splendor of science in this state.
In this very domain, however, it becomes evident that the ruler's will has its limit in the means available and in the overall course of development.

The course that knowledge takes cannot be commanded, least of all nowadays, when it is no longer determined by a few predominant literary figures but by the cooperation of many, determined, as it were, more democratically than aristocratically.

People are wont to describe the societies that are established by the state for the recognition of pure science, without practical applications and without aiming at the instruction of youth,
as an aristocracy of the sciences—sometimes with good will, sometimes with ill will. Such a one is ours; and the more Frederick William IV esteems pure science without self-interest, the more have we too been able to enjoy his favor and his confidence.

But this favor and this trust, in accordance with what has been said, cannot be justified by us through our directing science onto entirely new paths or marking out its ways in the highest decision: we must content ourselves with contributing our modest share to the scientific activity and capacity of the age.

Nor can we, nor do we wish to, exercise over the nation the influence that the French Institute exercised over France for a time: the Germans have never in the field of scholarship allowed themselves to be governed by an academy, and they never will; our means, moreover, are too limited for an activity extended in every direction, and the activity of the men who form this circle is claimed by so many other things that they can devote only a small part of their energies to the Academy.
To give each year a brief survey of what the members have accomplished in the bosom of the Academy is one part of the purpose of today's celebration.

I begin this survey today, allowing myself to reach further back, with a subject that became a matter of the heart and of the mind to the high-minded King: if he has placed it in the hands of the Academy, how should we not be permitted to recognize precisely therein a sign of his highest confidence?

At the same time it is a subject of very serious significance, because it concerns nothing less than the expression of the spirit and of the innermost being of the great ancestor, who has become one of the moving principles and forces of the history not merely of this realm but of humanity, a fellow-executor, out of his ownmost freedom, of the destinies—the outward and the intellectual—which Providence has marked out in advance for the race, in one person the epitome of his age, of its intellectual as of its political life.
I am speaking of the writings of Frederick the Great, with the publication of which the Academy was commissioned by His Majesty the King.
The new edition of the same will be brought to completion in these days.

When the centenary of the
accession of Frederick the Second approached, Mr. Professor Preuss published his rich and instructive work on Frederick the Great as a writer and therein made proposals for a complete edition of the latter's works.

In January 1837 he sent the Academy his paper, to be sure, without any specific proposal, yet with the suggestion that it would be worthy of the Academy to carry out this undertaking and thereby to fulfill an obligation toward its restorer, or rather its founder; in March of the same year the superior ministry addressed the inquiry to the Academy whether it intended in any way to take into consideration Mr. Preuss's proposal to produce a complete edition of the works of Frederick the Great.

The Academy then declared, toward the end of April of the same year—and, if I remember rightly, especially at Wilken's instigation, who was at that time one of the permanent secretaries of the Academy and at the same time a member of the Royal Board of Censorship—that although a new edition of those works was desirable, the Academy's direct participation in it might be open to objection; for if it were to appear in a manner worthy of the Academy, the Academy would have to be put in possession or use of the original manuscripts and be permitted a complete and unabridged communication of the writings of the great King; but for the fulfillment of these two indispensable conditions there was probably no prospect under the given circumstances.

Minister von Altenstein concurred in this judgment, and it soon became evident that the Academy's assumption had been well founded: the original manuscripts would not be permitted to come into its hands, and it was not to be regarded as permissible to have them printed unabridged.

Hereby the matter, insofar as it concerned the Academy, had at that time its conclusion, and I pass over that which relates to a plan drafted soon afterward, namely to publish the great King's historical works in a manner other than the one desired by the Academy: until His Majesty the reigning King, by cabinet order of October 5, 1840, entrusted the Academy with the publication of the complete works.

In this connection, Mr. Preufs, who had already earlier been chosen for the publication of the historical works, was to be
set to work; no less so Aug. Wilh. v. Schlegel in Bonn, a foreign member of the Academy, who had meanwhile offered his participation in the work of his own initiative.

On the part of the Academy, its philosophical-historical class was entrusted with carrying out the Royal command, and this class accordingly appointed a committee, likewise in accordance with the Royal determination, whose duties were designated as the handling of all preparations, namely the proposals concerning the use of the sources held in the Royal Archive, concerning the external form of the two editions—both the deluxe edition for the immediate disposal of His Majesty the King and the smaller edition intended for the book trade—further the distribution of the work, and finally the continuing supervision over the execution of the work.

The election to this committee fell, apart from the two class secretaries, Wilken and the speaker, upon the members of the class, Messrs. Ranke, Eichhorn, and Fr. von Raumer; the full academy, which had reserved to itself the right to add a few members of the academy, unanimously expressed the wish that Mr. A. von Humboldt might join the committee, and he not only approved this wish but has also continually promoted the undertaking, to which he had devoted himself with love from the very beginning, through counsel and action in a quite outstanding manner.

Several of the original members were withdrawn from the Academy in the course of its work; they were replaced by Messrs. J. Grimm, Zumpt, and von Olfers. The last of these first joined as a deputy of Mr. von Humboldt through election by the full Academy, and has to date taken the most eager part in the work together with Mr. J. Grimm; in particular, he has attended to the furnishing of the work with copper engravings, tailpieces, and similar artistic additions with the greatest care and self-sacrifice.
The position on the committee left vacant by Zumpt's death was not filled again, because the work was already considerably advanced.
At its very first meeting, the committee elected its present speaker to the board.

Furthermore, His Majesty the King had already commanded on December 14, 1840, that a military commission should cooperate in the publication of the writings relating to military affairs, under the supreme oversight and direction of General of Infantry von Krauseneck
and with the special participation of Lieutenant General von Lossau, in particular in order to add such explanatory notes, maps, and plans as might be appropriate.

Between the latter and the chairman of the committee, repeated negotiations also took place, but without anything being achieved thereby; on the other hand, in the recent period, when the military-scientific part of the works came up in turn, we had the good fortune to enjoy the active assistance of General von Reyher and of Lieutenant Generals von Hahn and von Brese.

Besides the deliberations and negotiations concerning the division, printing, and publication of the work—the latter only with reference to the smaller edition—the gathering of the material had been the next concern: Mr. Preuss had long since made extensive preliminary studies for this, which he had only to complete; a public appeal by the Academy to the owners of documents of Frederick the Great for their communication was met from many quarters with great readiness; the use of the archival sources was indeed for a long time subject to significant difficulties, but was at last carried out entirely to our satisfaction, in the sense in which the Academy had originally wished it, with the ready support of the Royal archive officials, by Mr. Preuss with untiring activity.

Soon afterward a review of the works was necessary—not, to be sure, in order to determine what should be omitted, since rather a large part of Mr. Preufs's labor must have been directed toward restoring the original in place of what had been falsified, nor again in order to improve the style, of which the great man was master enough, but in order to purify them with respect to grammar and here and there to append short notes beneath the text by way of explanation or also of correcting small oversights of the sublime author.
The latter were drafted by Mr. Preufs and submitted to the committee for deliberation.

The grammatical correction of the text was initially attended to by the French scholar Paul Ackermann; when the latter had in the year 1846 fallen into an illness that soon brought about his death, Prof. de la Harpe took it over; Dr. Fr. A. Märcker, to whom the correction of the printed sheets was entrusted, also took some part in
these revisions.

I hardly need to say that August Wilhelm von Schlegel too, as a scholar of the finest and most cultivated taste and of a rare knowledge of French—in which, apart from Mr. von Humboldt, he acknowledged no German as his equal—had to have a leading voice in this purification of the text; and since he had already come here in 1841 for the purpose of his collaboration, the best success could be expected from it.

The principle was established and maintained that the committee was not entitled to make changes beyond what is grammatical—what, in contrast to this, one is accustomed to call "the rhetorical"—since this would encroach upon the author's individuality.
Schlegel himself acknowledged this; but regarding the application of this principle or the determination of its limits, people could not come to an agreement with him.
I would not mention this if it had not been brought up by him himself in the complete works published after his death in accordance with his instructions.

In the eighth volume of the same, which appeared in the year 1846, there is found a "preliminary draft of a new edition of the works of Frederick the Great" from the year 1844, which had already earlier come into the hands of the academic committee, and therein something of his participation in our proceedings: he refers to a communication of the principle just touched upon, which was made to him at that time, and to his reply, in which he had examined the concept of the grammatical and the extension which must be given to it in the present case, not without 'gentle complaint that he had received no written answer to this so important discussion, which he calls the result of his ripest reflection; to which, since he was a present member of the committee, the latter had no occasion.

In the well-known peculiarity of this distinguished man, who seems to me to have a greater merit for German education than is commonly acknowledged, there lay an insurmountable obstacle to any fruitful cooperation with him, especially given his increasing ill health: should the correspondence concerning the works of Frederick the Great, carefully collected by him and delivered to the Academy after his death, ever come to light, then
one will be able, not without amusement, to form an idea of his irritability, his pretensions, and his arrogance, which it does not become me to set forth here.
He also sought to reverse the complete printing of the works, contrary to the Academy's original intention.

He had been commissioned by His Majesty to compose an introduction to the new edition of the collected works, and thus believed—to use his own words—that the task had been set for him "to grasp the peculiarities of the great King as historian, as thinker, as poet, as a witty mind and founder of an intellectually lively sociability in his circle, to follow the course of his development, and to portray the influences of the age upon him and his powerful counteraction"; a fine and great subject, worthy of him and one to which he was above all equal: but despite all reminders and entreaties that, following his enthusiasm for Frederick the Great and forgetting the small disagreements between himself and the academic committee, he might set his hand to this monument—for which he would have been a thousand times better employed than in correcting the great man's grammatical errors, with or without inclusion of the rhetorical—he resolved too late upon this work, which would without doubt have become a masterpiece.

With regret we miss this at the head of the academic edition; the editor's preface and the introductions by him placed before the individual writings or volumes have a different purpose, and thus cannot compensate for this deficiency.

The tasks of the editor and of the committee touched on thus far could not be completed before the beginning of printing, because printing had to be started as soon as possible, so that no doubts might arise as to the timely furtherance of the work; those tasks therefore continued, diminishing proportionately, into the last years.

Printing was begun in the year 1844; since that time 32 volumes of the deluxe edition—two more than had been intended and planned—have come from the press of Mr. Decker, who has left nothing undone in order to give the work a [character] worthy of the reputation of the printing house. Of these, only 200 are to be given typographic value.

Copies were drawn off for the immediate disposal of His
Majesty, and a parchment copy, which has been incorporated by His Majesty into the Royal Library.
At the same time, the smaller edition intended for the book trade was advanced in the same number of volumes.
Only the portraits entrusted to the most distinguished artists have not yet been delivered in full.

Nor have we been able to bring the material together to such an extent that additions would be impossible: in particular, the letters of the great King are so scattered that, despite all the effort applied, some of them have escaped us or have not reached us in time, as is the case with the correspondence with Maupertuis that appeared shortly ago.

A redaction of the political testament of 1768, running to a hundred closely written quarto pages, which would well have deserved to be received into the series of historical works, has likewise come to our knowledge too late.

As editor of the whole, only Prof. Preufs is to be regarded; and it is precisely my duty to acknowledge his merit in particular, all the more so as I can bear witness to the manifold cares and even plagues that weighed upon him in this business.

He recognized in this work his life's purpose, and equipped with all the knowledge required for its completion in a measure such as none of his contemporaries possessed, he devoted his energies to it out of enthusiasm for the hero of the previous century, without any regard for personal advantage.
His awareness of this is his noblest reward.

And if the execution corresponds to the expectations of the exalted prince who ordered it, the Academy will count itself fortunate to have contributed its part thereto.*) *) Here followed the survey of the Academy's achievements in the past year.

div.head: XXXVII. Einleitungsrede gehalten in der öffentlichen Sitzung der Königlich Preuſsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zur. Feier des Jahrestages Friedrichs des Groſsen am 28. Januar 1858.
Von Friedrichs des Grofsen Urtheil über den Werth der Philosophie im Vergleich zu Kriegsthaten und von d'Alemberts Einleitung zur Encyklopädie

p.s: When four years ago, on the memorial day of Frederick the Great, I spoke of the philosophical education of the celebrated man, I was led to begin from a question that Plutarch had considered with reference to Athens—namely, whether a state becomes more famous through deeds of arms or through science and art—by a judgment that he is said to have pronounced upon his own worth as a philosopher and a general.

Reflections of this kind are subject to great fluctuations: their material is very pliable and can be turned this way and that, so that, depending on whether the one or the other answer is more appropriate to the purpose which the investigation serves, much can be adduced for the one or for the other; and even without one's being guided by regard to a particular purpose, under different circumstances and the different moods occasioned by them, the one or the other way of answering presents itself involuntarily to one and the same person.

To be ready to purchase with one's life the victory whose fruits one will no longer enjoy is certainly the highest sacrifice: to make this sacrifice with full awareness—only the highest and noblest elevation of the spirit enables one to do so, and that is worthy of the greatest glory.

In this respect, and in several others, a quarter of a century before that lecture (in the year 1829), on the occasion of another celebration, I agreed with Plutarch when he ranks the world-battles of the Athenians higher than their glorious activity in the domain of peace, in art and knowledge—though, to be sure, without failing to recognize what renown states acquire through the cultivation of the arts and sciences.
Turning the other side outward, I found in the lecture for the birthday celebration of the great King that one may well be angry with Plutarch when he prefers the power of arms to the power of the spirit; for the fruits of purely intellectual activity are at least equally beneficial for the nations, the consequences of their victories outlast the consequences of warlike ones, and the warlike ones are worthless unless through them goods are protected that have imperishable value for their own sake.

Even if the two views are not incompatible when the proper closer specifications and limitations are applied, the precariousness of such comparisons nonetheless becomes evident, and one would therefore warn against them, as against all comparisons that are undertaken in order to set one thing over against another, or even one person over against another, to highlight the one or to cast the other into the shade: let each thing and each person rather stand in its own worth or unworth.

If, nevertheless, I return today once more to a consideration akin to one that occurred earlier in this place, I find myself moved to do so by the fact that the remark attributed to Frederick the Great concerning the value of his own deeds of war and of his philosophizing in comparison with one another—a remark which I was earlier able only to set aside as unsubstantiated—has meanwhile been more decisively set aside, and in its place has come a more general judgment of the great King concerning the value of deeds of arms as against merit in the field of intellectual activity: it seems not inappropriate to the celebration of today to set this in a clearer light.

Our corresponding member Christian Bartholmèss, who died too early, cited—as I remarked earlier—from the "Mémoires sur la civilisation des différentes nations de l'Europe," as from a work of King Frederick and as words that he had written about himself, the judgment: "I believe that, if one weighs the voices, the works of the philosopher will be held in higher esteem than those of the warrior." Mr. Preufs had recognized that by this was meant the "Mémoires historiques et critiques sur la civilisation de l'Europe aux XVII et XVIII siècles," which by J. Alex.

Published by Borrelly in Paris in the year 1807 and in Quérard's "France littéraire,"
they are designated as a work of Frederick the Great.
That Bartholmèss himself saw this book I doubt, since his citation, contrary to his habit, is very imprecise; Mr. Preufs has not seen it either, and neither have I.

Upon repeated investigation, which was undertaken by our colleague Mr. Pertz and other officials of the Royal Library, it has now emerged from a notice of the work in the "Journal général de la littérature de France," 10.

At least by 1807 (p. 174) it had been made sufficiently clear that the work bears the title: “Mémoires historiques et critiques sur la civilisation des différentes nations de l'Europe, aux dix-septième et dix-huitième siècles, par Frédéric le Grand,” and that it was printed at The Hague already during the King's lifetime, in the year 1780, but was reprinted at Paris in the year 1807.

The editor had no intention of foisting a work upon the King, but may well have wished to attract readers and buyers by the great name on the title page. According to the notice in that journal, he says, he is giving a compilation of extracts from the writings of Frederick the Great, and he wished to bring these extracts into connection as far as possible; however, one will find interruptions, gaps, and frequent transitions from one subject to another that are as abrupt as they are unexpected.

Borrelly, then, has taken that judgment from the king's writings; but whether he has presented it as Bartholmèss understood it, as a judgment of Frederick upon his own merit, I do not know: what is certain, however, is that the king did not mean it so.

Mr. Preuss, namely, in the recently published "Catalogue raisonné des écrits attribués à Frédéric," which is appended to the Table chronologique générale, has shown that although the work from which Bartholmèss cites that thought of the King does not belong to him, the words were nevertheless actually written by him and are found in a letter to d'Alembert of November 20, 1780 (Oeuvres de Fréd. le Grand, vol. XXV, p. 166); the King, however, is not speaking of his own philosophical works, but of d'Alembert's, which he modestly places above his own military deeds.

Now, to be sure, the correspondence of the King with d'Alembert was not printed until the year 1788, whereas Borrelly's work had already appeared for
the first time in the year 1780: it is therefore not possible that Borrelly already knew the King's words at the time of the first edition of his collected work, and one must assume that they were added only in the second edition.

Now, in order to determine precisely the sense in which it was written by Frederick, one must consider it not only in its immediate context but also in connection with d'Alembert's letter, which the king answers.
D'Alembert writes on November 3, 1780: "It is today, November 3, twenty years to the day since Your [Excellency]..."
Major ... covered themselves with glory on the plains of Torgau by wresting from the Austrians the victory which these flattered themselves they had already carried off.
Your
Majesty, you have added to this glory by being Germany's peacemaker and avenger, in your own states the reformer of the legal system, and in Europe the model of warriors and of kings.
What a distance, Sire, as Terence says, there is between one human being and another! and how sadly I feel this for myself when I [consider] Your...
Major, come closer; for I do not venture to say [it], when I compare myself with you!

The little strength that I still possessed twenty years ago in my intellectual and moral faculties has almost entirely vanished; nothing of energy remains to me except in the deep feeling which binds me to Your...

Maj. [Majesty] holds one spellbound, while you still preserve in their full strength those rare qualities which, since the forty years in which you have occupied the throne, have made you so venerable in the eyes of Europe." There follow complaints about his weakness, exhaustion, and despondency, and remarks on other subjects, which I pass over.

The King answers everything point by point: to confine myself to what alone comes into consideration here, he says right at the beginning of his letter: "Many men have won battles and conquered provinces, but few men have written so perfect a work as the Avant-propos de l'Encyclopédie is; and since it is a rare thing to appreciate all human knowledge according to its true worth, and a more ordinary one to put to flight people who are already afraid, I believe that, if one weighs the voices, the works of the
philosopher should be held in higher esteem than those of the warrior, if we consider these matters from the side of utility."

Knowledge well developed in detail and rightly appreciated endures forever; books transmit it to the most distant posterity; whereas the transient successes of a war that claims the participation of only a few peoples in a small corner of Europe are forgotten as soon as they have passed.

That is how it stands with the philosopher and the warrior." This letter of the King's is almost throughout a letter of consolation: it is natural that one should place the person whom one wishes to console as high as possible.

If d'Alembert feels himself very small in the presence of the great prince, the latter wishes all the more to raise him, in that he values his achievements more highly than his own—at least the military part of them—for comparison of which with great services to science d'Alembert's letter itself gave him occasion.

It is a courtesy toward the oppressed friend, and at the same time a noble trait of mind, a self-denial, when he sets back that in which he especially excelled in favor of that in which his friend was distinguished: for he well knew that he himself was more a lover than a master of science, and did not wish to be a school-trained philosopher, but a thinker.
Yet what is said in that letter is no courtesy at the expense of what he held to be true.
Frederick states it quite generally and without any regard for persons, that he places the successes of the philosopher higher than those of the general.
Even with respect to fame, he judges similarly many years earlier, in a letter to Voltaire of January 3, 1773 (Oeuvres vol. XXIII.

However much sense of glory he may have, he says, he nevertheless does not flatter himself that princes have the greatest share in it: the great writers, who combined the useful with the pleasant and instructed while they entertained, enjoyed a far more lasting glory, because the life of good princes passes entirely in activity and the change and the pressing mass of succeeding events obscure those that came before; whereas the great writers are benefactors not only of their contemporaries but of all the centuries.

The name of Aristotle
would resound more in the schools than that of Alexander; one reads Cicero more than Caesar; the great writers of the previous century (the seventeenth) would have made the government of Louis XIV more famous than the victories of the conqueror; the names of Fra Paolo, of Cardinal Bembo, of Tasso, of Ariosto, would surpass those of Charles V and Leo X, even if the latter claimed as strongly as he might to be the vicar of God; one speaks a hundred times of Virgil, Horace, and Ovid for once of Augustus, and moreover this is seldom to his honor; one is more curious about little stories of Newton, Locke, Shaftesbury, Milton, and Bolingbroke than about the soft and voluptuous court of Charles II, the wretched superstition of James II, and the paltry intrigues that stirred the government of Queen Anne.

Thus may the expectation of the teachers of the human race, when they strove for fame, be fulfilled, while the hopes of princes were often deceived, because the former labored for all centuries, the latter only for their contemporaries.

"One no longer lives with us," he says, "when a little earth covers our ashes, and one converses with all the fair spirits of antiquity, who speak to us through their books." D'Alembert's Introduction to the Encyclopedia (Discours préliminaire des éditeurs) appeared in the year 1751, at the head of the great work.

It goes without saying that he sent it to the King at once, and Mr. Preuss finds an indication of this in a letter from d'Alembert to the same, which he dates to the year 1751 (Oeuvres vol. XXIV, p. 369).

On May 12, 1760, the King writes from Meissen, shortly before the start of a new campaign, to Voltaire that he had read many newly published books and regretted the time he had spent on them: "I have found nothing good except a new work by d'Alembert, especially his Éléments de philosophie and his Discours encyclopédique; the other books that have fallen into my hands are not worth being burned" (Oeuvres vol. XXIII, p. 83).

Thus this introduction appeared to the King not merely transiently, but over a long series of years, as a masterpiece; and to this his comparison of the successes of intellectual works with military successes attaches first of all.

One is
therefore involuntarily driven to take a closer look at that introduction here.
I shall therefore give a very brief overview of it, and dwell relatively longer on the first and principal part.

D'Alembert sets down as the twofold object of the work he introduces that, as an encyclopedia, it should set forth as far as possible the order and interconnection of human knowledge, and that, as a "Dictionnaire raisonné des Sciences, des Arts et des Métiers," it should contain the general principles on which these rest, and the essential particulars that constitute their body and substance.

With regard to the former, he seeks, so to speak, to develop the genealogy, the descent, and the connection of our cognitions, the causes from which they arose, and the distinguishing marks that differentiate them; he seeks to go back to the origin and the generation of our ideas.
He divides all our knowledge into direct and reflected.
We obtain the former through the senses: we therefore owe all our ideas to our sensations (sensations).

The first philosophers are said to have established this principle, and the Scholastics defended it because it was old; but at the rebirth of philosophy it was followed by the system of innate ideas: now people are agreed that the ancients were right.
We need only reflect on these feelings.
They teach us first our own existence, then the existence of external objects, to which our body also belongs.
Our first reflected ideas must therefore fall upon ourselves, upon our thinking principle; the next upon the external world and upon the part of it nearest to us, our own body.

This would soon be destroyed if care for its preservation and the removal of pain did not occupy us; the necessity of guarding our body against pain and destruction leads us to consider the external objects that can benefit or harm us.

Among them, however, we find some that are entirely similar to us and that have exactly the same needs as we do; and in order to recognize and distinguish in nature what can preserve us or harm us, we find it advantageous to join ourselves with those beings.

The principle and the support of this union is the communication of ideas, and this requires the invention of signs.
This is the origin of the formation of societies, out of which languages had to arise.

In society, as a counter to the right of the stronger, there takes shape the idea of the just and the unjust and of the moral nature of actions: this should then also lead us to ask what in us is the principle of action, or the substance that wills and thinks, and to the recognition that we consist of two different natures, which are in an indissoluble connection with and dependence on each other.

This slavery, which is independent of us, joined with reflections on the nature of the two principles and their imperfection, should furthermore lead to the contemplation of an almighty intelligence and to its veneration.
These purely intellectual concepts were, he said, the fruit of the first ideas occasioned by our sensations.
From care for the body spring agriculture, medicine, and all the absolutely necessary arts, and further, partly for the sake of necessity and partly for entertainment, the whole study of nature.

From here d'Alembert, by a path that for the sake of brevity I shall not specify in detail, arrives at the mathematical sciences; and after he has brought these to their highest point, at the science of magnitudes in general. He then considers how mathematical abstraction returns once more to the physical body, to which impenetrability belongs, and how thereby the laws of equilibrium and of motion, the object of mechanics, are formed, and further the whole body of the physical-mathematical sciences, at whose summit he regards astronomy, the most sublime and surest application of geometry and mechanics; its progress, he holds, is the most incontestable monument of the successes to which the human mind can raise itself.

But also for the investigation of earthly bodies, the use of mathematical knowledge is no less important: in this case what matters above all is a reflective study of the phenomena, the comparison of them, and the reduction of a large number of them to a single one, which he explained more closely with reference to magnetism.

All the knowledge that may be granted to our natural understanding lies between two limits: between the idea of ourselves, which leads to the idea of the Supreme Being, and that part
of mathematics whose subject is the general properties of bodies, of extension, and of magnitudes. But between the two lies an immeasurable interval, and the small number of certain cognitions does not suffice for all our needs.

As for the former limit, the nature of man is said to be an impenetrable mystery to himself, if he is enlightened by reason alone; the same could be said of our present and future existence, and of the essence of the being to whom we owe it, as well as of the kind of veneration which that being demands of us.

So let a revealed religion be necessary for us, one that nevertheless confines itself to what is most necessary; but through the art of the insights that this religion has communicated to the world, even the common people should be firmer and more decided on a great number of important questions than all the sects of the philosophers.

Even the mathematical sciences, which form the other boundary, would not all possess the same certainty, nor be as rich as they appear; even mathematical theorems, considered without prejudice, would come back to a very small number of original truths: the theorem immediately following, which is inferred from the preceding one, would be nothing but the preceding one, which changes its form in the transition from the one to the other.

The same applies to physical truths and to the properties of bodies, insofar as we recognize their connection: all these properties are nothing but a single and unique cognition; if others, in greater number, appeared to us as distinct truths, then we owed the multiplicity of these cognitions solely to the weakness of our insights, and this wealth is only the sad consequence of our poverty. "The universe, for him who could comprehend it under a single point of view, if it is permissible to say this, would be only a single fact and one great truth" ("L'univers, pour qui saurait l'embrasser d'un seul point de vue, ne serait, s'il est permis de le dire, qu'un fait unique et une grande vérité", p. IX).

I must deny myself even a single excerpt from the following parts, however compressed, such as the previous one is, partly because it does not seem appropriate to me to give almost nothing but material from others, and partly because I must limit the scope of this introductory address. I shall
therefore remark only this much more.
D'Alembert turns first to the cultivation of logic, then of grammar, of rhetoric, and of history together with chronology and geography.

To this extent he has developed the part played by human cognition, which consists either in the direct ideas that we have received through the senses, or in the combination and comparison of these ideas—a combination that one calls philosophy in general.

But another kind of reflected knowledge consists in the ideas that we ourselves formed, in that we represented beings to ourselves through the imagination and combined them in such a way that they are similar to those which are the object of our direct ideas.
This is the imitation of nature through the fine arts: painting, sculpture, architecture, poetry, music.
He attaches to this still further remarks on the distinction between the sciences and the arts, and on the mechanical arts.

Then he constructs a genealogical tree (arbre généalogique ou encyclopédique) of human knowledge, divided into three principal parts under the aspects of memory, reason, and imagination—in some respects somewhat external and aggregative, on the whole following Bacon, though with not a few deviations.

The second part of the entire treatise is formed by the consideration of the Encyclopédie as a Dictionnaire raisonné des Sciences et des Arts; but before he enters into the details of this, he shows the then present state of the sciences and arts, and by what gradual stages men had arrived at it, yet he goes back only as far as the restoration of the sciences; of which I cannot give any further outline here: the remainder serves to instruct more particularly concerning the work that had been set on foot, and is founded in part on Diderot's Prospectus, which had appeared earlier.
It scarcely needs to be remarked that one can expect nothing mediocre from d'Alembert.
