I admire the power and solidity of the presentation, the definiteness and precision of expression that are peculiar to the French writers, the abundance of stimulating and fruitful thoughts that spread over the whole domain of human knowledge: everywhere spirited insights, especially also in the preliminary consideration to the second part, which gives a brief history of intellectual
development since the restoration of the sciences in its main points.

What relates to mathematics and physics may indeed be the more distinguished part, whereas some of the propositions contained in the principal section are hardly adequate to the historical course of the spirit and are also, philosophically, not exactly deep.
However strictly one may judge this; one will nonetheless, even against one's will, be carried away by the author.
The entire scientific culture of the age, and especially the French, is concentrated in him, and that without any admixture of the poison which the Encyclopedists are said to have spread.
The standpoint, to be sure, is only that of empiricism and sensualism: it is Locke's philosophy, to whom he also pays great homage, and Frederick the Great fully shared it.
Yet d'Alembert himself, starting from this standpoint, arrives at an idea of the greatest speculative consequence.

I regard as the summit and crown of the entire treatise the proposition to which he arrives in a highly methodical manner: that the universe, to one who could comprehend it under a single point of view, would be only a single fact, one great truth.
How small, from there, is the step to the Monas monadum of Leibniz, or, to use the later expression, to the Absolute!

And I do not know whether the added caveat, "if it is permitted to say so," did not arise from the feeling that with this thought he was boldly overstepping the boundary of the prevailing views, or also offending against the positive faith, which, moreover, he spares with great circumspection far more than his pupil Frederick.
But however beautiful the work is, and however much it deserves immortality, its influence has, so far as I know, not extended so far as to have become authoritative for the science.

"The physical constitution of the literary world," says d'Alembert himself (p. XXXII), "brings with it, as does that of the material world, violent upheavals, to complain of which would be just as unjust as to complain of the change of the seasons."
Thus in the intellectual life one direction displaces another, and often the greater must temporarily yield to the lesser.

The work to which Frederick attributes the greatest perfection has by no means had so lasting an after-effect as a single battle won by the King;
and I believe, too, that the complete works of that distinguished French philosopher have not had so lasting an effect as all the military deeds of the royal commander, which founded a significant state.

But these deeds would nevertheless by no means have become truly beneficial if Frederick had not at the same time joined to military distinction that of the statesman—I mean not so much a statesman who manages external affairs with art and skill, but the true politician who orders and guides the internal affairs of the state: they would have been of little use to the country and people if he had not joined the arts of peace to the art of war.
Through these, even apart from his activity as a writer, he not only acquired the lasting reputation of a practical sage but also exercised the lasting effectiveness of a philosopher on the throne.

Thus he did not by any means work only for his contemporaries, but also for posterity; and surely, with regard to himself, he underestimated the achievements of the princes if, in the words cited just above, he confined them to the present.

Yes, we live and still commune with him even beyond his writings: for—to confine ourselves today to his activity on behalf of Prussia—he has implanted in this state a spiritual principle of life, on which the happiness and the splendor of this realm rest just as much as on its military power.
It is to this spiritual principle, the soul of this land, that our celebration today is above all devoted.
Whoever does not acknowledge this principle cannot worthily commemorate the memory of the great Frederick.
May no one ever be able to say that in this land it is no longer possible to commemorate worthily, because this land is no longer animated by Frederick's spirit!

Yet comforting hopes for the near future, comforting hopes for the more distant future, after the heavy fate and sorrow that have befallen the land together with His Majesty the King, cast rays of light into our minds and let us await in joyful foreboding the fulfillment of all that we wish and implore for the welfare of the King, of his exalted house, and of the land, for the present and for time to come, for ourselves and for our children and children's children.

div.head: XXXVIII. Zur Begrüfsung der Herrn Weber, Parthey und Theodor Mommsen als neu eingetretener Mitglieder der Königlich Preufsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften in der öffentlichen Sitzung derselben zur Feier des Leibnizischen Jahrestages am 8. Juli 1858.
Zur Begrüfsung der Herrn Weber, Parthey und Theodor Mommsen in der Akademie

p.s: If I reply in a joint address to you, esteemed gentlemen, three of whose words we have just heard, then I need no further justification for doing so than that you all move within the field of antiquity, that you have all grasped not merely the one or the other principal aspect of the study of antiquity—which one is accustomed to divide into the linguistic and the substantive—but both together, as it ought to be.

To be sure, the fields of your studies are very different in place and in time: in place, India, Egypt, the Roman Empire, which was indeed a world empire but nevertheless had its center in Rome and Italy; in time, in that the study of India and Egypt ascends to the primeval ages of humanity, whereas Roman philology, at least for the most part, moves within the light of history.
Yet there is no lack of points of connection, chiefly through Hellenic mediation.

India and Rome are not connected solely through the commonality of the Indo-Germanic language family; rather, after Alexander's arms had carried Hellenic culture to the distant East, even that primeval land—as you, esteemed colleague Mr. Weber, suggest—could not resist the influence of the Hellenic, to which Rome likewise owes its finer literary culture. And though the Egyptian form of culture, in its rigid peculiarity, is sharply separated from the Greek, an early influence of Egypt upon Hellas, and thus indirectly upon Italy, cannot be denied so hastily as some have done. After the later fusion of Greek culture with
the Egyptian through Macedonian rule, however, the culture of the Romans was in many ways determined by the Alexandrian, until Egypt itself became a Roman prefecture.

If more recent times have produced an even stronger interaction of peoples and states with one another, the prejudice is nonetheless steadily disappearing that in antiquity nothing but hostile isolation prevailed everywhere.
Nevertheless, highly esteemed gentlemen, your studies diverge very widely indeed.

To leave many differences out of account, I single out only this: that Roman philology, as the last speaker has just remarked, has the advantage of the benefits and drawbacks of a tradition many centuries old, whereas Indian and Egyptian philology are new creations.

But this makes no difference to the difficulty and importance of the work: for if, in a new field, the lack of prior work demands greater independent activity, then a richer store of prior work requires greater exertion to master it; and the more predecessors one has, the more one must be on one's guard lest one be misled by those predecessors, and the more strength one must devote to a careful critical sifting. One must first clear a clean path in order to reach the goal in a straight course, and this clearing away, this removal of error, is often more difficult than the direct finding of truth.

So let them all be equally welcome among us—those who break new ground and those who continue the intellectual cultivation of soil long since plowed; no field of knowledge has yet been exhausted to the point of barrenness, and everywhere new truth remains to be brought to light.
But I say nothing new when I assert that the most important inventions or discoveries are brought about by the natural course of the sciences.

Once knowledge has advanced to a certain degree, certain deficiencies, gaps, and needs make themselves felt; new tasks arise, which loom more vaguely before one person and more clearly before another: even a dim feeling of a hidden treasure, for whose recovery one would like to have a divining rod, has a stimulating effect in scholarship.

The new discoveries must come as soon as the time for them has arrived in the course of knowledge; even if they seem to be made
by chance, one can maintain that this chance could not have taken place had science not reached the point to which it had reached at the time of this chance—and thereby chance ceases to be chance, because it is conditioned by what preceded it.

Indeed, had this discovery not first succeeded for this man, it would soon have had to succeed for another: hence, too, several things were discovered by more than one person at roughly the same time.

In saying this we do not wish to diminish the merit of the inventors: it is, after all, a great thing if this particular spirit was chosen to be the instrument of the whole human spirit for bringing forth a new truth—that spirit which, in the course of the centuries, rears up the gigantic edifice of human science as it strives toward the divine.

But much here depends on each scholar's intervening in the whole at the right time and in the right place, on his feeling his calling and, in accordance with it, producing something distinctive; if he does this, he will surely also fulfill his calling in science.

Whether you, gentlemen, to whom these words are addressed, have done this and are doing it—on that point the Academy's judgment is already settled, and not only through the election in consequence of which you have appeared here today as speaker, but already through the earlier relations between the Academy and yourselves.

You, Herr College Weber, began a moment ago by noting that for twelve years the Academy has shown itself favorable to your work; if you turn this so that the recognition that has now fallen to you applies not to yourself but to the importance of those studies which the Academy has deemed worthy of unremitting support, then I must reply that this assistance was not directed to those studies in themselves alone, but insofar as they were yours, and that through them you have powerfully intervened and will continue to intervene in the solution of the tasks of Indian philology that you have just now more closely designated; and if within the scope of these tasks you name the transition of the Vedic period into that of the Indian Middle Ages and India's relations to the countries in the West as the field to which you have turned, especially in literary-historical respects, then I recognize—particularly in recollection of your academic lectures on Indian literary
history and of other smaller essays—as your pre-eminent calling for the advancement of these studies the important sifting and determination of works according to their ages, in which you have already demonstrated your complete impartiality and freedom from prejudice.

To you, Herr College Parthey, who without laying claim to a public teaching post devote your life to science out of genuine academic impulse, the Academy already long ago, on the occasion of your prize essay on the Alexandrian Museum, turned its attention.

You have chosen as subjects of your studies, on the one hand, ancient geography in general and that of Egypt in particular; on the other hand, the criticism and interpretation of the ancient writers, too long neglected, who relate to Egypt and to the Egyptian circle of intuition and thought hovering between myth or mysticism and philosophy; and, finally, the Coptic language, so important for the understanding of the Egyptian linguistic monuments.
How timely and adapted to the present state of research on Egypt you have set your tasks is self-evident, without my dwelling on it.

You too, Herr Mommsen, our youngest colleague, have for a series of years stood in connection with the Academy, not only as a corresponding member, but also quite pre-eminently in consequence of the great inscriptions work assigned to the Academy by His Majesty the King, of which you have spoken in fuller detail; you too have in your address emphasized a definite task that has been set for you, and have discussed its scholarly significance.

This is, to be sure, not your only field; your activity extends to linguistic research, to the history of the Roman state and of Roman public institutions, to jurisprudence, especially Roman law, to pass over other things; but you grasp these studies all together in their interconnection, and you have yourself shown how this interconnection, and with it an expansion and refinement of epigraphic study, is demanded precisely now by the course of scholarship, into which your particular activity fits and intervenes with an admirable capacity for work and insight.

No one can feel more keenly than I with what self-sacrifice the task you have so aptly described is bound up—that of ordering the archives of
the past and, what is more, of first gathering together and purifying the material of these archives: may your election as a member of our Society and the free position granted to you afford you some compensation for the sacrifices already made and those still to be made!
Accept, esteemed gentlemen, this unassuming reply as a friendly and heartfelt greeting on the occasion of your ceremonial entry into our midst today!
